0.chip: Hangs material skipping queen trade (often queen)
0.label: Constant at peak: player declines an available queen trade (Qxe2+/Qxd3/Qxe7+) and the undefended queen falls along the open e-file; at medium it blurs to losing a minor piece (knight via Bxc6+/Qe4+ fork or a bishop trapped on g4/h5) after the same skipped trade.

8.label: Top boards are constant pawn captures (e.g. exd4, gxf4, dxc5, hxg6) that resolve central tension or break a key defensive/blockade pawn, letting the opponent recapture into a winning structure (passed pawn or centralized king); medium broadens to king/bishop recaptures and even a non-capturing rook trap, and the cluster is fuzzy since some boards are 0cp/best moves and one is a missed queen-check win.

2.label: Top boards miss the specific Nf6+/Nxe6+ winning knight fork or check (sometimes forced mate) in favor of a passive queen/pawn move; medium broadens to other forcing knight checks/forks (Ne7+, Nd6+, Nh6+, Ne2+, Nf3+) including wrong-square knight choices.

3.label: Top boards consistently play a quiet queen move (Qf3/Qg2) or pawn push that bypasses an immediately winning capture (Nxh8, cxb5, exd4, Bxf1) or invites a fork/mate; medium blurs into any non-forcing quiet move (king step Kf7, castling, bishop retreat Bh6/Bf6, pawn h6/g6/h3/g3) that likewise skips the forcing best move — about half merely miss a free win (materially safe) while the other half hang material in the 2-3 move refutation, so the constant is 'failed to play the winning/forcing move,' not one hung piece.

9.label: Top boards are tightly clustered: in a won endgame the player captures a passed pawn with a heavier piece (queen, bishop, or rook — and once a pawn-push that drops the rook) and is recaptured into an insufficient-material draw; medium broadens away from the passer-grab to plain hung material (a knight retreat dropping the g2 pawn) and even a borderline non-blunder, weakening the 'grabbing a passer' specificity.

5.label: Top: every board is a premature opening knight sortie (Ng5/Nb5/Nb4) where the unsupported knight is won by the queen (Qxg5, or Qa4+/Qa5+ then Qxb4) or at least loses two tempi; medium keeps the 'piece lands undefended and is refuted by a queen capture/check (Qa4+, Qb5+)' core but broadens to other knight excursions and greedy pawn-grabs (Nxe4/Nxe5) and even non-knight pieces, with a few boards drifting into missed-win/passive moves instead of strict material loss.

6.label: At the peak the player invariably overlooks an undefended enemy QUEEN that could be taken for free (often playing an unrelated move that even leaves their own queen hanging); at medium activation this blurs to skipping free captures of other hanging pieces (rook, knight, bishop) and, more loosely, missing other clear wins (forced mates, promotions) while in a winning position.

7.label: Top boards (all winning positions) decline a decisive forcing capture-with-check — most often a knight check like Nxe7+/Nxg7+/Nxc7+ (occasionally a bishop check Bxe6+/Bxc6+) — in favor of a routine pawn/piece capture, letting a winning eval collapse; medium boards keep the knight-tactic theme (best move still a knight check/capture) but the played move instead actively hangs the player's own piece, so direction blurs from 'missed win' to 'hangs material'.

12.label: Top: a materially-safe, passive move skips the clearly best continuation — usually a winning capture (Rxf5, Bxf3, Bxh2, Qxg3, Qxa7) or, occasionally, the only drawing/forcing line; medium: same passivity, but the missed 'best move' blurs beyond captures into quiet positional/defensive improvements (Qe7, Qd6 trade, Rd4, Ne4) rather than just material grabs.

4.label: Top: in losing positions the player makes a king move instead of the only saving rook capture/exchange, leaving their own rook hanging (a few walk into forced mate); medium broadens to non-king moves (queen Qxc5, rook Rc1, pawn dxe5) and to other consequences (back-rank mate, abandoned bishop), but still anchored on declining a defensive rook trade in a lost position.

1.label: At the peak, a tempting natural move—usually a greedy capture, sometimes a 'safe' castle/king move—throws away a decisive/winning position, split roughly half-and-half between missing a forced win or mate-in-one (e.g. Qc8#) and hanging material to a refutation; medium boards blur toward capturing or developing moves that hang material to a specific refuting tactic (fork, pin, trapped queen, or pawn promotion), so the 'missed mate' half fades and the 'walks into a tactic / hangs material' half dominates.

10.label: Constant at the peak: a clearly winning/saving position where the player skips the ONE forcing best move (fork, check, or free capture like Bxe2/Nf5+) and instead plays a natural-looking alternative—greedy capture, quiet consolidation, or king centralization—throwing away the decisive edge; the direction is genuinely split, ~half hanging own material or walking the king into mate/forks and ~half merely missing the win, with no dominant piece (king/queen/knight all appear). Medium blurs from 'decisively winning' down to merely-better or defensible positions and passive tempo-loss moves (e.g. b6 instead of Bg4, Rxf7), where the same natural move squanders the concrete resource.

14.label: At the peak, White is in a won endgame and shuffles its queen right past a free, undefended enemy queen (a trivial Qxq) throwing away the win; at medium it broadens to declining other free captures (e.g. a hanging rook via Bxd1) and quiet/checking moves that instead hang own material or forfeit a forced mate.

20.label: Top boards uniformly squander a forced checkmate delivered by the player's own queen (mate-in-1 to mate-in-10); medium positions blur this by broadening to mates delivered by other pieces (e.g. Be2#) and to a few squandered near-winning queen attacks that fall just short of forced mate.

15.label: Top boards are uniform: an unprovoked ...Bxf3 (once Bxf6) met by Qxf3, planting the queen on a commanding central post and handing over the bishop pair plus the development/positional edge; medium boards keep the voluntary bishop-for-knight trade but broaden the recapture square and piece (Bxc3/Qxc3, Bxa4/Qxa4+, Bxf6/Qxf6, Bxd5/Qxd5, occasional bishop recapture) and sometimes the dominant recapture also nets material via pin/fork/hanging piece.

16.label: At the peak it's a knight capture (typically ...Nxd5) hung to White's c4-bishop/queen battery aimed at f7 in the opening; at medium it broadens to any piece or pawn (queen abandoning c2, bishop hanging on e6/g4, b-pawn, etc.) dropping material, sometimes already in the middlegame.

11.label: Top: a tempo-wasting pawn lunge chasing an enemy bishop lets it retreat to safety while skipping a clear win—most often a free capture of the (frequently hanging) bishop or a clean tactic; medium keeps the bishop-chasing pawn/quiet move but the missed win blurs into assorted tactics, and the slow move itself more often self-inflicts material or king-safety damage (shading toward 'hangs').

19.label: Top boards are passive queen retreats/relocations that skip a saving queen trade and abandon a defender, hanging material or allowing mate; medium blurs to other passive piece/pawn moves where the missed save is a capture rather than a queen trade but the result is the same lost material.

13.label: Constant across all boards: an unsound bishop sacrifice on f7/f2 with check (Bxf7+/Bxf2+) that simply hangs a full piece for one pawn after Kxf7/Kxf2 with no real attack; top activations are the cleanest one-punch sacs and include both the white Bxf7+ and its mirror black Bxf2+, while medium positions are uniformly Bxf7+ in messier/non-classical setups, often with a fizzling follow-up check (Qh5+/Qf3+/Ng5+) before the king walks back to safety.

18.label: Top: a developing bishop move (Be6/Be3) self-hangs to a checking knight fork (Ng5+/Ng4+) that wins the piece in a winning opening position; medium broadens to other pieces walking into checking knight forks (Kd6→Nf7+ winning the queen) or knight sorties that squander a winning edge, while ~3/10 top boards are off-pattern endgame queen moves that miss capturing a hung rook on h1 (a missed-win).

22.chip: Hangs piece, ignores en prise bishop
22.label: Top boards uniformly ignore an enemy bishop demanding immediate recapture on f3/f6 and instead play a quiet developing/king move, hanging a full piece; medium blurs the en prise bishop to other squares (e3, c6, h6, f5, e2) and partly flips direction — sometimes hanging one's own bishop to a pawn/knight, sometimes merely missing a free capture of the loose bishop.

17.label: Top: a passive, materially-safe rook move in a drawn/winning endgame that forgoes the decisive active rook continuation (active rook, winning capture, simplification, fork); medium blurs to any passive/inferior move by other pieces (king, bishop, queen) that squanders the position, often by allowing opponent counterplay or tactics rather than purely missing one's own win.

25.label: At the peak the move is a greedy queen capture (Qxd8→Rxd8#, Qxh2→Nxh2, Qxc7/Qxa7→mate, Qxb1) that ignores the opponent's immediate forcing recapture or mate; at medium it blurs to king walks, pawn pushes and other-piece moves (Kf2, Ke3, fxg6, d5, Ne8+, Qg3) that likewise overlook a forcing refutation, losing material or getting mated.

28.label: Top boards: a slow/passive move (often a king move) ignores an immediate material threat and hangs a specific unit (bishop, knight, pawn, even a queen-trade); medium boards blur this into queen moves and positional/tempo slips that likewise fail to address the material situation, with ~2/10 instead being missed captures of a hanging enemy piece — the only true invariant is 'fails to meet the immediate material threat.'

24.label: Top boards are dead-consistent: a routine developing/king move ignores a forced mate-in-one on the weak f7 (or f2) square in front of the king (Qf7#/Qxf2#); medium blurs to other opening developing moves that ignore a forced refutation losing decisive material rather than mate (pin winning a piece, trapped queen, attack on the fianchetto).

32.label: Top: an opening move cleanly drops a minor piece (knight or bishop, occasionally a pawn) to a one-move capture or simple trap with no compensation; medium broadens to queen hangs and moves that lose the material more slowly via structural/king-safety collapse (opened lines, tempo-chased pieces) rather than an instant clean drop.

23.label: Top boards are constant: a misplaced/passive queen (occasionally rook) abandons or trades away the attacking piece and skips a forced winning tactic or mate (two instead hang the player's own piece by leaving a defended square); medium blurs the piece type — rook, knight, pawn, even a quiet king move — making an imprecise move that squanders the one forcing continuation, sometimes only the move that held a draw.

26.label: At the peak the player hangs the QUEEN in the opening — typically by moving a knight/pawn that was shielding it on a diagonal (Bg5xd8, Bxd1, ...Bxf3), leaving it en prise for nothing; medium activations keep the 'leaves own material loose in the opening' core but broaden the victim to knights, bishops/the exchange, and even pawns won over a short refutation (plus a few unsound f7 sacs).

36.label: Top: a greedy capture removes the sole guardian of the king/back rank, allowing a near-immediate (usually back-rank) checkmate; medium keeps the same greedy-capture-of-a-key-piece impulse but the refutation only wins material (or a positional edge) via a follow-up tactic rather than delivering mate.

29.chip: Hangs material via knight push (often central e4)
29.label: Top boards are near-uniformly a knight planted on an unsupported central outpost (e4, sometimes d5) that drops a clean pawn after Nxe4 dxe4 Qxe4/Bxe4; medium keeps the 'hangs own material' core but broadens to knights jumping to other weak squares and even rook/bishop/king moves that lose a pawn or whole piece.

33.label: Top: a slow king/pawn move ignores doubled-rook tension on an open/contested file, hanging a full rook to the RxR-RxR-RxR sequence (3/10 the attacking side instead missing the winning RxR); medium keeps the same neglected rook-file tension but blurs the material swing—often single-pair tension dropping only an exchange or pawn, occasionally just a positional concession.

21.label: Top: from a winning position the player recaptures (or develops) with the wrong piece and leaves their own KNIGHT hanging for free, almost always a botched recapture decision; medium keeps the 'careless move drops a piece in a won position' core but blurs the piece (bishops and queens too) and the mechanism (defender removal, a loose developing move, or walking into a pin/fork/mate rather than a pure recapture).

30.label: At the peak, the player is in a won position and overlooks a direct capture of the opponent's undefended QUEEN (Bxa6, Nxg4, Nxb5, Nxd1, Nxe2, Bxd8, Nxh4, Bxe8), choosing a safe but lesser move; at medium the target blurs to other winning material (a hanging rook via Bxd1, the exchange via Bxg6) and to passive/tempo-losing moves that squander the win, with a few cases drifting into hanging one's own piece in the same already-winning setting.

38.label: At the peak the player skips a clean forced mate or decisive piece-winning simplification in an already-winning endgame, playing a slower still-winning move; at medium activation this blurs to missing simplifying queen/rook trades into won pawn endgames — but the feature is genuinely mixed, with several optimal 0cp moves and one hung-queen blunder, so it reads more as 'winning-endgame conversion moments' than a single recurring error.

27.chip: Hangs major piece, ignores free capture
27.label: Top: in the opening the player ignores a free capture (typically the enemy queen, or a bishop/knight that is itself attacking their queen) and plays a natural developing/pawn move, hanging their own major piece — almost always the queen, occasionally a rook. Medium keeps the same 'free enemy capture available in the opening is ignored' theme but blurs in direction and target: roughly half still hang the queen (e.g. Bg2/Qh5/O-O/Qf6), while the rest are materially-safe misses that merely skip a free win (Bxa6, gxh4, Bxb5, Qxg5), plus a minor-piece/positional case (d5d4).

31.chip: Lets own piece get trapped (often queen)
31.label: Top boards are near-uniformly natural-looking developing or greedy/grabbing moves that let the QUEEN get geometrically trapped and lost over 2-3 moves; medium keeps the trapped-piece core but broadens the victim to rooks/bishops/knights being entombed or forked and blurs into adjacent king-safety walk-into-mate and squandered-winning-advantage cases.

43.label: Top boards are uniformly Nxf7 'Fried Liver'-style knight sacrifices that simply hang the piece to ...Kxf7 for at most a pawn; medium blurs to other unsound knight sac/fork attempts (Ne6, Nxc7, plus a few non-knight cases) that are refuted by a quiet recapture or intermezzo, and sometimes throw away a win rather than hang material outright.

45.label: Top boards consistently drop a minor piece—usually a knight on f3/f6/d5/d6 left to a pawn capture after a passive pawn move in the opening; medium blurs into hanging pawns and weakening/positional moves that also concede material.

46.label: Top boards are a bishop left hanging to a one-move pawn capture in the opening (either moved onto a pawn-attacked square or abandoned by a developing move); medium broadens to knights and a middlegame bishop lost to a pawn (plus an occasional missed capture of a hanging pawn).

34.label: Top boards are almost all bishop-takes-rook exchange wins on f1 (Bxf1), the player declining the safe capture; medium broadens to other capturers and squares (knight Nxf8/Nxb8, Bxg8, Bxd1) and occasionally a full-piece win, with a few off-theme hangs (Bb7, Qf3) loosening the cluster.

39.label: Top: in an equal/winning opening the player plays a developing or repositioning move instead of the forced central PAWN capture that resolves the tension (fxe5, cxd4, exd5, fxe4), sliding into a worse position; medium keeps the 'neglected central resolution' theme but broadens the missed move to non-pawn captures or central knight jumps (Bxh6, exf5, Nxf7, Nd5) and more often the played move directly hangs material rather than just drifting positionally.

40.label: Top boards all decline a free capture/recapture of an outright hanging enemy piece (usually a bishop, sometimes a knight) in the opening, letting it retreat while staying a clean piece down; medium boards blur into middlegame positions where the skipped capture wins a loosely-defended or tactically-vulnerable knight/bishop — sometimes via a recapture or fork — rather than a strictly free piece.

42.label: Top boards almost always leave a rook (sometimes queen/bishop) hanging for a free capture in a won/drawn endgame—often via a king or rook move onto/away from an attacked square; medium blurs to hanging lower material (pawns, knight, bishop) and a few cases that merely give up the win rather than drop a major piece.

50.label: At peak the feature catches a self-improving endgame move (king march or pawn push) that walks into a decisive forcing reply — Ra8# mate or a move-order Qxe3 hanging the queen; at medium it blurs to materially-safe king-centralization moves that only drop a few centipawns (9cp) in already-decided positions, so the constant is the 'plan-following king/pawn advance' while the punishment severity (fatal vs negligible) is what varies.

41.chip: Exposed own king to mating attack
41.label: Top: king or queen moves that abandon defense and walk the player's own king into a clean forced checkmate (Kg6/Kg3/Qb5-type); medium keeps the same self-destructive king/queen moves but broadens the punishment from strict forced mate to a decisive king-hunt or outright material loss, plus a couple of outliers that instead miss a winning tactic.

35.chip: Hangs defense via ignored threat (often rook)
35.label: Top: a counterattacking move (almost always attacking an enemy rook) is simply ignored by the opponent because it abandoned a key defender or king-safety duty, leading to a decisive counterattack and lost king/material; medium keeps the abandoned-defense/ignored-threat core but blurs the target beyond rooks to greedy pawn-grabs and trapped pieces, and contaminates with a few opposite-direction missed rook-captures.

44.label: Top: from a winning position a tempting queen check that either hangs the queen outright (Nxd3+/Nxf5/Qxd5/Nxc4/Nxb4) or forces an equalizing queen trade instead of the quiet winning capture; medium: same self-defeating queen check, but the damage blurs from a clean queen-hang to a mere forced trade or wasted tempo (one case barely loses anything).

52.label: Top boards consistently make a non-urgent move (king walk, queen relocation, or promotion) that ignores a forcing defensive resource and walks the exposed king into a forced checkmate; medium boards keep the 'ignored the position's forcing demand' core but blur the consequence from mate to general material loss (hanging a rook/knight, dropping the exchange, losing a pawn) or, occasionally, a missed mate/draw.

51.label: Top: a developed bishop (Bc4/Bc5) is left en prise to a pawn (d-pawn dxc4 / dxc5) after an unrelated developing move, dropping a clean piece; medium keeps the opening-blunder theme but blurs to other material—different hung pieces (Ba3, Qf3 trap), pawn losses (c6 dropping e5), multi-move tactical refutations (Nc6→Nxc6/dxc5), and even semi-positional/tempo errors.

55.label: Top: a non-forcing or greedy move (usually a quiet queen move) throws away a forced checkmate against the exposed king, ignoring the killer check; medium keeps the 'skipped the forcing blow' core but broadens the prize from mate to any decisive forced win (winning the queen via Re8+/Qf8+ back-rank sac, the exchange via Qxf1+), with a few cases where the greedy/wrong move also gives back or hangs material.

53.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed one-move capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen (player makes a lesser move/capture instead); medium blurs the same pattern to include a hanging rook (Nxh4) and move-order/intermezzo slips (Bxf7+ before Bxd6, Rxh5 before Bxe7) that squander the clean queen win.

59.label: Top positions uniformly overlook capturing a completely undefended ROOK, instead playing a safe/passive king or pawn move; medium broadens the hanging target to any major piece — adding free queens (Nxf1, Kxd4, Qxf6) and a wrong-piece capture — but the core 'declined a free winning capture' pattern holds throughout.

54.label: At the peak it's a tempo-losing queen sortie (frequently to the h-file) that throws away a forced mate or decisive material gain, handing the opponent the defensive tempo; at medium it blurs to other pieces and slower/greedy/trading moves that squander a winning advantage instead of converting—plus a few outliers that actually hang material or aren't even mistakes.

58.chip: Hangs piece to uncaptured knight (often queen)
58.label: Top boards consistently hang the queen (occasionally rook/bishop) by playing some other move instead of capturing a dangerous enemy knight that then grabs the piece; medium positions keep the uncaptured-knight constant but blur the lost unit to any major/minor and broaden the punishment to knight forks, discovered checks, mating nets, and even missed captures of a free knight.

62.label: Top boards consistently drop a full piece (queen, rook, bishop, or knight) either outright or a move or two deep via a trade, pin, fork, or zwischenzug; medium boards keep the lose-your-own-material core but blur outward to include dropped pawns, move-order tactics, king-safety/mating lapses, and even a few purely positional concessions (and one missed capture).

57.label: Top: voluntarily trades the last rook via a capture (usually with check) into a clearly lost king-and-pawn endgame; medium blurs the piece (adds bishop/knight/queen) and the resulting ending (minor-piece or removing-a-key-defender captures), with a couple of near-equal or actually-correct cases.

37.label: Top: reflexively captures an active enemy knight with the bishop (a routine trade) instead of a stronger intermediate check/fork that wins material or a king-safety move; medium broadens to knight captures (Nxe5) and to cases where the trade itself directly loses material to a recapture fork or even allows mate.

56.chip: Hangs rook while losing (often into mate)
56.label: From an already-lost (occasionally drawn) endgame, the player makes a material-losing move that usually converts a resistible loss into forced mate; top boards consistently hang a rook (sometimes the queen) directly into mate, while medium boards broaden to king-walks, defender-removals, and pawn-grabs that likewise lose material or hand over the mate.

48.label: At the peak, a passive move (king step, pawn push, or aimless check) skips a clearly winning/equalizing capture; at medium it broadens to passive king moves/pawn pushes that ignore the one forcing defense and walk into a forced mate or hang material — direction (missed-win vs self-hang) is genuinely mixed.

61.label: Top boards all hinge on the queen as the decisive piece in a winning middlegame tactic—about half miss capturing the enemy queen (typically a bishop grab like Bxf4/Bxg4/Bxe2) while half hang their own queen/material in the multi-move refutation; medium positions keep the queen-involved material-tactic theme but blur the decisive piece toward rooks/minor pieces and broaden to fork/pin motifs.

64.label: Top: queen makes a material-grabbing capture that backfires—taking on a pawn/piece-defended square so the queen hangs, or opening lines (f-/d-file) into a crushing attack; medium blurs to the same greedy-grab idea with other pieces and to squandering a won position (ignoring threats, missing mate/fork) for a refutation.

69.label: Top boards are uniformly flashy knight fork-with-check moves (Nc2+/Nc7+/Nf7+) that win at most the exchange but lose the forking knight to a recapture along a diagonal or to being trapped; medium broadens to other checking captures that likewise surrender a strong piece for too little — non-fork knight checks (Nxf3+, pointless Ne2+) and even a bishop check trade (Bxe6+) that hand back the material edge.

67.label: Top boards are tightly uniform — an unsound knight (once a bishop) sacrifice/grab on f7 or f2 that hangs the piece for at most a pawn and is cleanly refuted by a calm Rxf7/Rxf2; medium blurs the square and motif, broadening to a knight (occasionally bishop/queen/rook) that captures or sorties to other squares (g2, d5, b7, c2, d6) and similarly loses material to a quiet recapturing refutation.

60.label: Top boards are uniformly failures to play the g4/g5 thrust that challenges the bishop pinning/pressuring the f3-knight, allowing Bxf3/gxf3 or Nxf6+/Bxf6 to shatter the kingside; medium blurs to any missed pawn-break that should challenge a developed/pinning bishop — adding queenside b5 kicks, trapped-bishop wins, and even an allowed Qa4+ fork.

47.label: Top: a loose king move or greedy capture throws away a won/equal game by walking into forced mate or perpetual check; medium broadens to pawn-shelter weakenings and slower material-winning checking sequences (often from already-worse positions).

65.label: At the peak the player reliably declines a loose free bishop sitting near an exposed king (Kxf7, Qxf5, Nxe2, bxc4, Nxg8), never capturing; at medium activation this blurs badly into a generic tactical-blunder feature—sometimes missing other captures/tactics, but just as often hanging its own knight/rook or walking the king into attacks or mate, so direction (missed-win vs hung-own) is genuinely split ~50/50 and needs human review.

71.label: Top boards are clean one-move minor-piece hangs (bishop or knight) snapped off by the active enemy king in a king-and-pawn endgame; medium keeps the enemy-king recapture but blurs into losing trades and mis-exchanges that drop a minor piece into a lost pawn/rook endgame (occasionally even a non-king recapture).

72.label: At the top, a safe centralizing king move (or botched underpromotion) skips a forced mate-in-1-3 or a decisive check/skewer that wins the rook; at medium it blurs to quiet king/pawn moves that miss the single winning forcing check (Rg2+, Ra6+, Rf7+) or tempo shot, with smaller (~400cp) but still game-deciding margins.

70.label: At the peak, Black answers with a passive king walk or pawn push instead of a forcing winning continuation—usually a clean capture (Bxd6/dxc3/Nxd5) or sharp tactic (Bc5+)—letting the advantage slip; at medium the pattern blurs to either color making a slow/non-forcing move that not only skips the win but often outright hangs material or flips the eval.

63.label: Top boards: player declines the one critical capture of an attacking piece (almost always a knight, via a king/queen move) and walks straight into a forced mate; medium boards broaden the spurned target to bishops/rooks (and occasionally a passive non-capture) where the punishment shifts from mate toward simply hanging material or conceding a lost endgame.

66.label: Top: minor-piece (usually knight) developing/retreating moves that drop the piece in the opening, refuted by a queen check (Qa4+/Qb4+) or simple recapture 1-3 moves later; medium blurs to pawn moves and dropped pawns, plus a stray positional loss and one missed fork.

73.label: At the peak, the constant is a pawn advance played WITH CHECK in a winning/near-winning king-and-pawn or passed-pawn endgame that hands the enemy king its ideal BLOCKADING square directly in front of the pawn, squandering the technical win on tempo grounds (and several flagged moves — h3+, b5+, g6+ — are actually engine-best, so it fires on the pattern itself); at medium it blurs to checks that instead grant a CENTRALIZING/counterattacking king square, occasionally a non-pawn check (Be3-c5+), and stretches to bigger errors that drop real material (fxg7+) or throw away a forced mate (f4+ over Ne6+).

75.label: At the peak: a natural opening developing move—canonically Black's bishop to e6—that hangs a piece to the d5 pawn fork (bishop + Nc6) or a removal-of-defender sequence; at medium it blurs to other pieces and pawns (knight, e5/c4 pawns) lost via forks/overloads, and bleeds into quieter moves that don't strictly hang material but squander a big advantage through tempo loss or structural concessions.

68.label: Top: a routine opening fianchetto/develop/castle move lets a free, undefended enemy bishop go uncaptured (Bxa6/Bxh3/Bxh6/Bxb7/Nxa3/Nxh6), and in ~half the lines the same move also hangs the player's own piece to the recapture (Bxb7→Bxa8, Bxg7→Bxh8, Bxb2); medium keeps the identical missed-free-bishop theme but blurs to also include routine opening move-order/positional slips.

80.label: Top: a developing minor piece is left undefended on an aggressive square (overwhelmingly bishop to g4/g5, with rare h6 or knight-to-g5 variants) and snapped off for free by the enemy queen; medium narrows to purely a bishop hung on g4/g5 and captured by the queen.

82.label: Top boards are all hung queens—left en prise by moving onto an attacked square, ignoring an existing attack, or removing its defender; medium keeps the queen as the dominant victim but broadens to other pieces dropped the same way (a rook/exchange in #1 and #8, a knight in #7).

84.chip: Greedy queen move hangs bishop (often pinned)
84.label: Top boards are greedy opening queen recaptures (…Qxd5) that hang the undefended g4 bishop by skipping the forced …Bxe2 pin-resolution; medium blurs into other loose queen sorties (Qxd4/Qf5) causing tempo loss or a queen+bishop pawn-fork, plus a missed free bishop capture (…cxb5).

87.label: Top boards peak on an undefended-rook bishop capture that wins the exchange (with a few that grab the queen instead, e.g. Bxb6/Bxd5), skipped for a slow safe move; medium boards are uniformly the same bishop-takes-rook exchange win (Bxe8/Bxd8/Bxb8/Bxb1) passed up for a quiet positional move.

74.label: Top boards are king moves—mostly captures (Kxa2, Kxb6, Kxg7)—that throw away a won/drawn passed-pawn endgame by abandoning the blockader or entering a lost K+P ending; medium blurs to non-capturing king moves losing the opposition/blockade square (Ka1, Kd1, Kf7) plus occasional piece tempo/order errors (Nf4, Nd7, Bf6) that let the passed pawn promote.

85.label: Top boards are aggressive/forcing moves (centralizing, capturing, or a reflexive check) that directly hang the player's own piece by abandoning a defensive duty or walking into a refutation; medium blurs to materially-safe active moves that instead squander the edge by missing a forcing win/draw (perpetual, tempo, intermezzo) or liquidating a key piece.

78.label: Top boards are pointless/premature QUEEN checks that let the enemy king flee a forced mate or clearly winning position; medium keeps the missed-win-via-check core but blurs into wrong-piece or wrong-move-order checks (rook/bishop were the right check, or capture-before-check) and an occasional non-check tempo-waster, all squandering the win without losing material.

83.label: Top: in a clearly winning position a clean decisive material-winning capture is available but botched — roughly half passed up by a quiet/passive move (missing the win) and half replaced by a move that hangs own material, often the queen, over 1-3 moves; medium keeps the 'winning position, critical move botched' core but blurs from clean captures to any single best move (missed fork/check like Nxf7+, king-safety preservation, defensive queen trades, positional moves).

77.label: Top boards consistently skip a single decisive winning shot in a favorable/tactical position — usually a clean forcing capture (Rxh7, Bxg7, Qxd4+, Qxb7) — though several instead hang the player's own piece to a free capture or short refutation; medium positions keep the 'failed-to-find-the-critical-move-in-a-won-position' core but blur it into hung pieces (Nf3, Rf6) and into positional/king-safety lapses (missed g4 break, Bxg4/f4 opening the king) rather than a clean material-winning capture, with no single recurring piece.

76.label: Top boards are uniformly QUEEN moves played instead of a needed KING-safety/escape move, usually conceding a perpetual-check draw (sometimes dropping material) from a winning position, with the queen often blocking its own king's escape; medium blurs both the piece (rook/knight/bishop too) and the required reply (not always a king move — pawn break, sac, or back-rank guard), and widens outcomes to hung material and forced mate.

89.label: Top boards are critical-moment king moves in won pawn endgames that fail the unique winning continuation (Kxh4, Kc6 squandering the win); medium blurs to a pawn push (f4) that misses the only defensive resource (Ne5+) and hastens a loss — so decisive piece (king vs pawn) and direction (missed-win vs hastened-loss) both vary.

79.label: Top boards lose material in the opening with a knight as the moved or capturing piece—hanging a minor piece outright (Nd5, Nxf2, Be6/Bf5 to a knight) or allowing a knight fork/sac for a clear piece-down verdict; medium blurs into king-safety and tempo lapses (Kh8, g3, Bd3/Bc1, Kd7, e6) that are punished by knight tactics—forks, recaptures, central breaks—often costing just a pawn or the advantage rather than a full piece.

81.label: Top boards uniformly hang a major piece (usually the queen, sometimes a rook) to a trivial knight capture after a tempting forcing check; medium boards blur this to king walks into knight checks/forks, the occasional minor-piece grab, and a few cases of missing a faster win or forced mate rather than strictly hanging material.

90.label: At peak activation the move is a passive/wrong reply that neglects the king's sole defensive resource and allows a forced mating attack (Re8+, Rxh2!, Nf3!, Qe5+, Nc2+); at medium activation it broadens to any failure to play the one critical defensive move, still often a king attack/mate but also bleeding into plain material loss — hung or trapped pieces and even an enemy pawn promotion.

95.label: Top: captures the enemy queen with the very rook guarding the 8th rank, allowing an instant recapture back-rank checkmate; medium blurs to any greedy capture that strips the back-rank defender (incl. promotion-with-check recaptures and removed bishop/file shields), often mate-in-several rather than immediate.

91.chip: Missed win via wasteful check (often queen)
91.label: Top boards are almost all queen checks that throw away a forced mate by letting the king escape or inviting an interposition/queen trade; medium broadens the piece (rook, knight, bishop checks) and the goal—squandering wins like missed forks or merely extended mates rather than only pure forced-mate omissions.

88.label: Top: a rook (queen once) swings to the 1st/8th rank for infiltration/back-rank threats but squanders a held edge—most often by inviting an attack-killing simplifying trade, otherwise hanging the piece or abandoning a defensive/blockading duty; medium blurs to other major pieces and softer squanders (trade-or-hang plus occasionally just dawdling past a faster win).

99.label: Top: all opening positions where moving the queen's SOLE shielding knight off the bishop's diagonal (g4–d1 or g5–d8) lets the enemy bishop grab the undefended queen; medium keeps the 'remove the queen's line-blocker → bishop wins the queen' core but broadens the moved blocker to pawns/bishops (and other diagonals, sometimes via discovered attack), with a few looser queen-hang variants.

96.label: At the peak, boards are clean missed forced wins where a rook supplies the decisive blow—back-rank mates and check-led forcing lines (Ra1#, Rb1+, Rh2+→Qf2#)—the player instead doubling rooks or making a materially-safe move; at medium the pattern blurs to wins led by other pieces (queen/knight/bishop, e.g. Qb4#, Nf4#, Bxa1) and to material-losing or winning-to-drawn blunders, with one board not a mistake at all, but a rook stays in the decisive play of nearly every position.

93.label: Top: from a clearly winning position the player squanders a forced mate or a free capture by choosing a tempting flashy check instead of the simple decisive capture/mate; medium broadens to any inferior forcing or tempting move (not always a check, sometimes a quiet positional/retreating one that even hangs material) that throws away the best continuation, and the prior advantage blurs from 'forced win' down to merely 'better'.

92.label: Top boards consistently fail to convert a decisive knight-based tactic from a winning position — usually missing a winning knight fork or knight-driven discovered attack (the knight is the key piece in the refutation), with the player's king/queen move just sidestepping the shot; medium blurs the direction toward hanging the knight itself or walking the king into a knight tactic, so material is actively lost rather than merely a win being skipped.

100.label: Top boards uniformly hang the queen to an immediate one-move capture (Qe4 into Nxe4, Qa5 into Qxa5, Qxh5 into Rxh5); medium boards blur this, with the queen lost more indirectly (trapped on a2, left hanging when its defender moves, unable to recapture due to a pin) plus a mix of non-queen material/tempo/king-safety blunders that only loosely fit the 'hangs the queen' core.

103.label: Top boards are uniformly a knight fork checking the king and winning the player's own queen for a knight (one outlier is an analogous knight discovered-check dropping the exchange); medium broadens the fork's prize from queen to rook/exchange or two rooks, and blurs further with a couple of near-fork collapses (an undefended-queen capture, a king walking into mate).

101.label: At the peak a clearly winning side (endgame) skips a decisive forcing shot — usually a knight fork or forcing capture — and plays a slow routine king/piece move that lets the win drift to equality; at medium strength the missed idea broadens to any tempo-gaining tactic (pawn forks, forcing strikes) and the slow move sometimes outright hangs material rather than merely missing the kill.

94.label: Top: a natural opening developing/castling move ignores the f7/c7 weakness and hangs the exchange (often queen+rook) to a clean knight fork — 5.Nxf7 or 5.Nxc7+; medium keeps the same f7/c7-counterstrike motif (skipping the critical ...d5) but blurs into related f7 tactics (Bxf7+ sacs, Nxf7 discovered attacks, multi-move material drops) and a few cases that instead MISS a winning ...d5 break, so the direction (hangs vs missed) is partly inconsistent.

102.label: Top: a superficially natural developing move, check, or capture/sac that ignores the concrete demand and hangs a piece or queen (with a couple of missed wins and one non-blunder); medium broadens to dropped pawns, allowed forks, trapped queens, and positional collapses—but the same theme of a natural move abandoning the position's real duty.

98.label: Top boards are pure one-move oversights of a hanging enemy rook (occasionally queen) that should simply be captured for free; medium broadens to other hanging pieces (knights) and to multi-move winning captures via forks, discovered attacks, and winning simplifications, with a few cases also hanging the player's own piece.

97.label: Top: in a clearly won endgame the king (or a promotion) walks into a knight fork/skewer that hangs the queen (boards 2-5), with a rook-hang variant; medium blurs the lost piece (rook/bishop) and direction, mixing in missed wins/conversion slips and even some non-blunders.

86.label: Top: trading bishop for a centralized knight lets the f-pawn recapture, opening the f-file and a central pawn against the uncastled king; medium keeps the capture→punishing-pawn-recapture engine but broadens to knight/pawn captures, the h-file, and consequences like forks, connected passers, or mating attacks.

106.label: Top boards are king moves that botch the critical race geometry (corner/opposition/blockade) in a king-and-pawn or rook endgame, squandering a held draw or a won race; medium blurs to pawn-push move-order errors (advancing without the saving check), and ~4 of 10 are 0cp non-blunders that merely share the pawn-race king-move shape in already-lost positions.

104.label: At the peak, a roughly equal position is thrown away by an unrelated/idle move (a pawn push, repositioning, or king step) that leaves an attacked, undefended piece — usually a bishop — to be captured for free; at medium strength it broadens to dropping pawns or removing a key defender/blocker, opening a file or allowing a fork so the material loss comes over the next move or two.

105.chip: Hangs to queen on exposed king (often check)
105.label: Top: a king-exposing move (frequently castling, or a rook/queen retreat that vacates a key square) lets the opponent's queen deliver a tempo-gaining check and win a rook or bishop a move or two later; medium broadens to any king-weakening move punished by queen infiltration—often still a check but sometimes a quiet grab of a pawn/piece or even mate, not always winning a full rook/bishop.

108.label: At the peak it's consistently a routine queen recapture or passive queen retreat that skips a forcing bishop/knight zwischenzug; at medium the same 'plays the natural move instead of the critical in-between/forcing move' broadens to any piece (bishop, knight, rook, king), with the consequence split ~50/50 between hanging own material and merely throwing away a winning tactic.

111.label: Top boards are king-safety catastrophes (greedy queen-grabs gxh5 and a busted Bxf7+ sac walking into immediate mate) that throw away a clearly winning/advantageous position by losing material; medium blurs into the same 'won-to-lost' core but via a quiet positional/tempo-loss move (f3 instead of f4) with no material hung and no recurring piece, so the only constant is 'converts a good position into a bad one' and direction is genuinely split between hung-material disasters and missed forcing wins/saves.

109.label: Top boards are uniformly an opening bishop check (Bb4+/Bb5+/Bg5+) that a single pawn move (c3/c6/f6) hits with tempo, so the side wastes two tempi and drops material (the hung unit varies — bishop, knight, or pawn); medium keeps the same pawn-refuted bishop sortie but blurs to include a non-checking Bg5 development hung to ...Qxg5, occasional non-bishop sorties (Qc2, Nd4) refuted the same way, and a couple of cases that are really missed wins (skipping Qh4+/Qf3/Qxd5+) rather than direct hangs.

112.label: Top: uniformly a bishop given up for one pawn via a checking sac on f7/f2 (Bxf7+/Bxf2+) that the king safely takes (Kxf7/Kxf2), expecting an attack the undeveloped pieces can't deliver; medium keeps the same f7/f2 attacking-sac idea but blurs how it's refuted — non-king recaptures (Nxf7/Qxf7), a free piece making the sac needless, and one outlier rook exchange-sac on h6.

107.chip: Hangs material skipping forcing trade (often e-file rook)
107.label: Top: a passive/slow move (retreat or quiet push) skips the critical open-file rook exchange (Rxe8+/Rxe1+), hanging own material to a forcing refutation (Bxf6/Nxd5 fork, ...Bxf3, ...Rxe1+ winning a deflected defender); medium keeps the 'passive instead of forcing' theme but blurs the forcing resource and punishment — sometimes still e-file rook play, sometimes a missed queen-sac win, an allowed back-rank mate, or a queen-losing knight fork.

115.chip: Missed endgame capture (med: any saving move)
115.label: Top: in a dead-drawn or won endgame the player makes a passive king (occasionally knight) move and skips the single free capture — queen, rook, or pawn — that wins or holds; medium blurs this to any aimless move (pointless check, wrong capture order, slow pawn push) that misses the one saving/winning resource, which is often but not always a capture, and even includes some 0cp near-best moves.

123.label: Top boards uniformly miss capturing White's completely undefended bishop with a knight (Nxc4/Nxf4), the refutation just retreating it; medium keeps the free-piece capture theme but broadens the capturing piece to queen/rook (and occasionally targets a hanging knight or recapture rather than strictly a bishop).

119.label: Top is laser-tight: in a winning/critical endgame the player ignores a completely undefended enemy rook (a queen in one board) and plays an irrelevant king/pawn/rook move, throwing away the free capture (Bxh8, Bxd8, Qxd8, Nxd2, Qxa2...) and a forced mate or won ending; medium blurs this into general tactical oversight — hanging one's own piece (Bxc5, Nxc5, Bxh3), walking into back-rank mate (Rd8), or missing a discovered-attack tactic (Rdh7), so 'free hanging rook' broadens to 'any decisive tactical miss' and direction mixes missed-win with hung-own.

118.label: Top: a slow materially-safe move declines the one decisive rook trade (e.g. ...Rxe3) that would win a pawn endgame or dodge a knight fork — constant is the missed/declined rook simplification; Medium blurs in the other direction too, mistiming the swap (offering losing rook/queen trades like Re3, Rd8, Rg7) plus a few non-trade slow moves that skip a decisive tactic, so the rook-exchange core is steady but the timing direction and piece (queen) broaden.

121.label: Top boards uniformly push a passed pawn or shuffle the king instead of a forcing rook check or back-rank checkmate that wins outright; medium boards keep the same missed-forcing-move theme but broaden beyond pure rook checks/mates to other winning resources (queen mate, bishop capture, exchange-sac intermezzo) and to winning material rather than always mating.

117.label: At the peak it's invariably a speculative flank queen sortie (Qg4 or Qb3–b6) that vacates a central/defensive post, hanging the piece or square the queen was solely guarding; at medium it blurs to any aggressive sortie (incl. knight Ng4/Nf4 and bishop Bg5) and the punishment spreads across hung material, allowed forks/back-rank/mate, missed wins, and pure tempo/positional drift.

110.label: Top boards consistently play a quiet, materially-safe move that overlooks a free queen capture; medium blurs the target to grabbing a full hanging piece, landing a winning fork, or seizing extra material rather than a queen specifically.

113.label: Across both tiers the player flunks the single critical only-move in a decided endgame; at the peak the pivotal piece is almost always a bishop (either a winning Rxf7/Rxa2-type capture missed, or its own bishop left en prise), while medium blurs to missing a winning capture of any undefended piece (bishop, but also rook on Kxc3 or queen on Nxe7).

120.label: At the peak the player mishandles opening central pawn tension—skipping the precise capture/break (dxe4, cxd5, Bxd4, Bxd5, exd4) in favor of a tempo-losing developing or pawn move that squanders a winning/equal position (material usually safe, occasionally hanging a piece); at medium it blurs into general pawn-move-order/tempo errors, including mistimed pawn breaks and king-and-pawn endgame timing (push-pawn-vs-advance-king), still materially safe but throwing away the win.

116.label: Top: a forcing check — almost always a queen (or queen+rook) check — compels an unfavorable exchange that liquidates into a clearly lost, material-down position; medium broadens to any check (discovered, capturing, or centralizing) that simply hangs the checking piece outright, where the lost unit can be a rook or bishop rather than the queen.

122.label: Top boards are clean missed decisive captures in losing endgames (dxe4, fxe5, Qxe5, plus one missed mate via Rd6+); medium positions blur the pattern into self-hangs (en-prise/trapped pieces) and king-safety/tempo collapses, so neither the Missed-vs-Hangs direction nor any single piece dominates.

124.label: Top: from a clearly winning position, plays a safe/passive rook or king move and skips a forcing rook capture (often a temp sac) that wins material via a fork (Bc4+/Bd5+/Nd7+) or pin after the forced recapture; medium keeps the 'missed forcing tactic' core but blurs to non-recapture wins (in-between Nxe4, winning checks, missed prep) and even flips direction into self-inflicted blunders that walk into the opponent's forks/mate in non-winning positions.

129.label: Constant at the peak: an undefended enemy ROOK is left uncaptured for free, the win typically taken by king or bishop (Kxf3, Bxd6, Bxd1, Kxf5); at medium the target stays a hanging rook but the capturer broadens to queen and pawn (Qxf6, Qxc8, fxe6), with a few near-misses being move-order/material-grab variants rather than the clean omission.

127.label: Top boards are won king-and-pawn endgames where the player slows or throws away the win by pushing the passed pawn prematurely or sidestepping the king to a passive square instead of leading actively with the king; medium broadens to rook and passed-pawn endgames with the same failure to advance the king first (though many flagged moves are actually 0cp/optimal, weakening the signal).

128.label: Top: a winning position is thrown away by directly placing/leaving a piece (queen, rook, knight, or exchange — type varies) on an immediately capturable square; medium keeps the same material-losing theme but blurs to losses realized over 2-3 moves (removing one's own defender, deflection) and includes a few materially-safe moves that merely skip a forced win.

125.label: Top: in a losing/holdable endgame cleanly trades the SOLE defensive bishop (for a knight, or by grabbing a pawn) and gets recaptured into a lost K+P or bare-king ending; medium broadens the mechanism to hanging the bishop with a king move or a move-order pawn-grab that still loses the only defensive piece/the game.

131.label: Top: a piece deserts its duty guarding material or blocking a tactic and is punished by a forcing refutation that wins clean material (knight, queen, or pawns); medium keeps the abandoned-duty/walks-into-refutation theme but blurs to king-safety and positional collapses where the punishment is invasion, a fork, or mate rather than direct material gain.

133.label: Top boards hang a piece outright to a single direct capture (most often the queen, plus knight/bishop, with one king-walk-into-mate outlier); medium boards broaden to own material lost over a 2-3 move refutation — knight/pawn forks, skewers, decoordinated or removed defenders, and king-safety walks — but the constant is a move that loses one's own material for nothing.

137.label: Top boards uniformly play a materially-safe but passive move, missing a winning Qh4+/Qh5+ check that exploits the opponent's f-pawn-less kingside (often with a Nxf4+/Ng6+ fork follow-up); medium boards keep the 'missed winning tactic against an exposed king' core but blur the specific shot — other queen checks (Qc5+/Qg5+), a clean pawn grab (Qxe4), or a faster forced mate (Qa1) — plus a couple of passive retreats that merely concede the win.

126.label: Top: queen+rook tactics where a central (d/e) file rook is the decisive piece—split evenly between MISSING the winning rook move (Re6, Rad1, Rde8, Rce8) and self-inflicting loss by removing the rook's defender (Qxh5, Nd1), blocking its own e-file x-ray (Be6), or walking into back-rank/king mate (Rxa7, Ke6); medium keeps the rook-on-open-file/queen-battery theme but blurs to any file and other hung defenders (bishop g6, rook e6/c8/h3), with the same genuinely mixed Hangs-vs-Missed direction.

132.label: Top boards consistently capture/trade a rook (occasionally a bishop) to simplify directly into a clearly LOST pawn endgame, surrendering the very active piece that was the key defensive/winning resource; medium blurs the piece (adds queen and bishop trades) and the severity (some are queen-trade simplifications that merely squander a winning edge or draw rather than always reaching a lost K+P ending).

134.label: Top boards are uniformly tempo-losing ROOK checks that drive the enemy king to safety and squander a forced win (frequently a forced mate); medium boards keep the same 'patzer-check throws away the win' pattern but broaden the checking piece to queen/bishop (and discovered) checks, with a few that additionally hang material or are even borderline-correct forcing checks.

138.chip: Hangs king to ignored sac (often Qxh7+/f7+)
138.label: Top: a quiet/developing move ignores a forcing queen/bishop capture-with-check on a kingside weak square (Qxh7+/Qxf7+/Qxf2+/Qxh2+) that rips open and exposes the king; medium keeps the 'neglected king attack' core but blurs to other refutations — knight forks via f7 (Nxf7), pawn breaks (gxf7+), c-file rook sacs, and king-walks straight into mating nets.

141.label: Top: a calm/greedy move skips a forcing queen capture-with-check (Qxa1+/Qxc1+/Qxg8+/Qxe1+) or queen mate that wins a rook/minor or forces mate; medium broadens to other queen-led forcing wins — multi-move mates and checks occasionally delivered by rook/knight (Rg8#, Nd6+, Nb3+) plus missed perpetual saves — but the missed forcing shot, usually queen and usually with check, stays constant.

136.label: At the peak it's uniformly a greedy queen capture-with-check (Qxf7/Qxf2-style) onto a defended square that donates the queen for a pawn; medium blurs to broader greedy opening grabs and sacrifices — bishop sacs on f7/f2, queen pawn-grabs/raids without check (Qxa2, Qxd5, Qb7), and a defender-stripping knight move — all losing material.

144.label: Top boards are unsound 'Fried Liver'-style knight sacrifices on f7/f2 cleanly refuted by the king simply recapturing (Kxf7/Kxf2) for a piece-for-pawn loss; medium positions keep the same f7/f2 knight sac but broaden the refutation to counter-tactics exploiting the knight's departure (e.g. Qxe4+, Qxg2) rather than just the king grab.

139.label: At the peak, a winning-opening side plays a natural developing/castling move (Bg7, O-O, Nf6, d4, e6) instead of grabbing a free hanging enemy piece — almost always a knight, frequently on d5 — squandering a full-piece edge; at medium it blurs into premature/overextended pawn pushes (d5-d6, e4-e5) that skip the same free capture and hand back the advantage.

143.label: Top boards uniformly play a quiet/natural move (O-O, h3, Bb3, h6) and miss the Bxf7+ sacrifice exploiting the uncastled king and a loose Bg4 (Ng5+/Ne5 then Qxg4); medium broadens to other missed opening strikes against the king-in-center on f7 (Qb3, Qd5, Bxf2+, Bd5), with the move staying materially safe but squandering a near-winning edge.

147.label: Top boards uniformly skip a forced winning/mating CHECK—grabbing material (capturing a bishop/rook/pawn or trading off the key attacker) instead of delivering the decisive blow; medium boards keep the 'missed the one crushing continuation by grabbing material' core but blur the check requirement, where the winning move can be quiet (rook penetration, discovered-attack capture, or king repositioning) rather than a check.

142.label: Top boards consistently play a quiet developing/retreating move instead of a forcing knight fork or check (Nc2+, Nc7+, Nf6+) that wins material; medium boards keep the same 'quiet move skips a forcing win' theme but broaden the missed shot to other forcing tactics—rook-sac back-rankers (Re8+), discovered checks, queen grabs, and even forced mates (Nf3#).

130.label: Top boards are clean, materially-even bishop captures that the enemy queen recaptures, liquidating a key attacking bishop and squandering a winning/equal edge; medium broadens to leaving the bishop hanging to the queen (queen grabs it for free, sometimes via a non-bishop move, and once a rook instead), so the loss shifts from an even trade toward outright material loss.

146.label: At the peak it's uniformly a reflexive rook/queen check in the endgame that concedes a tempo (or a better square to the enemy king) instead of the direct converting move — capture/king-march — though ~4/10 flagged checks are actually best/0cp; at medium the pattern blurs beyond checks to tempo-wasting king moves and other quiet non-conversions that hand the opponent's king or passed pawn a free tempo, with material kept safe at the single-ply level even where the multi-move refutation eventually costs.

151.label: Top boards consistently hang the player's own knight (once a bishop) by playing a developing/retreating move instead of the forcing Nxf3+/Nxf6+ zwischenzug-capture; medium boards keep the 'skipped Nxf3+/Nxf6+' constant but blur the consequence to merely losing the advantage/a pawn or missing a piece-winning capture rather than always dropping a clean piece.

148.label: At the peak, a move (frequently a greedy queen capture) deserts a back-rank/rook defender and loses own material in a forced rook-exchange or back-rank mating sequence; at medium it blurs to the same abandonment of a key control square but on the queenside, where a piece (rook/knight) vacates a promotion/blockade square and lets the opponent's passed pawn queen.

140.label: Top: an unsound sacrifice or defender-removing/relocating move that drops a minor piece (knight or bishop) to a deflection/removed-defender refutation a move or two later; medium blurs the material to any value (exchange, rook, queen) and bleeds into king-safety/mating collapses plus a few materially-safe 'missed the cleaner win' cases.

149.label: Top boards are consistent: from a winning/equal position a move (usually a greedy capture, sometimes a king or pawn move) hangs the player's own material to a forcing tactical refutation (discovered check, recapture-with-check, knight fork); medium positions blur this by adding tempo/positional moves that squander a winning edge without an immediate material hang (missed-win), so the lost material ranges from pawn to exchange to rook.

114.label: Top is a constant pattern of a bishop greedily grabbing a 'free' opening pawn (Bxb4/Bxg4/Bxc5/Bxc4) and hanging material to a tactical refutation (Bxg7 winning the exchange, Qxb7, forks); medium blurs this to any piece and even non-capturing developing moves (Bf5, Bc5, Na5, Qf5, Nxe5, cxd5) that still leave own material hanging to an opening tactic.

152.label: At the peak the player leaves their own queen en prise to an enemy knight (Nxd8/Nxf6/Nxd1/Nxf7) while developing, capturing, or castling and instantly loses it; at medium it blurs to ignoring other direct threats while grabbing material — back-rank mate (Rxd4→Rg8#) or a knight recapture-with-check — still dropping the queen or major material.

153.label: Top boards: a quiet queen move forgoes a forcing winning capture/check/mate (constant: queen + clear missed win); medium blurs this to other quiet pieces (knight/rook/bishop moves, missed perpetual) and ~4 cases where the quiet move also hangs the player's own material, mixing missed-win with self-inflicted loss.

150.label: Top boards are pure one-move queen blunders — placing/leaving the queen en prise, very often as a flashy check that simply gets captured (check blindness) or capturing into a rook/king that takes it back; medium keeps the hung-queen core but blurs to include squandered queen advantages and missed queen captures/draws (e.g. skipping Qxe6+ or a saving perpetual).

145.label: Top boards uniformly walk into a clean forced mate (mate-in-1 to -3), almost always via a greedy capture or by pulling a key piece off king defense; medium keeps the threat-neglect idea but blurs—some are slower forced mates, others are non-greedy tempo-losing or misplacement moves that simply concede decisive material/position rather than immediate mate.

154.label: Top boards consistently miss an immediate forced mate by skipping a queen check (Qe2+/Qxf7+/Qh5+/Qg6#/Qxd8#), instead playing a quiet knight/bishop retreat or grabbing a pawn; medium boards broaden to forced mates/wins thrown away by skipping any winning check — bishop checks (Bg4+/Bh5+), discovered-check sequences (d3+), or non-immediate queen checks (Qb5+) — over one or several moves, occasionally also trapping the player's own piece.

155.label: Top boards uniformly hang a rook or queen by a (usually greedy) capture/piece move that opens a file or diagonal or strips a defender, letting the enemy queen/rook win the major piece; medium blurs this to hanging minor pieces/pawns and to king-safety opens that allow forced mate, plus a couple materially-safe missed-win omissions.

158.label: Constant at the peak: in a winning position the player ignores the forcing Rxh8+/Rxh1+ capture-with-check that wins the open-h-file race and instead grabs a pawn/piece elsewhere (Nxg5, Nxg4, Qxg4, Bxg5, Nxc3, Bxd5), leaving their own h-file rook undefended so the opponent captures with check first and wins material; at medium activation it blurs from greedy captures to merely passive or relocating moves (Qe7, Ne5, d5, Ng1) that likewise abandon the h-file and forfeit the rook.

156.label: Top: in pure king-and-pawn endgames the king blockades or centralizes instead of advancing its own passed pawn, losing a tempo in the promotion race; medium keeps the race-tempo-loss theme but broadens past strict king moves to rook/queen/bishop endgames and to slow captures or pawn moves that fail to push the passer.

159.label: Top boards are constant greedy captures/pawn-grabs (Bxd4, Nxe4, Bxe4, Qxh7, Kxf5) punished by a larger material loss or king-safety collapse; medium blurs into broader hung-piece, tempo, and positional blunders (Qf3, Ne4, Bd4, g6, b5) plus a few missed decisive wins/mates (Re1#).

160.label: Top boards uniformly vacate the defender or diagonal-blocker of the a-file corner rook, hanging it to Qxa1+/Qxa8+ WITH CHECK; medium broadens to any piece left undefended after moving its guardian — back-rank rooks (a1/a8/b1) plus minor pieces (c4 bishop, d2/f3 knights) — captured by the enemy queen, frequently WITHOUT check.

162.label: Top boards cleanly hang a piece in a winning position—mostly a knight/minor piece, plus a rook and bishop, often via a greedy capture or bad trade; medium blurs into pawn-losing positional errors, missed wins, and even allowing mate, with one top board actually the best move.

161.label: Top boards are near-uniform Bxd4 grabbing the central pawn and hung to Qxd4 (missing Nxc4); medium broadens to other greedy bishop pawn-grabs (Bxh3) where the bishop/material is lost to a knight fork over 2-3 moves rather than by immediate recapture.

168.label: Top: a natural-looking developing/centralizing/pawn-grabbing move ignores the opponent's most urgent threat and is refuted decisively—either forced mate (Qh7#, mating nets) or loss of a major piece (queen/rook hung over 1-3 moves) or a crushing central breakthrough; medium keeps the 'ignored urgent threat' theme but the punishment blurs into smaller/slower losses—forks, trapped bishops, move-order pawn losses, positional collapse, and king-walks—so the exact thing lost (piece vs mate vs pawn) is inconsistent.

164.label: Top boards hang an undefended minor piece in a winning opening—almost always the e5-knight dropped to dxe5 (a couple hang a bishop/queen, plus one greedy trade); medium blurs this to hanging a pawn (Bc5 allowing fxe5) and even a missed exchange-winning combination.

163.label: Top boards uniformly lose the promotion race—greedy captures (Rxh3, Bxh4, Kxh7) or stepping the rook/king off the promotion file—letting the enemy passed pawn queen, often with a deflecting rook-sac (Rf8+/Rh8+ then c8=Q/a8=Q); medium blurs into broader passed-pawn race mishandling, where tempo-wasting maneuvers, pointless checks, or premature own-pawn pushes squander the race rather than directly conceding the queen.

135.label: At the peak the player cleanly leaves a minor piece (most often a bishop) en prise—frequently to the enemy king—converting a clearly winning position into a draw; at medium it broadens to knights and to unfavorable captures/recaptures and tactical refutations (knight forks, discovered checks) that still throw away the advantage by losing or mistrading a minor piece.

170.label: Top boards are passive/prophylactic bishop relocations that vacate a square doing critical active or defensive work and thereby hang material; medium boards broaden the relocating piece to king, knight, queen, rook or pawn and dilute the outcome toward tempo/positional losses (plus one missed tactical win), so the constant is the self-inflicted passive repositioning while the punished material varies.

157.label: Top boards: a natural developing/king move ignores an infiltrated enemy QUEEN's threat and hangs the corner rook to Qxh1/Qxh8 (the constant peak pattern); medium blurs to other hung pieces and other capturers — knight/bishop snapping the h1-rook, a queen grabbing an undefended bishop, or a pawn/exchange lost over 2-3 moves — but always losing own material to an infiltrated attacker.

167.label: Top: in winning passed-pawn endgames a quiet bishop/king repositioning skips the decisive continuation (promotion push, winning capture, or pawn break)—and several are actually 0cp non-blunders; medium blurs to rook moves, middlegame, and even losing positions, adding genuine catastrophic blunders (into mate, a missed promotion-stop) and one greedy capture.

173.label: Top: initiates a capture (rook takes bishop) that loses the exchange when recaptured by a pawn; medium broadens to hanging a whole rook/knight outright in a capturing move.

171.label: Top: a knight move (often Nf3/Nb1-d2) abandons a defensive duty and hangs material to a multi-move tactic, almost always a knight fork (e.g. Nxf2+, Nxc2, Nc3); medium keeps the loose knight move but broadens the refutation to pins (Nxf3+/Bg4), recaptures on d5, and pure positional concessions—and ~3/10 instead are materially-safe knight/castling moves that miss a winning continuation.

165.label: Top: in a won endgame the player pushes/promotes a pawn instead of an immediate winning capture that removes the opponent's only active piece (usually a rook); medium blurs to slow king/bishop moves (or a short forcing tactic like Qd8+/Qxh8) skipping that same capture, with ~30% of cases actually hanging material in the refutation rather than just squandering the cleanest win.

169.label: Top boards overlook a one-move back-rank mate or rook check and instead play a careless king/pawn grab; medium boards blur to missing any forcing resource—discovered checks, queen attacks, perpetual-check draws—and occasionally hang material outright.

176.label: Top: in a won endgame the player declines the decisive queen trade into a trivially winning pawn endgame, instead making a passive/exposing king move; medium broadens the simplification to rook exchanges/sacs and other king misroutes that squander the win (a minority even hang material in the refutation).

172.label: In a won endgame the player advances their own passed pawn or plays a tempo check instead of the precise winning move; top boards consistently miss capturing the enemy's dangerous passer/hanging rook with the knight (Nxa6/Nxa4/Nxd6), while medium blurs to other missed winning captures (wrong knight, hanging exchange/rook) and king-first technique (Kg5 before pushing).

174.chip: Missed free queen capture (corner rook→any hanger)
174.label: Top boards are uniformly a skipped queen capture of an undefended corner rook (Qxa8/Qxa1) along an open diagonal/rank in a winning position, played a safe developing/recapturing move instead; medium blurs to other missed winning queen moves—snatching the wrong target (Qxh7 not Qxg8), grabbing undefended pieces elsewhere (Qxh1+, Qxd2, Qc8/Qxa8), or passing up the only strong queen move (Qe4, Qe6+, Qxb2).

175.label: Top boards are all gratuitous rook/queen checks in won endgames that waste tempo or blur the clean conversion instead of the precise quiet/centralizing/king move; medium broadens to any instinctive forcing move (checks but also pawn pushes, captures, king retreats), mixing harmless 0cp checks with the few that genuinely squander the win — materially safe throughout.

177.label: Top: a 'tempo' pawn push (b6/g6/g3) meant to chase the enemy queen instead wrecks the king's own shelter, letting the queen reroute deeper (Qa6/Qh6/Qh3) for a crushing attack or mate; medium keeps the chase-the-queen pretext but broadens the weakening push to other squares (g4/h6) and adds back-rank-collapse versions of the same idea.

179.label: Top boards are almost uniformly a rook dropped en prise—typically moved onto or beside the enemy queen, or the wrong rook played—losing it outright in the middlegame; medium positions blur the constant by broadening to other hung/lost pieces (wrong-piece captures, bishops, allowed forks/skewers) rather than purely a rook-to-queen hang.

180.label: Top boards are materially-safe moves—predominantly king retreats, plus rook/knight/bishop—that skip the single precise winning-or-saving forcing resource (almost always a tempo-check, knight fork, or back-rank defense) in losing endgames; medium blurs toward missing defensive checks/perpetuals against mate threats and occasionally letting material hang over the refutation.

182.label: Top boards are consistently a premature forcing check (most often a knight: Ne7+, Nf2+, Nf6+) that either hangs the piece to a simple recapture or trades away a forced mate, whereas medium blurs the signal — the forcing/checking move broadens to other pieces and even quiet tempo-losing moves (f4, g3, Qg2) that skip a win, and includes several near-zero-loss false positives.

181.label: Top boards are uniformly f-pawn captures (fxe5/fxe4) that strip the e1-h4 / e8-h5 diagonal and lose a pawn with check to a crushing Qh4+/Qh5+; medium broadens to assorted greedy opening pawn-grabs and loose developing moves (exd5, bxc4, exd4, Bd6, Bc3, Rb6, Ng5) that simply hang material or expose the king, with a couple of dxc4 grabs that are instead missed wins—so direction is mixed.

189.label: Top: a natural developing/structural move (fianchetto, castle, develop, or retreat) in a won opening ignores a clear knight-based tactic — a hanging knight (Nxe5), a knight fork (Nb4/Nxc2+), or knight mate (Nd6#) — losing material/structure over 2-3 moves; medium blurs the piece (bishop grabs like Bxh3, discovered attacks) and the direction (some boards merely miss a free capture/favorable trade rather than self-inflict the loss).

186.label: Top boards are razor-consistent: a capture or fork chasing material abandons the defense of the player's own piece, which then hangs (queen/rook/knight/bishop) — usually via an in-between check or trapped-piece refutation in the middlegame; medium blurs the same theme into broader defensive lapses, where the greedy/careless move neglects king safety or a key defender and is punished by either lost material or forced mate.

187.label: Top: a knight greedily grabs a central d4/e5 pawn (or plants on d5) and is lost to the refutation, the knight being the decisive piece; medium broadens to other knight sorties—failed forks/unsound sacs on e6/e3 and loose positional excursions (Na6, Nxb5, Nc4, Ne5)—that hang material or squander the advantage, with a few cases instead missing a stronger material-winning shot.

191.label: Top boards center on an endgame rook capture/recapture moment where the player usually hangs the rook (sometimes a knight) onto a square for simple recapture, but also flips to the mirror error of skipping a winning king-recapture (Kxh2/Kxb3); medium blurs this into capturing the wrong piece or a tempo-losing king/bishop move that throws away the win, so the direction is genuinely mixed around a rook-centered endgame recapture.

188.label: Top boards consistently grab material—usually the queen or a rook—while overlooking a FORCED MATE, almost always mate-in-one; medium boards blur to missing the strongest/fastest forcing WIN (material-winning skewers, forks, or check-sequences, and efficient conversion), often by playing a greedy or premature capture instead of the cleaner forcing line.

166.label: Top: an undefended enemy queen sits en prise and the free capture (almost always by the rook, once by the king, e.g. Rxg8/Rxa3/Kxb3) is the ONLY move avoiding forced mate, but the player declines it for an unrelated move and gets mated; medium keeps the same ignored hanging queen but broadens the saving capture to other pieces (e.g. knight Nxc4) and mixes in a couple of near-zero-loss non-errors (g5+).

183.label: Top: in an already-lost position the player makes a self-inflicted QUEEN move that abandons a defensive post or walks into a tactic, converting a survivable loss into forced mate or queen loss; medium blurs to rook moves and to missing the only saving defensive resource (e.g., a perpetual or stalemate trick), so the king is mated rather than material strictly hung.

190.label: Top boards drop a rook, bishop, or knight outright (no single piece dominating) with self-inflicted moves in already-lost positions, a few instead abandoning king defense to walk into forced mate; medium positions keep the same one-move piece drops but broaden to pieces lost via tactics (skewer, fork) and to trading off the last defensive piece.

192.label: Top boards are king walks or shelter-pawn pushes that force immediate mate (king central to every refutation); medium broadens to king-exposing or passive moves that lose decisive material to checks/forks/skewers, plus a few non-king material drops (trapped bishop, passed pawn, missed win).

194.label: Top: a king-safety/repositioning move (almost all are king moves) that ignores the position's critical demand—either skipping a winning capture or walking into a refutation, so it misses a win or hangs material; medium broadens the moved piece beyond the king (quiet pawn pushes, bishop/queen repositionings) that likewise skip the critical tactic, with direction genuinely mixed between hanging material and missing a win.

184.label: Top: an opening pawn/developing move clears or fails to guard c7, allowing a knight royal fork (Nc7+ hitting king on e8 and rook on a8, winning the exchange); medium keeps the c7 theme but broadens to a bishop infiltrating c7 (Bc7) winning the queen and to ordinary developing moves that simply ignore the standing fork.

193.label: Top boards liquidate a won rook-vs-minor game by capturing a piece with the rook (usually a bishop, often with check) and recapturing into a drawn-or-lost king-and-pawn endgame; medium positions keep the same rook-trade-into-pawn-ending mechanic but broaden the captured piece to knights as well as bishops.

195.label: Top boards are pure back-rank mates allowed by pulling a rook/king/bishop off the back rank or key defensive square; medium broadens to king-safety collapses permitting other forced mating nets (exposed-king and 7th-rank mates), with minor non-mate/non-blunder noise.

196.label: Top: hangs a rook in the endgame via a non-defensive move that drops it to a free capture (often a bishop, sometimes a pawn or knight fork) or a losing trade; medium broadens to hanging other pieces (e.g., a knight in the opening) by a careless advance that leaves it undefended.

199.label: Top boards are uniformly the queen failing to grab a free undefended central d-pawn (Qxd4/Qxd5, occasionally capturing with the wrong piece and hanging the queen instead); medium broadens to other squandered best queen moves and central captures (e.g., Qxe7 winning a piece, or wrong-piece central recaptures).

198.chip: Hangs piece to deflecting check (often rook)
198.label: Top boards are king moves (rarely rook/bishop) that walk into a deflecting or skewering check, winning a rook outright or forcing a losing rook trade into a lost pawn endgame; medium blurs to broader endgame slips—tempo-losing/passive moves that concede material more diffusely (with only a couple still being true deflection checks, plus one non-blunder).

185.label: Top: an already-losing endgame where a king move squanders a critical tempo in a passed-pawn promotion race (sometimes letting the pawn queen with check), with a couple outright piece hangs; medium keeps the 'worsen a lost endgame' core but blurs to non-king moves (rook/knight/pawn pushes) and other king inaccuracies (king-safety, wrong-direction) plus more hung-piece cases.

200.label: Top: pawn pushes/trades (many at ~0cp) that hasten an already-lost king-and-pawn endgame, with peak constant = a pawn advance/liquidation; medium blurs to king moves and minor-piece moves worsening assorted lost endgames (rook, passed-pawn, promotion races), and even a thrown-away win — so it tracks 'a move that accelerates a lost endgame' more than one specific tactical error.

201.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player passes up a forced decisive rook trade/simplification on an open file (typically Rxe8/Rxd7 enabling c-pawn promotion or a won pawn endgame) in favor of a slow positional/pawn move; medium blurs this to other missed forcing shots — a simple queen capture, a knight check, a b-file rook swap — and even one case where a 'safe' king move allows a queen fork that actually drops material, mixing missed-win with hung-material direction.

202.label: Top: in already-lost middlegames the move vacates a key defensive square or removes a back-rank/king blocker, accelerating an essentially inevitable forced mate; medium broadens to king/queen moves abandoning a guard square that convert a still-defensible position into a fresh forced mate.

205.chip: Hangs major piece contesting file (often rook)
205.label: Top: a rook is moved to contest an open file or back rank and lands on a square where it's captured or lost to a forced (often back-rank) exchange sequence; medium keeps the same heavy-piece-into-a-contested-file pattern but broadens beyond rooks to queen moves (and file-opening pawn captures), still dropping material to forced recaptures.

208.label: Top boards: player declines an immediately available capture of a completely undefended queen/rook/knight (often with check) in a clearly won endgame, throwing away a forced mate or free piece; medium broadens to capturing pieces that aren't purely hanging—overloaded/only-defenders or a promoting pawn—and to less-won (even near-drawn) positions, but the constant is a skipped decisive winning/saving capture.

206.label: Top boards uniformly play a quiet, safe move that skips a clean one-move material-winning capture (Rxc6/Bxb8/Bxf8/Nxh4) netting a piece or the exchange; medium blurs to broader missed tactics — multi-move combinations, fork/mate shots, and correct-capture-order wins — in already-winning positions.

204.label: Top: opening move hangs own material to a short, knight-driven tactic (forks/free captures); medium blurs to non-knight refutations (queen/rook captures, back-rank mate) plus pure tempo and positional losses into the middlegame.

197.chip: Purposeless check squanders win (often hangs checker)
197.label: Top boards are consistently 'patzer sees a check' errors — mostly rook checks (in winning/won positions) that hand the enemy king an escape square and throw away a winning advantage, twice even hanging the checking rook outright; medium blurs into bishop/knight/queen checks that either hang the checking piece (Bxe5+, Qxf3, Bxf3) or merely waste a forced mate by a tempo, and includes a few near-zero-loss 'checks' that aren't real blunders, mixing the hangs-piece vs skips-the-win direction.

207.label: In already-lost positions, the player skips the only defensive queen trade/capture (Qxd7-type); at the peak this is a king-tuck or queen sortie that either hangs the queen outright or allows forced mate, while medium boards blur toward king/queen moves that consistently walk into a forced mate.
