209.label: Top positions surrender material outright — a bishop/knight/rook left hanging or sacrificed for too little; medium blurs into endgame king/rook moves that squander a forced win or burn a critical tempo, so neither the piece nor the direction (hung vs. missed) stays constant.

213.label: Top boards play a slow, materially-safe move (often a quiet pawn push or aimless piece retreat) that abandons a key file/square/tempo and throws away a clearly winning position, collapsing it to equality; medium broadens the same 'squandered win' theme to include greedy pawn grabs and outright piece losses (forks, trapped bishop, hung minor).

214.label: At the peak, a pawn capture or queen placement opens a file/rank and drops the own queen to an enemy rook for a rook (board 10 hangs a rook instead); at medium it still hangs the queen but the attacker blurs to bishops/knights and includes promoting a new queen straight into capture or ignoring a queen already under attack.

220.label: Top boards consistently leap/centralize a knight onto a square where a pawn simply recaptures it (Nd4/Nxd5/Nf4/Ne4/Ne5) for a clean piece loss; medium blurs the piece type—still mostly a knight hung to a pawn, but broadening to a flat-out hung pawn (g5) and a greedy pawn-grab refuted by recapture (Nxe4)—yet every case drops the player's own material in the opening to a trivial recapture.

210.label: At the peak the player is in a clearly won endgame/forced mate and hangs a major piece — usually the queen (incl. a fresh b8=Q to ...Rxb8, Qxe3, Qxc5+) or a rook (Rxc1+) — collapsing the win to a draw/loss; the medium board blurs this to hanging a rook to the opponent's passed pawn from a roughly equal (not yet won) position, and a couple of top boards are noisy (missed-mate or 0cp non-blunders).

215.label: Top: a queen move that declines a forcing, material-winning capture-with-check (overwhelmingly Qxrook+, e.g. Qxa1+/Qxh8+/Qxc8+, sometimes a deflection move-order or forced mate); medium blurs to other forcing wins (back-rank checks/mates, quiet winning moves like Re1) and to a few cases where the player's move instead hangs own material to an enemy tactic.

211.label: Constant across both: a pawn is shoved straight to queen instead of first playing the needed prep move (king-safety step or intermediate check); top boards are punished catastrophically by immediate back-rank/forced mate or a check/skewer that wins the fresh queen, while medium boards blur to simply losing the newly-promoted queen to a routine recapture (Rxc1/Rxf1/Nxg8) or squandering the winning line for a smaller material loss.

203.label: Top: a tempting move—usually a greedy queen capture—abandons a key square defending its own king and walks into forced mate; medium blurs the direction, where similar queen/rook moves instead hang material or, conversely, miss a winning tactic or forced mate in a forcing position.

219.label: Top: in a lost middlegame a passive or greedy move fails the only defense and lets the opponent's king attack mate via forcing checks (fxg3→Qxg3+, fxg6→Rxg6+); medium blurs to any decisive material lost to a check/capture refutation, plus a few missed forced wins and endgame draws thrown away, so the constant 'forcing-check mate' shrinks to 'hangs material in a critical position.'

216.label: In an already-winning opening the player skips a forcing winning capture; top boards constantly miss a knight capture (Nxf3+/Nxf6+) — often after a passive Bh4/Bh5 retreat — while medium broadens to other winning captures like Qxd4 or Nxg3.

218.label: Top boards are uniformly king moves that step off a safe square into a forced mating net or decisive tempo-checks while ignoring an available queen-trade defense; medium blurs to other piece moves (rook/bishop/knight/pawn) that similarly expose the king or hang material, plus a couple that throw away a forced win.

217.label: At the peak, the move hangs a whole piece outright—with a knight almost always central (the dropped piece or the forking/refuting attacker, e.g. Nf6 allowing Ne6+ or Bg7 dropping the d4 knight); at medium it blurs into lighter material losses (a pawn, an overloaded-defender piece) and squandered winning advantages via short tactical refutations, with the knight only sometimes involved.

222.label: Top boards reliably play a quiet/retreating/repositioning move instead of a decisive kingside piece sacrifice (Bxg6/Bxh3/Bxh6/Nxg6/Rxh3 or exchange sac Rxe3); medium keeps the 'quiet move skips the kill' theme but blurs the strike type to any missed decisive tactic — central breaks (cxd5/d6), pawn promotion (fxg6), rook-lift batteries (Rd3), the Greek Gift (Bxh7+), or even a forced mate.

226.label: Top boards uniformly leave the queen en prise in the opening to an enemy knight (one bishop exception), losing it outright for a minor piece; medium keeps the hung queen but blurs the capturing unit (pawn, bishop) and broadens to one case of allowing a knight fork that wins the exchange.

178.label: Top: in a lost position the player ignores the only defensive resource (often a saving capture) and a slow king/pawn move allows a forced mate via king-safety/back-rank collapse; medium: the same failure-to-meet-a-decisive-threat, but the king itself more often wanders into the mating net and 2-3 boards just hang a piece or squander a winning edge.

224.label: Top boards are uniformly passive king-walks toward the edge/corner that accelerate one's own checkmate in already-lost endgames; medium blurs this to other passive king/pawn moves and even rook/queen/bishop moves that worsen the endgame result—sometimes squandering a win or draw rather than strictly hastening mate.

225.label: At the peak, a winning/mating position is squandered by a tempo-losing queen check instead of the decisive open-file rook check, letting the king escape or castle; at medium the squandering move broadens to bishop checks, wrong-rook moves and greedy captures, and the missed forcing line widens from open-file rook checks to knight forks, quiet centralizations, and mate-in-1.

228.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a crushing forcing tactic—almost always a pin/trap/geometric shot that wins the enemy QUEEN—after a natural capture, check, trade, or retreat; medium boards keep some queen-wins (forks, queen traps) but blur to skipping other decisive gains (winning pawns, the exchange, the bishop pair) or a winning attack, sometimes by greedily grabbing material instead.

227.label: Top: a greedy or careless move—usually a queen capture/reposition—that skips the forcing check or rook exchange first and so hangs own material (rook, queen, or pawn) or walks into a forced mate; medium blurs to a materially-safe but slow move that only delays an already-forced mate rather than losing material.

236.label: Top boards all overlook a pawn capture that wins a hanging enemy knight for a pawn (player instead playing a quiet developing/central move); medium boards keep the pawn-grabs-loose-piece pattern but broaden the target to any hanging minor piece, including a bishop on f4.

223.label: Top: a quiet/passive/greedy move ignores the critical forcing line and usually exposes the player's own king to a decisive attack or mate (occasionally skipping the player's own winning fork/free-piece); medium broadens to ignoring forcing tactics that drop material via pins, discovered attacks, hanging pieces, exchange loss, and back-rank mates.

229.label: Top boards consistently squander a forced checkmate by grabbing material with a greedy queen/rook capture (Rxf4, Rxe1, Qxh6, gxf3, Rxh7) instead of the forcing line; medium boards blur this to any inferior move—quiet pawn push, premature check, wrong-piece capture, or self-hanging tactic—that throws away a forced mate or decisive winning continuation.

233.label: Top boards consistently throw away a won position with a materially-safe but tempo-wasting move — a pointless check or abandoning a dominant outpost instead of advancing the decisive pawn; medium broadens to outright squandering of advantage via hanging pieces and allowing tactics (forks).

212.label: Top: a queen capture/trade meant to 'simplify' from a balanced position backfires, losing material to the recapture/refutation (most often a knight fork winning the exchange, or an undefended piece); medium blurs to other faulty captures/moves (pawn captures, queen-trapping tries) that backfire into material or positional loss.

231.label: Top: in losing positions a rook move walks into a decisive enemy check, losing the rook to a capture/skewer or allowing forced mate (one board is actually the engine's top check); medium blurs to other pieces (king/knight/bishop/pawn/queen) and to general worsening of a lost position—purposeless checks, tempo loss, and allowing pawn promotion.

239.label: Top boards consistently make an inferior bishop trade (e.g. Bxf6) that throws away a won game, typically by trading instead of grabbing a free hanging piece like Bxh5; medium boards broaden to other suboptimal captures—wrong capture order, grabbing a pawn, or other pieces—that likewise squander the winning advantage.

234.label: Top boards are uniformly a bishop failing to capture an undefended rook (winning the exchange, opponent rescues with tempo); medium keeps the undefended-rook target but broadens the capturing piece to knight, queen, or rook.

232.label: Top: a quiet king/piece move that ignores an immediate tactic and hangs a rook or the exchange; medium keeps the 'ignored-tactic quiet move' theme but broadens the lost material to bishops, knights, and pawns and drifts toward skipping a free winning capture or pure king-safety/tempo errors.

235.label: Top boards constantly decline the correct resolving opening capture and instead play a passive minor-piece move (almost always a bishop, occasionally a knight) that hangs, traps, or surrenders the piece; medium boards keep the same 'skip the capture' core but blur the offending move to any quiet developing move — pawn pushes, castling, even a wrong capture — that drops material to a trap, hanging piece, or fork.

243.label: Top boards almost always hang the exposed queen to a trap or fork—either a queen sortie that gets trapped or a quiet pawn/developing move that ignores a vulnerable queen; medium keeps the 'loses own material to a 2–3 move tactic' core but broadens the victim to knights, bishops, rooks, and even pawns, and the tactic type from trap/fork to discovered attacks and pins.

238.label: Top: a non-forcing slow move (pawn push, prophylaxis, or greedy pawn-grab) throws away a forced mate or decisive winning eval, handing the opponent counterplay/perpetual; medium: the same tempo-wasting move only blurs the win — slower mate or still-winning — with much smaller cp losses (sometimes near-noise).

221.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a precise, often quiet move that traps, wins, or favorably trades the opponent's queen; medium keeps the queen central in about half but broadens to general precise tactical/defensive resources where the queen is only tangential.

237.label: Top: a premature queen sortie to an exposed flank square (a4/a5/h4/h5) is met by a developing/tempo-gaining attack on the queen that wins material (trapped queen or now-undefended piece falls); medium: blurs to assorted opening moves by any piece (knight, bishop, pawn, occasionally queen) that hang material to a tempo-gaining hit or tactical refutation.

241.label: Top boards are uniformly greedy queen captures/trades that backfire—typically a zwischenzug recapture-with-check (e.g. Bxd7+ before Bxh6) that hangs the player's own queen/piece (~7/10) or, less often, squanders a forced win by trading queens (~3/10); medium blurs from pure captures toward any queen move that walks into a refutation (e.g. queen chased/trapped by ...Bc2) and includes near-noise zero-cp moves.

240.label: Top: aimless queen relocations to active-but-irrelevant squares that abandon a defensive duty/tactical threat and hang own material (pawn/bishop/knight) or skip a clear winning capture; medium keeps the aimless-relocation idea but broadens the moved piece to king/knight/bishop/rook and blurs the outcome from clean hangs toward positional/tempo losses and missed wins.

242.label: Top boards consistently miss a forced king capture of a hanging rook/knight in a losing endgame (with a secondary cluster that promotes a pawn straight into capture, plus one king-safety mate), while medium boards blur into broader material-losing blunders—a positional knight retreat, a tempo-losing pawn push, and a greedy queen grab.

244.label: Top boards: an active-looking rook/bishop move leaves the player's own knight hanging (e.g. Qxc3+) or walks the king into a knight-aided mate; medium broadens to hanging bishop/exchange/pawn or tempo-losing trades where the knight only sits peripherally in the refutation, with a couple of missed-tactic cases blurring the hang-vs-safe split.

248.label: Top boards squander a winning/equal edge with a materially-safe but inferior move that misses the one precise reply—almost always Ba3 to keep the enemy king from castling (refuted by ...O-O); medium broadens to other precise misses (Kf1, c3, Qxe6+, Qd3) plus a few free-piece/pawn grabs, but always letting the opponent consolidate rather than losing own material.

247.chip: Failed to stop pawn promotion (rook→any piece)
247.label: Top: rook/king moves in R+K endgames fail to control the promotion square, letting a passed pawn queen (frequently with check); medium broadens to other pieces (queen, knight, dark-square bishop) and to missed tempo-gaining checks/zwischenzugs that allow the same forced promotion.

250.label: Top: a non-addressing move leaves the unresolved f5/f4 light-square bishop tension (Bd3-vs-Bf5) standing, so Bxf5 wins the undefended bishop or a central pawn; medium broadens to other undefended minor pieces and pawn-forks left hanging in the opening (e5-knight, c5-bishop, Nc6/Be6 fork) after a similar tension-ignoring move.

249.label: Top boards are premature queen sorties (esp. ...Qxd4/Qd5 grabbing a pawn) that hang material to a tactical refutation; medium broadens the losing move to pawn pushes (b6, f6, g4, a4) and minor-piece moves (Nd7, Bh6) plus other queen excursions, all dropping own material in the opening, with a few near-equal missed-win cases blurring the edge.

255.label: At the peak the player invariably skips an immediate free capture of an undefended enemy queen (throwing away forced mate or decisive material for a quiet move), while at medium strength the target blurs to grabbing/playing a lesser move instead of snapping off a hanging rook or other undefended major piece.

245.label: Top: in a won endgame the player passes up a completely undefended enemy ROOK, playing a quiet non-capturing king or pawn move (sometimes even hanging its own rook in the refutation); medium holds the same 'free rook left on the board' core but blurs to other passive piece moves and to grabbing a lower-value piece instead of the free rook.

253.label: Top: player passes up an available winning pawn-capture of an attacked/undefended knight (almost always the dxc6/dxc3/exf3 pattern) in favor of a natural developing or repositioning move, throwing away a decisive material edge; medium keeps the 'natural move skips the forcing win' core but blurs the win itself — the capture is sometimes of another piece (cxd5 bishop, fxe5/Bxe4 knight) or a different motif (capture-with-check, en-passant), and several boards shade from a pure missed win into allowing a fork/back-rank tactic instead.

230.label: Top: a developed bishop captures on d4/d5 and the enemy queen recaptures, centralizing and dominating the board (twice bishop-for-pawn); medium broadens to other central captures — a knight or even the queen — that outright hang material to the queen recapture or a deflecting check.

246.label: At the peak it's a passive queen move that skips a forcing queen check (usually a saving perpetual, occasionally a mate or material-winning check sequence); at medium it broadens to any quiet piece move (rook/king/knight/pawn) that misses the forcing check, still nearly always a queen check but once a rook check.

257.label: Top boards greedily capture the enemy queen but hang their own queen to the recapture (Bxc7/Bxe2); medium blurs to hanging other material (bishop, exchange, pawn) via move-order errors and multi-move refutations, with a couple of outliers closer to a missed win/fork.

251.label: Top boards uniformly hang an undefended kingside bishop (g5/h4/g4) to a ...Bx, Nx, Qx sequence winning a full piece with a knight recapturing; medium boards blur into hanging assorted pieces/pawns plus broader opening positional, king-safety, tempo-loss and fork errors.

256.label: Top: a greedy/unsound or move-order capture (usually a pawn capture or Bxf7+) leaves the player's OWN bishop hanging to the enemy queen (dxe4→Qxb5, cxd5→Qxb4, exd4→Qxg4, Bxf7+, O-O→Bxh6); medium blurs the captured piece to a knight or shifts to king/pawn moves that walk into mate or drop material — plus a few top boards merely squander a winning advantage rather than hang a piece, so the invariant is genuinely fuzzy.

259.label: Top boards all revolve around an uncastled king in the open center where the decisive resource is a forcing e-file queen check (Qe2+/Qe7+/Qxe4+)—but direction is split, roughly half self-inflicted hangs (Bxc3, Bxf7+, O-O into Qd4+ fork, Bxg5, Nf4) and half missed checks/wins (skipping Qe2+/Qxe4+/Qe7+); medium positions keep the open-king-in-center theme but blur the key move beyond the queen check to other central captures (Nxe4, Qxd5+) and even a plain queen hang (Qf4).

254.label: Top boards uniformly waste a tempo (premature check or non-urgent pawn push) instead of the single immediate decisive capture—almost always eliminating an enemy passed pawn (Rxa2, Nxa6, Nxa4); medium blurs the 'right move' beyond pure captures to other urgent tasks (blockade Rf1/Re8, queen retreat, central break) and even includes greedy mis-captures that ignore the critical continuation.

261.label: Top: small tempo/precision king moves escorting a passed pawn in already-won K+P endgames (several actually 0cp-optimal); medium broadens to moves that hang real material or throw away the forced win/mate (hung rook/queen, lost decisive passed pawn, even non-endgame cases).

263.label: Top boards miss a forcing check on an exposed king — either a mate-in-one (a3#, b3#, Rh8#) or the only saving check that draws/escapes (c5+, e5+, g5+), often walking the player's own king into mate instead; medium boards keep the missed-check motif (usually a pawn check like f5+/h4+/f6+/h6+) but blur from mate to checks that merely win material or preserve a winning advantage rather than deliver checkmate.

265.label: Top boards are uniformly premature pawn pushes in pawn/piece endgames that let the pawn be captured for free or traded so its passed/connected/restraining value vanishes; medium keeps this push pattern but blurs to include king moves that walk off a pawn's defense (and a few near-zero-cp cases).

267.label: Top boards uniformly leave a KNIGHT en prise to an immediate pawn capture (exf6/dxc3/exf3) in the opening, dropping a minor piece for at most a pawn; medium boards keep the 'piece hung to a pawn capture' core but blur it by adding bishops and multi-move intermezzo refutations rather than a single-ply grab.

252.label: Top boards play a move that ignores a decisive enemy QUEEN attack/battery and fail to defend or trade, so they hang material (bishop/rook/knight) or walk into mate; medium blurs this to other ignored threats—back-rank mates, a fork, and especially missed queen-trade defenses—where the failure to neutralize pressure costs material or squanders a winning/holdable position.

272.label: Top boards are kingside attacking sacrifices/lunges that hang a major piece (most often the queen, sometimes a rook) or walk into a back-rank mate; medium positions keep the same unsound-attack motif but blur toward rook sacrifices and queen moves that drop material or step into forced mate—unified by 'own piece falls' rather than any one piece.

269.label: Top boards uniformly hang a centralized d4/d5 (or f3) knight by stripping its sole defender via a queen retreat, king step, or pawn/bishop push, losing it to a capture—usually with check along an exposed a2-g8/a7-g1 diagonal; medium blurs to hanging any defended minor piece (a kingside defender or knight on d7) by removing its protector, without the diagonal-check motif.

268.label: Top boards are passive (usually king) moves that skip an immediate promotion and squander a winning/drawing endgame result; medium broadens to other non-forcing endgame choices (a greedy king capture, a quiet pawn push) that pass up the decisive forcing resource (skewer, pawn-race tempo) instead of an actual promotion.

264.label: Top: in a won (mostly rook) endgame, a materially-safe but inferior move — a tempo-losing 'patzer' check or wrong-square/wrong-piece rook/king move — throws away the win instead of the decisive continuation; medium keeps the 'squander a winning position with an inferior safe move' core but blurs into missed tactical wins, move-order errors, and occasionally hung material.

262.label: Top: an impulsive opening developing/'free check' move that drops a minor piece to a trivial pawn capture — constant pattern is Bb5+/Bb4+ (and a stray Bf4/dxc5) walking into axb5/axb4, plus knights jumping to d5/f5/e4 that a pawn simply takes; medium blurs from clean piece-hangs into broader opening material/tempo squander — a purposeless Bb4+ check losing tempo, castling into a trapped piece (O-O), missing a strong tactic (Ne5), and even declining a free piece (Kf8 instead of Kxf7).

274.label: Top: a developing move (usually a bishop to d6/f4/e3/d3) lets a single pawn advance (e4/e5/d4) fork two minor pieces — almost always bishop + knight — netting White/Black a clean piece; medium keeps the pawn-break-forks-two-pieces motif but broadens the victims to include the queen (d5 forking Q+Nc6) and blurs into related 'pawn break wins material' cases (trapped bishop, tempo loss, c5/d5 thrusts).

275.label: Top boards are uniformly premature QUEEN trades (Qxf3/Qxf6/Qxc4 etc.) that liquidate a winning attack or dynamic edge into an equal/worse queenless position; medium blurs to bishop and rook captures (Bxc4, Bxg4+, Rxe5+) that simplify into inferior or lost piece/pawn endgames, the constant being a needless simplifying capture that throws away the better side's resources.

271.label: At the peak it's a materially-safe queen/bishop move in the opening that skips a free rook on the open long diagonal (Qxh8/Bxh8 after a fianchetto gap); at medium it blurs to other missed opening tactics (Bxa8, Qh4+, Nxf7) and some queen moves that not only miss the win but allow enemy counterplay/forks.

276.label: Top boards all drop an undefended minor piece (overwhelmingly a bishop, e.g. Bb5/Bf5/Bg4) for free in one move in the opening; medium broadens to other ways of losing opening material — knight/queen forks, trapped bishops, ignored exchange-winning captures, and even dropped pawns.

273.label: Top: an inferior B/N/Q/P move—usually a greedy capture or a piece relocation/retreat that abandons a defensive or tactical role—loses material within 1–3 moves (clean hang, back-rank mate, or a missed forcing win) while a sharper forcing tactic was available; medium blurs to plainer greedy grabs or defender-removals that simply drop a pawn/exchange with a smaller eval swing.

279.label: At the peak the player hangs their own queen — moving it onto an attacked square (Qe4, Qf5) or removing the pawn/diagonal shield that protected it (e5/dxc5/Nc3 → Bxg4/Qxd3); at medium it blurs to skipping a winning queen move, most often a Qh5+/Qe4+ attack on the exposed king (or a missed Nd5 queen-fork / Qh5+ perpetual).

277.label: Top boards are queen moves from a winning/mating position that throw away the advantage—hanging the queen for a pawn, missing a forced mate, or skipping a winning queen trade; medium blurs to rook moves with the same conversion failure, but several flagged boards (both tiers) are in fact engine-optimal or near-0cp moves.

280.label: Top: in pure K+P endgames the king walks the wrong direction and abandons a defensible pawn that the enemy king captures for free; medium blurs this into pawn-push weakenings and opposition/infiltration slips that concede material or ground rather than a direct free pawn.

286.label: Top boards all hang a knight to an enemy pawn in the opening (moving it into the pawn's reach or ignoring the threat); medium broadens to bishops hung to pawns and the occasional piece lost to a non-pawn attacker or positional concession.

278.label: At the peak, in a won endgame the player skips the trivial capture of an undefended rook—almost always a king recapture (Kxh2/Kxg7/Kxa2)—playing an aimless check or tempo rook move instead and tossing the win; at medium it blurs to other winning/won endgames squandered by a tempo-losing or non-forcing move (e.g. Rd8 instead of Ra1+), with a couple of looser positional/king-safety slips rather than a literal hung-rook grab.

282.label: Top boards are already-losing positions where a defensive move (usually a king move) exposes the king and walks into a forced mate, missing the one saving resource; medium boards blur to other weakening/non-addressing moves (pawn pushes, knight or queen moves) that instead allow a decisive attack, a fork, or simply drop material — plus a couple of off-pattern passed-pawn endgame inaccuracies and one missed mate, making the invariant fuzzy.

284.label: Top: in winning endgames, skips capturing a (passed) pawn—usually grabbable with check—to instead fire a pointless tempo-check; medium broadens to missing any winning capture (pawn, or even mate) where the substitute is a quiet pawn push, king/piece move, or even a move that hangs material.

281.label: Top boards squander a winning passed-pawn/promotion race by playing a slow quiet move (pawn push, retreat, king step) instead of the forcing rook sacrifice or check that forces/clears promotion; medium blurs to other forcing resources (back-rank king-steps, knight checks) needed in similar winning positions.

289.label: Top: player consistently hangs or trades off their own ROOK (frequently captured by a pawn) sealing a hopeless, often endgame, position that was already losing; medium blurs to surrendering other material (knight, bishop, the exchange) and even positional/king-safety concessions, sometimes from an equal or better starting position.

260.label: Top boards uniformly decline a forced/winning capture of an enemy knight (almost always on c6 or c3 via bxc6/bxc3), letting it escape or win material in return; medium positions blur into broader 'ignored the one critical move' errors (a needed central developing move, or a king move that hangs a pawn) where no knight capture is even on the board.

285.label: Top: player self-destructs king safety to speed up an existing loss — usually marching the king straight into a forced mating net (Ka3→Qa1#, Kg5, Kh3, Kb1 back-rank) but also stripping away its last defender/back-rank guard (Rxd6, Rxa4, self-blocking Rg3); medium narrows to pure king-walks into the open onto forced mate (Kd4, Kc6, Kf5), converting a defensible loss into a faster checkmate.

287.label: Top boards are clearly winning/favorable positions where the player skips the single strongest conversion — wrong piece, skipped forcing intermezzo/check, or a bad trade — shrinking or losing the win; medium broadens to murkier or smaller-advantage positions where the error blurs into outright hanging a piece (b3c2, b6c5, d8d6) or positional/endgame drift (f5f4, c4c3, h6g8).

288.chip: Hangs piece on greedy grab (often queen)
288.label: Top boards are uniformly the queen left en prise on g4 after a greedy/irrelevant pawn or knight capture in the opening (punished by ...Bxg4); medium blurs to other hung pieces (e.g. bishop on c4 after Nxc5) and adjacent greedy opening grabs that lose material or expose the king (fxe5 → Qh4+).

283.label: Top: in a won endgame the player makes a natural pawn push/quiet move instead of the single decisive converting capture, almost always a king capture (Kxf6/Kxb7/Kxa2); medium broadens to a pawn endgame where the missed converting move is a precise king advance (Kf7) that wins without capturing.

293.label: Top boards almost all decline an undefended enemy rook in a winning endgame, playing a king or pawn move instead of the free capture; medium stays in the endgame but blurs the captured piece to knights and broadens to general king-and-pawn / passed-pawn technique slips (premature checks, wrong rook placement, blocking the king).

291.label: Top: a free, undefended enemy queen is available to capture/win outright and the player plays an inferior developing or attacking move instead (one mate-in-3 the lone outlier where the win isn't a queen-grab); medium: identical pattern — an undefended enemy queen (Qxc2) ignored for a flashier move, just with a smaller swing.

290.label: At peak, boards consistently miss a tempo-gaining rook lift (Rg1/Rg8/Ra1) that saves material while harassing the exposed/infiltrating enemy queen, choosing a passive or self-damaging move instead; medium blurs into other tempo-hits on the queen (Bg4, Nh5, Ne5, trapping Bd6) and drifts toward general passive/self-damaging moves that miss forks or hang own material.

292.label: Top boards are uniform: a natural developing/pawn move ignores an enemy knight that, instead of retreating, leaps forward to a royal fork of king+rook (e.g. Nc7+, Nxf7+, Nf2+), losing the exchange; medium blurs to other knight tactics (queen/rook forks, discovered checks, Nd6/Ng6 outposts) and looser positional or king-safety lapses that aren't strictly forks.

298.label: Top boards squander a winning/drawing endgame through an imprecise tempo-losing or passed-pawn-neglecting move where the decisive piece varies (rook/king/bishop); medium blurs to mostly king and pawn tempo-losses in the same pawn-race/conversion theme — but several boards (Qc8+, Nd5+, Qb1+, c6) are actually best moves, making this a genuinely mixed conversion feature.

266.label: Top: a pointless dark-square bishop check (Bc5+/Bb6+/Bh6+) that the opponent simply sidesteps with Kh1/Kh8, wasting tempo and squandering the position; medium keeps the same sidestepped-check pattern but broadens the checking piece (adds Qb6+) and the consequence — which ranges across outright hanging the bishop (Rxc5/Nxa3/Rxb4), dropping material a couple moves later, and missing a stronger winning continuation (Qd4+ fork).

302.label: Top: an opening move (usually the c8-bishop leaving) hangs a piece or pawn that the enemy QUEEN snatches for free (Qxb7/Qxc5/Qxd4); medium keeps the same hang-in-opening core but broadens the punisher beyond the queen — a bishop grabs the loose piece/pawn (Bxf4, Bxb4) or a removed kingside defender leads to a queen mating raid (Qxg7#).

297.label: Top boards are king moves that walk the monarch onto an exposed central/open square inviting forced mate or queen-loss via fork/skewer; medium keeps the king-exposure theme but blurs to include pawn/piece moves that open lines on the king and to consequences short of mate (heavy material loss or a winning attack).

294.label: Top boards are uniformly f-pawn moves/captures that self-weaken the king or structure and hand back material (a piece to ...fxe5, or king exposure to Qh5+/Qh4+); medium blurs the f-pawn anchor, broadening to any self-weakening opening move that loses material — removed defenders, forks, trapped pieces, and bad trades.

296.label: At the peak it's constantly a rook passively committed to blockade/chase a passed pawn (tempo-losing/over-committal vs a more active rook); at medium it blurs to king marches and other piece commitments toward the passer, and—like ~3 top boards—fires on several 0cp/best moves, making it genuinely mixed.

301.label: Top boards almost always skip the single converting move—usually a free capture of a hanging knight/bishop/rook or the correct (queen) promotion—in a won endgame; medium blurs the same fault to imprecise king-march/tempo moves that squander winning pawn and rook endgames (and even a few near-zero-loss cases).

305.label: Top boards consistently botch a king-safety crisis—mostly walking the player's own king into an immediate/forced checkmate (Rg1/Kh1/h3/Rc5/Rxa7), with two outliers reversing direction by throwing away the player's OWN forced mate (wrong knight to f7); medium blurs from pure mate to king-safety/attacking blunders that hang material instead (discovered attack winning a rook, Qxg2 winning a rook) plus one still-mating Ke5.

299.label: TOP: a safe king move/capture declines a forced winning promotion or material-winning blow (dxe8=Q, axb1=Q, Qxf4) in a clearly won position; MEDIUM blurs to general squandered winning technique — passive rook moves and king misrouting in endgames that throw away the advantage without a clean promotion on the board.

307.label: Top boards uniformly miss the classic Greek Gift bishop sacrifice on h7/h2 (Bxh7+/Bxh2+) launching a forced mating attack; medium blurs to missing other decisive kingside mating shots against the castled king (Qxg7#, Qxg2#, Nf3+→Qg2#).

295.label: Top: a queen capture-with-check (often grabbing a knight/pawn) is recaptured or hung, collapsing a winning endgame to a near-draw; medium blurs to queen-for-rook capturing-checks that lose material but stay nominally winning.

304.label: Constant across both: a voluntary capturing trade (frequently a check) that liquidates a winning/drawing position into a worse pawn or simplified endgame; top boards blur the traded piece across queen, rook, and one bishop (and 2/10 are actually optimal trades), while medium boards narrow to pure queen trades that surrender a winning bind.

300.label: Top: in an endgame the player gives up their active rook (occasionally a key minor piece) for a pawn or knight that is immediately recaptured, collapsing into a lost position; medium broadens to smaller-eval drops — simply hanging the rook to a clean capture or prematurely swapping off a strong attacking piece, sometimes with queens still on the board.

303.label: Top boards are nearly all the same ...Bxh6/Bxh6 deflection sac (dragging the queen off c3 to win material) that the player skips in favor of a slow quiet move; medium blurs to other overlooked tactical shots (pins like Bb5/Bb4, forks, grabbing a hanging piece) and shades into actively hanging own material rather than just declining a win.

258.label: Top fires on skipping the winning Nxh4 capture of an exposed h4-knight (missed-win, 2 boards), plus one self-inflicted rook trade into a lost pawn endgame; medium blurs to dropping a winning advantage by carelessly pushing a passed pawn in a rook endgame, so direction (missed-win vs hung/squandered edge) is genuinely mixed.

308.chip: Hangs material to knight fork (any tactic)
308.label: Top boards are pure knight forks (often winning a full piece/bishop) where a careless pawn push or bishop move walks the king/piece into Nxf-type fork-with-check; medium keeps the 'committal move loses material' invariant but blurs the punisher — only ~half are knight forks (Ne8+, Nc6+, Ne2+), the rest being rook infiltrations, hanging pawns, or even tempo-losses/missed wins.

306.label: Top boards are K+P endgames where a passive/centralizing king move skips the decisive pawn push or escort technique—often throwing away a forced mate while losing no material; medium blurs into broader endgame tempo errors (wrong-direction king moves, mistaken pawn pushes like h4/b4, and bishop/rook endgames) that miss a plain win rather than mate, with several near-noise non-blunders mixed in.

312.label: Top boards squander a clean forced mate in a winning endgame (missed mate-in-1 or abandoned mating sequence via a materially-safe move), while medium boards blur toward merely prolonging the win or losing tempo with a slower safe move.

309.label: Top: voluntarily gives up the queen WITH A CHECK (trading queens or queen-for-rook), collapsing a winning/holdable position; medium keeps the checking-queen-giveaway but broadens to hanging the queen to an unsound check and to other position-collapsing moves (rook trade, king/pawn blunders).

315.label: Top: in a won/decisive endgame the player addresses the wrong target — captures the harmless pawn (Nxg7 vs Nxh4+), or sends the king/bishop to the wrong square (Kh5, Bb3) — neglecting the opponent's passed pawn and letting it promote; medium blurs into general mis-targeted/missed captures in passed-pawn-decisive moments (wrong capture order, or skipping a free piece like Rxe2), with several boards actually engine-best (Kd2, Bh3).

317.label: At the peak the player throws away a won position by overlooking a free winning capture (Nxe5, Bxg7); at medium activation it blurs into broader winning-position squanders — vulnerable queen/knight placement, trapped pieces, and missed breaks/tempo (Qe7, Ne7, Be3).

314.label: Top activations are knight checks (especially Ne2+ leaving a dominant outpost) that let the king step to safety; medium blurs to bishop/rook/queen checks (Bc5+, Rg8+, Qf1+) that equally waste a tempo and squander the advantage by skipping a clearly stronger move.

318.label: Plays a natural/passive/greedy middlegame move and overlooks a forcing tactical resource; at the peak this is almost always an exchange sacrifice or a check that wins material (often the queen) or saves a drawn/losing position, while medium boards blur toward simpler forcing moves (plain checks, tactical captures) and even quiet positional/defensive alternatives.

316.label: Top boards are tightly unified: in winning positions the player skips a decisive back-rank/forcing rook check (Rd8+, Ra1+, Rb8+, Rb1+, Rg8+) that wins material or mates, instead playing a quiet move; at medium the rook-check idea still dominates (Rc7+, Re1+, Ra7+, Rc4+ fork) but blurs to include other forcing shots (Bd3 mate, Qc1+ perpetual) and the direction splits — several boards don't merely miss a win but hang own rook/exchange to a knight fork (Nxc5, Nxd6, Nxe6+) or to Qxa1.

310.label: At the peak, an inferior move squanders a winning/favorable position via a sharp concrete refutation—forks, deflections and hanging pieces lost over 2-3 moves—or a cleanly missed winning tactic (top 1-4: royal fork, mate-net king walk, queen/exchange hangs); at medium it broadens to king-safety collapses forced to mate plus slower positional/structural concessions (opening a diagonal, releasing central tension, allowing a favorable queen trade, king walks that drop a piece), so direction (hangs own material vs misses a win) and the piece involved are genuinely mixed.

313.label: Top: player makes an even-for-even bishop trade/capture instead of eliminating the opponent's strong centralized knight, and the knight recaptures or survives on a dominant square (best line removed the knight); medium broadens the same advantage-squandering swap to other pieces — trading off one's own strong knight (Nxd7) or a premature rook sacrifice (Rxg7+) — so the constant is the losing trade leaving the enemy knight thriving while the specific piece blurs.

319.label: Top boards are king-safety collapses where the move abandons a key defender (f6-knight, f2/central pawn, or kingside-guarding queen), exposing the king and conceding a decisive attack; medium broadens to premature pawn advances, knight sorties, and tension releases that merely overextend, waste tempo, or shed a pawn—and even reach endgames and a missed winning break—worsening an equal-or-better game without cleanly hanging a piece.

320.label: Top boards are uniformly a premature central e-pawn push (e5/e4, occasionally d-pawn) left wholly undefended and snapped off for free; medium broadens to other premature pawn advances (d4-d5, e5-e6, even flank b4-b5) where the push either hangs the pawn directly or opens a diagonal/file that costs the pawn or a piece, with a few cases blurring toward opening-line/king-safety damage.

311.label: Top: a queen sortie (typically to h3/g3) abandons a defensive duty—an unguarded piece, square, or counter-pin—and hangs material (exchange/piece/pawn), with a few quiet queen redeployments instead squandering a winning tactic or mate; medium keeps the 'abandons a duty and ruins a won/equal position' core but blurs the piece (rook, knight, bishop, king, pawn) and tilts more toward missed wins/mates alongside the hung material.

322.label: Top: in a lost middlegame a rook (occasionally a pawn) abandons a key defensive post—back rank or open file—letting pieces converge into a forced mate; medium broadens to any king-safety-weakening move where the punishment blurs from forced mate to plain material loss (forks, hanging) or positional/endgame collapse.

324.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where releasing pawn tension or a careless king move hands the opponent a decisive passed pawn or king penetration (losing the race or throwing away a winning passer); medium broadens to minor-piece and rook endgames with the same passed-pawn-race theme, but is diluted by several statistical non-blunders and an unrelated back-rank mate.

327.label: Top boards are uniform: a passive opening move (Be2/d4/h3/Bf4) overlooks the winning Nxe5 that nets the now-undefended pinning bishop on g4/h5 once the pin breaks; medium keeps the missed-win theme but blurs to other winning knight strikes (Nxe4, Ng4).

328.label: Top boards consistently hang a piece—most often the bishop—by abandoning its defense, self-interference, or stepping into a fork/pin (losing the queen); medium boards broaden to hanging knights, pawns, and the queen via skewers, removed recaptures, and rook invasions, so the lost material varies while the theme stays a middlegame move that drops the player's own material.

323.label: Top boards are uniformly identical — a missed free capture of an undefended enemy rook on the open long diagonal with the fianchetto bishop (Bxh8/Bxa8/Bxh1/Bxa1/Bxb1), playing a quiet move that lets the diagonal be blocked; medium blurs this to other free diagonal captures (rook by queen on a1, bishop takes a3-knight, Bxb8 on the f4-b8 diagonal) and bleeds into adjacent missed/allowed tactics like an undefended bishop or a knight fork.

330.label: Top: a materially-safe, slow/passive move (rook shuffle, knight reroute, bishop retreat) that fails to grab a cleanly hanging central pawn (d4/e4/d5/e5/c6) for a clean win; medium blurs the target to any squandered material win (pawn-with-check, exchange, tactical Nxd5) and even tips into the passive move itself conceding material — hung piece (Rd6, Nc3, Nd3, e5) or back-rank mate — so the direction is no longer purely 'missed'.

325.label: Top boards are premature pawn-to-queen promotions (often with check) where the new queen sits adjacent to the enemy king/piece and is captured immediately, throwing away a winning or drawn endgame; medium blurs into broader endgame-conversion errors — a wrong-piece recapture that kills a passed-pawn win and a promotion grabbed by a knight rather than an adjacent king.

333.label: Top boards uniformly neglect king safety—grabbing material or chasing an enemy piece while ignoring a decisive threat that yields a crushing attack or back-rank mate; medium blurs the theme to ignoring other decisive threats (pawn promotion, hanging pieces, lost queen/pawn endgames) with a couple being simple missed material wins.

332.label: Top boards under-trade or hang a dominant knight on a capture that the opponent simply recaptures (usually with the king), throwing away the advantage; medium blurs the lost piece to bishops and a rook (exchange sac) and even includes non-capturing moves (pawn pushes / knight retreats) that leave a piece hanging, plus a couple of missed-win/near-best cases.

331.label: Top boards uniformly answer a slow/developing move (f6, Bb7, O-O, Bd7, c3, Na5, Ng6, c5, Bb2, Bg4) instead of the demanded central capture (exd4/dxe4/dxe5), allowing the e5 break—frequently a pawn fork netting a full piece; medium blurs to other breaks (e4, f5, f4, c4, cxd5) that mostly seize tempo/space rather than win material outright.

336.label: Top boards are uniformly knight checks that trade away or hang the player's own best minor piece — almost always the checking knight itself (or its trip ends in being trapped and losing the queen); medium broadens to include a non-checking bishop development that simply hangs, plus another Nxf3+ that sacrifices the dominant knight for a pawn.

326.label: TOP: every board skips a one-move capture of a free, undefended enemy piece (8/10 a rook, plus one queen via Bxc4 and one bishop via Kxe4), throwing away a won endgame; MEDIUM: blurs to missing the best winning move generally—usually still a capture (free knight Bxa3/Rxc4, winning pawn grabs Rxg2/fxg5, mating Qxb1) but also non-capture wins (setup Bd3, Qh2), so the 'free hanging piece' specificity softens to 'missed winning capture/move'.

329.label: Top boards uniformly capture with a rook (a minor piece or pawn) only to be recaptured, surrendering the exchange in the middlegame; medium blurs to dropping a full rook for a pawn and to materially-safe rook moves/trades that skip a stronger winning continuation.

337.label: Top: a natural-looking opening/developing move hangs material (pawn most often, also bishop/knight/queen) and is refuted by a pawn capture; medium broadens to middlegame quiet moves with varied refutations (piece captures like Bxd2, structure-wrecking queen trades, king-safety pawn storms) plus an occasional missed pawn-win.

334.label: Top: a won (usually endgame) position is thrown away by skipping a simple free capture of an undefended piece — typically a rook move like ...Rxd6/...Bxe2/...Rxb6 — choosing a pointless check or pawn push instead; medium keeps the 'winning position squandered' core but broadens the mechanism to walking into forks, missing forced mate, wrong-pawn promotions, greedy material-losing trades, and drawing a won pawn ending.

340.label: Top boards leave an undefended minor piece (repeatedly the d4 knight, plus a hanging e5 bishop / f3 knight) to be grabbed by a one-move capture, while medium blurs into rooks and removed-defender pieces (Bg4, a1 rook, e5/f5 knights) and shades toward positional/king-safety material losses.

335.label: Top boards are rook-takes-rook on/next-to a promotion square letting the enemy pawn recapture-promote to a queen with immediate check or mate (back-rank); medium broadens to any greedy capture that frees an enemy passed pawn to promote or simply win material, not always with mate.

338.label: Top boards uniformly hang an undefended central knight in the opening (very often the e5-knight to Nxe5, also d5/d4/e4) for a clean full piece, either by leaving it loose or removing its sole defender; medium boards still orbit a vulnerable central knight but blur into removed-defender forks, kingside/structural collapses, tempo-wasting moves, and even missed knight-captures, so direction and exact mechanism vary.

343.label: Top boards convert a clearly winning position into dead equality via a forcing rook/queen trade (usually a capture-with-check that overlooks the loss of a sentinel or a zwischenzug); medium broadens to any premature simplification—promotions, passed-pawn pushes, wrong-piece captures, or mate-throwing checks—that hands back the win.

339.label: At the peak the move hangs the queen—usually to a knight fork (Nf6+, Nh4+, Nf4+)—or misses a decisive queen shot (Qxg7#, Qxf3+) in a winning position, with the queen always the decisive piece; at medium it blurs into losing other material (exchange/pawn) or pure positional/king-safety collapse where the queen is no longer central.

348.label: Top: in an already-won position the player avoids the immediate forcing check (Qxc4+, Rb8+, Qa3+) and plays a slow centralizing/quiet move that only delays a forced mate; medium keeps the 'skipped the forcing check' core but blurs from pure mate-delays to missing material-winning forcing sequences (forks, deflections, intermezzi), occasionally even hanging the queen by ignoring the available check.

345.chip: Hangs to ignored knight tactic (usually a piece)
345.label: Top: a quiet developing or pawn move skips capturing a loose enemy knight (e.g. Qxg4/Qxg5) and hangs a bishop, queen, or rook to an immediate capture or knight fork in the opening, with a knight always central; medium keeps the knight central but broadens to hung pawns and looser positional/tempo/king-safety errors, sometimes drifting past the opening.

350.label: Top: in a won endgame the player skips an immediate capture of an undefended rook (sometimes a queen), playing a check or king move instead and throwing away the win; medium keeps the 'squandered won endgame' theme but blurs beyond captures into missed pawn pushes and inefficient checks/technique that bleed or forfeit the win.

341.label: Top: a faulty capture/exchange — wrong target, wrong move-order, or premature recapture — throws away a winning position (and often hangs own material in the refutation); medium broadens to non-capturing moves (knight to the rim, king/pawn pushes) that abandon a dominant piece or defensive post and let the opponent equalize.

321.chip: Hangs piece declining bishop capture (often c6/c3)
321.label: Top: player declines to recapture an intruding bishop on c6/c3 and ends down a full piece as it retreats to safety; medium keeps the 'don't take the intruding bishop' core but blurs the square (h6/a6/f5/e5) and shades from hanging-own toward simply missing a free or forcing capture.

349.label: Top boards uniformly play a safe developing move and overlook a winning bishop capture (Bxd6/Bxd3/Bxc5) that nets a full, unrecapturable piece from a winning position; medium boards still miss bishop captures but on more varied squares (Bxc6/Bxf5/Bxf3/Bxc4) and for gains ranging from a full piece down to a pawn, with a few non-capture missed-win outliers.

344.label: At the peak the recurring error is a knight move that abandons the c4 bishop and hangs it (Bd3 the only fix, refuted by ...dxc4), with a minority instead skipping a winning Nxe5/Nxe4; at medium this blurs into a grab-bag of central-tension mishandling — missed Nxe5/Nxe4 captures alongside other hung pieces and allowed forks — so the direction (hung vs. missed) is genuinely split.

352.label: Top: pure king-and-pawn endgames violating 'king before pawn'—advancing the passed pawn (or stepping the king the wrong way) throws away the win and lets the enemy king blockade to a draw; medium broadens to general endgame king/pawn-timing errors (wrong king route, premature pawn pushes, wasted tempi) in piece-and-pawn races and positional endgames, often only costing advantage rather than the whole point.

355.label: Top boards are forcing checks (or check-captures) that hang a piece to the checked king's/recapturer's reply — rook, bishop or queen varies; medium boards blur into checks that instead force a losing trade or lost pawn/rook endgame, with the harmful check constant (100%) but the hung piece and win-vs-loss outcome varying.

353.label: Top boards uniformly miss a forced queen mate against the enemy king (almost always Qxh2# / queen-lift to the h-file); medium boards broaden to missed winning king attacks via other pieces and sacrifices (rook lifts/sacs like Rxh2 & Rxh7, Greek-gift Bxh7+, longer forced mates), blurring further into a few non-mating tactical/material wins (Qxa7, Bxb6, fork-winning Qh5).

351.chip: Squandered win with plausible move (opening→all phases)
351.label: Top boards: in clearly winning OPENING positions, a natural developing knight/bishop move or a tempting empty check is played instead of the unique precise continuation (typically a central pawn capture like fxe5/fxe4 or a quiet mating move), throwing the advantage away — mostly materially-safe squandering, though Bb4+/Bc5 directly hang a piece over 2-3 moves; medium boards keep the same 'plausible move that squanders a better position' idea but blur outward to the middlegame and endgame with assorted imprecise tries (premature pawn pushes, wrong-square piece moves, defensive-piece relocations, move-order errors) and occasional outright hangs/trapped pieces.

354.chip: Walks into forced mate (else hangs material)
354.label: Top boards are uniformly immediate forced checkmates where the player's own king is sealed in a self-made mating net (move ignores Qxf7#/Rxh#/walks the king into mate); medium keeps some forced mates (back-rank, slower nets) but blurs into forced losses of major material—queen to knight forks and discovered attacks—plus a few positional/missed-win cases, so the constant 'forced punishment of a losing move' holds while the penalty shifts from mate to dropped material.

347.label: Top boards consistently hang a piece on an undefended/loose square (rook most often, also queen and bishop) that's then collected by a tactic (fork, discovered attack, or in-between check); medium blurs to mixed concessions—missed winning captures, abandoned passed-pawn blockades, and king-safety lapses—where the material loss is indirect or merely positional.

346.label: At the peak the player skips a free capture of a completely undefended major piece (queen or rook), instead playing an idle king/pawn move and throwing away the won endgame; at medium the target is almost always an undefended rook and the missed shot occasionally blurs into a non-capturing best move (a winning pawn take or precise positional move).

356.label: Top: a quiet/tempo king or rook shuffle leaves a piece (varying — queen, bishop or rook) hanging by ignoring a forced recapture/trade on a contested square; medium keeps the same 'tempo move that fails to resolve tension' pattern but is dominated by king/queen moves that drop the queen, plus a few exchange-loss/bishop cases over 1–3 moves.

358.label: Top boards throw away a won position by a clear material error—most consistently hanging or failing to capture a major piece (rook/queen) along an open line; medium blurs this to hanging knights, allowing knight forks, and quiet/tempo-losing moves that skip the decisive winning capture.

361.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a passive/wrong-square king move squanders a tempo or the opposition in an already-lost position (no material hung); medium blurs to add bishop endgames and king retreats that concede a key blockade/promotion square, the constant being king-only moves that worsen a losing endgame without hanging anything.

357.label: Top: a greedy capture or passive/king move that ignores a forced checkmate against one's own king (clean mate-in-1-to-3); medium blurs to broader king-safety collapses where the abandoned defense costs decisive material via a king-hunt rather than immediate mate, plus a few non-king material/positional blunders.

359.label: Top: White hangs an undefended knight (usually g5) in the opening that Black grabs for free, typically ...Qxg5; medium broadens to hanging other minor pieces (e.g. Bc5) and dropping material to simple opening tactics—forks, trapped knights, overloads—plus some king-safety/missed-win drift.

364.label: Top: self-inflicted middlegame moves that flip an unclear/holdable position to lost, mostly by losing material in a 2-3 move refutation (bishop/rook/knight/pawn) plus a few king-into-mating-net walks; medium keeps the same holdable→lost collapse but blurs toward tempo-losing retreats and direct one-move piece hangs across varied pieces.

363.label: Top: pure king-and-pawn endgames where a passive king move (or inferior pawn push) skips the one decisive pawn break/breakthrough, throwing away the win or draw; medium blurs the same idea into knight/bishop endgames (passive/greedy piece move over activity) and tempo/move-order misses, and includes a few near-0cp non-blunders.

370.label: Top boards sacrifice a bishop on f2/f7 with a tempting check for a single pawn that White simply recaptures (Bxf2+/Bxf7+), leaving a piece down for nothing; medium broadens to knight sacs hung for a pawn (Nxe5/Nf3+), but in all cases a routine recapture refutes the unsound opening sac.

366.label: At the peak the player consistently hangs their own queen for little/no compensation (moving it en prise, sac'ing it for a pawn, or capturing/playing on while it's attacked); at medium this blurs to hanging minor pieces (knight/bishop) or surrendering material and advantage via a tactically-refuted move.

369.label: Top boards take a piece (usually with the queen, sometimes a rook) in an already-won position instead of the faster forcing check/mate — often missing an outright mate-in-1/2; medium keeps the same grab-material-over-forcing-win habit but blurs the direction, with one capture actually hanging the queen and another squandering the win into a draw.

365.label: Top: a king move (or kingside pawn push) in an already-lost endgame that either hangs a rook/pawn or accelerates a forced mate, with the king the decisive piece; medium broadens to king walks that expose it to mating-check nets, abandon a defended pawn, or occasionally squander a remaining win/draw, often with smaller cp swings.

368.label: Top: a greedy minor-piece grab (usually capturing the enemy bishop) in an endgame that abandons the decisive task of stopping a passed pawn from queening—or once ignores a one-move back-rank mate—flipping a win/draw into a loss; medium blurs to materially-safe endgame pawn/piece moves (e.g. g5+, Bc5) that are actually the correct, 0-cp choices (false positives).

371.label: At the peak it's king/pawn/knight moves in already-won K+P and knight endgames that squander a pawn or pawn-tension/structure (several top boards are actually 0cp-optimal noise, and the 'hung piece' SEE signal is contradicted by multi-move pawn-loss refutations); at medium it broadens to rook endgames and larger swings that can outright throw the win, so the true invariant is just suboptimal endgame conversion rather than hanging material.

367.label: Top boards are quiet king moves in endgames that skip the one holding/saving resource (Bxb6, Kxf8, Nxd4+, Rxd3), turning a draw or salvageable loss into a clear loss punished by a hung piece, enemy promotion, or mate; medium blurs to other quiet pieces (bishop/rook/pawn shuffles) that likewise pass up the sole correct move, with more varied and sometimes milder punishment.

372.label: Top boards are pawn endgames where a king move (Kh2/Kf2/Ke4/Kd6) skips the single precise pawn capture that holds (fxg5, gxf5, bxa6, bxc6), losing the pawn race to an unstoppable passer; medium blurs to tempo/move-order errors (a4 before gxf5) and king moves that skip the resolving capture or follow-up tactic, with smaller eval swings.

360.label: Top: a quiet/greedy move (often a pawn grab like Qxg7/Qxa7) overlooks a forcing material-winning tactic that is almost always a CHECK (Bb3+ skewer, Ne4+/Nd6+ fork, Re3+/Be2+ deflection); medium blurs the 'forcing-check that wins' core into slow or greedy pawn-grabbing/offside moves (Qxa2, Nxa2, Rd1, Rc1, Qa5) that skip the position's critical defensive or central resource and let the opponent seize a decisive attack rather than purely missing a self-win.

377.label: Top boards uniformly hang the player's own QUEEN via an in-between attacking move (or move-order error) in a winning position—attacking an enemy piece while leaving the queen capturable instead of cashing in; medium blurs the constant queen-loss into hanging a rook, allowing a back-rank/mating attack, or a materially-safe check that simply squanders the won position.

381.label: From a winning position the player chose a quiet, materially-safe king/rook move and skipped a forcing win — at the peak almost always a knight check/fork or sacrifice (Nf3+, Nf6+, Nb3+, Nxe3+, Nxf6+, Ne7+, with a single Bxg7+ outlier); at medium the win blurs to other forcing shots (e.g. the rook strike Rxg2) alongside the knight check Ne7+.

376.label: Top: declines a forcing rook OR queen trade (Rxd8+/Qxe1+/Qxd7+) that liquidates into a won—occasionally drawn—pawn endgame, keeping the major piece on instead; medium: same missed simplification but narrowing to passive rook moves that skip Rxc4+/Rxf7+ into a winning king-and-pawn ending.

374.label: TOP is razor-consistent: in a won position the player plays a safe/consolidating or material-grabbing move (c3, cxd4, Qxd5, fxe5, Qxb6) and misses a decisive rook lift to the third rank (Rf3/Re3/Rd3/Re5) launching a winning—often mating—king attack; MEDIUM blurs to generally missing the single precise forcing/tempo move (other-rank rook lifts, checks like Re1+/Bf4+, tactical strikes, even defensive rook lifts) where the same quiet or greedy choice squanders the win or the hold.

373.label: At peak, a winning side skips a decisive back-rank/first-rank rook invasion (or favorable rook trade) for a greedy capture or passive queen/piece move; at medium the missed move broadens to any critical rook move (7th-rank invasion, check, file-contesting trade, defensive resource) and bleeds into unrelated tactics (missed captures, hung pieces), sometimes in merely difficult rather than clearly winning positions.

385.label: At the peak the player skips a single winning forcing CHECK—almost always a bishop check (Bd4+, Be6+, Bxf4+, Bf3+, Bc4+) that squanders a clear win; at medium the pattern blurs to other forcing checks (knight Ng5+, queen Qd5+/Qf5+) and even non-check best moves (Re2, Kg6, Qa7), and the direction is mixed since a couple of boards actually hang the player's own queen/rook or trade into a lost ending rather than merely missing a win.

375.label: Top: an inferior ROOK move throws away a winning/clearly-better position—missing a forced mate or material win (#1,6,7,9), losing tempo by abandoning an active square (#2,5,10), misplacing the rook (#3), or walking it into a trap (#8); medium blurs the moving piece (queen, king, knight, pawn also appear) and often the squandered resource is itself a rook tactic (Rxc2/Rxc6/Rxg7/Re7), but the constant is a materially-safe, passive/inferior move that squanders a winning edge.

342.label: Top: a slow, natural queen-or-rook move (doubling, retreat, idle attack) forgoes an available forcing mate/material-winning line in a won position; medium blurs this—still mostly a slow queen move, but now it not only skips the win but directly hangs a pawn or the queen (or invites a king attack) to the refutation, so direction splits ~evenly between 'missed win' and 'hangs material.'

387.label: Top boards consistently hang the QUEEN to a pawn capture in a winning/forced-mate position (squandering the mate into 'merely winning'); medium broadens to hanging other material — rooks, knights, or the queen to a recapturing piece — and bleeds into a few missed-win/non-blunder cases.

379.label: At the peak: a routine developing move (usually a knight) overlooks a fully undefended enemy bishop on g4/g5 that the queen could capture for free in the opening; at medium it blurs into other missed winning tactics (Bxf7+, ...Nxe4, ...e5) and routine moves that instead allow opponent forks/pins/discovered attacks (mixing missed-win with self-inflicted hangs).

389.label: Top: from a winning position plays a slow, materially-safe move—almost always skipping a decisive kingside pawn break (f5/f4) or a key capture (Nxc7, Kxa3, Bxe6)—wasting the one tempo that wins and conceding a draw; medium keeps the 'missed the only winning resource' theme but blurs the resource into wrong-piece recaptures (Kxd4 vs cxd4) and outright tactical shots (Rxc5 knight-fork combo), with one near-equal/non-blunder case as noise.

378.label: At the peak the player advances a pawn or grabs material while ignoring an enemy passed pawn about to promote or a forced mate (the one defensive capture/move that neutralizes it); at medium the overlooked threat blurs into general tactical shots — knight/pawn forks, a queen-winning attack, and an uncaptured enemy passer — but the core stays 'pursue own plan instead of meeting the opponent's decisive threat.'

383.label: Top boards make the decisive losing move in an already-lost endgame by hanging the rook, trading it for a pawn, or skipping the one saving capture—collapsing a fightable position into forced mate; medium blurs into broader non-material errors (tempo loss, premature pawn pushes, move-order/king missteps) in critical endgames, sometimes only drawn/winning, with far smaller eval swings.

388.chip: Missed winning pawn push (K+P at peak)
388.label: At the peak these are pure king-and-pawn endgames where pushing the passed pawn to the seventh rank is the only winning move and the king move throws a forced win into a dead draw; at medium the same king-instead-of-push error appears but the loss is softer (win stays winning, smaller eval swing) and can involve extra pawns rather than bare K+P.

384.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a slow king move or passive pawn push squanders the single winning/holding pawn break (g4, h5, f5, h4, a4) with material staying safe; medium broadens to middlegame and other tempo-losing slow moves, where the neglected break instead lets the opponent strike (pawn forks, exchange, lost pawns) and material is actually dropped over 2–3 moves.

380.label: At the peak it's a queen moved onto a square where it's captured WITH CHECK—almost always disguised as a trade offer—turning a playable/winning game into a loss or forced mate; at medium the pattern blurs to hanging or trading away other material (rook/bishop/knight, even pawn or defender moves) that drops the queen/piece or exposes the king to mate, frequently without the check or the trade pretext.

391.label: Top boards are uniformly an undefended bishop dropped onto a free-capture square in the opening (Ba6, Bh3, Ba3, Bg4, or refusing the Bb3/Bc4 retreat), captured immediately for a full piece; medium keeps the bishop hangs but blurs to broader opening material loss, adding a weakening pawn push (g4) that bleeds material via king exposure over several moves.

392.label: Top boards are all bishop captures played in the wrong move-order—grabbing a rook/piece while a queen, knight or pawn hangs to an intermezzo, intermediate check, or undefended piece in a winning position; medium broadens to other pieces and even quiet repositioning moves (and an occasional missed-mate/bigger-win) that likewise overlook a refutation and drop material.

393.label: A slow tempo-grabbing pawn push (usually one that kicks an enemy bishop) ignores a more urgent matter: at the top it ignores a forced mating attack or decisive tactic and gets mated/loses heavy material; at medium the same slow push merely squanders a winning/equal position by dropping a pawn or tempo without immediate mate.

395.label: Top boards almost all leave the player's own knight en prise in the opening (failing to retreat an attacked/loose knight before castling, capturing, or pushing a pawn); medium broadens the hung material to pawns and other pieces, often lost over a 2-3 move refutation (zwischenzug/discovered attack).

400.label: At the peak, every board passes up a winning queen check (Qa4+ or Qa5+) that forks the uncastled king and an undefended bishop on b4/b5; at medium strength it broadens to include the Qb5+ variant and forks whose secondary target is a knight (e.g. c4) rather than strictly a loose bishop.

394.label: Top boards are almost always a purposeless QUEEN check that throws away the position—hanging the queen to a king capture/interposition or dragging it off a key defensive square into mate (sometimes skipping a forced mate); medium keeps the pointless-check theme but broadens to knights, bishops and even quiet non-check blunders that similarly drop material or walk into mate.

390.label: Constant at the peak: a slow queenside expansion pawn push (a-/b-/c-pawn) that squanders a critical tempo and is refuted by a concrete tactic — usually dropping own material (Nxb5, Bd5 trapping the rook, Nxf2 fork) and occasionally a king-attack or thrown-away win; at medium it blurs to kingside flank pushes (g4/h4/g5) and even slow non-pawn developing moves, where the punishment widens from lost material to merely a missed central break or surrendered initiative.

399.label: Top boards center on a bishop being lost or traded into a lost/defensible ending (plus a few missed material-winning Bxa1 captures); medium blurs to hanging assorted minor pieces (bishop, knight) and structure-collapsing pawn pushes — constant is botched endgame material, but direction varies (hang/trade/missed).

386.label: Top: in a won position the player passes up a fully undefended enemy ROOK—playing a king move, a check, or a lesser capture instead—throwing away the win; medium keeps the same 'free hanging target ignored in a winning position' theme but blurs the piece to a bishop or even a pawn (and the refutation more often punishes by mate or by costing the player's own material).

402.label: At the peak the player voluntarily captures/trades a powerfully-centralized KNIGHT (usually a recapture-equal trade, often with check) for a passive enemy piece, throwing away a winning fork or attack by missing a far stronger continuation (e.g. Nc2 fork over Nxe2+); at medium the dominant traded piece blurs to bishops and rooks (Bxc6, Bxf3, Bxg3, Rxe2 — occasionally even conceding the exchange), but the constant is swapping off the cornerstone piece while skipping a stronger tactical/positional move.

404.label: At the peak it's strictly hanging one's own knight in the endgame—a king or knight move leaving it undefended or trading it for a pawn; at medium the hung material blurs to other minor pieces and rooks, and bleeds into slow/tempo-losing king moves in already-lost endgames.

401.label: Top: a quiet opening developing/prophylactic move ignores a pawn's direct attack on the player's own knight, losing it (one loses a rook/trapped instead); medium blurs to other hung pieces (bishop), allowed tactics/forks, and structural or endgame concessions beyond the opening.

396.label: Top boards are clearly winning positions with exactly ONE decisive move available, which the player declines—about half the played moves hang material outright (Nf5, Rf1-into-fork, Rxd5) and half merely skip the win (g5 not Bg5, h4 not Re1, d4 not Rc1); medium broadens to positions that are only advantageous or even difficult/losing, and adds greedy pawn-grabs (Qxb2, Nxb5, Qxd4) and king-safety lapses that likewise bypass the sole correct move.

403.chip: Greedy capture hangs own piece (often knight)
403.label: Top: a greedy material-grab or wrong capture-order that hangs the player's own piece (most often a knight) or invites a refuting fork, squandering a winning/equal position; medium blurs to wrong-piece recaptures and 'natural' moves that skip a forced/clean win.

382.label: Top boards consistently forgo a forced mate or a tactic that wins the enemy queen in favor of a materially-safe tempo move (often one that merely chases the queen); medium boards show the same instinct to attack/chase the enemy queen for tempo, but there the inferior move typically drops material in the 2-3 move refutation rather than just leaving a win on the table — so the direction blurs from 'missed win' toward 'hangs material'.

398.label: Top: a quiet developing/retreating move from a won opening misses a free one-move capture of an undefended piece (9/10 a hanging bishop, e.g. Bxg4/exf5/Bxf5); medium keeps the won-opening + passive-move skeleton but broadens the missed win to knight double-attacks (Nxf7), Greek-Gift sacrifices (Bxh7+), check-tactics (Qa5+/Bxb2) and central breaks (d5), losing the specific 'free bishop' flavor.

407.label: Top boards uniformly miss a forced mate delivered by a queen capture/check (e.g. Qxb6+→Qb7#), while medium boards still miss forced mates but the initiating/delivering check broadens to rook- or knight-checks alongside queen moves.

409.label: Top boards are all greedy/careless rook moves or captures that hang the rook or strip a key defender (back-rank/king cover) for self-inflicted material loss; medium keeps the rook-capture motif but the hung piece blurs (bishop/knight via removed defender), and ~3/10 instead simply miss a winning line (incl. throwing away a won endgame), so direction isn't fully uniform.

397.label: Top: a knight lunges at the enemy QUEEN hoping to win a tempo, but she sidesteps to a superior square (or checks), so the raid mostly just squanders tempo and the misplaced knight—and in several cases hangs outright; medium broadens the target from the queen to bishops/other pieces and the refutation now usually wins material directly (the sortie piece is simply captured, opens a diagonal onto a rook, or vacates a key defender).

416.label: Top boards consistently hang the player's own material to an overlooked knight tactic — knight forks or captures like Nxc5+, Nxc7, Ne6+ and Nxh8 that win a pawn/exchange/piece with tempo; medium boards blur this into broader losses of advantage (passive/tempo and positional king-safety errors that drop a pawn or invite invasion without a direct knight shot), plus a couple of squandered forced wins, making the direction mixed.

414.label: Top: imprecise king/pawn moves in winning or drawn endgames that throw away the result (incl. king moves walking into a knight-check-fork like Kf4→Nd5+, missed en passant, broken winning pawn structure), though a couple of top boards are actually optimal; medium narrows to pure king-and-pawn endgames where an imprecise king/pawn advance squanders the win.

413.label: Top boards uniformly play a forcing CHECK that throws away material—the hung unit varies (queen, rook, knight, or bishop) and two endgame cases are active-rook trades that surrender the position—while medium boards drop the check requirement, broadening to quiet tempo moves (pawn pushes, king moves) that hang a piece or hand back a winning/drawn position.

406.label: Top: a materially-safe, passive move (Qe2, quiet pawn push) declines the single winning continuation—almost always a pawn capture, frequently en passant—turning a clearly winning position into equal/losing; medium broadens the missed move to any one critical resource (knight captures, central breaks, prophylactic c5) and bleeds into a few cases where the passive move actually allows an opponent tactic (fork, even mate).

415.label: Top boards are clean queen-for-queen trades/captures where the recapture immediately promotes (or makes unstoppable) a passed pawn, frequently with check, converting equal/losing positions into clearly lost ones; medium is the same motif — a queen capture (Qxb2) that lets the opponent's passed pawn run, just without the promotion-with-check element.

410.label: Top boards uniformly lose own material by ignoring or walking into a bishop pin (Bg4/Bg5/Bb5), almost always refuted by h3; medium boards keep the opening material-drop theme but broaden beyond pins to unsound f2/e5 sacrifices, plain hanging pieces, and forks.

405.label: Top: king greedily captures a pawn and steps off the passed pawn's square/blockade, so the enemy passer queens unstoppably; medium broadens to any losing king (or even bishop/knight) move that abandons the critical square—letting a passer promote, opening lines into a mating net, or squandering a won pawn endgame.

417.label: Top boards consistently capture/swap the last active rook or queen into a lost king-and-pawn ending where the opponent's pawn majority and king decide; medium blurs to broader endgame-conversion errors (premature pawn pushes, wrong recaptures, simplifying while down material).

418.label: Top boards are quiet bishop/knight developing-or-retreating moves that hang material by abandoning a defender or ignoring a live tactic (fork or hanging piece); medium broadens to materially-safe moves that instead squander a winning advantage or miss a winning tactic.

412.label: At the peak the feature fires on an unnecessary, materially-safe simplification of an easily-won endgame (queen-for-knight trade that collapses a piece-up position into a bare pawn ending); medium blurs to other won-endgame conversion errors that keep material safe—e.g. a pawn push allowing en passant/an unstoppable passed pawn—plus noisy near-best moves, making the unifying theme 'threw away the clean win in a winning endgame' rather than any one tactic.

408.label: Top boards are uniformly missed winning knight forks (Nxc2+/Nxc7+/Nxf3+ against an uncastled central king, often netting the queen) where a quiet developing move let the king escape; medium keeps the knight-fork core but broadens to any squandered winning tactic — queen grabs, loose-piece shots, and capture sequences — with a few drifting toward outright positional/hung-piece errors.

419.label: Top boards consistently relocate a MINOR piece (bishop ~5/10, knight ~3/10) to a square where it either hangs to a short tactic (Be3, Nd4, Nxg5, Bb3) or goes passive/overextended (Bc6, b6, Bxe4, Na5); medium boards blur to ANY piece type — queen (Qh5, Qf4), king (Kf8, Kf2), or pawn (g3, d6, f5, h5) — dumped onto a losing or weakening square, keeping the shared theme of a piece sent to a bad square but losing the clean minor-piece/material-hang signal.

423.label: Top: a safe/routine move skips a forcing winning knight fork, almost always Nb5/Nd5→Nc7+/Nb6+ (or Ne3+) winning the king+rook exchange (one outlier is a Bxb1 combo); medium blurs to other missed knight tactics — Nxf2, Nf3+, Nd4, Ng4 — that fork or hit the queen/pawns rather than the c7/b6 fork specifically.

424.label: Top boards are almost all queen moves that desert a critical defensive square — leaving g2/b2/f2, a hanging bishop, or the king unprotected and losing material or getting mated; medium keeps the same 'piece abandons defense → gets punished' core but broadens the moved piece beyond the queen (castling into an unaddressed pin, a knight vacating a key defensive square, a wrong-piece/rook capture) that likewise hangs material.

425.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a king or pawn move mishandles the structure—wrong move order, locking the position, releasing tension, or skipping a key (often en-passant) capture—squandering the draw or worsening the loss; medium broadens to rook/knight/bishop endgames where a king/pawn move similarly damages the position by losing tempo, walking into checks, allowing tactics, or trading into an inferior endgame.

421.label: Top: hangs own material (piece/exchange) by declining the forced open-file rook trade (Rxa8/Rxc8/Rxc1) and allowing an invasion or fork in the refutation; medium keeps the same skipped-rook-exchange theme but blurs in direction, often just dropping a winning/drawn position (missed win) rather than always hanging a piece.

422.label: Top boards: in a losing/drawn position an over-ambitious capture or check (often a rook) hangs a piece to an immediate tactic (fork, skewer, undefended capture); at medium the pattern blurs to any aggressive king/rook/knight move that abandons a defensive duty or wastes tempo, losing material over the next 2-3 moves rather than at once—no single recurring piece or motif.

430.label: Top: a quiet/non-forcing materially-safe move throws away a short, clean forced mate against an exposed enemy king; medium broadens to longer forced mates and decisive king-attacks/promotions that are missed either entirely or via near-right execution slips (wrong move-order, wrong check square, wrong capture/discovery target), with one outlier being an actual hang of the attacking piece.
