420.label: Top boards consistently skip a clean forcing win — a decisive check or capture (Qxf1, Bg5+, Qh2+, Rd2+) — in favor of a greedy grab, passive king move, or purposeless check; medium blurs this into squandering any winning/equal position by replacing the single critical move (often now a quiet king-centralization or prophylactic only-move rather than a forcing shot) with a passive, greedy, or tempo-wasting one, frequently walking into mate or material loss.

429.label: Top boards constantly skip an obvious free capture of an undefended enemy major piece (peaking on a hanging queen, also rooks) via a passive king/quiet move; medium blurs to missed rook captures plus broader winning-position squanders like greedy pawn-grabs, wrong-piece moves, and tempo losses.

431.label: Top boards are all opening failures to play the resolving central pawn capture/break (...dxe5, ...dxe4, ...d5, cxd5/cxb5), choosing a passive developing move and squandering a won/equal position; medium broadens to any unresolved pawn-tension capture (kingside/flank f4-g4-h6 breaks, later in the opening) and occasionally to a hung minor piece.

427.label: Player blows a won (or drawn) position by hanging their own material—top boards consistently dump the QUEEN (or another major piece) on a tempting check/capture or a 'no-look' pass instead of the simple win, while medium blurs to a minor piece, e.g. an unsound knight fork (Nc2+) that just gets taken; piece type varies and one board (#4) isn't actually a blunder.

432.label: Top boards are losing/lost endgames where a passive KING move (or occasional pawn push) wastes the one critical tempo—skipping the urgent capture (Kxb4, Kxb3, bxc4, Nxb5, Kxf6) or defense—and lets White promote or mate; medium blurs to pawn and bishop tempo-wasters in drawn or merely-worse positions that just let the opponent consolidate or queen.

436.label: Top boards are queen checks in won positions where a quiet capture of a hanging piece or a faster forced mate was the cleaner win (though ~4/10 are actually 0cp best-move checks); medium blurs to rook/knight/pawn checks with smaller cp losses (tempo-wasting or fork-instead-of-bigger-capture), so the feature really tracks 'delivers a check in a winning position' more than a clean blunder.

438.label: Top boards are uniformly unsound bishop sacrifices on f7/f2 (Bxf7+/Bxf2+) that drop a full piece for a pawn or two with no attack; medium blurs the piece/method—adding knight sacrifices on f2 and a pawn push (f6) that traps the e4 knight—but every case hangs a minor piece in the opening for no compensation.

426.label: Top: in the opening the player attacks a hanging enemy piece (knight/bishop) with a pawn or developing move instead of the free queen capture (Qxd5/Qxg4), letting it escape from a winning position; medium blurs away from this clean 'missed free Qx-take' signal into later-phase material misplays — sometimes a missed non-queen capture, but often the opposite direction (moving a piece onto a square where it's taken, or a king-safety/tempo error), so direction is mixed between 'missed' and 'hangs'.

433.label: Top: queen greedily snatches a b2/d4 pawn while underdeveloped and is trapped or loses more material to tactics (Rb1/Nb5, Bxc6+, Nc7+); medium blurs the grabbing piece (bishop Bxe4/Bxc2, even Kxf1) and target (pawn→minor piece) plus queen sorties that abandon a defender, all refuted by traps, forks, skewers, or mating attacks.

434.label: TOP is a slow flank pawn push (a4/b3/h3/a3) that fails to challenge Black's dominant rook on the 2nd/7th rank, squandering the edge and often dropping material a few moves later; MEDIUM keeps the passive/non-confronting move theme but blurs the target — sometimes still an active rook (open file, back-rank, doubling) but also king moves, knight retreats or queen swaps that ignore forks, mate threats, or winning technique.

440.label: Top boards are direct material hangs—the player's own queen, rook, knight, or pawn captured within a move or two of the refutation; medium boards blur this into king-safety/walk-into-mate blunders plus a few pure missed wins/draws, so the constant is 'critical move throws away a winning/drawn game (usually hanging own material)' while the piece and exact mechanism vary.

437.label: Top: the queen is parked on a fully open diagonal and grabbed for free by a bishop (clean queen-for-bishop, ~6pts); medium keeps the bishop-takes-queen-on-a-diagonal motif but broadens to lines the move itself opens (pawn pushes, capture-order slips, discovered attacks) and to queen-for-rook trades and a mating-net capture.

435.label: Top boards consistently hang a rook—usually delivering a check—to an enemy bishop that captures (often blocking the check) in an already-lost/difficult endgame; medium blurs to broader lost-endgame material blunders where a pawn advance or capture loses pawns (pawn- and bishop-endgame errors) rather than specifically a rook to a bishop, with two top boards being missed captures and one a false positive.

439.label: Top: passive queen (occasionally rook) moves in winning positions that skip a forcing material-winning capture/tactic (Qxb2, Qxf7#, Qxe6+); medium keeps the 'only-move squandered' theme but blurs the piece to knight/king/rook/pawn and broadens into ignored king-safety, positional drift, and a few that hang material.

442.label: Top: while already winning, plays a quiet move (usually a king step) instead of grabbing a hanging/undefended enemy piece—overwhelmingly the queen—letting the free material and the win slip; medium blurs toward missing winning shots more broadly (forks, exchange-winning captures) and inferior/positional moves that squander a clear advantage rather than a literal free queen-grab.

443.label: Top: a knight/bishop capture of a rook or queen grabs material while skipping a forced mate-in-1-or-2 (the captured-from piece was the linchpin of the mating net); medium: still a tempting material grab/forcing capture, but the missed continuation blurs from clean forced mate to any decisively stronger win (a bigger attack, more material, or a longer forced mate), with a couple of non-capturing tempo-wasters mixed in.

441.label: Top boards consistently swap a forcing CHECK (usually ...Rd2+ / Re7+ / Rxe7+ types) that wins material or holds a winning edge for a slow natural piece move; medium keeps the same slow-move habit but the skipped precise continuation broadens beyond checks to pawn breaks (d5, h6), active rook placement (Rh8, Rc2) or restraint (Qa4) — and the outcome splits ~50/50 between merely squandering the advantage (single-ply material-safe) and walking into a multi-move refutation that drops a pawn or piece.

445.label: Top: an aimless, non-saving king walk in a drawn rook endgame leaves the rook en prise to immediate capture (e.g. Kxh2); medium: broadens to king moves that lose a bishop or pawn or burn the only drawing tempo, dropping material over the next 2-3 moves rather than instantly.

428.label: Top: in the Qb3/Bc4-vs-Qb6/Bc5 queen-bishop battery, players mostly hang queen/minor/the knight itself by mishandling the c3-knight tension (b3, e3, Qd2) or miss the winning Na4/Na5 double-attack — the decisive piece is always the battery knight; medium keeps the battery/knight theme but the direction blurs toward missed wins and broadens to varied knight forks (Nf4, Nh5-g3, Nc3, Nxb5) and tempo-losing moves in similar opening structures.

452.label: Top: queen/rook captures or trades made to 'win material' or simplify, overlooking a recapture/zwischenzug that nets the material back or a transposition into a lost K+P endgame; medium blurs to knight trades and pawn pushes that likewise miss a winning tactic or walk into mate.

448.label: Top boards: a winning/clearly-better position is thrown away by an inferior move—most often an unnecessary capture/trade that frees the opponent's piece or releases tension (with occasional missed mate/fork, a move-order slip, and one true pawn hang); medium boards narrow to clearly unfavorable trades, typically surrendering a key bishop, that relieve a merely-better position.

453.label: Top boards consistently skip an immediate free capture of a hanging enemy piece—peaking on undefended bishops (Rxg8/Rxb8/Qxd6)—while still touching loose queens/rook; medium blurs to any hanging piece type (queen, rook, or bishop) left en prise as the player plays a routine developing or attacking move instead.

449.label: Top boards consistently miss/avoid the rook exchange-sac (most often Rxd4) that eliminates Black's centralized knight—sometimes then hanging material to that knight; medium broadens to general missed strong rook captures hitting bishops, rooks, or pawns (Rxd5/Rxe4/Rxf6/Rxe6/Rxc4), with the fuzzy edge slipping into ordinary missed-conversion moves.

444.label: Top boards are clearly winning middlegames where a concrete forcing win (forced mate, royal fork, or intermediate check) is passed up for a slow/greedy passive move that squanders the advantage; at medium the edge is only modest (better/equal) and the 'squandering' blurs from a clean missed forcing tactic into general positional drift and outright piece-hanging.

447.label: Top: in a winning rook endgame the player gives a check or grabs a pawn with the rook and the enemy king simply recaptures, hanging the whole rook for a pawn (twice for the exchange); medium keeps the rook-for-pawn hang but blurs to include tempo-losing checks (e.g. Re1+) that squander the win even without dropping material.

454.label: Top boards are won endgames where White delays immediate promotion with a tempo-wasting check, king move, or pawn push (usually 0–16cp, no material lost); medium broadens to any winning position where the cleanest conversion is skipped — slower than a forced mate, missing a winning fork/tactic, or declining a clean simplification — occasionally even squandering the forced win or walking into mate.

450.label: Top: in a won endgame the player moves a unit into a simple one-move capture, hanging a major piece (queen/rook on 1,3,8) or a key pawn (h3/g5 on 2,4,6) and dropping into a draw; medium blurs to premature passed-pawn pushes and tempo-wasting advances (g6 blockaded, a5) that squander the win over several moves rather than via a clean single-ply capture (board 5 even shades into a missed promotion).

446.label: Top boards uniformly hang material on the a1-h8/h1-a8 long diagonal—almost always by skipping the freeing ...Bxg2/Bxg7 fianchetto trade or moving a piece that left the b2/g7 bishop and back-rank rook exposed; medium blurs the motif to hanging any piece or pawn by deserting its sole defender (and occasionally missing a win), on assorted lines rather than strictly the long diagonal.

455.label: Top boards are all queen checks that backfire—hanging the queen outright or via a forced trade into a lost endgame (with a couple costing a knight/tempo instead); medium broadens the checking piece to bishop and knight checks that hang the checker, plus some purely tempo-losing 'patzer checks'.

458.label: Top boards consistently promote a pawn to a queen that is captured for free on the next move in a king-and-pawn endgame (where underpromotion or a king move was the right call); medium boards keep the same premature-queening theme but blur in cases where the loss comes over a short refutation sequence or by ignoring a more urgent defense (e.g., allowing the opponent's own promotion/mate) rather than a single immediate free capture.

457.label: At the peak the move is almost always a tempting but unsound capture/sacrifice (Bxh7, Nxe5, Bxf3, exd5, Bxh2) that drops a piece, pawn, or even the queen by removing a defender; at medium it blurs to quiet retreats and piece relocations (Nd7, Qc7, Rb7, Na4) that hang material to forks/undefended pieces, plus some pawn pushes that instead crack the king open.

456.label: Top: in a lost/difficult middlegame a passive non-forcing move (often a wrong-wing pawn push) skips the single critical resource—a saving capture (exf6), counterplay (bxa3), or king defense—most often allowing forced mate by removing a king guardian or dropping material; medium blurs to king moves that walk into mate and direct material-losing/greedy captures plus a few near-equal positional/endgame omissions, so neither error type nor piece dominates.

459.label: At peak activation the player ignores a fianchettoed/diagonal bishop attacking a corner rook and plays elsewhere, dropping the exchange or whole rook for nothing; at medium activation the motif blurs — the ignored attacker becomes any piece (knight on the rook, a fork, a skewer) but the player still hangs material, usually the exchange/rook.

451.label: Top: in a won/drawn position the player overlooks the single best move, almost always a winning or saving capture (frequently winning the queen) with a lesser piece/pawn; medium broadens to missing the only good defensive king-retreat, positional, or endgame move.

461.chip: Hangs major piece taking passed pawn (often rook)
461.label: Top boards are rook captures of a passed/advanced pawn with check, immediately recaptured by the king for a single pawn in a won endgame; medium broadens to queen captures and bishop recaptures of the major piece, with the constant being a reflexive major-piece grab of a dangerous passer that surrenders the whole piece.

460.label: Top: an inferior rook move that skips the engine's rook-doubling / seventh-rank (or second-rank) maneuver, with the result split ~50/50 between outright hanging material (back-rank/mate, loose pawn or exchange over 2-3 moves) and merely forfeiting the stronger rook plan; medium blurs the constant rook focus to other pieces (king, queen, pawn, castling) that likewise abandon the doubling/best plan, so direction (Hangs vs Missed) needs human confirmation.

462.label: At the peak the squandering move is almost always a queen move that abandons a decisive continuation in a winning/better position (queen the moved or key piece in ~9/10); at medium the central piece blurs to rooks/king/knight and the refutation is genuinely mixed between missed wins (Qxd4, Rc1, Rxe7) and self-inflicted losses (king-weakening that allows mate, hung pieces, queen-for-rook trades), so no single 'Missed X'/'Hangs X' direction holds.

465.label: Top boards are all forced back-rank mates delivered by a rook check on the open/8th rank; medium broadens to queen-delivered back-rank mates and back-rank tactics that win heavy material (occasionally even allowing the opponent's own back-rank mate).

464.label: At the peak, a materially-safe passive/retreating move overlooks a winning or game-saving forcing check (Re8+, Rxg7+, Rb8+, Rd1+, Rg3+, h4+); at medium it broadens to skipping the engine's best continuation generally—captures (dxe4), defensive king moves (Kd3, Kf4-to-survive), or quiet positional improvements (Bd6, f3)—often not a check.

469.label: Top boards are constant: an opening pawn move that opens the e8-h5/h4-e1 diagonal and lets a queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+) fork king and rook for material; medium blurs to opening moves that hang a piece by other means—leaving a knight simply en prise (exf6/exf3) or a bishop to a fork—plus a couple of purely positional/missed-win outliers.

472.label: Top boards are queen moves in winning endgames that skip the cleanest forcing win — a forced mate or stopping/blockading a passed pawn before promotion (material stays safe); medium blurs the piece to rook/knight conversion moves and dilutes severity, with several near-0cp 'inaccuracies' that aren't true blunders at all.

468.label: Top: a queen lands on the open d-file (d4/d5), usually snatching a knight, and is simply recaptured for a minor piece; medium keeps the 'grab-then-lose-the-queen' theme but broadens beyond the d-file to other squares (g4/f3) and other recapture mechanisms (diagonal bishop, Nxc7+ fork), with a couple of cases blurring into a knight loss or a bad forced queen trade.

471.label: Top boards consistently leave an own bishop undefended on an open diagonal for a free capture (either moving the bishop itself onto a loose square or vacating its defender); medium blurs the piece type to any hung unit — knights, the exchange/rook, and squares that lose their defender when a pawn or piece moves — with one or two outliers that are positional or a greedy missed-mate rather than a clean hang.

463.label: Top boards are uniformly h-pawn captures (hxg4/hxg5) that grab a piece but rip open the h-file straight at one's own castled king, inviting a crushing attack; medium blurs to other greedy captures and pawn/king moves that open files (a-file, kingside) or remove the king's shelter, exposing it to a decisive assault.

470.label: Top boards make a plausible-but-irrelevant move (king flee, queen shuffle, pawn push, capture) that ignores an immediate mating attack and self-walks into forced mate; medium broadens to ignoring any decisive threat, most often self-inflicting material loss via hanging piece, fork, or pin.

473.chip: Abandons defensive square, allows mate (often rook)
473.label: Top: a rook (occasionally bishop/knight) vacates a back-rank/escape/defender square, self-exposing the king for forced mate; medium keeps the same self-exposure motif but broadens the moved piece (pawns, king) and softens from forced mate to merely losing material/tempo.

478.label: Top positions leave a piece en prise in the endgame—overwhelmingly a bishop hung to the enemy king/knight/rook (one knight and rook case, one losing bishop trade); medium positions keep the same hang-a-piece theme but blur the piece toward knights and rooks (plus a few material-losing trades/positional slips), all turning a tenable endgame into a lost one.

411.label: In every position the player ignores the forced Qxd8+/Qxd1+ queen exchange WITH CHECK on the open d-file, instead developing/grabbing/retreating a minor piece; at the top this reliably hangs material (a knight or pawn, or the exchange via a Qxd8+/Kxd8/Nxf7+ fork) or strips the king of castling, whereas medium boards blur toward pure tempo/positional damage (knight stranded on the rim, bishop shuffling) and one case where the forcing resource isn't even the queen trade (Nxf6+).

475.label: Top: king strays out of the passed pawn's 'square' (or makes the wrong capture/tempo move) in K+P endgames, losing the promotion race and flipping a won game to lost; medium broadens to wrong-tempo pawn pushes, opposition losses, and a few near-equal false positives where the played move was actually fine.

485.label: Top: the queen passes up capturing an undefended back-rank rook WITH CHECK (usually a forced mate) in favor of a materially-safe but vastly inferior move; medium keeps the same missed winning queen-takes-undefended-rook but the check/forced-mate blurs (no-check captures like Qxh8/Qxb1, or self-blocked diagonal preventing Qxa8+).

476.label: Top boards squander a clearly winning position by playing an inferior trade, grab, or check instead of the clear winning continuation (usually a material-winning capture like Qxc7/Bxa5/Qxb1+); medium blurs the 'winning move' to forced mates, simplifications, or king-safety moves, while a couple of boards instead hang the player's own piece and one is not actually a mistake.

477.label: In an already-lost middlegame, top boards are clean piece sacrifices/hangs — knight, bishop, rook or queen, often the last defender — given up for a single pawn or an empty check; medium blurs into king-weakening pawn pushes (g4/g5/g6/h6) and defender-removing moves that don't just lose material but allow an immediate forced mate.

479.label: Top boards are slow king moves that delay an immediate winning/drawing promotion in a pawn race (often letting the opponent promote with check off the badly-placed king); medium blurs into other imprecise, materially-safe endgame moves—king, rook, or bishop—that skip the one precise active move (immediate promotion, correct capture order, or rook activation).

466.label: Top: a natural active rook/queen move squanders a winning middlegame by missing the single saving move, almost always a quiet queen reposition (Qh2/Qa4/Qe1/Qh3+) that sustains the attack; medium keeps the 'only-move-in-a-won-position' frame but blurs the save to rook/bishop/king moves and to declining a queen trade, with ~3/10 outright hanging material.

482.label: At the peak every move is a king advance/centralization (refusing the only safe retreat like Kh7) that walks straight into a forced checkmate; at medium the same king-into-danger theme persists but blurs from pure mate to king moves that merely expose the monarch and drop decisive material (Kc5, Bc7, Kd6), and occasionally non-king moves that strip the king's shelter.

484.label: Top boards are king-and-pawn endgames where a pawn push or suboptimal king advance loses a tempo (occasionally throwing the win to a draw, as in boards 1 and 10), while medium boards blur into rook and other endgames with king-misplacement or tempo loss—but with many 0cp non-mistakes and only minor inaccuracies, making this a mixed 'won-endgame king imprecision' detector rather than a clean blunder finder.

483.chip: Misroutes king in pawn endgame (often passer)
483.label: Top boards are passed-pawn races where the king goes to the wrong square and fails to stop/escort the passer (peak constant: passer escort, many with near-zero cp loss in already-lost positions); medium blurs to general king-and-pawn endgames where the king simply heads the wrong direction (toward a pawn that runs away, or onto a square allowing promotion with check).

474.label: Top boards are tempting forcing checks (queen ~52% / rook ~48%, played 100%) that squander a forced mate or clearly winning position—usually hanging or trading the checking piece itself (Qxf1, Qxa8, Qxb1) or letting a single blocking move (Re1/Rd1/Ng1) erase the win; medium broadens to knight-fork checks (Nf2+) that expose a back-rank rook, queen-trade checks while down material, and even some sound/0cp checks, blurring between truly hung material and merely missed conversions.

489.label: Top boards constantly miss the one precise tactical shot that wins or traps the opponent's QUEEN (pin/deflection/skewer/alignment); medium blurs the target outward to winning the exchange, forcing a favorable queen trade, or exploiting a back-rank/mate threat, and in both tiers a couple boards instead simply hang the player's OWN piece (Kd8, Bg4, h3-rook, Bxd7), so the direction is mixed (mostly safe-but-missed-win, occasionally self-hang).

493.label: Top boards consistently miss a forcing QUEEN check (winning attack/mate or saving perpetual) in safe/winning endgames, choosing a quiet pawn push or greedy capture that hands over the decisive tempo; medium boards blur the constant—broadening to any tempo-wasting quiet move (flank pawn push, rook leaving an open file) that surrenders the initiative without necessarily skipping an actual check.

492.label: Top boards consistently overlook a single forcing check/fork that wins material outright (Be6+, Ra7+, Bf5+, Be3+) while playing a slow routine move; medium broadens to missed non-check captures (Bxb7), missed mates, premature/wrong-order checks, and even quiet winning resources or positional pawn breaks — but always squandering a clearly winning position.

481.label: Top: a passive/tempo-wasting move (piece retreat or flank pawn push) leaves the e4/e5 pawn tension unresolved, letting the near-constant ...fxe5/...fxe4 break win material or rip open lines toward the king; medium blurs to other mishandled tensions and wrong capture-timing (dxe5/c5/cxd5/hxg5, omitted exf4), sometimes punished by king attacks, forks, or hanging pieces rather than a clean central pawn break.

491.label: Top: a clearly winning (sometimes equal) position is thrown away by a tempting flashy check / greedy-or-lesser capture / pawn push instead of the clean material-winning move — typically leaving a freely hanging enemy piece uncaptured and hanging own material within 1-3 moves; medium broadens the same 'squander the advantage' theme to quieter tempo-losing or positional moves (castling, slow pawn/knight development, misplaced queen) that forfeit the edge without an immediate hang.

490.label: At the peak it's king/queen checks/centralizations in already-won endgames that give an inferior continuation—throwing away the forced win (Qb4+→draw) or slowing the mate; at medium it blurs into rook-endgame technique slips (failing to cut off, wrong file) plus a hung exchange, and several flagged moves are actually optimal, so no single clean error recurs.

486.label: Top: in a clearly winning middlegame the player makes a quiet/positional move and overlooks a one-move pawn capture that wins the hanging enemy queen; medium blurs this — the missed grab is sometimes a rook instead of the queen, and some boards flip direction, where a natural pawn push attacking an enemy piece itself walks into the opponent's refuting tactic (fork/exchange sac) and squanders the advantage.

494.label: Top: in losing positions the player declines a forced Bxd8/Bxe8 bishop-takes-queen trade, repositioning the queen and leaving the bishop en prise; medium broadens to hanging any piece (queen, knight, or bishop) by moving it onto an attacked square instead of making the saving capture.

467.label: Top: a queen move (often a greedy capture) that ignores a forced mate on the player's own king; medium broadens to rook/knight/pawn moves and shifts from immediate mate to squandering a winning attack or missing the only decisive forcing line.

480.label: Top boards hang concrete material—piece, exchange, or pawn—to an immediate or short (2-3 move) tactic (overloaded defender, hanging piece, fork); medium keeps some clean piece-hangs (Bxc6, Bxg5, c2+ winning the queen) but blurs into tempo-loss and king-safety/positional blunders that squander a winning advantage with non-material refutations.

496.label: Top: queen (sometimes rook) snatches a pawn—usually a2—abandoning a forced mate while staying materially safe; medium keeps the 'squander a forced win' core but broadens the distracting move beyond pawn-grabs to king moves, slower mating captures, and wrong-pawn pushes, occasionally even hanging material to a tactic (skewer/fork).

495.label: Top boards are rook endgames where a greedy pawn-grab deserts a decisive passed pawn (its support square or promotion), throwing away the won game; medium keeps the 'squandered winning endgame' core but broadens to other pieces (queen, knight) and other failure modes—tempo loss, premature pushes, abandoned blockades/files, and even a missed mate or material-winning shot.

500.label: Top: a premature CENTRAL pawn break (d5/e4/f4/f5/c5) that demolishes the player's own center/pawn chain and loses a pawn by force; medium keeps the self-undermining pawn push but broadens to queenside flank advances (b3/b4/b5) and the forfeited material widens from a pawn to a piece or the exchange.

487.label: At the peak the move botches a forcing king-side MATE—most often self-inflicted by f3 (or Bd3/Qe1) collapsing the king's shelter and walking into Bh2+/Qh1#-type sequences, occasionally an offensive missed forced mate; medium blurs to broader king-attack tactics (pins, exchange-winning shots, mate played a tempo too early) and a couple of non-king tactical/positional slips, with direction genuinely split between getting mated and missing the win.

499.label: Top boards are pure pawn/passed-pawn endgames where a passive king (or bishop) move skips the one resolving pawn capture/exchange and hands the opponent a decisive passed pawn; medium keeps the 'quiet move instead of the needed capture' core but blurs into middlegame king-safety and capture-tension positions where the passive move instead opens lines, hangs a piece, or walks into mate.

502.label: Top boards are all winning positions where a clear decisive/forcing move (capture, fork, breakthrough) is skipped for a quiet/routine one—about half then hang material in the multi-move refutation (no consistent piece: queen/exchange/pawn/knight) and the rest are pure missed shots; medium keeps the 'threw away the win' core but blurs into quiet positional drift and even an unsound sacrifice rather than crisp tactical misses.

488.label: At peak, a quiet pawn/king/developing move replaces the one required bishop move — either a winning capture (Bxb5/Bxb4) or a forced defensive trade (Bxd5/Bxg5); medium keeps the same 'skip the bishop capture' theme (Bxg4, Bxe7, Bxd6, Bxc5, Bxg5) but blurs into occasional non-bishop tactics (Rxe3, knight forks), with direction split between missing a win and hanging material over the refutation.

497.label: Top boards are greedy captures (Bxf6/Nxc3/Nxe6) that overlook an immediate refutation and hang the queen or walk straight into mate (Qxf7#, Qxh2#); medium keeps the same 'ignore the refutation' theme but blurs the trigger (now including pawn pushes like e5/e6/f5, not just captures) and the loss (dropping a rook, exchange, or knight—or still getting mated—rather than always the queen).

503.label: At the peak, the player throws away a forced back-rank checkmate (typically a queen-sacrifice deflection) by grabbing a natural capture or rook trade instead; at medium it blurs into missing other forced tactical wins (knight forks, discovered checks) and greedy captures that simplify away or outright hang the decisive blow — with one near-false-positive where the capture was actually best.

501.label: Top boards uniformly skip an immediately available knight capture that wins material—almost always Nx winning the exchange (knight takes rook)—by instead grabbing a pawn, giving a check, or playing a slow move that lets the attacked piece escape; medium broadens to missing winning captures/tactics in general, where the saving piece isn't always a knight and the gain isn't always the exchange (full piece, queen, defender removal), and one case even hangs the exchange to the opponent's knight.

509.label: Top: plays a safe but slow endgame move, missing a forcing check—almost always a knight fork (Nf4+/Nd6+/Nc2+)—that wins a rook or queen; medium broadens to other forcing checks winning material (rook skewers, bishop/rook checks) and occasional missed mate/trade conversions.

505.label: Top: a critical king defender (or the king itself) is removed, misplaced, or blocks the king's escape, forcing checkmate or a decisive king attack; medium keeps the defender-abandonment/line-opening idea but blurs toward simply losing material (hung bishop/knight, even an endgame rook misstep) rather than always forcing mate.

507.label: Top: a passive king/pawn/queen move skips a forced mate that is almost always an immediate mating queen check (Qg4#, Qc1#, Qb7+→mate); medium broadens to missing the precise winning check — rook mate (Rh7#), a slower/faster forced mate, or just the best winning queen check rather than an outright mate-in-one (with the odd outlier giving up material).

514.label: Top boards throw away an outright forced mate (almost always available via a forcing check) by playing a materially-safe but slow/greedy move; medium boards keep a clearly winning position but the move merely skips the most forcing path — prolonging the mate or missing a faster tactical/check finish rather than discarding the win entirely.

511.label: Top boards consistently hang a rook — usually by moving/capturing it onto a square where it's freely taken (often via a greedy capture or hollow check) — while medium boards blur to hanging knights and other minor pieces, with a few cases that instead surrender a winning advantage through a needless queen trade or missed tactic.

512.label: Top boards squander a concrete forced mate (mate-in-N) via a king walk, quiet move, or greedy capture instead of the forcing line; medium broadens to forfeiting a decisive winning advantage—missing the one forcing continuation that wins major material or a slower mate, sometimes letting own material hang in the refutation.

498.label: Top: in an endgame the player grabs a (dangerous) passed pawn with a rook—also bishop or queen—and allows an immediate clean recapture, losing the piece for the pawn (often turning a win/draw into a lost or insufficient-material position); medium broadens to non-passed pawns, more piece types (knight/king), and to multi-move refutations (deflection, zwischenzug, removed defender, or trade into a lost pawn ending) rather than a direct recapture.

506.label: Top boards are remarkably uniform: a slow, quiet non-forcing move (Rd7, Qc3, Rb1, Bd5) that overlooks a winning or drawing forcing check / back-rank sacrifice (Qd6+, Rc8+, Rd8+, Rf1+); medium blurs the direction—it adds missed forced mates via sacrifice (Rxg6+, Re8+, Rxf8+) but also slow moves that let the OPPONENT's forcing check/mate through (allowing Qd2+/Qd1#, Rh1#, Qc4+), plus a few flagged non-blunders, so 'missed forcing resource' is the constant while win-vs-self-harm is the variable.

510.label: Top: a strongly-posted knight moves directly onto a square an enemy piece covers and is captured free for a full piece (a couple just trade away the key knight); medium keeps the knight-loss theme but blurs to indirect/multi-move refutations (pins, forks), smaller pawn-only losses, knights left hanging by a non-knight move, and a few pure tempo/positional misplacements.

508.chip: Slow move hangs material (skips queen trade)
508.label: Top boards play a slow, non-forcing move that skips the available forced queen trade (Qxd1+/Qxd8+/Qxe2) and get punished by a multi-move tactic that wins material; medium broadens to any tempting slow/flashy move (a superficial check or rook lift) that skips the best forcing line, in one case merely missing a free capture/win rather than directly hanging material.

517.chip: Hangs rook on long diagonal (often delayed)
517.label: Top boards are tight: a fianchetto-style pawn push (g6/b6/b3/a3) clears a long diagonal so an enemy bishop grabs the undefended corner rook in one move (one case via queen); medium keeps the cleared-diagonal rook loss but blurs it—captures come delayed via a knight unmasking the bishop, the queen takes the rook, and it bleeds into adjacent diagonal-opening tactics (forks, pins, king exposure).

516.label: Top boards are clean self-inflicted material hangs from winning positions punished by a simple refutation (the hung unit varies—pawn/knight/bishop/rook—and twice the move walks into mate); medium boards blur to positional/tempo concessions that throw away the advantage without an outright material loss.

519.label: Top boards are uniformly unsound opening sacrifices or illusory forks—Bxf7+/Bxf2+ bishop sacs and Nc7+ 'royal forks' that the queen/king simply captures for a clean piece; medium broadens to other premature piece sorties that drop material in the opening (trapped bishop via Ba4, over-extended knights on e5/g5/f7), so the constant is 'loses own piece in the opening' while the specific Bxf7+ sac motif blurs into general premature-sortie material loss.

515.label: Top: a knight/bishop/rook (or the exchange) hangs to an immediate clean recapture or short tactic — typically a greedy capture or a miscalculated 'fork' onto a defended square; medium broadens to overextensions and backfiring pawn-grabs whose material loss only materializes over a multi-move refutation, with a few cases shading into positional/tempo concessions or even missed wins.

523.label: Top boards hang (or fatally expose) a developing minor piece—usually a bishop—to immediate free capture in a near-equal opening; medium keeps the hung-own-material core but broadens to dropping queens/rooks and to multi-move tactical refutations (forks, pins, discovered checks), occasionally past the opening.

521.label: At the peak the move overlooks a single loose piece — mostly self-inflicted by moving its defender or opening a line so the piece hangs, occasionally by failing to grab an en-prise enemy piece; medium positions broaden the same blind spot to forks, back-rank shots, and king-safety tactics that net the loose material.

522.label: Top boards are uniform queen retreats off d5 (Qd8/Qd7/Qa5/Qe6+) that skip the resolving 7...Bxf3, squandering near-equality and getting hit by the d5 break with tempo on the c6-knight; medium blurs the piece, broadening to other misplaced pieces (bishop sorties/retreats, a premature d6 pawn push, even a queen offside on a5) that lose tempo and squander an opening advantage, punished by central pawn breaks or tactics.

504.label: From a winning/favorable middlegame the player makes a tactically-refuted move that throws away the advantage; top boards almost always hang the QUEEN (twice a rook) to a one- or multi-move refutation, while medium broadens to hanging rooks AND minor pieces (plus greedy pawn-grabs, missed winning captures, and one drawing perpetual), making it genuinely mixed between 'hangs material' and 'squanders the win.'

520.label: Top boards are almost uniformly the queen-baiting ...Bg4/Bg5 (or symmetric) that drops a full piece to a zwischenzug knight check (Nxf6+/Nxf3+ then Qxg5/Qxg4) or simply hangs b7 to Qxb7; at medium the motif blurs into any overlooked forcing reply — hanging other pieces (Bxe5, Nc3, e5) or allowing a king-safety/back-rank mate.

531.label: Top boards consistently leave an own piece (knight, bishop, or rook) undefended where the enemy QUEEN snaps it for free, often with check (Qxd5/Qxb5/Qxa8+/Qxa1+); medium blurs the capturer to any attacker — pawn (exd5), rook (Rxc2), or knight fork — and even drifts into non-capturing drops of advantage (tempo loss, forced queen trade).

527.label: Top boards are uniformly rook checks that hang the rook for nothing—almost always snapped off by an enemy knight; medium broadens the same 'sees-a-check, gives-a-check' reflex to other aggressive checks (queen and even pawn) that drop material, with the capturing piece varying (bishop, king, pawn).

524.label: Top: in a won middlegame, pulls the queen (or bishop/rook) off a defensive square and allows a forced back-rank/king-safety mate (or misses a forced mate by playing a non-forcing/greedy move); medium: same squandering of a winning position but blurs from outright mate to simply hanging a piece (queen/bishop/knight) or pawn.

532.label: Top: in a winning position the player skips the decisive passed-pawn push/support, instead making a slow king/rook move or grabbing a lesser pawn; medium broadens to general mishandling of the passer — wrong blockading piece, breaking the pawn chain that backs it, or a tempo-wasting king move — sometimes hanging a pawn rather than purely missing the win.

529.label: Top boards uniformly leave/move a rook onto a square where an enemy minor piece (knight or bishop) grabs it free, blowing a winning endgame; medium keeps the hung-piece-in-a-won-position theme but broadens the dropped piece (bishop, even queen) and the capturer (including rook-takes-rook) across both endgame and middlegame.

530.label: Top: a quiet, non-forcing move that throws away a forced mate which should have been started with a rook check (overwhelmingly Ra7+/Rb7+ on the 7th/back rank, or Rxh7+ sacs); medium keeps the missed-forcing-check theme but broadens from strict mate to any decisive winning line (winning material, gaining tempo, or even holding a draw) and occasionally a non-rook check like Bxg3+.

526.label: Top boards are almost all self-inflicting moves from a winning position that walk into a forced checkmate (mostly king moves like Kh8/Kc1/Kh6, plus pawn/bishop moves opening mating lines); medium blurs the mechanism—still mate at the peak (a rook blocking the king's own escape square into Qf8#), but broadening to non-mating self-sabotage that merely hangs material or abandons a pawn/tempo, with one board a false positive (a 0-cp check).

528.label: Top boards are clean, decisive-material moments (SEE floor 100%, mostly rook endgames) where the player throws away a winning position either by hanging a piece/pawn (boards 2,4,7) or by skipping the one winning capture/promotion/tempo move (boards 1,3,6,10); medium blurs the same 'squandered win' theme into middlegame king-safety/positional errors that merely allow a tactic, plus near-zero-cp slips in already-lost positions — so it conflates hung-material and missed-win directions rather than detecting one clean piece or direction.

533.label: At peak activation, a knight is centralized to an undefended d4/d5 in the opening where the enemy queen simply captures it for free; at medium activation this broadens to hanging any piece (or pawn) by moving/removing its defender or abandoning a guarded square, captured most often by the queen but sometimes via another major piece or a fork.

535.label: Top: an aggressive queen sortie or rook invasion (Qe8+/Qc7/Qg4/Rd7) abandons a defender or steps into a refutation that wins back the player's own piece over 1-3 moves, the lost unit varying (knight/bishop/rook/exchange); medium blurs to other careless moves (bishop hangs, exposing king) plus ~2/10 that are positional drops or missed wins rather than outright hangs.

518.label: Top boards constantly walk into a refuting opponent pawn break/lever (e4, d4/d5, a5, c4, b4) that wins material or seizes decisive initiative; at medium the refuting instrument blurs to piece captures/retreats (Bxc4, Bxf3, Nd5, Rdc8) and the player's own error type widens (hung piece, missed tactical win, positional/king-safety slip).

525.label: Top: in already-lost positions the player declines the sole saving queen trade/capture with a king or queen move and is forced into checkmate (once just hanging the queen); medium: same lost-position theme but the spurned resource is any defensive move (and may be a rook move), and the punishment is heavy material loss or a collapsing eval rather than forced mate.

538.label: Top boards consistently skip a forcing queen-check sequence (Qh8+, Qc1+, Qb1+, Qa5+, Qd5#) that wins fastest in an already-won endgame; medium broadens to other forcing wins with non-queen pieces (king/pawn moves, deflections like e5+/c4+, faster mates), with a couple optimal moves and a couple hanging-piece refutations making the pattern mixed.

537.label: Top: opening pawn-pushes/developments (g6, c4, Bf5, Ne7…), usually tempo-grabs against the enemy queen, that open a line or undefend a square—letting White's queen win a rook or deliver Qxf7#; medium keeps the queen as punisher but broadens to non-tempo developing/middlegame moves that simply leave a pawn or piece hanging (Qxb2, Qxg2, Qxd3, Qxb7).

543.label: Top: king moves in pawn endgames that abandon the blockade/escort of the opponent's passed pawn (or capture the wrong way, removing the blocker), letting it run to promotion; medium broadens to other pieces (bishop/knight) leaving the blockade and tempo-wasting pawn/king moves that lose the king-race against the runner.

513.label: Top boards are constant: Black plays a slow opening move (flank pawn a6/b6/h6, early ...Qb6, or passive ...Be7/...Bd6) instead of the thematic ...d5/...e5 break, surrendering the center and the advantage; medium broadens to either color missing a central pawn break (d4/e5/d5) and into the early middlegame, plus two unrelated knight hangs (Nh5, Nd5).

534.label: Top boards consistently move or trade a piece off its critical defensive/blockading duty (usually a rook holding back a passer or guarding another piece), hanging own material or letting a pawn promote (with 2 pure missed wins—mate/fork); medium blurs this into greedy pawn-grabs, weakening pawn pushes, and natural developing moves that likewise desert a defensive role and drop material to a refutation (often an allowed fork).

544.label: Top boards uniformly decline a forced queen trade (Qxd4/Qxc5/Qxd5/Qxf7) and leave their own queen hanging with check or walk into mate; medium keeps the same 'declined-saving-trade' signature but blurs the loss to a hanging bishop/rook or a pure forced checkmate rather than a literal queen capture.

547.label: Top: a simplifying rook/queen capture trades cleanly into a lost-or-worse king-and-pawn endgame (recapture by king is even but positionally losing); medium broadens to greedy/undefended captures that outright lose material to a straight recapture or zwischenzug (queen for rook, hanging rook).

540.label: Top boards are consistently a bishop snapping off a centrally-posted enemy knight (Bxe4/e5/d4/d5), surrendering a key defensive piece or walking into a fork/zwischenzug that loses material; medium blurs to pawn (and other minor-piece) captures of central pawns/pieces that rip open files and diagonals toward an exposed king, collapsing into material loss—plus a couple of outliers (a missed-win capture and one non-capture).

549.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a single wrong king step surrenders the opposition/blockade and converts a dead draw (eval 0) into a forced mate; medium broadens to king tempo-losses around passed pawns and already-lost positions merely accelerated to mate (with a couple of stray pawn-push outliers).

539.label: Top boards are uniformly the skipped open-d-file queen exchange (Qxd1+/Qxd8+) in the opening—the player develops or pushes a pawn instead, losing castling rights or hanging the e4/e5 pawn (or g4-bishop) in the forced refutation; medium boards blur to other forcing queen trades (Qxd7+, Qxe7+, Qxf2+, usually with check) on varied squares with mixed payoffs (winning the exchange/a piece, declining an unsound Bxf7+, or being punished by the opponent's own Qxd1+ zwischenzug), plus a few off-theme cases (trapped bishop after b4, premature Bxf6).

552.label: Top boards are winning positions where the player skips a free hanging queen (or rook) capture, playing a quiet developing/repositioning move instead; medium blurs to missed bishop/rook captures plus a few pure self-hangs and a missed forced mate, so direction is mostly 'missed win' but mixed.

551.label: Top boards uniformly hang a rook with a tempting check or capture (Rd8+/Rxe2+/Rxg2+) that nets nothing; medium broadens to quieter greedy rook grabs and infiltrations (Rxc6, Rxa5, Rc1) plus the occasional knight hang or passive move that drops material.

541.label: Top boards are constant: a slow/greedy non-forcing move (pawn push, decentralizing/greedy queen move, self-blocking rook) ignores a decisive threat and is punished by forced mate or an outright hung queen, with the queen central as mater or victim; medium boards keep the same core—skipping a required forcing queen check/defense (intermezzo, perpetual, recapture-with-check)—but the outcome blurs from mate/hung-queen to ordinary material loss or a squandered win/draw.

542.label: Top boards are consistently opening moves that fail to contest the center, punished by a central pawn break (d4/d5/e4) that seizes space or wins material; medium blurs to other piece losses (rim-knight traps via b4, undefended-piece forks, g3 pins) and missed central/kingside breaks.

548.label: Top: a clean hang of an own piece—often the knight itself—by removing its defender or stepping into a direct capture/tactic; medium blurs into broader advantage loss (positional misplacement, tempo-wasting knight moves, even missed tactics), with a knight featuring in nearly every position even when it isn't the piece lost.

546.label: Top boards are purposeless rook moves to a passive square (a-file, h1, or 7th rank) that squander a tempo and abandon the critical defensive/active task in rook endgames; medium broadens to other passive piece placements—including queen retreats to flank squares (Qh1/Qa7/Qb7) and sometimes middlegame positions—that similarly waste tempo or vacate defense, with a few cases crossing into outright hanging material or a missed capture.

557.label: Top boards consistently skip a forced checkmate or decisive king attack—usually grabbing a pawn instead of delivering the queen check that mates; medium boards broaden to missing any decisive winning tactic (knight forks, deflecting checks, material-winning sequences) where the played move is materially safe but throws away the forced win rather than necessarily a mate.

558.label: Top boards are pure endgame moves that throw away a winning or drawing position through tempo loss—wrong move-order, aimless checks, or a losing trade/liquidation; medium blurs the mechanism to include king misplacement, blocked passers, and missed tactics (forks, back-rank mates), with some examples drifting out of the endgame entirely.

553.label: Top boards are near-uniform Bxf7+ Greek-Gift bishop sacrifices that hang a piece on a check with no real follow-up (simple Qxf3/bxc3 recapture was correct); medium blurs to other checking pieces and squares (Nb5+, Bh7+, Re1+, even h1=N+) plus a couple of non-check tempo-grabs, but the constant is a flashy tempo/attack check that drops material when a quiet recapture won.

536.label: Top: pure king-and-pawn endgames where the king marches to the wrong side to grab a peripheral pawn, abandoning the critical zone and turning win→draw or draw→loss; medium broadens to general endgame mistiming—tempo-losing king/rim moves plus wrong pawn pushes and even a knight move that abandon the key task across rook/bishop/knight endgames.

550.label: Top: in a lost position, a reflexive rook check that hands the rook over outright (Kxrook → forced mate, back-rank/2nd-rank net); medium broadens to rook checks that merely waste a tempo and centralize the enemy king, trade the rook for a pawn, or even a defender (queen) abandoning the back rank — all just accelerating the loss.

559.label: Top boards almost uniformly pass up a decisive FORCING rook continuation—a rook check/mate-in-one or seventh-rank rook penetration winning a piece—in favor of a slow non-forcing move; medium boards keep the 'skipped a concrete forcing win' core but blur the executing piece (adding bishop/knight tactics like Bxg5 or Nd8/Rc6) and soften into general tempo/positional misses, with a minority of boards instead hanging the player's own knight/pawn rather than missing a win.

555.label: Top boards are pure pawn-endgame tempo errors—premature pawn pushes (c4/a5/g6/f5) or king moves that block the king or lose a tempo, dropping eval with no material hung (instead of centralizing or timing a break); medium keeps the same mistimed king/pawn move but blurs the context out to rook endgames, passed-pawn races and king-safety positions, with several flagged moves actually being 0cp non-mistakes.

562.label: Top boards are constant: from a winning/critical position a tempting capture or queen/knight centralization is met by a forced refutation that wins material (the queen most often the piece lost or misplaced); at medium it blurs—still a tempting inferior move, but the punishment shifts toward pure tempo loss letting the opponent castle/consolidate, plus endgame/king-safety technique slips that merely throw away the edge rather than dropping a piece.

556.label: Top boards are uniformly rook checks in a winning endgame that squander tempo and let the enemy king centralize/escape instead of pushing the passed pawn or promoting; medium broadens to checks by other pieces (queen Qa8+, bishop Bh2+) and checks that even skip a concrete tactic (missed rook fork), while also catching several borderline cases where the check is actually the best move (false positives).

554.label: Top boards are razor-consistent: White's quiet Be3 vacates c1 and hangs the b2 pawn to the b6 queen (the resolving dxc5 was needed); medium blurs to other non-resolving developing moves that hang varied material — pawns or pieces via forks, pins, or structural collapse — instead of the central-tension-breaking capture.

561.label: Top boards are uniform: a missed crushing queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+) exploiting the open e1-h4/e8-h5 diagonal left by a missing f-pawn in the opening, all in already-winning positions; medium boards blur the motif to other missed/allowed king-safety shots (allowing or skipping Qh5+) and further out to entirely different missed wins—trapped/hanging-piece tactics, tempo-losing retreats, and positional/endgame conversions—so the constant is 'skipped the winning continuation in a better position' while the specific queen-check-on-open-diagonal signature dissolves.

560.label: Top: a queen move that offers/initiates a queen trade or challenges the enemy queen backfires, hanging material to a follow-up tactic (often a knight fork) or even allowing mate; medium blurs this to include greedy queen captures/grabs and other backfiring queen moves refuted by forks, deflections, hanging-piece tactics, or mating attacks (with a few that merely surrender counterplay or miss a stronger capture).

567.label: Top: in a won opening the player skips an immediate one-move capture of a free, en-prise enemy QUEEN, playing a quiet developing/pawn move instead; medium broadens the hanging target to include a minor piece (a free bishop), with a couple of non-fitting outliers (a sound check and an allowed knight fork).

565.label: Top boards uniformly skip the centralizing capture (Nxd4/Nxd5) that eliminates White's dominant knight and wins material in an already-winning position; medium broadens to missing other key minor-piece captures (e.g., Bxf3) or the right winning capture entirely, occasionally even hanging a piece instead.

568.label: Top: in winning openings plays a natural developing/castling move and misses the crushing Qd5 queen-centralization that double-attacks f7; medium keeps the 'superior side skips a forcing win' theme but broadens the missed blow to other tactics (knight forks like Nxc7+/Nxf7, Bxf2+ sacs, queen double-attacks) across phases, with a few cases outright dropping material.

563.label: Top: a natural/aggressive move hangs concrete material to a forcing refutation—back-rank, knight/pawn fork, discovered check, or abandoning a key defender/blockader; medium blurs this to also allowing forced mates (king-safety walks) and includes ~2 missed-win cases rather than true hangs.

566.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed material-winning queen pawn-grab (almost always Qxg2, also Qxb7/Qxg7) passed up for a quiet developing/castling move; medium broadens the capture target to other loose pieces/pawns (Qxc6, Qxa8 rook, Qxb2) but also mixes in several boards where the played move instead hangs the player's own piece/king, making direction impure.

577.label: Top boards consistently skip a forced BACK-RANK mate (usually mate-in-1/2) in favor of a safe capture or developing move while staying winning; medium broadens to forced mates via other mechanisms (e.g., discovered check) rather than strictly back-rank, but the constant is choosing a material-safe move over an immediate forced checkmate.

564.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a suboptimal king move or wrong pawn break/trade throws away a won or drawn position with no material hung (king-activity errors); medium broadens to rook and bishop endgames plus milder king-activity inaccuracies, with a few off-theme outliers (opening, mate-allowing pawn moves, near-zero-cp non-blunders).

570.label: Top boards are constant: an active rook/queen move that abandons a defensive duty (king-cover, a hanging piece, a deflectable defender) and loses material or the king to a multi-move tactic; at medium the piece type blurs to any move (pawn recapture, king step, endgame push) that similarly neglects defense and loses to a tactic, with ~3/10 boards instead being missed winning shots (Nef3+, Ne4 fork, Nxg4) rather than self-inflicted hangs.

575.label: Top: loses a bishop or central pawn by mishandling unresolved central tension (cxd5/dxe4-type exchanges, bishop the usual victim), with 2-3 boards instead missing an undefended-queen capture in an already-won position; medium broadens to assorted pawn-push/pawn-break errors (f5, d4, b5, Bd3/Bd7) that drop a pawn or piece.

574.label: In passed-pawn endgames the player plays a natural king-walk or pawn-push instead of the lone precise move; at the top that move is consistently a simple capture, knight relocation (Na4/Nd5), or promotion fork in a won position, while at medium it broadens to defensive-only saves (Qf1, Rf8, b3), tactical forks (Ne6+), and avoiding back-rank/king-safety mates — plus occasional near-noise.

573.label: Top: in a won middlegame, plays a greedy queen/pawn move and overlooks a forcing bishop capture+check exploiting king–queen alignment (Bxe6+, Bxc6+, Bh6); medium keeps the missed bishop shot but the played move blurs to rook moves and the motif broadens to deflection, back-rank and discovery—plus a few cases where own material is actually hung, mixing 'missed' with 'hangs'.

571.label: Top boards are aggressive knight/queen checks and captures that hang or badly trade away the player's own material in the opening (a forcing-looking move that loses the piece); medium broadens to bishop/queen sacrifices and trapped pieces, with two cases that instead skip a winning capture (e.g. missed Qxc2), making the direction genuinely mixed.

572.label: Top: the queen is placed next to the enemy king by a check or check-promotion and the king simply recaptures it for free, discarding a win or forced mate; medium keeps the 'check the opponent just captures' theme but blurs to queen-for-rook trades, recaptures by a rook (not only the king), and even a hung rook.

578.label: Top boards hang own material almost always via a king move—wrong-way king dropping a pawn in pawn endgames (and undefended opening knights); medium keeps the hung-material core but blurs into greedy captures and skipped material-winning tactics (promoting intermezzo, fork).

579.label: Top: in a winning/drawn position the player races or rushes a passed pawn to promote, hanging material to a forcing tactical refutation (knight fork, winning check, or mate-in-one); medium keeps the premature pawn push but blurs the punishment toward slower squandering of the advantage—king-activity/positional errors and quieter tactical oversights, with occasional non-pawn moves and near-optimal false positives.

582.label: At the peak the move is a decisive self-inflicted blunder—either directly hanging a piece (often a knight) or fatally exposing the king to a mating attack/breakthrough; at medium strength it blurs into slower tempo/positional moves that squander a winning or holdable position (sometimes still hanging material over the refutation, sometimes just giving back the advantage).

580.label: At the peak the mistake is almost always the dark-squared bishop on b4/a5 left hanging or trapped by a passive/mistimed move (refuted by b4 trapping it or Qa4+ forking it); at medium it blurs into hanging other material (queen, rook, pawn via Nxd3+) and a couple of materially-safe moves that skip a winning capture.

581.chip: Hangs piece to unsound check (often knight)
581.label: Top: an unsound aggressive opening check/fork (almost always a knight, e.g. Ne5+/Nc7+/Nf5+) drops the piece to a trivial recapture, with bishop/queen sac outliers at the edges; medium keeps the premature-check theme but blurs into other pieces and refutation flavors (capturing with the wrong piece, missed discovered-attack lines), still losing material.

576.label: Top boards are clean opening blunders that drop a piece for free—usually a bishop (Bd6/Be6) but also a knight, queen, or pawn placed on a square covered by an enemy pawn/capture; medium broadens to any material lost over a 2–3 move refutation (forks, pins, Qa4+ skewers) and blurs into a couple of non-opening king-safety/mating slips, so the constant is 'self-inflicted material loss' rather than the specific piece or phase.

584.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed winning knight fork hitting both rooks for the exchange, declined in favor of a natural trade/capture/developing move; medium blurs to other knight forks (relocations like Nc7, or fork-with-check) and occasionally a different missed/hung tactic, but the overshadowed winning knight fork stays constant.

569.label: Top: in a losing-but-defensible (sometimes drawn) endgame the player trades or hangs the last defending rook—occasionally the queen—for inadequate value, converting it into a clearly lost position; Medium broadens from an actual capture/trade to passive, tempo-losing piece moves (e.g., a quiet king or pawn move instead of a forcing rook check) that likewise surrender the holding/drawing chance.

588.label: Top: a bishop move parks the bishop on an undefended square where an enemy knight grabs it for free; medium keeps the hung-bishop core but blurs the trigger — the losing move is often a non-bishop move (rook, castling, capture) and the bishop falls to a knight, a pawn, or via an overload/pin (sometimes only the exchange).

591.chip: Skips central capture, hangs pawn (often piece)
591.label: Top boards constantly skip ...exd4, dropping the undefended central e5 pawn to dxe5; medium blurs to other central captures (cxd5/exd5) and to hanging a full minor piece or the exchange rather than just a pawn.

585.label: Top boards are uniformly a purposeless QUEEN check that drives the enemy king to a safer/more active square, throwing away a forced mate or won position when a quiet centralizing/improving move or capture won; medium broadens to checks by other pieces (knight Ng2+, bishop Bf8+) and even non-check tempo-wasting moves (rook reposition, pawn push) that all miss the single precise winning continuation.

590.label: In winning endgames the player skips an available material capture by interjecting a pointless tempo check—at the top almost always a rook check (Ra1+/Rc8+/Rg3+), while medium blurs to knight checks (Ng4+) and even wrong-direction king moves that likewise forfeit the capturing win.

593.label: Top: a routine castle or greedy capture that immediately hangs a piece for free or removes a king-defender allowing forced mate (Qh7#/Qxf2#); medium keeps the 'walks into the refutation' theme but blurs to natural moves (captures, pawn pushes, recaptures) punished over 2–3 moves by forks, discovered checks, or positional collapse rather than an instant hang/mate.

594.label: Top boards are greedy opening captures/pawn-grabs (dxe7, fxg3, dxc2) that pop open f2/f7 and lose to a classic bishop sacrifice (Bxf2+/Bxf7+) winning the queen or material; medium blurs to other king-exposing moves (axb4, dxc4, Qf6, Be7) punished by queen infiltration, pins, or knight forks rather than the pure f-square sac.

587.label: Top boards are uniform opening Scholar's-Mate setups where Black ignores the Qh5+Bc4 battery on f7 (the saving ...g6) and is mated or loses the king/knight/bishop; medium boards keep the Qh5/Bc4 kingside-collapse theme (e.g. Ne5 allowing Bxe5/Qg6+) but blur into assorted unrelated opening/middlegame blunders (tempo loss, hung knight, missed fork), so the falling target and direction (hangs vs missed) vary.

586.label: Top boards uniformly miss the opening central pawn break d5/d4 that wins the c4-bishop or rips open the c8-h3 diagonal to win the queen, playing a natural developing/flank move instead; medium boards keep the 'played a natural move over the decisive blow' core but broaden the missed win to other concrete shots—discovered attacks, knight forks, deflection sacs, and other pawn breaks (d6/e5).

596.label: Top boards are uniform: a bishop drifts off the only blockading/stopping square for an enemy passed pawn to a 'more active' diagonal, letting the pawn queen by force (a few cases use a knight or king as the blockader, or a rook trade that surrenders the stopper); medium blurs this into general defensive negligence — sometimes still a knight/king abandoning a passer, but often just shuffling the bishop to an 'active' square while ignoring an unrelated duty (hanging a piece, allowing a fork, or losing a key defensive tempo) rather than strictly a promotion.

600.label: Top boards lose own material in already-worse positions—hanging a piece (most often a knight, e.g. f6/Nc6/gxf3) outright or to a fork/tactic a move or two later, plus a few king-safety/mate collapses; medium broadens the material loss to trapped bishops/rooks and positional eval-drops while keeping the king-safety/exposed-king theme.

602.chip: Hangs piece on unsound sac (often Nxf7)
602.label: Top boards are uniformly unsound knight sacrifices on f7 (Nxf7, plus one mirror-image Nxf2) that simply hang the piece to Kxf7 with no attacking compensation; medium broadens to other premature king-side sacs and illusory forks — bishop sacrifices on f7 (Bxf7+) and knight forks like Nc7+ — that likewise drop the piece because the 'fork' is defended or the king just takes for free.

597.label: Top boards are middlegame king-safety lapses—usually king walks to the rim or other exposing/passive moves that turn a lost-but-defensible position into faster forced mate; medium blurs this into tempo-wasting/passive moves in endgames and pawn races (abandoned blockades, missed best defense) that speed promotion or material loss, all from already-losing positions.

603.label: Top: in a won rook endgame the player skips a forcing rook check that delivers forced mate (mate-in-1 up to mate-in-7), instead grabbing a pawn or retreating passively; medium keeps the same mate-skipping core but blurs to also include forcing rook sequences that win a piece/promote a pawn or merely the cleanest winning continuation.

599.label: Top boards are quiet/developing opening moves that hang a knight already attacked by a pawn (e.g. ...d6/3.Bc4 dropping the piece to a pawn capture); medium positions keep the knight central to the tactic but blur in direction, mixing hanging the knight with skipping a forced material-winning capture.

598.chip: Hangs piece via tempo attack (or position)
598.label: Top boards are aggressive 'with-tempo' attacks/repositionings (often a knight to b5 hitting the enemy queen) that leave the moved or another piece undefended and lost outright; medium blurs to the same overaggressive tempo moves that merely squander a tempo, weaken king safety, or concede a positional edge without dropping material immediately.

601.label: Top boards are uniformly a slow/passive opening move that squanders a winning edge by skipping the decisive e5/d5 central pawn break (often the Qf3/Bc4-f7 battery e5); medium broadens to other winning breaks (d4, f4) and even decisive forcing captures (Nxg5, Nxe5), from either color.

592.label: At peak the move is a greedy queen/rook pawn-grab that strands the major piece and abandons the defense of the player's own king, inviting a decisive attack or forced mate; at medium it blurs into pawn pushes, king walks and other loose piece moves (plus a couple of pure hung-material boards and an endgame tempo loss) that share the same self-inflicted king-exposure/material-loss motif.

595.label: Top: an imprecise king or queen move (or wrong-square check / wrong promotion) throws away a forced win or saving draw—often hanging the queen outright (Nd3, b8=Q, Kb6); medium broadens to rook and other piece moves that miss simplifying wins, blow forced mates, or create tactical vulnerabilities, with the constant being a single inaccurate move squandering the optimal endgame result.

607.label: Top: in winning queen endgames the player gives a non-mating queen check (or slow king/pawn move) instead of the forced mate or material-winning line, letting the king escape; medium keeps the same 'check instead of the decisive blow' idea but blurs to rook checks (Re8+, Rd1+), wrong-square perpetuals, and the occasional hung piece while still skipping the clean win.

604.label: Top boards are queen retreats in a winning opening that decline a forcing winning capture (rook/bishop/knight/pawn), with one outlier that actively hangs the queen; medium keeps the 'skip the winning opening shot' theme but broadens the moving piece to knight/bishop/pawn and the tactic to forks and central pawn-breaks, occasionally hanging/trapping own material instead of just declining it.

612.chip: Hangs bishop sac on f7 (sometimes f2/h7)
612.label: Top boards are uniformly unsound Bxf7+ bishop sacrifices that simply drop the piece for one pawn after Kxf7 with no attack; medium keeps the same premature-bishop-sac theme but broadens to other targets (Bxf2+, Bxh7+ Greek Gift) and to either color.

606.label: Top boards consistently skip a winning CENTRAL pawn break (most often e5, frequently exploiting a Bg5 pin on Nf6) in favor of a quiet developing/preparatory move; medium boards broaden to any missed winning pawn thrust—central or flank (d4, b4, a6, g5, c3)—and occasionally a non-pawn tactical shot, plus a few premature-capture cases that release the tension.

605.label: Top boards are uniformly a bishop diving to c7/c2/b7 to snatch a pawn and getting recaptured free by the queen; medium blurs to other undefended minor-piece grabs/sorties (Bxg7, Bxd4, Nb5) and even an occasional missed forcing win (Nc3 over f7+).

611.label: Top: a won endgame is thrown away by stepping the king or swinging the rook off its guard, dropping a defended pawn that's grabbed cleanly (often with check); medium blurs to hanging bigger material (a knight), abandoning promotion/queening squares, and a few missed forced mates.

610.label: Top: a clear one-move capture of an undefended enemy piece (constant = free hanging piece, usually grabbed by the king; piece varies across bishop/rook/queen/knight) in a winning position is skipped; medium blurs into general winning king-and-pawn endgame king moves that are often only mildly suboptimal or not actual blunders at all.

616.label: Top boards hang a trapped bishop on a greedy pawn-grab (with a couple queen-for-pawn trades and a missed mate mixed in); medium broadens to knight/queen pawn-grabs that merely squander a winning advantage rather than dropping a whole piece.

609.label: At the peak the move throws away a forced mate in a queen/pawn endgame (mate→draw or mate→merely-winning); at medium it blurs to other squandered endgame conversions/defenses (hung queen, faster-mate misses, even allowed forks), all materially-safe-looking endgame slips that skip the win.

608.label: Top: an opening pawn advance (c-/f-/d-pawn) that releases central tension and abandons support of a central/queenside pawn, dropping the now-undefended pawn to a clean recapture; medium keeps the same 'remove-the-defender' theme but blurs it across non-pawn moves (knight/queen retreats vacating a pawn's guard) and into middlegame positions, occasionally shading into a slow move that merely skips a win.

613.label: At the peak the player skips a forced mate (or back-rank/diagonal mating net), usually by greedily grabbing a pawn/piece instead of finishing; at medium activation this blurs into missing any decisive material-winning tactic (forks, free pieces, discovered checks) and bleeds into already-losing boards that simply hang material or collapse into a lost pawn endgame.

619.label: Top: pure king-and-pawn endgames where the player makes the wrong king move (or pushes the passer too early) instead of the precise king maneuver—king-before-pawn, taking opposition, or blockading the promotion square—squandering a totally won game into a dead draw with no material lost; medium blurs into rook/queen endgames, minor tempo slips, and even non-blunders or actual material hangs (back-rank pawn, king-safety, promotion-race), diluting the pure 'won pawn ending, wrong king move' signal.

621.chip: Hangs rook into lost endgame (often pawn)
621.label: Top boards constantly surrender the rook by moving it directly into capture or a forced trade, collapsing into a trivially lost pawn endgame; medium blurs the resulting endgame (also bishop or rook-vs-bishop) and sometimes loses only the exchange (rook for a knight) rather than a clean full rook.

623.chip: Hangs piece on greedy pawn-grab (often central knight)
623.label: Top: a knight greedily grabs a central pawn (e4/d4/d5) in the opening and is lost for a pawn to a recapture or Qa4+/Bd5-type fork; medium blurs to any piece (bishop, queen, rook, even a pawn) snatching a pawn and being punished by recapture, fork, pin, or trap.

620.label: Top boards are constant: a self-weakening/defense-neglecting move exposing the (often uncastled Ke1) own king to a decisive attack, usually the Nxe4→Qh4+ mate motif; medium blurs into general king-safety neglect—allowing discovered checks, back-rank mates, and mating attacks—plus a few that instead miss that same winning shot against the enemy's exposed king or drift into unrelated tactics.

618.label: Top: quiet pawn pushes and passive queen retreats that hang material (bishop/exchange/pawn) or skip a winning capture by neglecting a concrete tactic; medium broadens the move-type to king walks and greedy captures and the refutation to king-safety/mating attacks rather than pure piece-drops.

624.chip: Hangs piece on faulty kingside sac (often bishop h3/h6)
624.label: Top boards are uniformly unsound Greek-Gift-style bishop sacrifices on h3/h6 (and one f5/h3) that get accepted with gxh3/gxh6 and leave the player down a full bishop for one or two pawns with a toothless attack; medium blurs to other faulty kingside piece sacs (Greek-Gift Bxh7+, Bxh3 mating tries) plus broader greedy/unsound captures and hangs (knight sacs Nxe3/Nxg5, hung queen Qf5, bishop grab Bxh4) that all surrender material for inadequate compensation.

589.label: At peak, the player throws away a winning kingside attack with a natural, materially-safe pawn recapture (almost always fxg7/fxg2) that skips the one decisive continuation (Nxg5, Bxh7+, the precise promotion/mate); at medium activation this broadens to other tempting captures and pawn pushes (Qxb2, cxb7, c5, e4, d3) that squander the advantage and frequently hang material outright rather than just missing the win.

614.label: Top: declines the only/forced ROOK recapture-or-trade and either drops the rook outright or walks into a back-rank mate; medium: same 'skip the forced recapture' pattern but blurs to other major pieces (hanging the queen) and includes a couple of greedy captures and missed free-rook wins.

622.label: Both tiers play a slow/preparatory or wrong-square move that skips a forcing win and throws away a winning advantage; the top boards mostly squander passed-pawn pushes (plus a few forced mates and a free piece), while the medium boards mostly miss outright forced mates (plus wrong-piece/wrong-square recaptures).

617.label: Top boards consistently hang a major piece for a single pawn in a pawn endgame—a rook capturing a passer in ~6 cases, an existing/newly-promoted queen in the rest—immediately recaptured to convert a won/drawn position into a lost or worse king-and-pawn ending; medium boards broaden from this literal piece-for-pawn trade to general won-endgame mishandling (tempo-wasting pawn grabs, structural ruptures, and missed pawn pushes) that squander the advantage without actually sacrificing a piece.

628.label: Top: in won/equal endgames the player declines a free, completely undefended queen capture (8/10 boards, rook in the other 2), throwing away the win; medium broadens to skipping the free capture of any hanging piece (rook, bishop as well as queen) and now includes cases where not taking also permits a mating attack.

627.chip: Traded queens into worse endgame (or rook/knight)
627.label: Top boards are uniformly queen-for-queen captures, almost always with check, that simplify a winning or drawn position into a worse or lost endgame (sacrificing the active queen as sole compensation); medium blurs to non-queen captures—rook sacrifices (Rxg6+) and knight grabs (Nxf6)—plus move-order/intermezzo misses, where the simplifying capture similarly squanders the advantage or even hangs material.

635.label: From a clearly winning position the player surrenders material and throws away the game; at the peak this is almost always a flashy but refuted check that hangs the checking piece (Bd4+, Nf5+, Nf3+, Nd3+), while medium boards broaden to quiet hangs and losing 'simplifying' trades/exchanges, with the piece involved (rook, knight, bishop, queen) varying throughout.

632.label: Top boards all hang the queen by greedily grabbing a defended pawn on an open file (recaptured by a rook); medium broadens to any premature queen sortie that walks into a capture by a pawn or bishop.

633.label: Top: a middlegame move that strips away the sole guardian of the back rank, king-shelter, or a piece — refuted by immediate mate or decisive material loss (across rook/queen/knight/pawn movers); medium blurs from clean defender-removal into pawn-shelter-weakening pushes (f3/g5/g6), tempo losses, and missed defensive/winning resources.

634.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player chose a quiet king/piece move instead of the one forcing check that wins material—most often a knight fork, but also bishop or rook checks/capturing-checks; medium: blurs to missing the single winning resource that need not be a check (exchange sac, pawn break/push, correct recapture, deflection) and occasionally even hanging own material rather than purely skipping a win.

629.label: Top boards throw away a clearly winning/mating position with a flashy forcing move—a tempting check or greedy capture—that usually hangs the player's own piece (bishop/rook/knight/queen) or skips a cleaner mate; medium boards keep the 'squanders the win' theme but broaden away from forcing tactics into quiet tempo-wasting king moves and premature pawn pushes that surrender the advantage.

583.label: Top: a greedy capture or infiltration—most often the queen—that abandons a defensive/blocking duty and hangs material (twice even allowing forced mate); medium blurs to non-capturing moves that surrender a key positional asset (passed pawn, active rook/bishop square) and squander a winning-or-equal position without immediate material loss.

630.label: At the peak it's an opening squander with a knight as the key piece—a safe, non-capturing move that skips a winning idea (most often grabbing a hanging enemy knight on f4/e4, or a fork) and occasionally mishandles one's own knight; at medium the pattern blurs away from knights and the opening into any materially-safe but passive move that simply eases the opponent's task (e.g., a stranded rook in a won/lost endgame).

636.label: At the top this is razor-consistent: the player skips an available FORCING QUEEN CHECK (Qh5+/Qh6+/Qg6+ for perpetual or mating net, or Qxg3+/Qxc3+/Qxh3+ winning material) in favor of a slow or wrong-move-order move (Bh6, h6/h4 self-blocks, Nh4, Bxf2), throwing away a draw, mate, or won material; at medium the queen-check core stays dominant (Qc6+, Qf6+, Qxh4+, Qxe4+) but blurs to other forcing tactics — a rook check/mate (Rg4+→Rh8#) and a non-check capture (Rxe5) — and is diluted by a few 0cp 'alternative path' false positives (Nf7+, Nh3+) that aren't real blunders.

638.label: Top: a self-inflicted capture/forcing move—frequently grabbing material that removes its own blockader/defender—lets an enemy passed pawn promote and loses a piece; medium broadens to greedy, unprepared captures that simply hang a piece (and a few abandon-the-blockade promotion errors) without a passer always being the killer.

626.label: Top: in won endgames the player plays a materially-safe pawn capture (usually a king or queen grab) and overlooks a forced mate or decisive winning tactic; medium blurs the trigger to any tempo-wasting move—quiet repositioning or a slower capture—that merely delays or forfeits the fastest forced win.
