637.label: Top boards are consistently pawn captures/advances (d- and e-pawns) that release central tension or surrender a strong advanced pawn, squandering a winning/advantageous position; medium blurs this by adding a bishop recapture and routine pawn recaptures whose real fault is allowing a fork or missing a stronger tactical shot.

631.chip: Premature pawn push throws win (often K+P)
631.label: Top: almost pure king-and-pawn endgames where a premature pawn trade/advance liquidates a won position into a textbook theoretical draw (king should be improved first); medium broadens to pawn pushes in bishop/rook/knight endgames that squander or reduce a winning advantage, sometimes by also hanging material or allowing a tactic rather than purely drawing.

639.label: Top: a forced checkmate is missed by grabbing material with a routine capture; medium broadens to missed forced mates/wins thrown away via any second-best move (checks, quiet pushes, wrong move order), not just captures.

641.label: Top boards uniformly play a safe/quiet/retreating move (queen retreat, knight back, castling) instead of an available material-winning blow—a free capture (Qxh8, Qxd3, Qxg6) or forcing tactic/fork (Nxf7, Ndb4, Bxg8); medium broadens beyond captures to skipping the single precise winning move, which is often a quiet positional/initiative blow (pawn break ...e5/b4, queen centralization Qe5, knight leap Nb5) rather than a capture, and a minority of medium cases see the passive move actually hang or trap own material (Qd7 trapped, Qf3 forked, Qxc3 trade).

640.label: Top boards uniformly skip an available immediate (usually checking) pawn promotion in favor of a king/rook move or extra pawn push, squandering a forced mate or win in a clearly winning endgame; medium broadens to other conversion failures — wrong move-order (capturing before promoting), choosing the wrong promotion piece (under-promoting to rook/bishop), and abandoning the passed pawn's support — same theme of throwing away a winning promotion.

642.label: Top boards constantly play a natural quiet move (O-O, Qe2, Bd2) and miss the specific forcing shot axb4 winning the b4-bishop in sharp openings; medium blurs to other missed/ignored forcing tactics (discovered checks like fxe5+, knight jumps Ne5/Nb5, or letting the b4-tension resolve badly), with material outcome split between skipping a win and drifting into a loss.

643.label: At peak activation the mistake is a king-safety collapse—Greek-gift sacrifices, castling into a prepared attack, or king/pawn moves that expose the king and lose material or invite mate; medium positions blur this into plain hung pieces via forks, zwischenzugs, and greedy material grabs (often exploiting an uncastled king).

625.label: Top: a quiet pawn/king move that declines to capture the enemy's undefended queen (boards 1-3, also a free rook b4 / bishop b5), leaving material on the board and walking into forced mate; medium blurs both the piece and the direction—shifting to ignoring threats against the player's OWN material (hangs own queen b6, own minor piece b7) and king-safety lapses (b8), so 'missed enemy capture' broadens into 'hung own material'.

646.label: Top boards are quiet knight/queen retreats that abandon a concrete forcing resource (perpetual, fork, or winning check), split ~5/5 between directly hanging the moved piece and merely forgoing the win/save; medium broadens to bishop/pawn moves and softer, more positional abandonments of the key tactic, with a slight tilt toward outright hanging material.

647.label: Top: a clear winning shot — usually a forced mate (Qxh7#/Qxh2# Greek-gift battery) or a decisive capture — is passed up for a quiet developing/wrong move (frequently Qd3); medium keeps the missed-win core but blurs from pure mate to material-winning tactics (Bf7+/Nf2+ forks, free rook, deflections) and right-idea-wrong-move-order plays.

650.label: In passed-pawn/promotion endgames, a losing move (usually a king move that deserts a defender, or a premature promotion into capture) hangs material — top boards span the full range of pieces (knight, rook, queen, bishop), while medium boards narrow mostly to a hung knight and blur toward simple pawn-push/race misjudgments.

653.label: Top: squanders a clean forced mate by playing a passive, materially-safe non-forcing move (king shuffle, quiet pawn push, queen reposition) instead of the available check/forcing line; medium blurs the same pattern to missing forcing sequences that win material or merely shorten the mate, plus several near-0cp 'mistakes' that are actually best/equal moves.

645.label: Top: a clearly winning side plays a slow, non-forcing pawn push (e5/f5/a5) instead of the forcing decisive line, letting the opponent equalize or escape; medium broadens to other quiet piece/king moves—and near-equal positions—where the tempo-losing move more often directly hangs material or allows a concrete tactic (Rxa3, Nxc4, mate).

648.chip: Passive king move loses endgame (often draw)
648.label: Top boards are uniformly passive/wrong KING moves in pawn endgames that surrender the opposition, blockade, or key-pawn defense — converting a dead draw (eval 0) into a forced loss/mate; medium broadens the move type (some pawn and knight moves) and the direction (squandering a held WIN as well as a draw) with generally smaller eval swings, including a couple of borderline 0cp cases.

644.label: Top boards uniformly pass up a winning BISHOP capture—almost always Bxf3 (also Bxc3/Bxb3)—that removes a key defender (typically of e5) and instead play a safe-but-passive developing move; medium keeps the 'missed a forcing winning capture' core but blurs the piece/target (Bxf6, Bxe5, Qxf5, Nxf7, and move-order finesses like Bxc6+/Nxg3-first), with a few cases where the wrong capture order actually hangs material rather than just skipping the win.

654.label: Top boards uniformly squander a passed pawn by pushing/capturing it one move too early (almost always cxb2 onto the long diagonal, also f6g7/c6b7/b3b2) instead of first inserting a check, deflection, or queen trade, so it's simply recaptured; medium blurs to any greedy material grab (queen/rook/bishop/pawn captures, even a tempo-losing piece move) that ignores a stronger intermezzo, check, or deflection and gets punished.

651.label: Top boards are flank/passed-pawn pushes (or a skipped only-saving capture like Bxb2/Kxf8/hxg5) that ignore the opponent's promotion race and convert a drawn/holdable endgame into a loss; medium broadens the move type to passive king retreats and knight/bishop/rook repositioning that likewise fail the critical endgame defensive resource.

649.label: Top: a forced checkmate after a queen excursion or greedy capture pulls a key defender off the player's own king (back-rank/Qf-mate motifs); medium blurs to king walks into the mating net and softer king-safety lapses (allowing perpetual or just an eval-collapse), and the moving piece broadens from queen to king/rook.

656.label: Top: in a totally won endgame, a slow king/pawn misstep burns the one critical tempo and throws away a forced mate or win; medium broadens to any quiet conversion-killing move (wrong king-march square, premature pawn push allowing a knight fork-back, rook to the 7th over king support) that lets a winning ending drift toward a draw.

652.label: Peak boards hang an undefended own piece in the opening—almost always a bishop on a5/b5/b6 lost to a pawn (axb5/axb6/b4), occasionally a queen or rook; medium boards blur into materially-safe moves that instead miss a winning tactic (forced mate, a fork, or a winning combination).

662.label: Top boards: a natural-looking active move—usually a rook centralizing or a check—that throws away an equal/winning position by gifting tempo or open lines (with some outright piece/rook hangs); medium boards keep the 'active-looking move loses the advantage' theme but blur the piece (king, knight, bishop, pawn) and lean toward pure positional/tempo squanders of winning or holdable positions.

660.label: At the peak the player makes a quiet/pawn 'safe' move that skips capturing a fully hanging enemy knight in a winning opening (exf4/Bxd4); at medium the missed material blurs to hanging pawns (dxe4, Nxg5) and a minority instead grab a pawn at the cost of their own king safety/queen, so the constant is 'missed best material-winning capture' rather than one specific piece.

655.label: Top: in Q-vs-R and promotion-race endgames, a passive rook reposition or pawn push instead of the active tempo-gaining check lets the opponent's intermezzo check win tempo, the promotion race, or the rook outright; medium broadens to passive king/knight/bishop/queen moves in varied endgames that get refuted by a deflecting/winning check (and includes some near-negligible tempo cases).

658.label: Top boards uniformly hang an undefended piece—almost always the queen—by tunnel-visioning on one's own threat and abandoning the piece's defense (e.g. f4 leaving Qg6, Qxf6 into recapture, Bxg4/Qb5 walking onto attacks); medium boards blur from clean piece-hangs to defense-abandoning king-safety/back-rank moves that concede a mate (Kc1→Rd1#) or a major eval/material drop rather than a literal hung queen.

657.label: Top boards consistently vacate the sole defender of a critical square/piece, self-inflicting immediate mate (boards 2,4,7,8,9) or forced material loss (1,3,5,10) — the defender-abandonment theme is rock-solid at the peak; at medium it blurs away from literal defender-removal into tempo-wasting or passive/wrong-order moves (Rxa7, Bc2, Rc1+) that merely squander a winning or equal position rather than directly hanging a king.

663.label: Top boards are uniformly rook moves that abandon a defensive duty (back-rank guard or a defended piece) and self-hang material—often the rook itself into back-rank/queen mate; medium broadens to queen/knight/king/pawn moves that likewise hang material or walk into capture, with a few cases blurring into skipped wins (missed mate-in-one, declined free piece).

666.label: Top: an immediate back-rank checkmate (Rh1#/Rb1#) where the move pulls a rook defender off the first rank, blocks the king's own escape, or steps the king to a fatal square — almost always while the king is already boxed in; medium: blurs to broader king-safety collapses where the king walks into a forced mate or king-hunt, exposes itself to winning checks, or abandons a defender, not just the clean one-move back-rank pattern.

664.label: At the peak the player chooses a materially-safe but slow move (a wrong/premature pawn push, slow king/knight move, or one skipped free capture) instead of the decisive pawn advance or capture that forces a quick win/mate in passed-pawn promotion races; at medium it broadens to other winning endgames (rook/pawn) where the suboptimal move is often only a minor tempo loss or even a non-blunder.

669.label: Top: over-aggressive opening moves that directly hang a piece for nothing (frequently a knight grab/sac like Nxf2 or Qxh7); medium keeps the 'loses own material in the opening' theme but the piece is dropped to a one-to-three-move tactical refutation (fork/skewer) and the unit broadens (knight, but also rook).

668.label: Top: a quiet developing/recapturing move overlooks a winning Nxe4/Nxe5 knight capture that wins a piece or forks the queen; medium keeps the knight-capture core (Nxe5) but blurs into broader missed tactical shots — pin-breaking captures, wrong-piece recaptures (Rxe5 vs Nxe5+), and non-capturing tactical resources.

659.label: Top boards are decisive and clean: an intuitive capture or routine king/rook move either hangs a rook/queen/knight outright or skips a forced mate/fork/win; medium blurs the direction and severity, adding softer greedy pawn-grabs and king/pawn moves that merely squander a big advantage or walk into a tempo-gaining check sequence.

661.label: Top boards are king moves (plus a few greedy queen captures) that walk into a perpetual-check net, throwing away a forced mate/win while staying materially safe; medium blurs to other defensive piece moves (rook/knight/bishop) that vacate a key square and expose the king to decisive checks, now often conceding material or a mating attack rather than just a draw.

671.label: Top boards are uniformly a passed-up exchange-winning bishop capture on the long diagonal (almost always Bxa1/Bxb8 grabbing an undefended rook) in favor of a quiet move; medium blurs to the same skipped winning bishop capture but the target broadens to other pieces (e.g. Bxh6 winning a knight).

665.label: Top boards consistently abandon a decisive, usually forced-mate continuation (Nxc6, Rxc3+, b1=Q#, Nxg6+) for a tame, materially-safe move that throws the win away (one or two instead hang a piece in the refutation); medium boards blur this into squandering a winning edge via an imprecise, tempo-losing or positionally inferior move (Qxa4, c4, Nd3+, Qa4) that keeps only partial advantage—with one outlier walking into mate from a losing position.

670.label: Top boards are consistently passive or wrong-direction KING moves (occasionally a non-urgent pawn push) in endgames that squander a win/draw by failing to centralize/activate the king for the decisive march; medium blurs the constant from 'king' to ANY passive, tempo-losing piece move (rook/queen/bishop) that declines the active or forcing continuation, sometimes reaching into the middlegame and occasionally hanging material rather than just missing a win.

667.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a king/pawn move fails to capture or blockade the opponent's passed pawn and it queens; medium broadens to bishop/rook/knight endgames where the move abandons the key blockade square and the enemy passer runs decisively (outliers: a missed knight capture and a non-passer blunder).

673.label: Top boards consistently hang a bishop (sometimes queen/exchange) to a 2-3 move refutation crowned by an enemy knight capture, often with check (Nxf3+, Nxd3+, Nxh6, Nxd6+, Nxf6+) that wrecks the kingside; medium boards still surrender material but the refutation broadens to any short tactic — bishop/queen recaptures, forks, deflections, removing-the-defender — and the knight-with-check signature fades, with a couple drifting toward purely positional collapses.

677.label: Top boards uniformly drop the queen onto a square where a rook captures it (usually while greedily grabbing a pawn, sometimes via a king move that exposes the queen); medium keeps the rook as the punisher but broadens the hung piece to any major piece (queen or rook), throwing away a winning queen-vs-rook or mating edge.

680.label: Top is constant: from a clearly winning position the player skips a free hanging-piece capture (queen/rook/bishop) or a forced mate, taking a lesser edge; medium blurs to include non-capturing missed wins (mate-preserving pushes, key checks/promotions) and positional or king-safety inaccuracies, occasionally even letting material slip rather than simply forgoing a free shot.

678.label: Top: undefended rook lost to a bishop along an opened/undefended long diagonal (exchange); medium keeps the diagonal-rook-loss theme but the attacker can be a queen and a few cases blur into general tempo-loss material drops.

676.label: Top: a bishop grabs on b4/b5 is refuted by a queen recapture-with-check (Qxb4+/Qxb5+) along the diagonal to the uncastled e1/e8 king, dropping material or a winning edge; medium blurs to other capture squares/recapturing pieces (and even a checkless trade that surrenders a dominant attacking piece).

674.label: Top boards are passed-pawn promotion races where a natural king/pawn/rook move overlooks the one precise resource (usually a rook capture or sacrifice) needed to hold the draw or convert the win; medium blurs this to general endgame precision—king marches, deflections, and tempo moves—where the single only-move is likewise missed without immediately hanging material.

685.label: Top boards are constant: in the opening a knight forks on f7 and Black plays a queen move off d8 (Qf6/Qe7/Qh4), hanging the queen to Nxd8 or the d5-knight to Bxd5 instead of the only save Kxf7; medium blurs to other moves that equally ignore the f7 fork — developing/pawn moves (Be6, d6, Bg7, d5) and even a bishop-on-f7 case — still failing Kxf7 and dropping the queen or a piece.

684.label: At the peak the player skips a clearly mating/winning forcing queen check or capture (Qxh5+, Qh5+, Qa5+, or holding the blockading queen) and throws away a forced mate/win; medium blurs to missing the ONE precise winning queen check among several checking tries (the played check lets the king reach g8 or a pawn interpose), but ~6/10 top boards are 0cp joint-best non-blunders, so the feature mostly flags 'queen-endgame with a forcing-check option' rather than a consistent error.

675.label: Top boards are coherent: in a won endgame the player rushes their OWN passed pawn one square toward promotion (pawn push) instead of the prophylactic blockade/defense, letting the opponent queen with tempo, promote, or mate and throwing away the win; medium blurs the move type, broadening to any non-prophylactic move (king or bishop relocations, other pawn races) that fails to neutralize the opponent's counterplay before advancing, plus a few near-0cp false positives.

679.label: At the peak, the player makes a quiet/safe move (usually a pawn push) that passes up grabbing White's completely undefended queen; medium activations are pure clean missed free-queen captures (exf4, Nxg4), while the top set blurs slightly to other free wins — a hanging bishop/knight and a back-rank mate.

688.label: In a won endgame the player plays a safe repositioning move instead of an elementary free capture of an undefended enemy piece — the top boards are almost uniformly a hanging rook (Bxa8, Rxe6, Nxc5, Bxa7, Bxd6, Bxa2, Nxh6), while the medium boards blur to also include grabbing a hanging queen (Rxc6) or winning the exchange (Bxd8).

681.label: Top: a queen move permits a forced, materially-even queen trade that dissolves the player's attack/winning advantage; medium broadens to queen moves that outright hang the queen or mis-time a trade move-order, sometimes also missing a cleaner win.

682.label: Top positions uniformly miss a knight-fork check (Nf2+/Ne2+/Nf3+) that forks king and wins the queen, instead playing a passive/routine move; medium broadens to other overlooked single best forcing shots—rook checks, skewers, bishop sacs/checks—mostly winning material but sometimes a defensive saving resource.

683.label: Top: clearly winning positions where a quiet, materially-safe king/rook move ignores the one decisive shot (knight or pawn fork, promotion, or rook invasion); medium blurs to only slightly-better or equal positions where the same quiet move not only skips the win but actually permits the opponent's counter-tactic.

692.label: Top: a natural developing/positional move (castling, piece development, pawn push, king move) ignores a clean one-move material tactic—mostly hanging its own piece/exchange to a simple capture, sometimes skipping a winning/equalizing capture; medium broadens to multi-move tactical refutations and positional/king-safety collapses where the material link is looser and direction stays mixed.

691.label: Top: a materially-safe, soft/preparatory move overlooks a concrete winning capture or forcing tactic (Qxe6+, Qxa8, Rxd1+, Nxe5, Nxh4) that wins material or keeps a near-winning edge; medium keeps the 'soft move instead of the forcing best line' mechanism but broadens in direction — several medium boards not only skip the win but actively hang a piece (Bd4, Ng5, Nb4) or allow a king-safety collapse/mate (Nb3, Kf8), so it blurs from pure missed-wins into self-inflicted material loss.

672.label: At the peak the player consistently passes up the position's thematic central break/capture (d5/e5/f5/Nxe5) for a passive, prophylactic, or wing move — with a tight sub-cluster of unsound Bxf7+/Bf5 that simply hangs a bishop; at medium it blurs into any passive or loosening move that squanders an equal-or-winning position, more often hanging material outright (bxc4, Be6, trapped knights) than skipping a specific central break.

690.label: Top boards all discard a concrete forced mate (often mate-in-2) via a greedy capture or slow, non-forcing move; medium broadens to throwing away any decisive winning advantage with a slow/imprecise non-forcing move rather than a strictly mating one.

693.label: Top boards are near-king pawn pushes (g6/g4/b6/c4) aimed at chasing the enemy queen off an attacking square, which strip the king's pawn shield or open a line so the refutation wins material or mates; medium keeps the queen-chasing pawn push but blurs to pushes chasing a rook/bishop and a couple of non-pawn tempo moves (Qc3, Kd2), all punished by the same king-exposure/hanging-defender tactic.

689.label: Top boards consistently decline a direct material-winning capture (gxh3, Rxe2, Bxf4, axb6, Qxf3) in favor of a passive/inferior quiet move; medium boards blur into the same passive-move gesture but where the foregone best move is often a positional/tempo improvement rather than a clean capture.

687.label: Top boards skip the immediate winning pawn promotion (almost always the check-giving one, e.g. g1=Q+/c1=R), playing a king/capture/quiet move that throws the forced win away; medium boards broaden to missing the forcing tempo-check or queen placement that secures the promotion/win (Qa4+, Qf4+, Qxh2+), with one or two cases also hanging material into the refutation.

696.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed undefended enemy rook capturable by the QUEEN (frequently with check, e.g. Qxa1+/Qxd8+), the player instead choosing a slow pawn/piece move that lets the opponent cover the square and erase a winning edge; medium keeps the 'free rook ignored for a quiet move' core but blurs the capturing piece (bishop's Bxa1, queen w/o check) and bleeds into other squandered-win cases (missed best positional/defensive move, allowed skewer).

694.chip: Hangs to weakening pawn push (f-pawn check)
694.label: Top: an f-pawn push/capture vacates f2/f7 and opens the e1-h4/e8-h5 diagonal, losing material to a forcing Qh4+/Qh5+; medium keeps the f5 king-exposure cases but blurs into other opening pawn advances (c5, a5) that drop material to knight forks (Nc2+) or wrong captures.

695.label: Top: player overlooks a trivial capture of the opponent's completely undefended QUEEN (knight or rook simply takes), squandering a won position; medium blurs to missing other free material — undefended rook (Rxa8), pawn captures (Rxf2/Rxb6) — and even drifts into hanging one's own piece (Ng5), so the constant 'free hanging queen' peak generalizes to 'missed/mishandled free material'.

700.label: Top: hangs a piece (almost always the bishop) by greedily capturing a well-defended pawn in the opening — a clean ~2-pawn loss for nothing, occasionally tossing a forced mate to grab the pawn/queen; medium blurs into assorted advantage-losing blunders (pins, trapped pieces, king-safety drops, even a missed endgame win) where the greedy-capture motif fades.

699.label: Top boards are almost uniformly unsound Nxf7 knight sacs that the opponent just recaptures, leaving the player down a clean minor piece for a pawn; medium broadens to other overoptimistic opening capture-sacrifices (Greek Gift Bxh7+, ...Nxf2) plus a couple of quiet moves that hang a piece or skip a tactic.

697.label: Top boards are constant: a premature knight sortie in the opening (typically Ng5/Ng4 instead of the correct Nxe5 capture) that strands the knight and loses material; medium blurs the piece and the move itself, broadening to other careless opening pushes/developments (b4, d4, Be4) that likewise hang a pawn or piece — and the direction is mixed (mostly own material lost, but a few are materially-safe missed captures), hence low confidence.

703.label: Top: in a won middlegame the player skips an immediate free capture of an undefended enemy rook, playing a passive pawn/king/rook move instead; medium broadens to other win-squandering passive or self-blocking moves (king walks, self-blocking the rook, plus the occasional missed minor-piece capture or bad trade).

702.label: Self-inflicted move that ignores the opponent's threat and walks into a forced refutation costing own material or king; TOP boards are sharp and decisive — short forcing tactics ending in immediate checkmate (Qg7#, Qh7#, Greek Gift) or clean piece wins (discovered checks, forks, free knight) — while MEDIUM boards share the same 'walk into the punishment' structure but blur into smaller, slower losses (exchange, single piece, queen-trap, or positional material won over several quieter moves).

698.label: Top boards hang a bishop in a winning/unclear middlegame—left en prise or traded/sacrificed for a single pawn and simply recaptured next move; medium broadens the hung piece to other minors (knights to vulnerable squares) and includes a few materially-safe moves that skip a winning tactic (missed fork/mate).

701.label: Top boards are uniformly needless queen trades (Qxd8/Qxd1, etc.) that simplify a winning or attacking position into equality—often ignoring a free piece/pawn or a winning tactic; medium broadens to the same self-inflicted simplification with rooks, bishops, or knights (and occasional pawn captures), exchanging away the dominant asset and throwing away the advantage.

686.label: At the peak the player passes up a forcing rook move — almost always an exchange/capture on an open file (frequently ...Rxa1) or a rook check (Re8+, Rxb8+) — for a slow or unsound alternative that hangs material or squanders a winning/equal position; medium positions blur to include queen trades/captures and other forcing major-piece moves.

704.label: Top boards are king-safety blunders from a won position — a greedy capture (often queen/pawn-grab) exposes the king or throws away a forced mate; medium broadens to any careless move from an equal-or-favorable position that hangs material, allows a fork/back-rank, or simply misses the win.

706.label: Top boards are uniformly the Qh5+Ng6 queen-knight battery where Black skips the only defense ...Nf6 (playing hxg6/Kd7/Kd8/Nxc3/Nc6) and loses the h8 rook to Qxh8/Nxh8 or gets mated by Ne5+/Qf7; medium blurs to other ignored forcing king-attacks—back-rank Re1#, h-file discovered checks (Bxe4), Qh2+ king-walks—plus an occasional materially-safe missed fork.

705.label: At the peak the player hangs the queen (occasionally another piece) with an aggressive/checking move to h4/h5/e5/f2 that's captured for free; at medium it blurs to a materially-safe but pointless queen check (Qh5+, Qg6+) that throws away a forced winning tactic rather than losing material outright.

713.label: At the peak, the player drops a fianchettoed/long-diagonal bishop for a clean full piece (~500cp)—placing it (or a blocker-removing move) undefended on g7/b7/b2/f5/f4 where an enemy bishop or queen simply captures; medium activations keep the bishop-hang theme but blur in square and amount, adding placements like Bh6 and bishop moves that drop the exchange or even undefend g2 to lose a rook.

707.label: In already-lost positions, plays a move that shortens the opponent's forced mate; top boards are almost all king moves walking into a mating net (king exposure constant), while medium blurs to include pawn pushes that loosen the king's shelter/escape squares and accelerate the mate (with a stray rook-hang).

714.label: Top: a queen or rook vacates a critical square—hanging itself or dropping a defensive/file/back-rank duty—losing material to a forcing refutation; medium blurs to minor pieces (bishop/knight) and to tempo-wasting repositioning moves that abandon control or skip an available winning tactic (missed win).

711.label: Top: a winning middlegame thrown away by a slow queen/rook repositioning instead of the thematic fxg6 pawn-break knockout (or, in a couple, a forced mate); medium keeps the same 'skip the forcing strike' theme but broadens the knockout to other breaks (g6, fxg5) and queen-winning combinations, occasionally just dropping the spearhead pawn.

712.label: Top boards are uniformly a bishop snatching an edge/corner pawn (Bxa7, also Bxa2/Bxh2) and getting entombed by ...b6, losing a full piece for one pawn; medium broadens to other pieces grabbing pawns (Rxh7, Qxa2, Bxh3, Bxg6) or pawn moves (b3, f4) that leave a piece trapped and lost over the next few moves.

709.chip: Hangs material on flank pawn lunge (knight)
709.label: Top boards are uniformly premature flank pawn lunges (g4/g5/b5/f6/h3) launched to chase a knight, which hang material or fatally expose the still-central king via forks and open files; medium keeps the same chase-the-piece pawn push but broadens the target to bishops (f5, g4 vs Bh5/Be4) and dilutes the outcome from clean material loss to tempo-loss/positional collapses that wreck the eval without always dropping a piece outright.

708.label: Top boards are tempting forcing moves in the endgame — a material-grabbing capture or a flashy/spite check — that backfire by either hanging a piece (Q/B/N) or throwing away a forced mate/perpetual; medium positions blur this to quieter king retreats and non-forcing maneuvers (Kg7, Kg2, Nh5, Ra1, g4) that squander the win the same way, so direction is genuinely split between 'hangs' and 'missed'.

715.label: Top: a king-safety/back-rank blunder (walking the king into a net or removing the back-rank guard) that hangs a forced checkmate delivered by an enemy rook; medium blurs the mating piece (adds bishop mates like Bb5#) and weakens to king-exposures that merely drop material or a tempo rather than forcing mate.

720.label: At the peak it's almost always a PAWN check that hands the king an escape square and squanders a forced mate; at medium it blurs to checks by any piece (bishop/knight/rook, or a wrong-piece/wrong-order check) that throw away a forced mate or otherwise decisive win.

722.label: Top: a slow, materially-safe king (or pawn) move in an endgame skips the decisive pawn break or winning capture, throwing away the win/best defense; medium keeps the 'passive move misses the one winning resource' core but blurs to queen/rook/pawn moves and bleeds into a few that actually hang material over the refutation.

726.label: At the peak it's won/winning endgames where a materially-safe move—classically an underpromotion (a1=B, b8=R) or a wrong recapture (Kxe5 vs fxe5)—discards a forced mate or the fastest win; at medium it blurs into decentralizing/retreating king and rook moves (Rc8, Kg3) that merely lose tempo and let the win drift toward a draw, with a couple boards being no real mistake at all.

725.label: At the peak the player mishandles a passed pawn or promotion in a drawn/winning endgame (premature push, wrong promotion timing, or static-vs-dynamic error); at medium the pattern blurs into hanging a piece, missing a free capture/forced mate, and walking the king into mate, unified only by 'inferior endgame move that throws away the result.'

717.label: Top: a pawn PUSH that harasses the enemy queen/grabs space (or releases tension) hangs the player's own material, frequently refuted by a capture-with-CHECK against an uncastled king (clean pawn/piece win). Medium blurs the punishment outward — still a weakening pawn move (now including recaptures like axb5/gxh5/hxg3), but the refutation broadens from pure material-win to full king-safety collapse/mate, with a couple of cases that merely miss a win rather than hang.

721.chip: Hangs piece skipping knight capture (often Nxf3+)
721.label: Top: a quiet developing/castling/queen move skips the forcing knight capture (almost always Nxf3+, sometimes Nxd5/Bxc3) that resolves the tension, leaving a knight-anchored piece hanging to a knight tactic (Ng5 fork, Nxe4); medium broadens to other knight resolutions (Nd5, Nxe5) and even unsound sacrifices, where the failure sometimes only forfeits a winning advantage rather than a clean full piece.

724.label: Top boards consistently choose a natural-looking move that skips the one forcing winning continuation—usually a tempo-gaining check (Re1+, Bc5+, Bxc4+, Bb2+) in a won/equal position; medium boards broaden to playing the wrong forcing move (e.g. Qxe3+/Qf4+/Qf7+/Qe5+ instead of the mating or forking check Bh4+/Bc4+/Bg4#) and shade into outright material hangs (Bc7, Qb4, Nf3).

723.label: Top boards are tightly clustered on unsound Fried-Liver-style bishop sacs on f7/f2 (capture + check, no follow-up, refuted by simple Kx); medium blurs to any piece dropped in the opening — greedy central grabs (Nxe4/Nxe5), misplaced/trapped knights (Ng5, Ne4, Nh5, Nb5), hung bishops (Bg4), and even a declined free capture (g6 vs gxh6).

719.label: Top boards consistently decline the winning Nxe5 capture/recapture and hang a piece in the opening, most often a Bxf2+ bishop sacrifice for a pawn (the e5 knight as the constant tactical pivot); medium blurs to other skipped captures (Nxd4), fork-based refutations (Nxf7+), and safe-looking developing/castling moves that squander the winning edge rather than directly hanging material.

728.label: Top boards are uniform: in winning/equal endgames the player makes a passive king or rook move instead of the single precise pawn break (d4 or e6); medium broadens to middlegame pawn breaks (f5, h3) and other forcing shots (captures/tactical strikes) declined in favor of slow consolidation, with a few cases tipping into outright hanging material.

718.label: Top: in razor-sharp positions the player skips the single saving/forcing resource—almost always a queen check or queen trade that defends the king—and instead plays a quiet/slow/greedy move that walks into a forced mate on its own king; medium blurs the outcome from 'mate' to plain material, adding overlooked winning captures (Rxc5, Qxa8+), hung pieces, and a mishandled passed pawn, so the constant is 'one critical move missed' while the punishment shifts from king collapse to lost/missed material.

732.chip: Hangs piece on unsound check (often rook)
732.label: Top boards are constant: a forcing ROOK check/sacrifice (Rxh2+, Rxg6+, Re8+, Rxg2) that hangs the exchange or a full rook for a non-existent attack and is met by a simple recapture; medium blurs the sacrificed piece to bishop (Bxg3+), knight (Ne2+), and queen (Qe1+/Rg1+), and folds in defender-deflecting checks (Rf8+, Rxf7) — but in every case the check is refuted by a clean capture or forced trade that loses material.

716.label: At peak activation the player loses material through a faulty capture or simplifying trade (Rxa2, Bxd2, Nxe5, exd5—missing a zwischenzug or stronger recapture); at medium it blurs into broader self-inflicted blunders—king moves, repositioning, or abandoning a defender (Kh4, Ke3, Qc6, Nf6)—that hang a piece or even allow mate.

734.label: Top boards are opening moves that throw away material with the piece varying (often a bishop developing move that drops a pawn/piece, plus knight traps, losing trades, and a couple of outliers that miss a forced win/mate or are purely positional/endgame), while the medium boards tighten to clear material loss — a knight getting trapped, a pawn-grab refuted by a tactic, and a queen-for-bishop trade.

731.label: Top boards uniformly hang the queen on an open-file/exposed square—usually after an intermezzo check or discovered attack that deflects the defending king so the queen falls; medium boards keep the exposed-queen-on-open-line theme but blur to a different piece hanging (bishop), the queen merely being hounded/deflected, or a related tactic (mate, promotion, missed win).

735.label: Top: a slow developing/expanding move ignores an active opponent threat and hangs the player's own material, consistently king-safety related (loss via direct capture or a 2-3 move refutation). Medium keeps the same 'quiet move ignores live threat' core but blurs the consequence — beyond piece losses (knight/bishop/rook) it now includes walking into outright mating attacks and the occasional fork/positional collapse.

729.label: Top boards are passive queen retreats/sidesteps (rarely a bishop) that abandon a key square and skip a forced winning combination; medium broadens to rook/knight/bishop moves—often a needless check or wrong move-order—that likewise bypass the forcing tactic, with roughly 3/10 directly hanging material or allowing mate rather than just squandering a still-winning edge.

733.label: Top boards uniformly play a passive/routine move that squanders a winning bishop sacrifice on the enemy king (Bxf2+/Bxh7+/Bxf7+/Bxh2+); medium blurs to other missed decisive king-attacking shots — checks, mates and discovered attacks — plus wrong-piece-to-the-key-square choices and a few cases of allowing enemy tactics (fork/hanging piece).

727.chip: Passive blockade misses active save (often queen)
727.label: Top boards park the queen on a1/a8 to blockade a passed pawn instead of the forcing save (perpetual check or active king move), throwing away the draw/win; medium broadens to rook/king passive blockades that skip the active king activation or rook resource.

730.label: Top boards play a move that ignores the opponent's strongest forcing reply—a clean capture, knight/queen fork, or recapture that wins material outright (e.g. fxe7, Nxf6+ forking the queen, Nh4+ discovered check); medium boards keep the same blind spot but blur the outcome, with slow/passive moves that either hang material to a simpler tactic or merely throw away a winning edge via an unfavorable trade or a missed clean capture (Qxc2, Rxf5+).

737.label: At peak the player consistently passes up a knight fork (Nc2+/Nc7+) that checks the exposed king on e1/e8 and wins the exchange, playing a quiet developing/castling or pawn-grab move that lets the fork square get covered; at medium the pattern blurs to other missed forcing wins—bishop-check sequences netting the queen, forced mates, and free major-piece captures, plus the occasional case where the 'quiet' move actually walks into a refutation.

710.label: Top: a rook captures a centralized enemy minor piece (knight or bishop) that's pawn-defended and is simply recaptured (cxd4, gxf5, hxg5...), dropping the exchange with no compensation; medium keeps the rook-captured-then-recaptured signature but broadens the loss to a full rook/piece or to surrendered positional/attacking compensation (connected passers, king-safety, a mating defense) rather than a clean exchange.

736.chip: Declines forced trade, hangs piece (often queen)
736.label: Top: in a losing/inferior position the player skips the forced QUEEN trade that was the only damage-limiting move and instead plays a tempo-losing king move that leaves the QUEEN hanging; medium broadens to declining any forced simplifying trade (queen OR rook), hanging a rook or stepping the king into a losing intermezzo check (Rxc4+/Rxh1), with a few cases of declining a trade that merely skips a cleaner win.

738.label: Top: moving a piece/pawn off a defensive post hangs material outright (queen, rook, bishop, or exchange over 2-3 moves) or lets enemy pawns become unstoppable passers; medium keeps the 'abandoned defensive square' theme but blurs toward merely missing a faster win or a saving draw rather than losing material directly.

745.label: Top boards consistently hang a bishop or queen en prise, either directly or via a short 2-3 move refutation (check/pin/fork); medium boards blur to any hung material (knight, pawn, exchange) and mix in occasional missed wins and non-piece positional/endgame blunders.

740.label: Top boards are faulty pawn advances or premature promotions in (mostly pawn) endgames that flip a draw or win into a loss—occasionally hanging the freshly-promoted queen (3,9) but usually a tempo/structure loss or missed save; medium blurs the 'pawn' constant, adding king, rook, and knight moves that throw the endgame away in the same draw→lost manner, with direction genuinely split between hanging material and missing the saving resource.

746.label: Top boards consistently abandon a decisive continuation (forced mate or crushing attacking/material-winning shot) in a clearly winning position for a quiet retreating/developing/simplifying move; medium boards keep the missed-mate core (often mate-in-1/2 or wrong-piece execution like Qg6+ vs Bg6#) but blur into passive positional/tempo losses and a few cases where the chosen move also outright hangs the player's own piece.

739.label: Top: rook endgames where the player skips the single saving/winning CHECK (a perpetual-check drive or back-rank escape like Rf8+/Rd8+/Ka2), squandering tempo so the opponent's passed pawn promotes or a back-rank mate lands; medium keeps the 'one critical tempo resource was needed' theme but blurs it—broadening to non-check tempo/defensive moves (f4, Bc1, blockades), missed forced mates including mate-in-one, and allowed king-side tactics beyond pure rook endgames.

747.label: Top boards are constant: a move that fails to parry a concrete threat and walks straight into forced mate or loss of the queen/rook (decisive); at medium the same 'unmet threat' pattern blurs into smaller refuted material drops (hung rook/knight via fork), lost tempo, or pure positional concessions—plus one missed-win throwing away a draw.

743.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a forced winning queen check (almost always Qxc6+) and play a quiet/developing move instead; medium boards keep the forcing-queen-shot theme but broaden the square and motif — checks elsewhere (Qxc3+, Qxe4+, Qxe6+), non-check mate threats (Qg6), and occasionally non-queen tactics (Rg6+ exchange sac, Nb4 fork after a queen trade).

742.label: Top boards constant: a routine materialistic capture in a clearly winning position that skips the precise forcing tactic/check/mate, throwing away the advantage; medium blurs the move-type to passive retreats and pawn pushes (and king moves) that likewise squander the win, with the material direction genuinely mixed between hanging/trading into equality and simply missing the conversion.

751.label: Top boards are opening developing/repositioning moves (mostly Be3/bishop) that skip the needed Nxd4 and hang a piece to a knight capture, usually with check (Nxf3+/Nxe2+/Nxe3); at medium it blurs into broader dropped material and missed knight captures — non-check captures, a wrong-piece recapture, a knight fork, and a king-safety lapse refuted by a bishop check instead.

748.label: Top boards all play a move (often a greedy capture removing the king's last guardian, or ignoring a standing threat) that permits an immediate one-move checkmate, almost always Qxg7#/Qxg2# (occasionally Qxh2#/Qxb2#); medium broadens to forced mate-in-two and to plain decisive material/king-safety collapse rather than instant mate.

744.label: Top: in completely won endgames the player skips capturing the opponent's only surviving active piece (predominantly a knight, occasionally a bishop) via a king move, wrong-target capture, or prep move, throwing away a forced mate and letting the piece escape; medium: the same missed minor-piece capture (still almost always a knight, often via a non-capturing check or pawn grab) but typically downgrades a winning advantage rather than a forced mate.

741.label: Top: in a winning opening the player makes a quiet developing move and misses a knight blow (Nd4/Nd5/Nxe4 or ...Bb4) that punishes the opponent's exposed queen on c3/f3; medium blurs to other tactics against an exposed queen/piece (bishop double-attacks like Be5, g4 trapping a piece, Ne5/Nb4) and even some self-hanging opening blunders, so direction drifts from purely missed-win toward mixed.

756.label: Top boards are rook checks that walk straight into capture (Re8+/Rxd5+ → immediately taken); medium broadens to queen and bishop checks and pointless tempo-losing checks (Ra5+, Qxg4+, Bxc4+, Qe2+) that still hang material or hand the opponent free development.

749.label: Top: a tempting bishop check where the bishop itself gets trapped/captured a move or two later (with a few wrong-capture/bad-trades that forgo a bigger win); medium blurs to bishop checks that more often just squander a winning advantage or undermine coordination rather than cleanly losing the bishop.

758.label: Top boards uniformly skip a winning bishop check, frequently outright mate (Bb5+/Bxe6#/Bg6#/Bh5+), in favor of a quiet developing/retreating move; medium broadens to other forcing winning shots — queen, knight, rook or pawn checks and knight forks (Qa4+, Nc6, Re8#, e6+) — but the constant is choosing a calm move over an available forcing, materially-decisive blow.

755.label: Top: consistently hangs material by grabbing the Nxf7 'fork' instead of the winning Bxf7+ in the opening (knight gets trapped on h8, a piece falls, or king is mated a few moves later); medium broadens to other moves that pass up the decisive Bf7+! line (e.g. Bd5), which only forfeit part of the advantage rather than outright losing.

753.label: Top: in won endgames the player passes up a free capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen and instead fires off a pointless check, throwing away forced mate; medium keeps the 'tempting forcing move over the decisive win' theme but blurs the missed win to any best continuation (a quiet mating move like Kd3, a piece-winning Re7) and the discarded move is sometimes a greedy/offside capture rather than a check.

760.label: Top: a materially-safe move skips a forcing queen check (Qxg3+/Qxb6+/Qg6+/Qxh6+) that mates or wins decisively against the exposed king; medium keeps the missed forcing check on the king but broadens to capture-checks of hanging pieces and rook checks/sacrifices (Rxg5+).

754.label: At the peak the player passes up a promotion-with-check (e.g. c8=Q+, a1=Q+, or a queen instead of underpromoting to N), choosing a passive king move while staying winning; medium/lower boards broaden to skipping any single precise resource in a won/drawn endgame—a key capture, an equalizing knight check, or a defensive rook relocation—rather than hanging material outright.

762.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a queen capture-with-check (usually Qxc3+) that wins material against the uncastled/exposed king while playing a safe quiet move; medium positions keep the same theme—a quiet move skipping a forcing material-winning blow vs. the central king—but the winning shot blurs to other pieces (knight forks like Nd6+, Bxf2+, rook checks Re1+/Rd1+) and occasionally a non-check sac.

752.label: Top: in winning/drawn positions the player skips a forced mate or decisive tactic (Ne7#, Rd1#, Qh7#, Ne2+, Nxf2) and instead plays a materially-safe capture or quiet positional move, throwing away the win; medium blurs from clean mate-misses into broadly squandering a winning advantage with an inferior 'natural' move (tempo losses, greedy pawn grabs, weaker checks)—and a couple of boards instead walk the king into a mating net, mixing 'missed win' with 'allowed mate.'

750.chip: Hangs piece in opening center (often d4-grab)
750.label: Top: a bishop (or knight) captures a defended central pawn—almost always d4—hanging the piece for a single pawn in an equal opening; medium broadens to hanging a minor piece in the opening center more generally, including non-capturing developments onto attacked squares (Bd7–b5 into Bxb5+, Bf8–c5 into dxc5) and other central pawn-grabs/captures that drop material or a key square.

761.label: Top boards are uniform: the queen drifts to a passive square missing a forcing, material-winning queen-takes-rook capture (almost always Qxe1/Qxe8/Qxa8/Qxc1, typically an exchange- or queen-sacrifice exploiting the back rank); medium blurs to missing other forcing material-winning captures — rook captures launching promotion combos (Rxe8+c7), queen-grabs-rook (Qxa1/Qxa8), or a winning pawn-grab (Qxd3) — plus a couple where the quiet move also hangs material.

765.label: Top boards: a king-zone/key-square defender is moved off (or its post never taken), leaving the king's escape blocked or a square undefended so the opponent crashes through with forced mate; medium boards show the same defensive-neglect mistake but the breakthrough yields decisive material loss rather than mate, with the vacating piece varying (rook/queen/knight/pawn).

757.label: Top: in the opening a routine developing move abandons an infiltrating minor piece—almost always a bishop deep on c3/f3 (rarely a knight) that should have captured/traded—dropping it for free; medium keeps the 'develop instead of resolve' theme but blurs to other targets (hung knight/pawn) and softer cases where the developing move ignores a tactical or positional demand rather than cleanly hanging a piece.

763.label: Top boards are concrete missed forcing wins/mates abandoned by a passive queen or piece retreat (Qa3/Qb6/Qf1, Ne6/Ne1, O-O over Qe3+, Rg7/Qf1 over forced mate); medium blurs into any quiet/slow move—king walks, irrelevant pawn pushes, slow maneuvers, or a careless capture/develop—that squanders a winning or clearly better position, sometimes self-inflicting material or king-safety loss rather than only skipping a win.

767.label: Constant across all boards: the player picks a forcing check (top = mostly queen/knight checks) instead of the objectively best move; at the peak these checks reliably backfire—hanging material to a counter-tactic or walking into mate—while medium positions blur the consequence, adding rook/bishop checks that instead just miss a cleaner win or settle for a smaller advantage.

769.label: Top: in a won endgame, plays an aimless QUEEN check instead of the decisive queen capture/trade that simplifies into a winning (usually pawn) endgame; medium keeps the 'check-instead-of-the-win' theme but blurs to rook checks (Rf3+ over Rxb2), a wrong-square check that drops a forced mate, and even a greedy queen capture that hangs to Qxc5+.

772.label: Top boards are king moves that throw away a drawn/won endgame (king abandons a pawn, blocks its own pawn, or walks into checks/mate); medium broadens to non-king moves (pawn pushes, rook/queen/bishop/knight) that waste a tempo or hang material in equal-or-lost endgames.

771.label: Top boards are uniform: in a clearly winning middlegame a quiet, greedy, or passive move overlooks a forcing bishop strike (Bxh3/Bxh6/Bxg5/Bxg6/Bxe4/Be3); medium boards keep the same 'slow move skips the forced win' theme but the winning shot broadens to mate threats (Qf6), pawn breaks (d2, fxg6), or knight tactics (Nxg2/Nxg4), and a substantial share of boards instead just hang material outright.

775.label: Top boards drop a bishop outright or lose it within a 2-3 move refutation; medium broadens to any minor piece or pawn lost to a short tactic, plus tempo/positional concessions (and one outlier missed-win skewer).

759.label: Top: every board is an opening capture (knight ~67% / bishop ~33%) that backfires—removing a key defender or opening a line so the player drops material (rook, queen, knight) or walks into immediate mate; medium keeps the self-inflicted opening loss but blurs the trigger, adding non-capture loosening moves (pawn pushes like g4/d4, knight sorties, a pointless check) and leaning toward plain material loss rather than direct mate, so neither the lost piece nor the move-type can be pinned down.

779.label: Top boards: a natural opening developing move (usually a bishop) ignores a knight fork on f7 that wins the queen/exchange; medium blurs to c7 king-rook forks and f2 forks (plus a Bxf7-type sac), with one outlier missing a free rook capture instead.

777.label: Top boards consistently play a move that loses own material to a tactical refutation (undefended/wrong-order piece, pin, or overload) with the queen most often in the decisive line; medium blurs the victim piece and mechanism—forks, back-rank/king-safety collapses, hung pawns, plus a few tempo-loss/positional drops and missed winning tactics.

774.label: Top boards are unanimous: White plays a flashy queen check (Qh8+/Qh7+/Qh5+/Qe5+/Qe4+) instead of the correct simplifying queen capture (Qxd5/Qxf7+/Qxf6+), with the consequence genuinely split — half hang the queen outright (often into mate, boards 2/6/7/8/9) and half are materially safe but toss away a won game (1/3/4/5/10); at medium the queen-check-over-capture pattern blurs into any tempting non-forcing move that abandons the decisive line (a greedy Qxh5 that hangs, a missed Rxf2+ simplification, or a developing/pushing move that ignores a winning ...exf2+/mate threat).

776.label: Top boards are near-uniform ...bxc6 recaptures that open the a4–e8 diagonal for Bxc6+, forking the king on e8 and rook on a8 to win the exchange; medium blurs into other loose captures/moves that ignore a standing threat and hang material to a tactic (Greek-Gift Bxh7+, Bxf7+ sacrifices, king walks, opened-line recaptures).

770.label: Top boards play a tempting premature check (mostly knight, some bishop) that lets the enemy king escape and throws away a winning attack/mating net or dominant position; medium boards keep the same premature-check habit but broaden the checking piece to pawn/rook as well and more often see the checker itself hang or get trapped (Ne6+, Ng5+, Nf2+, Nc7+), so the direction blurs between squandered-win and outright hung material.

773.label: Top boards uniformly exchange (or allow the exchange of) the LAST ROOK, simplifying a holdable position into a trivially lost king-and-pawn (or B+P) endgame; medium blurs the piece — adding queen trades into lost pawn endings and a few looser simplification/hanging-material cases — but keeps the same theme of a voluntary major-piece swap that converts a defensible game into a lost ending.

780.label: Top boards are uniform: a bishop captures a defended pawn (usually on d7/e7) and after recapture has given a full piece for a pawn; medium blurs to bishop exchanges/captures that instead surrender a winning advantage or lose material in a trade.

781.label: Top boards are tightly consistent: a quiet, materially-safe developing/retreating opening move (Bb3, Nf3, Nc3, O-O, Bd3, a3) that skips a forced winning strike—usually a d5/e5 pawn fork or an Nxg5/Bxg8-type winning capture/fork against an uncastled king; medium keeps the 'quiet opening move misses a tactic' core (e5 fork, Nxg5, Bxb7) but blurs into adjacent error types—allowing the opponent's tactic (Greek-Gift Bxh2+), actually hanging own material (Na3→Qxa3), and even endgame/positional slips (Kxd4, g3, c6, O-O-O).

766.label: At the peak the mistake is a tempting knight capture (Nxe4, Nxf7) in a winning opening that is SEE-safe on the move but throws the game away by walking into a refuting tactic (usually a fork); at medium it blurs to other natural knight/pawn moves (Nf3, d6) that likewise concede the advantage by hanging a minor piece to a deeper tactical refutation rather than playing the one precise line.

786.label: Top boards are queen/king moves that vacate a key defensive square and walk into mate or heavy material loss (queen central to the refutation); medium blurs this to king-walks into checks and non-forcing/tempo-losing moves that merely permit a strong queen-driven tactical or positional refutation.

787.label: Top: from a clearly winning position the player plays a quiet, non-forcing move (knight retreat, pawn push) instead of a decisive forcing check — typically a mating pawn-break (f5+/h5+) or piece sacrifice; medium broadens to missing forced mates/wins that are queen checks (Qf2+, g3+) where the played move is itself sometimes a wrong check or an unsound attacking lunge rather than a pure quiet move.

768.label: Top: player inserts a needless intermezzo check (Bxf7+, Nc7+, Rxg2+, Re1+) that hangs the checking bishop/knight/rook/queen for far less than its value instead of the clean winning capture (usually just taking the hanging queen); medium blurs the 'check' constant — it becomes any purposeless quiet move (pawn push d2, rook shuffle Rf1) that likewise skips grabbing the free enemy queen and squanders the won position.

764.label: Top boards: king walks to the wrong square while declining a concrete saving/winning capture (Kxf8, Kxc2, Kxb6, Rxb8), flipping dead-draws into losses; medium boards blur to capture-free king misdirection that surrenders the opposition/tempo/defensive zone in pawn endgames.

784.chip: Hangs piece on tempting check (often knight)
784.label: Top: a tempting forcing check (usually a knight fork/discovery, sometimes rook) hangs the checking piece outright and spoils a winning position; medium blurs to more queen/rook checks and cases where the check merely substitutes for a stronger winning capture or forced mate.

791.label: At the peak it's queen/rook (and one bishop) checks that hang the checking piece and throw away a winning position; at medium it broadens to a knight check that loses a minor piece for a pawn — constant is 'a check that gives away the very piece delivering it,' blurring from major to minor material.

785.label: Top boards almost uniformly grab a piece and leave the queen hanging on the open d-file to an immediate Qxd8/Qxd1 (often a king move that fails to keep contact with the recapture square); medium boards keep the same greedy-capture-hangs-own-material pattern but the lost piece blurs to a rook, bishop, or pawn—and even when it's the queen it falls to a fork/discovery rather than the bare d-file.

794.label: Top boards all center on a mandatory queen exchange the player botches—either hanging the queen by wrong move order/ignoring the trade (Qxa4, Qxf5, Qxh4, Qxe5, Qxb7) or passively declining a winning/equalizing swap; medium keeps the same failed-trade core but broadens the punishment from pure material loss to king-safety mating attacks and tempo loss after queens stay on.

788.label: Top boards hang a piece directly—moving it en prise or playing a capture/advance that strips a defender or opens a line so a simple recapture wins material—while medium boards keep the same material-losing core but broaden to more indirect refutations (discovered attack winning the queen, removed-defender combinations on a centralized piece, and even an overlooked mate-in-one).

782.label: Top boards squander a favorable/winning position by either hanging a piece (bishop, knight, queen) to a recapture/fork/zwischenzug or skipping a clean pawn break/win (fxe5, c6, e5); medium boards blur this into broader positional drift, wrong recaptures, and king-safety weakenings that throw away the edge — no single piece or error type dominates, and the SEE 'bishop/capture/hung-100%' signature is contradicted by the varied actual moves.

790.label: Top: in a (usually losing) rook ending the player misplaces the rook—failing to get behind/blockade the enemy passed pawn—and lets it promote; medium blurs into allowing a related mate or hanging material (deflection check, fork/skewer, knight failing to guard the queening square).

783.label: Top boards hang a knight/bishop/pawn to an immediate capture, very often a tempo-gaining check against an exposed/uncastled king (Qxc6+, Qxd4+, Qxc3+, Rxc8+); medium boards broaden to pieces lost without check and to king-safety/positional moves that drop material more slowly after a central break (e5), with a few losing no clean material at all.

778.label: Top boards are uniform: a knight greedily grabs a pawn (Ncxb5/Nxb4) and is instantly recaptured, hanging the knight for one pawn in the opening (one Bxg4 bishop grab); medium broadens to other minor pieces and looser play—bishop/knight pawn-grabs (Bxg4, Nxg5, Nxe4), overextended sorties (Na4 trapped, Be4 kicked), an unsound sac (Bxf2+), and failing to retreat an attacked piece (Qd2, e3)—all dropping a minor piece for little or no compensation.

795.label: At the peak the player consistently hangs the QUEEN—via a capture or relocation that opens a line or strips its defender, losing it to the refutation (Qxe8+, Bxd1, Qxg2, Nxf3+, Rxd1+); medium blurs to hanging rooks/minor pieces or walking into forks (and includes pawn pushes/king moves rather than only captures), plus the occasional positional slip or missed free capture.

797.label: Top boards uniformly skip the forced e6 (or Ng5-on-f7) opening breakthrough from a winning position, playing a slow developer or pawn-grab and letting the win drain to equality; medium boards keep the 'missed a decisive pawn break/capture' theme but broaden the break beyond e6 (e5, f5, dxc6, cxb6) and out of the strict opening.

799.label: In a 100%-winning middlegame the player picks a natural/safe move instead of the one critical winning resource; top boards almost uniformly miss a specific knight tactic (Nxd4/Nf5+/Ng4 or a mating queen shot), while medium boards broaden to any single best move skipped (pawn breaks like cxd5/gxf5, queen centralization Qxe5/Qh4, rook captures Rxe7) — peak = knight, medium = any piece.

793.label: Top activations are pinning/developing bishop moves (Bb4, Bb5, Bxd5) that leave own material undefended and losing; medium broadens to any active or developing move — knight centralizations, queen sorties, pawn pushes, unsound sacrifices — that hangs a piece, with a minority (~3/10) instead skipping a clear win or forced mate.

792.label: Top: lost endgames where a king or pawn move mishandles a passed pawn—losing the promotion race or grabbing material into a lost pawn ending—plus two off-pattern missed Bxg7 exchange tactics and a false-positive best capture; medium narrows to king moves that lose a passed-pawn race in already-lost pawn endgames.

798.label: Top boards are uniformly premature/wrong-order pawn pushes (often with check) in a won K+P or minor-piece endgame—dissolving connected passers, allowing a blockading king or stalemate and converting a forced win into a draw or much harder edge; medium broadens to general move-order errors including king moves, but is heavily diluted with 0cp non-blunders flagged on the same 'advance-in-winning-endgame' pattern.

796.label: Top boards are constant: the king itself moves (Ke3/Kg3/Kg2/Kxd5...) straight into a forced mating net or a rook-losing check/skewer/fork; at medium it blurs by adding other pieces (Qc6, Rd6, Bd3) that expose the king to the same mating/fork attacks, plus a few slow tempo-losing king/pawn moves in already-lost positions.

801.label: Top boards consistently hang the player's own rook to a bishop capturing on a long diagonal (Bxh8/Bxf8/Bxe1/Bxa1) or trade it badly for a bishop; medium keeps the hung-rook theme but the capturer broadens to knights, pawns, and the king, with a couple of boards losing a different piece instead.

800.label: Top boards skip a faster forcing line in a winning position—usually a check (Rf2+, Rd4+, Rf4+, Nf6+, d5+) or pawn break (h5)—choosing a slow safe move instead; medium broadens to knight forks (Nd3+, Nxe5+) and simplifying captures/checks (Rxb3+, Re7+, f5), though about three flagged boards are actually 0cp non-blunders.

806.label: Top boards skip a free undefended-rook capture in a won endgame (advancing a pawn/king toward promotion instead); medium blurs to other free winning captures including queen trades and major-piece grabs.

802.label: Top positions uniformly overlook capturing the opponent's hanging queen—usually the only move to avert forced mate or material collapse; medium positions still mostly miss the free queen but broaden to overlooking other hanging major pieces (e.g., Nxa7 or Kxe7 winning a rook).

803.label: Top: in a won/drawn position a hasty forcing check or greedy capture hangs own material—frequently the queen—to an immediate recapture or zwischenzug (with a couple that simply miss a forced mate); medium keeps the hasty material-grab but broadens the refutation to a multi-move forcing king attack rather than a one-move recapture.

804.label: Top: the king marches the wrong way in pure king-and-pawn races, wasting the one tempo that loses the promotion race while material stays safe; medium keeps the lost-tempo/race theme but blurs to rook endgames, knight-check retreats, a promotion-with-check blunder and even a missed mate-in-one, sometimes at near-0cp in already-lost positions.

810.label: Top boards consistently put a knight at the heart of the decisive tactic—either missing a winning capture (often of an enemy knight/bishop, e.g. dxe4, gxf5, cxd5, Rxc5/Rxc2) or walking into/allowing a knight fork; medium boards blur this into more general middlegame material errors (hanging rooks, bishops, pawns, plus discovered checks and even mating attacks) where the knight is no longer the constant element, and the direction stays genuinely split between missed wins (~54%) and self-hangs (~46%).

814.label: Top boards hang a major piece (queen or rook) by moving it onto a defended square in a winning middlegame; medium blurs to also missing a material-winning capture or dropping a single pawn rather than a full piece.

813.label: Top boards consistently miss a forcing queen check (usually Qb4+) that wins material in the opening; medium broadens to other missed forcing shots—queen pawn-grabs (Qxb7), knight/queen forks, and strong centralizations—while still playing a materially-safe developing/castling move.

789.label: Top boards are uniform: a knight is advanced to a central outpost (overwhelmingly d4, also e5/d5/e4/f5) where the opponent simply trades it off, losing a pawn/piece or collapsing the pawn structure; medium blurs the square (flank/deep sorties like Nh5, Nf3+) and even the piece (Qc7, O-O-O) — non-knight moves that likewise walk into a simplifying capture or trade-driven refutation.

809.label: Top: Black ignores the d4-vs-e5 central tension—skipping the forced ...exd4 with a slow move (h6/a6/Na5/Nf6/g6/f6)—and drops the e5 pawn (sometimes a full piece) to Nxe5, dxe5, or a Bxf7+ shot; medium keeps the same loose-opening neglect but the lost material broadens to other things—a center pawn (d4/e5), the exchange (b6→Bd5), a piece (Bg4→Bxf7+ fork), or a trapped queen (Qg3→Bd6).

807.label: At the peak the player trades rooks (Rxb2/Rxd5/Rxa2/Rxd3) to remove an enemy passed pawn but liquidates into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn endgame where a connected/outside passer queens; at medium the act broadens to eliminating the passer with other pieces (Bxa3, Qxf7, Rxd3-missing-tactic) or king moves that allow the same trade-down (Ke7), and blurs into assorted losing-endgame inaccuracies and even some best moves.

817.label: Top: a slow/passive move squanders a clearly winning position by skipping the decisive capture or tactic (free piece/rook, forced mate, Greek-Gift sac); medium keeps the 'passive move forfeits a win' core but blurs to include positions already only equal/worse and moves that outright hang the player's own material rather than merely miss a win.

816.label: Top boards are all opening knight grabs of a central pawn (Nxe5/Nxe4) that are simply recaptured, hanging a knight for one pawn; medium keeps the 'grab a pawn, get recaptured' core but broadens to later phases and to other pieces (e.g. a bishop sac Bxh6) and varied recaptures (fxe5, Bxe5).

812.chip: Quiet pawn push forfeits win (→any quiet move)
812.label: Top: from a winning position the engine plays a slow luft/prophylactic pawn push (h3/g3/h4/g6) that skips a decisive forcing capture or forced mate (and ~4/10 simply hangs its own attacked rook/bishop/pawn); medium broadens to any passive king/bishop/queen move that squanders the win, similarly split between missed forcing wins/captures and hung material or allowed back-rank mate.

808.label: Across both tiers the constant is an enemy BISHOP the player fails to grab: top positions are clean, free captures of a fully undefended bishop where a quiet/king move simply lets it retreat to safety, while medium keeps the bishop as the target but blurs into sharper situations — the capture is the sole critical 'only-move' (Nxc5/Qxe3/Rxe6), sometimes a wrong-target choice (took pawn or h-pawn instead of the bishop) or a quiet move that also exposes own material to that bishop.

819.label: Top boards are the king marching the wrong way in king-and-pawn/passed-pawn endgames (incorrect blockade, too slow, or stepping away from where it's needed); medium blurs this into other slow or misdirected endgame maneuvers (rook, knight, queen) that lose a tempo and squander the win or deepen the loss.

811.label: Top: with the queen on d5 and Bg4 pinning Nf3, Black makes a passive, materially-safe queen retreat (Qd8/Qd7/Qe6+/Qa5) that skips the equalizing/winning 7...Bxf3 (or Qxd4/Qh5) and is punished by 8.d5 hitting the c6-knight with tempo (one board instead hangs Bg4 to hxg4); medium blurs to general passive/tempo-losing opening moves (Qd1, Qc3, e3, premature fxe4, allowing Nd4) that surrender the initiative rather than the specific Bxf3-skip.

805.label: At peak the move skips the forcing queen trade or queen capture the position demands and is punished by hanging the player's own material; at medium it blurs to skipping any critical forcing move (rook-sac mate, pawn-winning capture, defensive queen retreat), still usually queen-centric.

823.label: Top: a materially-safe move skips a clearly winning queen capture, almost always of an undefended rook on d4 (or an equivalent queen-led tactic); medium: still a missed winning queen capture/combination, but the target broadens beyond the d4-rook to knights, pawns, and other major pieces (with a few outliers that hang the queen or walk into mate instead).

826.label: Top boards pivot on a single queen interaction—either hanging own material to an enemy queen capture or missing the capture of an exposed/hanging enemy queen—with the queen as the decisive piece on both sides; medium boards keep the queen central but blur the direction into bad queen trades, failed attacks on the queen, and adjacent exchange/back-rank losses, so the unifying thread is misjudging a queen interaction rather than one consistent error direction.

822.label: Top: from a clearly winning position a safe, non-forcing/quiet move (or wrong capture order) overlooks a forced mate or decisive material-winning capture (often Qxe3/Qxg2-style queen/piece grabs or Rd1+/Qh6+ mates), downgrading the win to only a large edge; medium blurs into less-than-winning positions where the suboptimal 'safe' move actively throws the advantage away — hanging material, getting a piece trapped, or allowing an enemy fork — sometimes flipping into a loss rather than merely missing a bigger win.

821.label: Top boards uniformly skip a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (almost always a bishop, grabbed by the queen) in favor of a quiet/positional move; medium boards keep the missed-free-capture core but broaden the capturing piece (e.g. rook Rxf8) and blur toward quiet moves that ignore tactics generally — including ones that hang own pawns/pieces, lose tempo, or misplay the endgame.

820.label: Top: a piece or king vacates a guarding role and the defended target collapses—uniformly a hanging knight (boards 3,4,8,9) or a forced mate on the now-exposed king (2,5,6,7,10); medium keeps the same desertion mechanism but blurs to rooks/bishops/pawns hanging and softer king exposure (winning checks or a single pawn rather than forced mate).

825.label: Top boards are knight moves (plus a few greedy queen captures) that pull a piece off the king's-zone defense and allow forced mate; medium broadens to queen/king/pawn moves and to simply losing the now-undefended material rather than getting mated.

827.label: Top boards are consistently premature (passed) pawn advances in a winning/drawn endgame—pushing instead of activating the king or picking a sounder plan, so the pawn is blockaded/exchanged and the result is thrown away; medium blurs the move-type, adding non-pawn squanders (king/bishop shuffles, a missed capture) and cases where the push or move outright hangs a piece (knight fork, undefended bishop), so direction splits between 'missed win' and 'hangs material.'

824.label: Top: in already-lost positions a rook move abandons the sole defensive duty and ignores the opponent's immediate decisive threat (usually a forced mate, occasionally a perpetual/stalemate save), getting mated or losing material; medium keeps the 'ignored decisive threat' core but blurs across the moving piece (knight/queen/pawn as well as rook) and across outcomes (allowed mate, dropped material, bad queen trade into a lost ending, and even a missed forcing win).

828.label: Top: a queen capture-with-check is recaptured by the king, trading the queen (usually for a rook) and throwing away a forced mate; medium keeps the same queen-capture-check-into-recapture pattern but blurs the captured piece (incl. pawns) and the missed result (sometimes only a squandered winning advantage rather than mate, occasionally just a minor inaccuracy).

815.chip: Trades active bishop for knight (or hangs)
815.label: Top boards are uniformly an active bishop capturing a passive/undeveloped knight (a bad minor-piece trade surrendering the superior piece); medium boards blur into hanging or unsoundly sacrificing that bishop and a few other greedy captures that drop material in the refutation.

832.label: Top boards are king-/passed-pawn promotion races at the exact push-vs-king-activation decision, but mostly near-optimal 0–6cp moves with only a couple of genuine tempo/move-order slips (wrong king move or premature pawn push, no material lost); medium blurs into clearer tempo-losing king/pawn choices in races plus a few off-theme tactical/opening blunders (skewer, ...h6).

833.label: Top boards hang a freshly-promoted queen to a rook by queening immediately instead of inserting the required zwischenzug check; medium positions blur away from promotion to hasty captures/checks that likewise skip the precise intermediate move, throwing away a forced mate or won endgame (with one non-blunder mixed in).

836.label: Top: player consistently hangs own material by declining an available simplifying queen trade (Qxe7/Qxf2+/Qxd2+ etc.), letting the opponent win material in the refutation; medium drops the queen-trade element, instead losing material/position through a wrong recapture or pointless tempo-losing check.

838.label: Top boards are king moves that squander a tempo in passed-pawn/king-and-pawn races (failing to blockade or escort the passer, in positions usually already lost); medium blurs to knight repositioning and other slow moves that lose the race, sometimes shading into outright hanging a piece or greedy captures.

831.label: Top: a materially-safe king-exposing move—usually a king walk, queen retreat, or own file-opening capture—hands the opponent a forced mating series of checks; medium broadens to pawn pushes that strip the king's pawn shield and greedy/passive moves that surrender king safety or the checking initiative to the enemy.

835.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player hangs a piece (usually a rook, sometimes the queen or bishop) with a needless forcing check instead of the simple winning capture; medium broadens to squandering a won/near-equal position via other faulty 'active' tries — a passive rook retreat, a self-trapped knight, or an unsound fork — so it isn't always a clean check or pure material hang.

841.label: Top boards are uniformly a bishop placed or left on a pawn-controlled square (c5/f4/f5/b4/c4) and captured for free in the opening (incl. boards 8/10 where O-O or Re8 ignores the already-attacked c5 bishop); medium keeps the bishop-to-pawn theme but broadens to a bishop dropped via an unrelated move and the occasional knight hung to a pawn.

839.label: At the peak, every board is a drawn/defensible endgame where the player chooses a passive king- or rook-centralizing move instead of the one saving active resource—almost always a rook perpetual/defensive check (queen once); at medium the same 'skip the saving check' idea persists for rook checks but blurs into knight checks and other active defenses, diluted by a couple of non-blunders (Kd2, Kh1) and walk-into-mate cases.

834.label: Top boards consistently surrender/trade the ACTIVE ROOK that supplies the winning counterplay, converting a win into a draw or loss; medium blurs to giving up any decisive asset more broadly — trading the queen that shields a passed pawn, or recapturing immediately and skipping a winning zwischenzug.

837.label: Top: in a winning opening the player plays a quiet developing move that declines a free undefended capture, almost always Nxe5 (with a few Nxd4/Nxe4 variants); medium broadens to other missed free captures (Bxf5, Nxe4, Qxd8/Nxe5 tactic) and increasingly to quiet developing moves that instead hang the player's own material (knight, rook, b7-pawn).

830.chip: Pawn push over forcing tactic (usually pawn)
830.label: Top: a pawn push—almost always one attacking an enemy piece—played instead of a clean winning forcing line (fork/check/forced mate), which both skips the win and usually hangs own material to the refutation; medium blurs this to occasional piece moves (knight/rook) and to less-crushing skipped alternatives, where the push more often just drops material or concedes positionally rather than missing a forced mate.

842.label: Top boards all move a knight directly onto an undefended kingside-rim square (g5/g4/h5/h4) where the enemy queen snaps it off for free; medium broadens to knights left hanging by an unrelated developing/king move and to other squares/capturers (bishop takes, rook-for-knight exchange, queen-check forks), though it's still overwhelmingly a loose knight grabbed by the queen.

840.label: Top boards are dead-equal endgame king moves that abandon the saving/defensive resource and throw away the draw (hanging the rook, walking into a mating/check sequence, losing drawing perpetuals); medium broadens to pawn breaks that concede structure and even a knight move that misses a forced win, so both the piece moved and the direction (hang vs. miss) blur away from the king-move core.

848.label: Top: a greedy capture is instantly refuted by a recapture or zwischenzug — frequently with check or even mate — that wins back the grabbed material and more; medium blurs toward a materially-safe simplifying trade that overlooks a stronger tactical win (missed win).

844.label: Top: in a won opening a passive/careless move abandons the decisive queen line — a winning queen capture or mate (~6/10), or a queen retreat that lets the queen/piece fall in the 2-3 move refutation (~4/10), queen central throughout; medium blurs to non-queen winning moves (e.g., a passed-pawn push) and non-queen player moves where the queen is less central.

845.label: Top boards are constant: a rook (sometimes queen) lurches forward to chase/attack an enemy piece while abandoning a critical defensive duty (king's escape square, back rank, or open file) and gets refuted tactically for material; medium blurs the outcome — some still hang (queen/rook abandons cover and drops material to a fork/mate), but several are chases that simply fail (the hunted piece escapes with tempo) or moves that overlook a free capture/winning shot, mixing 'hangs' with 'missed win'.

852.label: Top boards are queen checks dropped onto a square covered by an enemy bishop's diagonal (mostly Qg4+ caught by the c8-bishop, the lone outlier a knight); medium keeps the queen-check-hang but broadens the capturer to knights and pawns and bleeds in a non-check hang, a missed mate, and a tempo-loss check.
