829.label: Top boards are almost all knights that wander to a rim/corner square (usually to snatch a pawn) where they're trapped and lost over the next moves; medium broadens the piece (queens/bishops also pawn-grabbing) and loosens the punishment—often a stranded or post-abandoning misplacement that squanders the advantage rather than a clean trap, plus a couple of pure tempo/positional outliers.

854.label: Top boards: against an exposed king, the player skips a forced checkmate or forcing king-hunt (Qe7+, Qd5+, Ra5#, Qd1#) and instead plays a slower greedy material grab — most often the queen snatching a rook in the corner (Qxa8/Qxa1/Qxh1); medium boards keep the same 'chose the non-forcing line against an exposed king' theme but blur to near-zero-cost tempo loss, where the move only stretches an already-forced mate by a few moves (mate-in-5→9, mate-in-14→16) rather than surrendering a win or material.

850.label: Top boards are mostly single-move material hangs—queen most often, but also rook/bishop/pawn, frequently with an exposed central king walking into a forcing check/deflection—mixed with a few missed forced wins or mates; medium blurs the same eval-flipping blunder further into trapped pieces, tempo losses, and missed captures, so neither direction nor piece is consistent.

853.label: Top: a rook move played to chase/challenge the opponent's queen that backfires by abandoning a defensive duty and hanging own material (a few instead miss a stronger tactic); medium keeps the queen-harassing intent but blurs the piece (adds bishop moves like Be3/Bc8) and the loss size, ranging from clear piece-drops to deflection/back-rank refutations and minor tempo/missed-win cases.

847.label: Top: in a clearly winning middlegame, the player overlooks a free capture of an undefended enemy rook by the king (Kxrook), with a couple blurring to a rook- or pawn-capture of any hanging piece; medium drops the 'missed capture' core entirely and broadens to squandering a won position by any single blunder—hanging a pawn (Qb3), structural/positional weakening (g6, g4), tempo loss (c5, Qc2), or king-safety lapses that allow counterplay or mate (Kg2, Nd4).

849.chip: Hangs piece, wrong capture order (often bishop)
849.label: Top boards are a tight cluster of move-order errors—grabbing a piece (usually with a pawn) before inserting the bishop-trade intermezzo, leaving the player's own bishop en prise; medium blurs this into hanging assorted pieces/pawns or skipping a winning intermezzo from non-capturing moves, with a couple being mere missed wins that settle into equality.

856.label: Top: unsound opening play that drops one's own material — classic f2/f7 bishop sacrifices and early-queen tempo-loss moves hanging a bishop, pawn, or queen, with a couple of boards instead missing a winning sac (Bxf7/Qb3); Medium blurs the mechanism and piece — greedy grabs (Qxb2), trapped/overloaded pieces (Bg4, Nxe5), pawn forks, plus more missed tactics/positional advantage-squandering, so direction wavers between 'hangs' and 'missed win'.

851.label: At the peak an inferior king or quiet move in a winning/mating queen endgame hangs the queen outright (or to a knight fork); at medium it blurs to merely missing the fastest win or losing smaller material (pawn, underpromotion, fork) — with a queen central to every position throughout.

843.label: Top: an exposed-king opening where the player refuses the only winning move—a king recapture of a sacrificed/hanging bishop (almost always Kxf7/Kxf2), letting it retreat and squandering a free piece; medium blurs to other missed recaptures of a hanging piece (Nxd3, Nxe4, Kxh2) and king/developing moves that fail to grab or defend the loose piece.

861.label: Top: pawn-endgame king moves to the wrong square, forfeiting opposition/key squares or a tempo in already losing/drawn positions (several truly negligible or optimal, one walks into a skewer dropping a bishop); medium keeps the wrong-square king theme but broadens to kings stepping into checks/mating nets and to tempo-losing moves by other pieces (rook/knight/bishop).

862.label: Top: a greedy capture (usually a rook, sometimes bishop) removes the sole back-rank defender and walks into an immediate forced back-rank mate; medium blurs into king moves/captures that walk into a promotion-check mate or open-board mating net rather than the pure back-rank pattern.

858.label: Top: a slow king-shuffle or quiet-pawn move that wastes the one tempo needed to push a time-critical passed pawn, letting it be blockaded and flipping a won/drawn endgame to lost; medium keeps the wasted-tempo theme but broadens beyond the passer push to any squandering slow move (passive king march, wrong recapture, abandoning the passer, missing counterplay).

855.label: Top: the queen consistently quits its defensive post (most often guarding the king) to chase offense/material and is punished by mate or a decisive material loss; medium keeps the abandon-defense-for-attack core but blurs to any piece (king, knight, rook, bishop, pawn) and other neglected duties—hanging pieces, back rank, move-order, promotion—still ending in a king attack or dropped material.

859.label: Top boards are queen checks that miss a forced mate-in-one or the single winning resource, letting the king flee to safety; medium broadens to weak checks that merely squander a winning advantage or allow a perpetual via the wrong checking angle/move-order.

866.label: Top boards play a move that loses material in the refutation—usually self-inflicted, with a knight frequently the dropped or attacking/forking piece (plus a couple of missed clean material-winning tactics like a skewer/fork); medium broadens beyond piece drops to hanging mere pawns and pure positional/king-safety lapses (even walking into mate).

865.label: Top boards consistently misjudge a knight capture in the opening — overwhelmingly failing to grab/recapture a free hanging knight (passing up a full piece, e.g. cxd5/dxe4/bxc3); medium blurs in the opposite direction too, hanging the player's own knight or queen and ignoring tactical refutations (Nc3 into dxc3, e3/d3 dropping the recapture, Qh5+).

863.label: Top boards squander a clearly winning position with a queen/piece trade or capture that either walks into a fork (hanging the exchange/piece) or skips a stronger forcing tactic; medium blurs this to a routine unfavorable piece trade that surrenders a positional edge rather than material.

869.label: Top: K+P endgames where the king goes to the wrong square—losing the opposition or vacating the pawn's promotion/blockade square so the pawn queens (huge swings to forced mate), but ~half are 0cp non-blunders; medium blurs into tempo losses, pawn-race delays, and minor 0–40cp king inaccuracies, even a non-pawn king-safety case.

868.label: Top boards lose the queen as the decisive piece—mostly left en prise directly or via a pawn/queen move that opens a line (Rxd7, Rxe7, Nxd4), plus a few queen trades that drop material or a winning position; medium blurs the target piece, adding a hung bishop, rook, or freshly promoted queen and positional queen trades that concede a dominant enemy rook.

846.label: Top boards are uniformly premature, pointless QUEEN CHECKS that drive the enemy king to a safe square while losing tempo, hanging the queen along a rank/diagonal, or skipping a forced win/mate; medium boards blur the pattern—some are still bad queen checks (Qh3+ hangs, Qxg4 squanders a win) but several are other careless king/pawn moves (Kf7, Kg8, Ke6) that instead walk INTO an enemy forcing check or skewer and drop material, plus one false positive.

857.label: Top: a piece move (most often the queen, but also knight/bishop/pawn/rook) that fails the position's decisive tactic—half hang material or allow forced mate by abandoning a defensive post, half are materially-safe moves missing a forced win—with huge swings; medium blurs to smaller move-order/tempo errors (any piece) that squander a winning advantage rather than cleanly hang or miss mate.

860.label: Top boards play a quiet/non-forcing move while a decisive forcing QUEEN CHECK was available (Qd1+, Qxc1+, Qf7+, Qa1+, Qb5+ — usually delivering mate or winning major material); medium blurs this to other forcing resources (Qa4+ knight fork, Rc2+ in-between check, Nh6+ perpetual, f6+ saving check) and mixes direction — roughly half are missed wins and half hang own material or walk into mate by ignoring the needed forcing line.

870.label: At the peak, the player declines a one-move pawn capture of an undefended minor piece (almost always a knight, occasionally a bishop) in the very early opening, throwing away a free piece; at medium the same missed pawn-grab broadens to more bishops, en-passant blindness, and slightly later opening moves, plus a few near-cases where the player instead recaptures wrongly or sacs rather than taking the hanging piece.

872.label: In a winning/forcing position the player chooses an inferior move that throws away the advantage; at the top this is almost always a premature/inaccurate CHECK (d6+, Bxa7+, Qh2+, Qxf2+) that gives the king an escape or lets a hung piece be saved, blowing a forced mate or hanging material — while at medium the check element drops and it blurs into quiet tempo/move-order or wrong-target errors (Bd4 vs Bc5, Qd1 vs Bf3) that merely forfeit a winning edge, so the direction is mixed between missed-win and self-inflicted material loss.

877.label: Top boards drop a piece—usually a rook—directly en prise for a free capture, frequently via a pointless spite check or greedy grab that ignores the hanging unit; medium broadens to any material (knight, bishop, or even a pawn) left hanging, plus a few near-cousins (a trapped knight, positionally-given material).

864.chip: Exposed own king to checks (king move)
864.label: At the peak, a king move to an exposed square (rarely a pawn push that strips the king's shield) walks into a forced check sequence — outright mate, a win-throwing perpetual, or checks that win material; at medium the trigger blurs to other shield-stripping/king-into-check moves and a few non-king-safety blunders.

873.label: At the peak it's a pointless queen check in a winning endgame that throws a tempo (letting the king escape/centralize) and squanders a decisive or forced-mate advantage instead of the precise consolidating move; medium blurs the piece and check requirement — adding king and rook tempo-wasters, wrong-direction checks, and a few that merely delay or even drop material rather than cleanly squander the win.

875.label: Top boards consistently lose material via a self-weakening move that strips a key defender or exposes the king, producing a clean hang of a varied unit (pawn, bishop, knight, even queen); medium boards blur this into material dropped through overlooked tactics—skewers, forks, discovered attacks, back-rank—plus a few near-positional/tempo concessions that only loosely lose material.

879.chip: Traded knight into lost endgame (often for pawn)
879.label: Top boards are razor-clean: a drawn endgame where the player captures/trades the knight—usually grabbing a pawn—and after the recapture liquidates into a lost K+P or rook endgame; medium broadens to losing the sole defensive knight by any means (hanging, deflection, leaving it undefended) and occasionally non-knight moves that simply surrender the same lost endgame.

878.label: Top boards are clean cases of declining a clearly winning capture (most often a bishop: Rxb2, Qxe3, Qxf4, Bxc3) in favor of a quiet, retreating, or wrong-move-order move that squanders a winning advantage; medium blurs the pattern into weakening/king-exposing pawn pushes (g3, f3, f6, h5, e5) and greedy or hung-piece moves where the missed best move is sometimes a defensive non-capture (b4, Bd6, Kc7) rather than a winning capture.

880.chip: Slow rook maneuver over forcing line (often missed mate)
880.label: TOP: a thematic rook maneuver (doubling on an open file, a rook lift, or a rook swing) is chosen over the concrete forcing continuation, almost always skipping a forced mate or decisive king-hunting check; MEDIUM blurs to any slow/passive piece move (queen, bishop, king as well as rook) that ignores a winning tactic, with roughly a third of cases having the quiet move itself hang material (pawn, knight, or even the queen) so the outcome direction is genuinely mixed.

876.label: TOP: in plainly won endgames the queen is the hinge of the decisive tactic—player either hangs its own queen (Qe6+→Rxe6, Kf4→Qxe2, Qc2→Rc6+) or misses a winning queen capture/mate (Rxc5, Nxc8+, Qxe6), but 3/10 are actually best 0cp king moves, not errors; MEDIUM keeps the won-endgame conversion theme yet blurs the piece (e.g. Bc6 missing Bxd1, a rook capture, not a queen) and the hang-vs-miss direction stays evenly split.

881.label: Top: a piece move that abandons a defensive duty or steps onto an attacked square, dropping a specific unit (b2/a2 pawns, a rook, or the exchange) within 1–3 moves; medium keeps the 'loses own material' core but blurs the mechanism into greedy pawn grabs (Bxb2/Bxh3), premature/positional advances (e5, Ng4), and the occasional materially-safe move that skips an immediate win (b5 instead of Nxa2).

888.label: Top boards are uniformly self-inflicted knight checks (Ng4+/Ng5+/Nxe5+/Ne4+) that simply hang the knight to a calm queen capture; medium keeps the same hang-on-check pattern but broadens the checking unit to include bishop checks (Bd3+) as well.

867.label: Top is constant: an unfavorable queen surrender — either an unsound check/sac that simply hangs the queen (Qh7+ Nxh7, Qh2+ Kxh2) or a premature queen trade that discards a winning advantage; medium blurs away from the queen (and from pure material) into general eval-collapsing blunders — pawn pushes (b6, g4), king-safety/castling (O-O-O), and tempo-wasting threats (Qh6) that squander a winning or equal position.

885.label: At the peak it's a quiet greedy move—usually king centralization in a winning position—that walks into mate or hangs a queen/knight to an overlooked tactic; at medium it broadens to other quiet/developing moves hanging material to forks, pins, and back-rank shots, with ~3/10 instead simply missing a winning capture.

883.chip: Exposes own king to check (often king move)
883.label: Top boards are near-uniform: a king move (occasionally a queen retreat) steps onto a diagonal/file or strips the king's cover, walking into a forcing check (skewer/fork/mating net) that wins the queen or mates; medium blurs this to line-opening pawn pushes (bxa5), greedy captures, and queen sorties that similarly expose the king to a decisive check or invasion, mixed with a few cases that are really just hung pawns or trapped pieces rather than pure king exposure.

882.label: Top: a tempo move attacking/challenging the enemy queen leaves the player's own queen, rook, or knight hanging and lost by force; medium broadens beyond queen-chasing to general hanging-piece oversights and unsound sacrifices that still drop material in the refutation.

889.label: Top boards drop the just-moved piece directly onto an undefended square (or grab a pawn and lose more) so the moved piece itself hangs; medium boards blur to losing material more indirectly—the move vacates a key defender or opens lines to the king, hanging a different piece/pawn—so direction stays 'hangs own material' but the hung piece and mechanism vary.

894.label: Top boards are king steps in won/holdable endgames that drop the undefended queen—mostly via a knight fork (Nc4+, Ne3+) or leaving Q en prise; medium blurs to losing other major pieces (rook, knight) through skewers, pawn forks, and deflections, with several false positives (best move flagged, missed forced mate) diluting the signal.

886.label: Top: a clearly winning position is squandered by a quiet/natural move instead of a forcing CHECK that wins material or forces mate (the played quiet move often invites a decisive counterattack on its own king); medium blurs to smaller-swing positions and non-check forcing precision/move-order wins (plus the occasional greedy capture), while still skipping the decisive forcing continuation.

871.label: Top boards are uniformly pointless rook checks that lose a tempo and let the enemy king escape to a safer/more active square, squandering a winning or better position (occasionally hanging the rook outright); medium broadens the checking piece to queen (Qa3+/Qa8+/Qb7+) and knight (Ne2+) checks with the same tempo-wasting/king-improving theme, though several medium cases are actually near-equal or non-blunder checks, diluting the signal.

887.label: From a won position the player skips the decisive blow; at the top it's almost always a knight strike (overwhelmingly Nxg6, plus Nxb3/Ng3+/Nxg3, with two boards instead hanging the queen), while medium positions blur the constant — still half knight shots (Ne5/Nxd4/Nd4#) but now also non-knight winners like Bd6/Bxb5, so the move-type generalizes from 'knight tactic' to 'any decisive blow.'

891.label: Top boards are tightly constant: the engine's best move is a clean queen exchange (Qxd6/Qxd5/Qxf3/Qxe4 etc.) that neutralizes an attack or wins, but the player shuns it for an active queen move (Qb3+, Qd4, Qg6, O-O-O) that hangs a pawn/piece or squanders a winning edge; medium boards blur around the same queen-trade axis but broaden the failure mode — mis-timing the trade (wrong move order on b8b3), taking it on unfavorable terms or letting the opponent trade favorably (Kh2), or outright hanging the queen (Rf6), with a few near-miss outliers that are queen-related tactics rather than strict trades.

893.label: Top boards consistently throw away a winning/favorable position with a materially-safe but inferior continuation—a wrong queen trade or a missed stronger check/fork/promotion (with one outright greedy capture that hangs material); medium broadens to greedy grabs and moves that lose material outright (trapped/hung pieces).

898.label: Top: a won K+P endgame is blown when the king greedily captures the wrong/minor pawn (Kxc4, Kxc3, Kxh4, Ke5) and abandons the strategically vital central pawn or square; medium broadens to non-capturing king commitments or pawn pushes (Kc4, Ke5, a5) that surrender the same critical square/pawn and collapse the win into a draw or loss.

896.label: Top: a flank/edge pawn 'puts the question' to an enemy bishop (a3/b4/h3/h6/b5) while ignoring central tension, and a short tactic (Bxd2, dxc4, dxe5, Bxf3+d4 fork, Bxf6+Nxd5) nets Black a full minor piece; medium keeps the same pawn-poke-at-bishop theme but the damage blurs from a clean minor piece to also winning the bishop directly (g5→hxg4) or ruining the king's pawn structure (h3→Bxf3, gxf3).

897.label: Top: an aggressive knight advance attempting a fork/attack abandons a key defensive or blocking role, most often opening a forced mating attack on the player's king; medium broadens to knight (occasionally bishop) thrusts and wrong-order captures whose refutation simply wins back a piece, so the punishment blurs from mate to merely hanging material.

901.label: Top: a routine developing/supporting move leaves a piece en prise to a direct attack and loses it outright — almost always the queen, sometimes a bishop (Bf4/Bg5/Bf5); medium: same opening piece-drops (queen on d5/e4, undefended bishop) but blurs to include tempo-losing queen relocations and premature breaks that concede material rather than a clean hang.

884.label: Top: queen greedily grabs a defended piece (often a rook) and is instantly recaptured with check or mate, losing the queen for inadequate material; medium blurs to forced queen trades into lost endgames and even non-greedy moves (a rook grab, a king walking into mate) that likewise concede a decisive checking recapture or mate.

900.label: Top: a king move in a passed-pawn endgame that worsens an already-losing position—letting the pawn promote or hanging the rook/knight to a deflection check; medium broadens to rook/bishop/pawn moves, other endgame types, and a few materially-safe missed wins, so the unifying error is a losing endgame move rather than one specific hung piece.

895.label: At the peak, a clearly winning passed-pawn position is squandered by a slow/passive move (usually a king or rook retreat, occasionally a careless trade) instead of the forcing line that eliminates the blockader and pushes the passer to promotion; at medium this broadens to missing other forcing wins in won positions — back-rank/mating shots, exchange-winning skewers, knight-sac mates, and queen-trade simplifications — where the specific passed-pawn motif (and the materially-safe direction) partly blurs.

902.label: Top: in an endgame the player hangs or trades a MAJOR piece (queen or rook), either dropping it outright (Qxa7, Ra6, Rxa4, Qxg4, Qd1) or trading into a lost king-and-pawn ending, converting a drawn/holdable position into a loss; medium keeps the endgame hang-own-material theme but blurs the piece type, adding hung minor pieces (Bd5, Nb2) and worsening-defense moves (king-safety/trapped-piece) beyond pure queen/rook blunders.

890.chip: Squanders win, inferior move (often queen check)
890.label: Top boards squander a winning position with an impulsive forcing move—almost always a queen check—that either misses a forced mate/win or hangs the queen/rook; medium broadens beyond checks to any imprecise move (knight repositioning, king march, rook/queen misplacement) that throws away the win or drops material, so the constant peak is the rash queen check while the unifying outcome (missed win vs. hung material) blurs at medium.

874.label: Across all boards the player ignores a hanging/dangerous enemy rook the position demands taking; at the peak it's a clean one-move rook grab (Rxf2, Qxg7, Nxe7, Qxe2, Qxc3, Nxe6, Nxg2) whose neglect — usually via a pawn-grab, lesser capture or retreat — drops material or allows mate, while medium blurs to rooks won through 2-3 move combinations, defensive rook-handling, or even missed forced mates.

905.label: At the peak the move hangs a minor piece (knight on boards 2-4, bishop on 7/9) by leaving it—or its sole defender (often the king)—en prise; at medium it broadens to hanging a pawn, usually by vacating the square that defended it (b7/e6/a2/c5/f5) or pushing into a capture, while ~4 top boards instead lose tempo or grab greedily and merely miss the decisive move.

907.chip: Threw away won position (breakthrough→any forcing win)
907.label: Top boards are winning endgames where a passive 'safe' move skips the single forcing passed-pawn breakthrough or promotion (e5+, g4, e2)—or mispushes/hangs the passer—while medium broadens to any squandered win: missed forks and forced mates, deflection/discovered-attack tactics, and misplaced pieces that drop material across both middlegame and endgame.

899.label: Top: rook greedily captures a (often defended) pawn and is recaptured, dumping the exchange or a whole rook for one pawn; medium broadens/flips to a greedy queen capture of a rook that wins material but throws away a forced mate.

909.label: Top boards are captures (pawn or piece) that open a file/diagonal toward the player's own king or strip a key defender, hanging material or allowing a forced mate; medium blurs this to include quiet defender-vacating moves (Rf2, Nc3) and pure structural/positional errors with the same self-exposing effect, plus several already-lost boards where the flagged move is near-best.

906.label: At the peak, boards consistently hang the player's own material (rook, knight, or pawn) via a quiet non-capturing move that vacates a defended square or ignores an opponent threat, letting the unit be taken (often over a 2-3 move refutation); at medium strength it blurs into passive/retreating tempo-losing moves that surrender the initiative or a forced win without immediate material loss.

908.label: Top boards hang a whole piece (rook/bishop/knight) en prise in a winning position—often by moving the piece's sole defender or grabbing the wrong capture; medium broadens to losing a pawn or the exchange via short refutations (decoys, forks, rook invasions, queenside-castle/king-walk that abandons a2), still rooted in leaving one's own material undefended.

911.label: Top boards are bishop captures (a few checks) made from a winning position that leave own material hanging — usually the queen — for a devastating recapture; medium blurs this into pawn breaks/pushes (g4, e5, exf6) and other forcing moves that squander the advantage, sometimes by missing a stronger capture or forced mate rather than directly hanging a piece, so the direction is genuinely mixed between 'hangs' and 'missed'.

904.label: Top: a greedy material-grabbing capture eliminates the player's own critical defender/blocker (or ignores a stronger in-between threat), collapsing the position within a few moves; medium blurs the 'capture' element to knight relocations and wrong-piece captures that likewise abandon a key defensive or tactical resource.

892.label: Top is razor-sharp: a forcing check captures a rook with the queen (Qxe1+/Qxd8+/Qxe8+/Qxd1+) but the queen is instantly recaptured, converting a winning position into a queen-for-rook loss; medium blurs the target/direction — same 'sees a forcing capture-check' impulse but broadening to hanging the queen for a mere pawn, trading rooks into a lost endgame, wrong-piece recaptures, and even grabbing material with check while missing a forced mate (missed-win), so it spans both hung-material and missed-win cases.

913.label: Top boards are slow/passive moves — retreats or pawn pushes (b5, Ba4, Bh4, Bh5, g5) — that ignore a live tactic and hang the player's own material (trapped queen, lost piece, dropped pawn); medium boards keep the passive/tempo-wasting move but blur toward king-safety lapses where the quiet move instead walks into a forced mate.

915.label: Top boards are uniformly premature passed-pawn advances in winning/drawing endgames that get blockaded or captured because the king/pieces weren't activated first; medium broadens to any premature pawn push that squanders the edge — overextensions opening invasion squares, tempo/king-direction errors, and even a middlegame passed-pawn lunge.

918.label: Top boards uniformly decline a forcing QUEEN check that delivers mate or wins major material against an exposed king, choosing a quiet centralizing/non-forcing move instead; medium boards keep the same 'pass up the killing king-attack' theme but broaden the missed forcing resource to pawn checks (a4+), rook checks (Rd8+), wrong-direction queen checks, and even non-checking mating moves (Re3 prep).

903.label: Top is uniform — a rook recapture/trade on the first rank removes the last back-rank defender and walks into a forced back-rank mate; medium blurs to any greedy or simplifying capture that strips the sole guard of a key square/piece, yielding a back-rank or king-side mate (or, in a couple, decisive material loss to a fork/pin).

914.label: Top boards are passive/loose ROOK moves that throw away the rook's own activity (occasionally hanging or trading it) and convert a drawn or defensible (often endgame) position into a loss; medium broadens to king and pawn moves that surrender rook activity in the same way—missing one's own rook's role or, more often, allowing the opponent's rook to infiltrate (7th-rank/cut-off/back-rank)—plus a few greedy rook grabs, with the rook remaining the decisive piece throughout.

912.label: At the peak the player squanders a won game by failing to grab a hanging enemy queen (free capture, often with check or forced mate, occasionally instead playing a king move or grabbing a lesser piece); medium activations keep the same 'ignore the free winning capture' idea but blur the target from queen to a hanging rook/exchange.

916.label: Top boards are near-pure king/rook passed-pawn races where one exact move was required—push/support one's own passer or get the king to the critical square (Kd2, a2, g2, Kb7) to win the promotion race; medium broadens to other pieces and adjacent promotion/tempo errors (wrong promotion capture hxg7, wasted king tempo, abandoned-file rook moves, even a missed forced mate).

920.label: Top boards are uniformly a skipped free capture of the opponent's hanging queen (usually Nxd4/Nxd5-style knight grabs, plus Bxg5/Nxe6/Qxd4), where a quiet developing move throws away a winning advantage; medium positions blur this to broader missed queen-winning tactics — a queen-pinning Bb5 instead of Bd5, an exchange-winning Bxg7, and even a 'natural' attacking move (Nf3) that abandons a blockade and walks into a forced mate.

924.label: Top: a freshly developed bishop is dropped on g4/g5 where it hangs for free to the enemy queen (Qxg4/Qxg5); medium keeps the 'hang a just-developed bishop' core but blurs the destination square (c5, f4, h3, b5) and the capturing piece (queen, bishop, or knight, sometimes after a short tactic strips the defender).

921.label: Top boards near-uniformly miss a forcing queen-check sequence (Qd5+/Qh5+ off the exposed f7 king) that wins the undefended c5 bishop, playing a safe developing move (usually O-O) instead; medium blurs to missing other material-winning continuations (knight on e4, a passed/wedge pawn) across middlegame/endgame, with rare outliers that actually hang own material.

917.label: All boards are self-inflicted material losses; the TOP is dominated by structure/king-weakening f-pawn pushes (…f6/f4/f3 inviting Qh5+/Re1) plus a few undefended developed pieces (Bg5, Bg4, Nb4), while MEDIUM blurs to varied pieces and pawns (Nc4, Ng4, fxe5, d3, h5) that ignore threats or walk into forks/pins, so the unit lost and the mechanism vary.

919.label: Top boards miss a clean forced mate or queen-winning combination in a won endgame, opting for a passive/greedy move that throws the win away; medium blurs to any missed decisive forcing continuation in the endgame—material-winning tactics, slower conversions, or even the only-saving capture.

925.label: Top boards are uniformly opening Bg4/Bg5 sorties whose bishop is won via deflection (Nxf6+/Nxf3+) or a pawn kick (f3/f6); medium keeps the loose-bishop-development idea but blurs the square (Bb4, Bf4, Bf5, Bh4, Bd5) and mixes in pure tempo losses and missed Ng5/Bxf7 wins.

927.label: Top boards uniformly hang a minor piece (bishop/knight) left en prise to a direct enemy pawn capture, usually after an h-pawn push or quiet move ignores the attack; medium keeps the hung-minor-piece core but broadens the loss to trapped knights and short multi-move refutations rather than a single pawn grab.

910.label: At the peak, the feature is a queen check (100%) in a decisive endgame that backfires—most often allowing a forced queen trade into a lost pawn endgame, but also wasting a tempo instead of grabbing a free pawn or simply hanging the queen; at medium activation the queen-and-check constants both dissolve, broadening to any backfiring endgame move (king walks, rook moves, quiet non-checks) that squanders a winning/drawn result or walks into mate.

929.label: Top boards: failing to resolve the Bg4–Nf3 pin with the thematic Bxf3, dropping a minor piece in the multi-move refutation (Nxd4 then Bxg4, or exf3) or fatally exposing the uncastled king; medium broadens to wider mishandling of the same f3/c3 tension—knight forks (Nxe5, Nxd4), hanging queen/bishop elsewhere, and skipped Bxf3/Bxc3 wins—so the f3-pin is constant at the peak but the resulting mistake type blurs.

928.label: Top boards consistently play a passive, materially-safe move that overlooks a clear winning knight capture/fork (Nxf3+, Ne6+, Nxc6/Nd5, Ne2+) winning the exchange, a piece, or the queen; medium boards broaden to other missed winning shots (Ne4, Bxf3, Qxe5, en-passant fork) and increasingly blur into quiet moves that also concede material to the opponent's pin or fork in the refutation.

931.label: Top: in a losing/critical endgame the player's KING move lets the opponent's passed pawn queen — classically walking into promotion-with-check (c1=Q+) or failing to capture/blockade/keep the lone defender of the runner; medium keeps the king-misplay core but broadens beyond pure promotion to general king-exposure blunders (king walking into checks, a mating net, or a fork) that concede material or decisive counterplay.

922.label: Top boards are aggressive opening pawn thrusts (e5/f5/e4) that collapse an equal-or-winning position by ceding key squares or walking into a fork; medium broadens to king-exposing pawn pushes (f3/g4) inviting a crushing ...Qh4+ attack plus a greedy ...Qxd4 that hangs a piece.

923.label: Top: from a winning position, misses the precise c-file knight capture Nxc6/Nxc3 that wins material—via a slow move or wrong move-order; Medium: broadens to other missed/mis-executed forcing captures (wrong-piece grabs like Nxf7/Nxg5, a missed pawn break, even a missed mate).

939.label: Top boards cleanly hang a piece (often a bishop captured back via a shared diagonal, plus knight/queen hangs and fork traps) to an overlooked recapture/refutation; medium boards blur the piece type and bleed into missed wins, bad trades, and endgame/tempo slips rather than clean hangs.

930.label: Top boards are tightly constant: the player declines the free, undefended b-pawn via Bxb2/Bxb7 on the fianchetto long diagonal (a sharply winning capture); medium activations blur this to other long-diagonal captures (Bxc3, Bxg2, Qxb7) and related fianchetto-diagonal motifs, where the chosen move frequently also hangs the player's own material (≈39% hangs vs 43% safe-but-missed-win), making direction mixed.

932.label: Top boards are quiet KING moves in clearly won endgames that hold the win but squander the fastest forced route (mate or promotion), with several near-zero-cp non-blunders mixed in; medium broadens to any quiet move (pawn/rook/minor) that lets the win slip slower or evaporate, plus a few that concede active counterplay/forks rather than purely missing speed.

934.label: Top: a natural opening move (castling/queen/bishop) consistently hangs own material to a forcing capture/recapture, with the pinned f3-knight and queen-losing recaptures recurring; medium keeps the 'hang in the opening' core but broadens the mechanism to knight forks (Nc7+/Nd5) and exchange-winning captures, with the hung piece type more variable.

937.label: Top: a king or piece move that deserts a key square near its own king (f7 recurs, also a8/f8), letting the opponent penetrate for a decisive attack or forced mate; medium: the same desertion-of-defense idea broadens to any guarded square, pawn, or piece anywhere (a2, b4, f3, d5, e-file, h6), allowing material loss or a strong attack rather than mate.

933.label: Top boards are uniform: a greedy pawn-grabbing capture (usually Qx/Rx/Nx) abandons a defensive duty and hangs an undefended own piece — queen, rook, or bishop — flipping a winning game to lost; at medium the pattern blurs to any defense-shirking move (often still a capture, but also weakening retreats/king moves) that drops material OR exposes the king to a winning attack/mate.

936.label: Top boards uniformly miss the elementary h-pawn capture hxg4/hxg5 that snares a hanging bishop on g4 in a winning position; medium boards broaden to missing the forcing material-winning move generally — the target piece (g4/f4 knight) and the winning shot (gxf4, b4 fork, Nd4+ sac, right capture bxc4) blur while the 'winning, quiet move thrown the win away' core stays constant.

945.label: Top boards consistently throw away an immediate forced checkmate (M1/M2) via a natural pawn push or king move; medium broadens to natural moves that skip a forcing material win (e.g., winning the queen by check) rather than mate, while a couple of outlier boards instead hang own material (e7 dropping the queen, Rc1 allowing Bxb4+).

941.label: Top boards directly hang a full minor piece (most often a knight) en prise for an immediate free capture; medium broadens to hanging pawns and undefended units, pieces lost over 2-3 moves via removed defenders or allowed forks, plus a few slower positional/tempo blunders.

940.label: Top boards consistently skip the tempo-gaining Nd5/Nd4 knight jump to the central outpost that hits the enemy queen and sets up the Nxc7 exchange-winning fork (a few instead use the wrong piece, e.g. Qd5, or hang material by allowing the opponent's own Nd5); medium boards broaden the same theme to other knight forks—winning the queen via Nxe2/Nxc2+—plus a couple of off-pattern tactical lapses (a missed mate-defense and an endgame exchange loss).

947.label: Top: an overlooked forced mate-in-one delivered by a queen capture (overwhelmingly Qxg2#, also Qxh7#/Qxc7#/Qxg7#), with the player making an irrelevant non-capturing move instead; medium broadens to longer forced mates and rook-led/rook-initiated mating sequences (e.g. Rcxb2+ mate-in-3, Rxg7+ sacrifice) that are likewise abandoned.

938.chip: Hangs exchange grabbing a pawn (or mate)
938.label: Top boards are uniformly a capture that grabs a (usually passed/advanced) pawn but opens a file or invites a recapture, losing a rook or the exchange; medium keeps the greedy pawn-grab-recaptured core but blurs to include defender-removing or quiet moves that hang a pawn, allow a fork, or walk into back-rank mate.

949.label: In a won opening the player makes a quiet developing/retreating move and overlooks a decisive queen blow; at the peak it's almost always a queen CHECK (Qe5+, Qxe5+, Qh5+, Qxd4+, Qxf7#), while medium positions blur to include non-checking queen captures/forks (Qxd4, Qa4+) that still win material or mate.

935.label: Top boards are uniform winning openings where the player retreats an attacked bishop (or develops/blocks) and overlooks that the attacking enemy knight is itself undefended, skipping a free-piece queen capture Qxh5/Qxh4 (two boards instead miss a Bxf7+ sacrifice); at medium the direction flips and broadens — quiet 'safe' moves now hang the player's OWN bishop (or knight) to an enemy knight, with a few outliers in trapped-piece, king-safety and endgame themes.

943.label: At the peak the player declines a forcing queen trade/capture (mostly Qxd5-style exchanges, plus Bxh4 grabbing the queen) in favor of a slow non-forcing move; at medium it broadens to skipping minor-piece captures (Bxe6, Bxf5, Nxe4) and exchange sacs — with downstream outcomes genuinely split ~50/50 between hanging own material and simply missing the win.

950.label: Top boards are won/better positions where the player skips the one precise winning continuation—usually a knight fork (occasionally a bishop fork); medium broadens to other missed forced wins (mate-in-one, decisive tactical strikes/desperados) with some cases also hanging the player's own material.

942.label: Top boards are queen-harassing bishop sorties (Bg4/Bg5/Bc5) that hang an undefended edge pawn (b7/b2/g7) or the bishop itself via an Nxf6+ deflection; medium blurs the target (g2, the bishop directly, captures like Bxg4/Bxd6) and the piece (knight moves like Ne4/Bxc3), with a ~38% tail that merely wastes tempo letting the harassed queen improve.

953.label: Top: in a clearly won position the player skips a forced checkmate (back-rank/king-safety mates) in favor of a slow queen-chasing or 'kick the queen' tempo move; medium blurs from mate to skipping a material-winning forcing tactic, where a move-order/tempo slip (Nxg7+ first) wastes the win and even concedes material.

954.label: Top boards consistently pass up a clean forced checkmate (mate in 1-5, king already boxed in) to snap off the queen; medium blurs to skipping any stronger winning tactic—mates, pins, royal forks, intermediate checks—by grabbing material (usually the queen, sometimes a knight).

948.label: Top boards are almost all self-inflicted queen drops, where a move walks the queen onto a square (or leaves it loose) that loses it to a discovered check or intermezzo refutation; medium broadens to losing the rook/exchange via knight- and queen-forks and to king-safety/back-rank collapses, so the constant queen-hang at the peak blurs into general material loss (and mate allowances) at medium.

955.label: Top: declines a defensive queen trade (Qxc6/Qxe6/Qxe7/Qxe5/Qxf6/Qxe3, plus a couple rook trades) and instead plays a king/queen move that hangs a piece or invites a decisive attack; medium broadens to skipping any material-saving exchange or defensive move (e.g., f3 instead of rescuing the e3-bishop), still losing material.

952.label: At the peak the move leaves a piece—almost always the queen—en prise for an immediate one-move capture (with a couple of rook trades into lost K+P endgames); at medium it broadens to losing one's own major piece (queen or rook) via a short 2–3 move forced refutation—knight forks, opened h-files, undefended pieces—plus a few borderline queen-trade/king-walk-into-mate cases.

944.label: Top boards consistently hang a MAJOR piece—usually a rook, sometimes the queen—via a greedy capture or careless move that's met by an immediate free recapture, converting an already-worse position into a lost one; medium boards blur this to minor pieces and the exchange, with more careless placements (not just captures) and positional/tempo overreaches that bleed material over 2-3 moves.

962.label: Top boards are uniform: a queen move voluntarily offers/allows a queen exchange that liquidates a decisive attacking queen and converts a winning or holding position into equality/loss; medium broadens to queen moves that also hang the queen outright or allow a trade-enabling tactic (knight fork, rook-collection) or skip a more forcing queen line.

956.label: At the peak it's the opening dxe7 grab that hangs the queen to Bxf2+; at medium it broadens to endgame king/pawn mishandling (e.g. Kd2) that lets a passed pawn promote — both throw away a clearly winning position into a loss, but the piece lost and the mechanism differ.

960.label: Top: in a clearly winning passed-pawn endgame the player pushes a pawn (or makes a slow king move) instead of capturing the lone enemy piece blockading/stopping promotion, throwing away the win; medium: blurs into general winning pawn-race imprecision (advancing rather than the exact winning capture), and several flagged moves are actually near-0cp non-blunders.

959.label: Top boards are aimless king/rook shuffles that ignore a live tactic and hang a rook (occasionally bishop/knight), usually also skipping the winning/saving capture; medium blurs the dropped material to the queen, an allowed back-rank/promotion mate, or a pawn lost in a rook endgame.

951.label: Top boards consistently inject a pointless check instead of the forcing capture that wins/holds material (capturing a hanging queen, rook, or bishop); medium blurs to other tempo-wasting or move-order errors—indirect attacks over direct captures, capturing before the key move, blockader/king misplacements—that skip the critical move and forfeit the advantage.

961.label: Top: in already-lost positions a piece or the king abandons its critical defensive square/duty and walks straight into a forced mate (king-safety dominant); medium blurs this into ordinary hung material and even passive/tempo-losing moves that squander a winning position (shading toward 'missed win').

957.label: Top: in a winning position, a safe/quiet move (passive retreat, castling, pawn push) misses a clean tactic—Bd4/Ra1/Rb1/Bc3/Rb8/c6—that traps or wins the exposed enemy queen; medium keeps the loose-queen theme but blurs from a clean trap to slower tempo-gaining harassment (Rg1/Rg3/Rb8) and other missed material wins, with a couple of cases actually hanging own material.

963.label: Top boards are slow king moves that skip the decisive ...f5/e5 kingside pawn break (forfeiting a win or draw); medium broadens to skipped queenside/other breaks (b4, c4, h4) plus one non-endgame consolidating-move tempo loss, with roughly half the boards being non-blunders where the king move is actually optimal.

965.label: Top boards uniformly skip an immediate one-move free capture of the undefended fianchetto bishop on h6/h3 (Bxh6/Nxh6/Bxh3) in favor of routine castling/development; medium blurs the win into multi-move tactics where Bxh6 deflects the queen to win a knight or the exchange, extends to other undefended bishops (Qxg4), and occasionally flips to actively hanging a piece.

966.label: Top boards are all greedy captures from a winning/better middlegame—usually grabbing or 'eliminating a dangerous' pawn—but the punishment is split (half miss a decisive material-winning capture like Nxe7/Kxc5/Bxd5/Nxe3, half hang own material into a mating net like Rxf2/Qxb6/g4/Qxf3); medium broadens beyond captures to quiet/positional misplays (Rd5, Kd6, Rxd5) that likewise let a winning or equal position slip.

964.label: A bishop or queen move that walks straight into the opponent's immediate refutation (queen check, pin, or trap); at the peak the punishment is most severe—forced mate or outright queen loss—while medium activations keep the same self-inflicted blunder but the loss blurs down to a bishop, the exchange, or a pawn (with one outlier being a missed winning tactic).

973.label: Top boards are textbook early rook lifts to the 3rd/6th rank that sit undefended and get grabbed by a bishop for the exchange; medium broadens to other active rook relocations (5th/2nd rank) that drop material, not always via a direct bishop capture and sometimes over several moves.

967.label: Top: a materially-safe queen move (usually a check) throws away a clean forced mate by not using the more forcing piece — a rook/bishop/knight check that mates or wins a piece; Medium: same wrong-piece queen check/centralization, but the missed prize blurs from forced mate to simply winning material or a big advantage (e.g. Rxf1+, Ne4+, Bxf7+), with a couple of cases shading toward defensive collapse.

968.label: Top: in an already-lost endgame, a pawn advance or capture that concedes a pawn or wrecks own structure, accelerating the loss; medium keeps the lost-endgame frame but blurs from pure pawn pushes to any move (king/knight/rook) that hangs material or merely hastens the inevitable defeat.

972.label: Top: in a won position, skips a simple free capture of a hanging enemy piece (often a pawn or minor capturing higher material) and plays a materially-safe non-decisive move; medium: broadens to skipping the single best move (a suboptimal capture or a positional/tactical only-move) that squanders the winning advantage.

971.label: Top: a winning king attack—often a forced mate—is thrown away by a slow, move-order-flawed, or tempo-losing move (e.g. Rg3 vs Rh2, premature Rh8+, walking the king into the attack), occasionally also hanging own material; medium broadens to greedy pawn/piece grabs and passive queen/bishop retreats that abandon the mating attack for material or safety.

979.label: Top boards are clean one-ply hangs—an aggressive-looking developing/attacking move (Bd3, Bf5, Ne4, d5, Bg6) drops a piece, queen, or pawn the opponent simply grabs; medium boards blur to material lost over 2-3 moves via pawn pushes, king-weakening, and tempo losses (with a couple of missed-win recaptures rather than outright hangs).

975.label: Top boards uniformly castle directly into a prepared attack or forced mate (king fatally exposed); medium boards broaden to other king-exposing moves—queen retreats that abandon defensive squares, pawn pushes that strip the shield, back-rank lapses—occasionally blurring into plain material loss rather than a pure king assault.

970.label: Top: a slow/greedy/natural move overlooks an immediately available decisive forcing shot, almost always a mate-in-1 (Qxh7#, Rh3#, Qb3#) — peak is the player's own missed mate; Medium broadens to other overlooked decisive forcing resources — knight forks (Nxd5), missed winning continuations (Qxf7), longer forced mates (mate-in-5), and allowed opponent mates — with endgame outliers missing perpetual/passed-pawn/stalemate draws, so direction blurs between missing one's own win and permitting the opponent's.

981.label: Top boards reliably hang a piece — usually a bishop left undefended, often by walking its guarding queen/rook off duty (Qb8, Qc2, Re1); medium blurs to hanging rooks, greedy grabs that trap a piece (Bxa2, cxd5), plus a few pure tempo/king-safety squanders and one missed tactic.

976.label: Top boards consistently skip an immediately available rook-capturing move (Nxe7/Bxd6/Bxd8/Nxc2) that wins the exchange, instead playing a quiet pawn or king move; medium keeps the 'failed the one critical move' core but blurs the target—broadening to other winning captures (Nxd7/Nxd5, or the wrong capture) and even position-saving/positional necessities (stopping promotion, avoiding f5) rather than strictly an exchange grab.

946.label: Top boards are opening knight moves that retreat or recentralize an attacked knight instead of the thematic ...d5 break, hanging it or throwing away a winning/equal eval; medium keeps the 'wrong move squanders the win' core but broadens to any piece or pawn (rook, bishop, king, pawn pushes/captures) across all phases, mixing outright hangs, allowed attacks, and a couple of missed wins.

982.label: At the peak the player surrenders an active centralized KNIGHT — either trading off the strongest piece / skipping a stronger tactic or hanging it outright — converting a winning position into equal-or-losing; at medium activation the surrendered piece blurs to bishop, rook or even a pushed passed pawn, and the mechanism splits more evenly between self-inflicted hangs and missed-win trade-downs.

983.label: Top boards voluntarily exchange rooks (Rx-) into a lost/drawn king-and-pawn (or minor-piece) endgame, surrendering the rook's active counterplay when a non-trading move held the edge; medium blurs to trading other pieces (e.g. a bishop) that likewise abandons a winning position/tactic.

926.label: At the peak the player invariably surrenders the queen (≈80%) or rook to a simple king recapture (Kx…), throwing away an available forced mate for a 'merely winning' position; at medium activation this broadens to giving up any piece—rook, knight, bishop, or even a non-recaptured queen—to assorted recaptures, and to abandoning a clearly-winning advantage or easier endgame conversion rather than a strict forced mate.

978.label: Top boards are uniformly missed knight forks (Ne2+/Nd6+/Nb6+) where a safe, passive move skips an outright win of the enemy queen; medium holds the 'missed winning tactic' core but broadens the motif to rook forks, pins, discovered attacks, and forced mates—still typically netting the queen or a major piece.

984.label: Top boards are pawn pushes/captures that misjudge the resulting king-and-pawn endgame (drawn/lost when assumed safe), throwing away a won/drawn position; medium broadens to king, knight and queen moves that release a blockader, hang a piece, or simplify into a lost knight endgame.

969.label: Top: in a clearly winning endgame a careless rook/king/pawn move (often a reflexive check) leaves the rook en prise, dropping into a lost king-and-pawn ending; medium keeps the hung-rook pattern but broadens to king moves that simply squander the win, including a king-safety blunder that loses the advantage without a direct material loss.

988.label: Top boards uniformly skip the forcing d4 central break that exploits the opponent's uncastled king to win material, opting for a slow developing move (Nbd2/b3/Bb2/d3); medium blurs to other thematic pawn breaks/forcing shots (d5, e5, fxe5, f4, even a winning capture) where the slow move likewise surrenders a winning advantage rather than always being d4 against an uncastled king.

980.label: Top boards consistently play a quiet/slow non-forcing move (usually a queen or pawn reposition like Qb3, Bb4, Rab1, Qa4, f3) that skips an available forcing tactical break and squanders a winning/favorable position while material stays safe; medium boards blur this into passive moves and careless captures that not only skip the critical move but actively hang a pawn/rook/piece (c6, Nxh5, Rd8, Qxd4) or expose the king to a forcing attack/mate (d3, Ra2, fxe5).

987.label: At the peak the move is a passive king walk (with some queen redeploys/captures) that ignores a decisive threat, giving immediate checkmate or hanging the queen/major piece; at medium it blurs into other non-defensive moves — rook shuffles, castling, pawn pushes, plus an occasional missed free capture — that leak material or tempo rather than always mate.

986.label: Top: in clearly winning endgames the player squanders the result with a premature check or aggressive king move instead of the one decisive continuation (passed-pawn push or rook activation), occasionally even hanging the game outright; medium broadens to passive/retreating king moves and wrong-pawn advances that throw away wins and must-hold draws alike.

977.label: Top boards play a materially-safe, passive move instead of an immediate decisive resource—almost always a promotion (often with check) or other forcing pawn-race win—throwing away a guaranteed win; medium boards blur the resource into other skipped critical moves (forcing queen trade, free capture, or the single only-move needed to hold), and several activations are really hangs where the passive move lets a fork/discovered attack win back material over the refutation.

985.label: Top: a materially-safe slow/preparatory move (developing, repositioning) instead of the one forcing pawn capture (fxe5/cxb6/exf5/bxc4) that resolves central, queenside, or kingside tension on the player's own terms, ceding the favorable break and squandering a winning edge; medium blurs into other tension-mishandling moves — wrong pawn pushes, premature breaks, or piece retreats — that surrender the structure and frequently hang material outright (queen/knight/pawn) rather than merely losing the initiative.

992.label: Top boards peak on overlooking the forcing Nd3+ knight fork (with a recurring cluster of bishop-sac checks like Bxh2+/Bxh7+/Bxf2+) that wins the queen or saves a lost king, while a quiet pawn/king move is played instead; medium blurs to other forcing-check resources (Bxb5+, Bxe3+ deflection) where the quiet move then allows mate or drops material.

991.label: Top: uniformly opening positions where a quiet developing/repositioning move ignores CENTRAL pawn tension and lets the opponent's d5/e4/fxe6-type break win material or decisive advantage; medium blurs to flank and middlegame pawn breaks plus broader critical-moment lapses (allowed forks, missed captures/mates, structural collapse) where the same 'wrong quiet move at the tension point' theme persists but the break is no longer strictly central.

989.label: At the top, the player uniformly forgoes a decisive centralizing knight leap (almost always Nd5, sometimes Nxb5) in a materially-safe winning position, choosing a slow/passive move (b3, f3, Be3, Bg5, Rb1) and surrendering the win; at medium the pattern blurs to other winning knight jumps/forks (Nc1, Nf5, Nd4) and even non-knight wins (pawn breaks d5/e7), and several boards cross from merely missing the win into actively hanging material in the refutation.

995.label: Top boards constantly ignore an immediate decisive threat by either hanging the queen (left en prise on a diagonal/file or grabbed-piece distraction) or walking into forced mate; medium keeps the same 'ignore the lethal threat' theme but blurs the victim—more king-safety moves that step into forced mate, plus an outlier missed-win tactic and a couple of plain material drops.

994.label: At the top the player queens straight into capture or loses the promotion race (new queen/pawn immediately taken, throwing away a won endgame); at medium it blurs to premature pawn pushes and king/rook tempo errors that wreck the same winning conversion.

997.label: Top boards uniformly leave an undefended bishop en prise to a pawn capture in the opening (bxc5 in the Evans, dxc4, exf4/gxf4) or an unsound Bxf2+ sac; medium keeps the bishop-to-pawn hang (bxc4, cxb4, gxf4) but blurs toward broader neglected opening tactics, occasionally just missing a free pawn or allowing a tactical fork.

999.label: Top boards consistently surrender a dominant/blockading knight via a bad voluntary trade (giving up a winning endgame, attack, or passed-pawn restraint); medium boards blur this into outright hanging the knight for a pawn (Nxb6/Ne3) and a weakening positional pawn push that loses the outpost.

998.label: Top: in the opening Black/White passively develops or retreats a minor piece (Nf6, Be7, Nf3) instead of the freeing ...d5 (or correct) central break, mishandling the d4/e5 (or e4/d5) tension and hanging the central pawn—or sometimes a bishop—to dxe5/Nxe5/cxd4 over 2-3 moves; medium keeps the 'wrong move, hangs material in the opening' core but blurs the cause beyond pure pawn tension—allowing a knight fork (Rd1→Nf2+), blocking a key file (Bd6), exposing the king (g6, f3), or just a passive offside bishop—so the lost unit and mechanism vary (pawn→piece, push→fork).

990.label: Top boards: a rook (sometimes queen) snatches a passed pawn in the endgame and is lost to an immediate recapture (Rxe5+, axb7+, Kxb7), turning a win or draw into a bare-king draw or a lost K+R-vs-K; medium narrows to the same rook-grabs-passed-pawn case (one example is actually only near-equal/mislabeled).

1004.label: At the peak the move ignores a direct attack and drops the queen to an unblocked bishop/knight along an open diagonal; at medium the loss broadens to other hung pieces (bishop, knight), self-blocks/back-rank, and king-safety collapses from unaddressed threats.

1005.label: Top boards retreat the queen instead of an available queen trade/capture, hanging a pawn (occasionally a rook or full piece) on the abandoned diagonal/file; medium boards keep the same trade-avoiding queen move but broaden the cost to a trapped queen or a squandered winning advantage.

1000.label: Top boards are uniformly missed mate-in-one delivered by a rook (lone outlier a winning-but-imprecise rook move); medium broadens to multi-move forced mates and missed winning lines delivered by queen, knight, or bishop as well.

1003.label: Top: a king-safety blunder—walking the king into the open or pulling away the only defender/perpetual-check resource—that abandons the sole saving line and allows a forced mate on one's own king; medium blurs to greedy pawn-grabs that ignore a mating threat and to defender-removals that lose decisively (or merely shorten survival) rather than always producing immediate mate.

1002.label: Top: clearly-winning positions where a single free, undefended enemy knight/rook (occasionally queen) is ignored in favor of a passive king step, throwing away the grab; medium broadens to also include hanging bishops, smaller-margin or multi-move capture wins, and other quiet non-capturing moves that skip the free piece.

996.chip: Hangs material via loosening pawn move (top: central capture)
996.label: Top boards are uniformly central d/e-pawn captures that prematurely release the tension and open a file or long diagonal the opponent immediately exploits (recapture-with-tempo, Bxb2/Bxc3+, discovered attacks) to win the player's own material; medium blurs the move-type, adding flank pawn pushes (b3, b6, a5, c5) and even piece retreats (Nd8, Be6) that remove a defender or open lines for the same material loss, plus a couple of materially-safe cases that merely squander a winning advantage (missed win).

1009.label: Top boards uniformly miss the crushing Qh4+/Qh5+ queen check against an uncastled/exposed king—instead grabbing material or playing a safe knight retreat; medium blurs this to other winning forcing checks and tactics exploiting the same exposed king (Bxd5+, Qxe5+, Nh4+, or slow moves skipping the Qh5+ shot).

1010.label: Top boards are uniformly queen relocations/centralizations that lose own material (queen trapped/won, or a defended knight/pawn abandoned); medium broadens the same 'repositioning into material loss' to other pieces (bishop, rook, knight, even a pawn push), where the moved or vacated piece gets won over 1-3 moves.

1006.chip: Hangs piece via greedy capture (often queen)
1006.label: Top boards consistently lose/hang the QUEEN after a greedy or wrong capture that abandons the attack or unblocks a defended line; medium boards broaden to hanging minor pieces and several materially-safe moves that miss a bigger capture or winning sacrifice.

993.label: Top: consistently neglects the opponent's passed pawn—failing to blockade, capture, or out-race it (or build a counter-passer)—so it queens and decides the game; medium keeps the passed-pawn core (promotion still common) but blurs into any neglected decisive threat, adding back-rank/mating shots and pure positional/structural concessions.

1001.label: Top: greedy capture of a poisoned piece beside one's own king (almost always gxh6, also bxa6/hxg6/gxh3) that rips open the pawn shield and lets the enemy queen crash in with a decisive/mating attack (Qxh6, Qxg6, Qxa6); medium blurs to any king-weakening or material-losing move — passive queen/king retreats (Qc8, Kg8) or pawn breaks that abandon h6, plus more general hanging pawns and positional/endgame slips that hand over the initiative.

1011.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a free capture of an en-prise rook in a losing position—playing a non-capturing king move instead; medium broadens to capturing other hanging pieces (e.g. bishop-takes-rook) and blurs further into king/pawn-direction blunders in already-lost endgames where no winning capture is available.

1013.label: Top boards are uniformly a premature BxN on f3/f6 that releases the tension, surrenders the active bishop, and converts the opponent's passive bishop into a long-diagonal monster (squandering a near-winning edge into equality); medium keeps the premature bishop trade but blurs across other capture squares (d4, c5, e4, g7, h4, g5) and shifts from merely giving up the advantage to occasionally hanging material outright.

1015.label: Top: a reflexive pawn-push CHECK that loses tempo and worsens the position (improving the enemy king's square, fixing/weakening the pawn structure, or hanging the pawn) instead of a quiet best move; medium broadens to tempo-wasting pawn advances WITHOUT check (b6, g4, f4) and even other purposeless tempo-checks/centralizations (Bd3+, Re3), still trading the quiet move for a self-damaging push.

1012.label: Top boards are all king moves from a winning position that walk into a decisive, usually mating attack (or block the king's own escape); medium broadens to other king-safety lapses—non-king moves (pawn/knight/rook) and softer cases that merely lose material or throw away the win rather than force mate.

1017.label: Top boards consistently hang a ROOK on a newly-open file/rank after a greedy capture or loose king move that converts a winning position to a loss; medium boards keep the same 'capture-then-hang' pattern but broaden the hung material to any piece (knight, bishop, queen) or even a pawn.

1008.label: At the peak the player declines an available forcing move — a capture, check, or promotion that delivers mate, a perpetual save, or wins material — in favor of a quiet/passive move (most often a king step), a pure omission with material left safe; at medium activation the pattern blurs from strict forcing tactics to simply missing the objectively best move, broadening to include quiet positional/king-safety improvements and pawn-grab avoidance where the best reply itself is not always forcing.

1021.label: Top: in critical only-move positions the player skips the unique forcing, material-winning tactic (exchange-win Bc3, knight fork Nxe6+/Ne6+, Rxf7+) for a plausible but empty move; medium blurs the same 'only-move' miss to include non-tactical only-saves and simplifications (defensive Bb5, queen-trade Qf3, centralizing Nd5), with a handful (Nxh5+ x2, Rb5) actively hanging material across the multi-move refutation.

1007.label: Top: a knight captures a centralized piece (Nxe5/Nxd5) and the pawn recapture forks two pieces—usually bishop+knight or queen+knight—dropping a full piece; medium broadens to other pieces capturing or advancing into a square where the pawn recapture wins material via single attack, pin, or opened file rather than a clean two-piece fork.

1016.label: Top: plays a quiet/developing move and misses a forcing QUEEN check (Qb4+, Qa4+, Qb5+, Qxc3+, or Qxf2#) that exploits the opponent's exposed/uncastled king to win heavy material or mate; medium broadens to knight-fork checks (Nxc2+) and other forcing tactics on the loose king, with a couple of boards instead self-hanging material into the enemy's exposed-king check.

1018.chip: Hangs material to discovered check (often queen)
1018.label: Top boards are tightly uniform: retreating the e-file-shielding knight or walking the king onto an open line/diagonal unmasks a discovered check that wins the queen; medium blurs the target and tactic — the same self-exposing king/shield move allows discovered checks (or pins, back-rank, exposure shots) that win a piece or force mate rather than always the queen.

1022.label: Top boards are all bishop retreats (Bb4/Bb3/Bb5) plus a rim-knight/rook shuffle that pass up a winning central knight capture (Nxd4/Nxd5/Nxe5/Nxe4); medium keeps the missed central knight grab (Nxd4/Nxd5/Nxe5) but broadens the skipping move to any quiet piece (rook, queen, king, pawn) and occasionally a non-knight central tactic (Nxc5, dxe4, Qh5+).

1024.label: Top: a greedy capture or pawn push that ignores a decisive threat hangs the queen (8/10, usually ...Bxh3/Bxf3) or walks into kingside mate (2/10); medium keeps the same materialistic, threat-blind capture/push but broadens the cost to a rook/exchange or king-attack — with a couple instances of merely missing a win.

1020.label: Top boards are pure move-order blunders—a flashy capture/check/fork is grabbed while ignoring a more urgent counter-capture that wins the player's queen or the exchange; medium broadens to general capture-priority errors: recapturing or capturing the wrong/lower-value piece, missing a free capture, or skipping a winning intermezzo, with the same own-material loss.

1014.label: Top boards skip a clear king recapture of a hanging rook or grab of a dangerous passed pawn in a lost endgame, playing an idle king move or pawn push instead; medium boards blur into general idle/wrong king-and-pawn moves that mishandle the endgame (losing opposition, abandoning a defended pawn, wasting tempo) rather than literally missing a capture.

1019.label: Top: captures with/trades off a strong active bishop for a passive enemy piece in an even trade, releasing tension or opening lines (b-/a-file) and throwing away a winning advantage instead of a stronger pawn thrust (d6/e5/g4), retreat, or developing move; medium blurs toward greedy bishop captures (often bishop-for-pawn or into a trap) that also lose material outright.

1025.label: Top boards are razor-sharp opening rim knight-sorties (Nh5/Nh4/Na5, plus Ng5/Na4) chasing an enemy bishop that hang the knight outright or abandon a central defender for a free piece; medium broadens to knight moves in any phase that vacate a key defender/outpost, conceding the exchange, queen, or just the advantage to a refuting tactic (fork, Bxb8, Bh5+).

1030.label: Top boards consistently vacate the defender of a pawn/piece or surrender an open file/key square, letting the opponent break through to win clean material (pawn, exchange, or even queen via fork/penetration); medium keeps the 'abandoned defensive duty' core but blurs the outcome — several are king-safety collapses ending in forced mate rather than material gain, plus a couple of trapped-piece and one missed-tactic cases.

1032.label: Top boards are king moves in already-lost rook endings — split between near-zero non-mistakes (often the engine's own best move) and catastrophic king walks into faster forced mate, a skewer, or a missed free-queen capture; medium blurs this further by adding non-king moves (pawn pushes like h4, a4) and other endgame types, so the only reliable constant is 'a king/pawn move in a losing endgame', with the actual mistake (if any) ranging from 2cp to forced mate.

1031.label: Top: trades/captures a rook immediately instead of first inserting a zwischenzug (intermediate check or pin) that wins extra material or forces mate; medium broadens to any premature capture/trade that skips a stronger winning continuation (an in-between fork like Ng4+, or a positional improving move like doubling rooks/Rfd1) rather than a pure zwischenzug.

1028.label: Top boards consistently desert the defender of a key piece, hanging a knight/bishop/queen to a tempo-gaining capture usually delivered with check or recovered by a fork; medium boards broaden to abandoning pawn/king defenders (hanging pawns or allowing knight forks) and blur into tempo-losses, trades, and missed passed-pawn pushes that merely squander the edge.

974.label: Top boards uniformly make a premature rook capture/trade (75% with check) that simplifies away a forced mate or winning tactic a quieter non-trading move would land (Rxf1+, Rxd1+, Rxc6, Rxg2+, Rxf8+, etc.); medium blurs the pattern outward—an unsound Rxh3+ sac in an already-losing position and even a non-capturing slow pawn move (...b5) that hangs the advantage to an opponent's fork—so the constant 'imprecise move throws away the win' holds but the specific 'rook trade with check' mechanism breaks down.

1029.label: Top: voluntarily marches the king into the open center (Kd2/Kd7/Ke7/Ke2/Kd1, or g6xh5 opening the king) into a forcing run of checks/mating net, almost always skipping the only defense g6/g3 that challenges the queen on h5/h4; medium broadens to other self-weakening moves — pawn pushes (g3, f4) or piece moves (Qf3, Na5, Bd7, Nbd2, Ke1) — that crack open lines or diagonals and hang material/expose the king to a decisive attack.

1034.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a free capture of the opponent's undefended queen—making a safe king/developing move or grabbing a lesser piece (rook/knight) instead—while medium positions broaden to missing other decisive winning resources (a hanging rook capture or a single precise winning move) rather than strictly the queen.

1026.label: Top boards are all forced checkmates ignored in favor of a materially-safe greedy capture (mate-in-1/short mates, grabbing queen/rook); medium blurs the prize from mate to any stronger forced continuation—knight forks, attacking tempo, faster mates—sometimes via retreats rather than captures (with one outlier that actually walks into mate).

1023.label: Top: in a drawn ENDGAME the player loses material—hanging a rook/piece by a greedy capture or by abandoning the sole defender of a promotion square so the opponent queens; MEDIUM keeps the 'balanced position turned lost' core but blurs the phase (adds opening/middlegame hangs like Bb5/Nd5) and the mechanism (tempo losses, passed-pawn races, deflection tactics) where the loss is sometimes a delayed promotion or positional collapse rather than an immediate hung piece.

1033.label: Top: in a winning position the player skips a clean queen capture (Qxd4/Qxe4/Qxf4/Qxf5+) that wins a full piece, playing a quiet developing/attacking move instead; medium keeps the available queen capture constant but blurs it into defensive queen grabs/sacrifices that were the ONLY move to avert a forced mate (Qxc7/Qxf4/Qxd2/Qxd4) — and occasionally the missed shot is a non-queen capture (Nxf7+/Ba4+).

1036.label: Top boards uniformly squander a forced checkmate by skipping a forcing king-side sacrifice (Qxh7+, Rxg7+, Rxh2+, Rxa7+) in favor of a slow/tempo-losing move; medium boards blur the same 'didn't play the most forcing line' error to include move-order/check-first sequences that win material rather than mate, and a couple of cases of failing to play the only defensive resource.

1038.label: Top: textbook Greek-Gift/Fried-Liver bishop sacs on the canonical squares f7/h7/h2/f2 (plus failing to rescue the f2-bishop) that the opponent simply accepts for a clean piece-for-a-pawn; medium keeps the same king-wing-sac-accepted theme but blurs to other capture squares (e.g. Bg6xh7) and plain ...Bxf2+ pawn-grabs, occasionally with marginal/'barely justified' compensation.

1041.label: Top: hangs a bishop in the opening by placing it on an immediately-capturable square for free (often greedy c7/a6/b7/h6 pawn grabs; one knight hang); medium blurs to general opening material loss — hanging pawns, undefending one's own piece, allowing a tempo/fork shot, or an unsound sacrifice, often refuted over 2–3 moves.

1035.label: Top boards are a move (usually a king tuck or a greedy capture) that ignores a forced mating attack on one's own king—often a back-rank mate; medium blurs the punishment from forced mate to slower material loss and positional/structural concessions, with the lost unit varying (king/queen/rook/exchange).

1039.chip: Missed free queen capture (sometimes for piece)
1039.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a one-move capture of the opponent's totally undefended queen (winning it for nothing on an open rank/diagonal); medium boards keep the hanging-queen theme but broaden to winning the queen for a minor piece, via a short forced sequence, or occasionally failing to rescue one's own en-prise queen.

1043.chip: Trades queen into lost endgame (or rook)
1043.label: Top boards liquidate the queen (usually a capture-with-check) into a lost king-and-pawn endgame, surrendering all checking/counterplay resources; medium broadens to trading the last rook into the same lost K+P endgame—though several top boards are actually fine trades (2,7) and a few are rook moves that simply hang material rather than trade (8,10).

1042.label: Top boards uniformly play a forcing queen check (often a queen-promotion check) that hangs the queen to immediate capture, throwing away a forced mate or won position; medium broadens to a rook check and to quiet/non-check queen moves, and to checks refuted by interposition rather than direct capture.

1027.label: Top boards are the same recurring position where the player skips the bishop capture (Bxg4) that removes a dominant knight and hangs the rook to an Ne3+ fork over 2-3 moves; medium boards blur this to a broader failure to neutralize a dominant knight (Bxc5/Bxc4/Bxc3/Nxe4), sometimes still a material-losing fork but often just conceding a powerful centralized outpost—so the dominant knight is the constant while the consequence (hung material vs. positional concession) is genuinely mixed.

1037.label: Top boards lose own material or allow queening with a passer one step from promotion—via vacating a key guard square, wrong capture, or wrong move order (with a couple of missed-win shots mixed in); medium broadens to general material-hanging moves (hanging a piece, walking into a double attack, weakening king safety) in passer-flavored middlegames that aren't always one square from promotion.

1045.label: Top boards capture/trade the last defensive queen into a king-and-pawn ending that's lost because the opponent's passed pawn promotes; medium broadens to the same fatal trade made with a rook (into a lost K+P or Q-vs-K ending).

1040.label: Top positions are razor-sharp and uniform: the player makes a passive king/rook move and overlooks an immediate capture of the opponent's totally undefended queen (Qxh5/Qxd2/Bxh7/Rxc1), usually throwing away a forced mate; medium positions blur this into generic catastrophic middlegame blunders—allowing forced mate via exposed king (Kf8/Kf2/Rd6), hanging own pieces to deflection/fork, or missing a mate-in-one (Qb8#)—rather than specifically a free queen grab.

1044.label: Top: a slow developing/prophylactic opening move ignores central pawn tension and skips a clean pawn-winning capture (dxe5/Nxe5/dxe4/dxc5) while the position is safe; Medium: same tension-neglect theme but blurs in outcome — sometimes still a missed pawn, sometimes it actively loses material (trapped knight Nh4, hung pawn b5) or collapses positionally (allows Qh5+, exf6, or bishop-chasing tempo loss).

1047.label: Top boards consistently play a move that ignores king safety and walks into a forced checkmate—almost always a back-rank mate boxed in by the king's own pawns (one outlier traps a rook)—squandering an equal/winning position; medium boards keep the king-exposure-into-mate theme but broaden to king-hunt mates and general king-safety collapses, with several merely losing material (hanging/trapped pieces, skewers) or even missing an endgame win rather than getting mated.

1049.label: Top boards are clean one-move hangs of a piece onto a square attacked by an enemy pawn (usually a bishop — Bf5/Bc4/Bf4 — plus pawn breaks like ...c5 that abandon a defender); medium boards blur into slower material/tempo losses, where a developing move walks into pawn-chasing (Bd3), ignores an already-attacked piece (Nc3 vs Bf4), or weakens with f3/f4 and concedes material/center over 2-3 moves.

1046.label: Top boards squander a forced mate or decisive tactic in an already-won position (peak cases miss a knight check/fork like Ne2+/Nc3+ or a clean mating sequence); medium blurs to natural moves—often a capture or 'forcing' check—that throw away a clearly winning edge via positional/tempo errors rather than a clean mate, with a couple of boards instead just trading/hanging the player's own piece, so human review is warranted.

1054.label: Top boards consistently play a slow/quiet move and miss an immediate winning bishop shot (frequently Bh6 or Bh5/Bc4/Bf3 pinning or winning the queen); medium broadens to other missed tactical blows — bishop attacks, a queen mate-in-one (Qb5#), and even a passive move that hangs a pawn.

1052.label: Top: a queen or bishop move hangs material by abandoning a defender or walking into a fork/capture (Qd5→Qxc7, Bc5→Rxc5, d6→Nxf7+), with a few boards instead missing a clean winning capture (Bxb3, Rxe2, Rxb2+); medium blurs into slower positional/tempo moves that drop a piece to a trap or squander a winning attack.

1056.label: Top: a natural quiet repositioning move (usually a queen relocation) in a roughly level/winning spot that overlooks the one decisive tactic—about half skip a winning shot (Nxf7/Nc3/Bxd2/Bxf4/Ng5+) and half desert a key attacker/defender so material hangs in the refutation; medium broadens the piece (knight/rook/bishop/king/pawn) and the motif (discovered attack, passed-pawn push, endgame king-walk), staying genuinely mixed between missed-win and hung-own.

1051.label: Top boards are uniformly self-inflicted bad bishop moves (Ba6/Bg5/Bh3/Bh6/Bb5/Ba3) to squares where the bishop is traded off or hangs, losing varied material (knight, pawn, exchange, or the bishop itself) often over a 2-3 move refutation; medium boards keep the losing bishop move but broaden the mechanism to abandoning a defender, tempo-loss, or greedy pawn-grabs, even slipping into the middlegame and one non-bishop move whose punishment merely runs through a bishop capture.

1050.label: Top boards are uniformly a knight planted on an undefended square in the opening and immediately snapped off by an enemy bishop; medium keeps the 'left a piece en prise for free' core but blurs the specifics — the hung piece can be a rook/bishop/queen-defended knight, the capturer can be a queen or long-diagonal bishop, and the loss may come via a tempo move, a trap, or a missed better capture rather than a one-ply opening grab.
