1055.label: Top: a completely won endgame where a king/pawn move loses only negligible tempo (~9-16cp) by skipping the most efficient promotion/centralization path; medium broadens to a still-winning but larger inaccuracy (capturing into +846 instead of taking a forced mate).

1059.label: In a winning/equal opening an overreaching developing or attacking lunge loses material: top boards are clean one-move piece hangs (a minor piece or queen left en prise to immediate capture, e.g. Ng5, Bg4, Bf4, Qd5), while medium boards blur into pawn/tempo lunges (c5, Qa5) and unsound sacs (Ncxe4) that drop the advantage rather than hang a piece outright.

1066.label: Top boards uniformly ignore a looming threat and walk into an immediate mate-in-1 (back-rank or exposed-king pattern); medium boards keep the same self-mating king-safety/back-rank blunder but broaden to forced mate-in-2/3 rather than strictly one move.

1061.label: Top boards are uniform queen-grabs (Bxd1) that walk straight into an immediate Bxf7#-style mate on the exposed king; medium blurs to other material grabs/defender-removals (knight or pawn captures) that allow a forced mate in 1-3.

1063.chip: Hangs material via bishop move (often Be3/Be6)
1063.label: Top boards are uniformly opening bishop developments to e3/e6 that hang material — Be3 inviting Bxe3/fxe3 to wreck the structure and expose the king, or Be6 walking into the d5 pawn-fork of bishop+knight; medium keeps the Be3 blunder but blurs into bishop relocations on assorted squares (Bg5, Bg4, Be2, Bb2, Ba6) that abandon a defender or walk into a tactic/trade, plus a couple of non-bishop moves and missed-win cases.

1048.chip: Greedy rook grab over forcing win (queen check/mate)
1048.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the rook makes a greedy capture (usually grabbing a piece/exchange) instead of the decisive forcing line—almost always a queen check or forced mate—squandering the win; medium broadens to a rook capture (even one giving check) that simply loses the exchange in an already worse, non-winning position.

1057.chip: Plays a losing check (often hangs piece)
1057.label: Delivers a pointless forcing check (usually a queen check) instead of the required quiet/capturing move; top boards constantly punish it by hanging a piece (knight/queen) or stranding it for a decisive material loss, while medium boards blur into pure tempo-loss, squandered wins, or bad trades where the king simply steps aside.

1064.label: Top boards are greedy material grabs (capturing a queen/rook/minor) that overlook an immediate forced mate while staying winning; medium broadens to non-capturing or wrong-piece moves — checks, pawn pushes, doubling rooks, or playing the right square with the wrong piece — that likewise downgrade a clean forced mate into a merely winning position.

1060.label: Top: a rook move squanders a forced mate by abandoning the key file/square that caged the enemy king, handing it an escape; medium keeps the same 'missed mate via freed king' theme but blurs the piece (adds queen/pawn/knight moves) and the mechanism (sometimes a greedy pawn-grab or even hanging material rather than a pure escape-square release).

1067.label: Top: in already-lost endgames the king drifts to the edge or out of play (Kh5/Ka6/Kh4/Ke1), converting a slow loss into forced mate or a lost K+P race with no material hung; medium broadens to king moves (plus a few piece moves) that also walk into checks/forks/skewers and directly lose material, sometimes from equal or merely difficult positions.

1072.label: Top is consistently a premature bishop sacrifice on f7 (Bxf7+) that drops a piece for a pawn to the trivial Kxf7 recapture; medium broadens the sacrificing piece (queen Qxf7+, knight Nxf7) and the target square (Bxf2/Nxf2, Nxc7+ pseudo-fork), all still refuted by a simple recapture with no attack.

1071.label: Top boards are materially-safe tempo losses — needless checks or king/pawn pushes in clearly winning passed-pawn endgames that at worst delay the forced result (mostly ≤7cp, ~half not real mistakes); medium blurs to include genuine tempo errors that actually squander a win or draw with large eval drops (Kh5, g4, b4, Be7), so the feature largely detects 'safe endgame move' rather than a true blunder.

1062.label: Top boards are near-uniform flank/wing pawn lunges (almost always ...g5, sometimes g4) thrown to chase White's bishop, hanging the pawn outright (Bxg5) or fatally exposing the king (Qh5+/Qh4+); medium blurs this to central pawn pushes (e5, d4, e6e5) and other piece-kicking moves chasing knights as well as bishops, where the refutation is often a fork or multi-move tactic rather than a plain capture, and some cases are positional/tempo concessions rather than clean material losses.

1069.label: Top boards consistently advance an endgame pawn that's immediately captured (hxg5/axb3/bxa5), flipping a draw or win into a loss; medium blurs to king/knight/rook moves that hang other material or only shed part of the advantage, with a few near-zero-cp false fires.

1053.label: Top boards are premature pawn captures/advances (fxg3, dxe5, e6, exd4+) that release tension or trade away the key attacking asset, dissolving a winning attack—sometimes a forced mate—into equality; medium blurs to bishop/knight trades, wrong recaptures, and tempting checks/forcing moves that likewise throw the win away.

1065.label: Top boards are consistently quiet/slow tempo-losing moves that squander a clearly winning position by skipping an immediate forcing pawn/central break (e3, d5, g6, f5, d3); medium blurs to only equal-or-better positions and broadens the missed resource beyond pawn breaks to tactics (pawn fork, mating net) while the punishment more often directly hangs a pawn or piece.

1068.label: Top boards are pure pawn/passed-pawn endgames where the king marches the wrong way—away from the kingside promotion/defense zone—and loses the pawn race without hanging material; medium keeps this wrong-direction king theme but blurs into slower tempo-losing king moves (some near-best) plus a few genuine tactical material losses (knight fork, hanging bishop, trapped queen).

1073.label: Top: a piece retreat from a dominant square (esp. the queen, also bishop/knight) overlooks a decisive forcing shot — a forced mate or material-winning capture; medium broadens to any quiet/passive move (pawn pushes like g4/c6, rook shuffles like Rb1/Ra8) that skips the winning tactic, and mixes in cases where the passive move instead lets the opponent's tactic crash through (~32% hang).

1058.chip: Failed to neutralize passed pawn (or break)
1058.label: Top boards constantly miss the specific neutralizing capture of a dangerous passed pawn (gxh5/axb6/cxd5/gxh6), letting it promote decisively; medium blurs to failing to resolve central pawn tension/breaks and mixes in looser tactical allowances (forks, hung rooks, tempo losses).

1074.label: Top boards are quiet king/queen moves that ignore capturing a hanging enemy QUEEN (e.g. Qxa2, Nxc4, Bxc2), often leaving the player's own queen hanging too; medium blurs the captured target to rooks/knights/pawns (cxd5, Rxc7, Qxc3) and the direction between 'missed the win' and 'hung own material', plus one speculative sac, so both piece and direction vary.

1070.label: Top boards uniformly skip the saving d-file queen trade (Qxd1/Qxd8) to defuse open-file pressure and instead hang their own queen/material or expose the uncastled king; medium broadens to skipped or wrong-order queen exchanges on other open files (h-, c-, a-, e-file, plus a few queen-safety retreats) that still leave the queen or material hanging in the refutation.

1077.label: Top boards uniformly hang the queen to an enemy ROOK on an open file/line (left en prise or moved onto it); medium boards still hang the queen but the capturing piece broadens to bishop/knight/rook, with a couple blurring toward tempo-losing/missed-win cases.

1079.label: Top: a routine opening move leaves the queen en prise to a bishop on an open g5-d8 or g4-d1 diagonal, captured instantly by Bxd8/Bxd1 (queen for bishop) — both via self-clearing the shield pawn/knight and via ignoring a standing bishop attack; medium keeps the identical queen-for-bishop loss but blurs to quiet developing/prep moves (c3, Nc6, Bg7) that simply ignore the pre-existing bishop on the diagonal.

1076.label: Top boards: a tempting capture—usually grabbing the queen—backfires by hanging material to a recapture, knight fork, or back-rank mate; medium boards blur the same impulse into trades/captures that throw away a clearly winning advantage without immediate material loss.

1083.label: Top: from a winning position the player ignores an undefended enemy queen they could simply capture (free queen, usually playing an idle king move instead), throwing away a forced mate; medium blurs the constant 'free queen' into missing the decisive winning move generally—a queen-capture-with-check, capturing a rook, the only winning quiet queen move, or a faster forced mate.

1081.label: Top: passes up a clean knight fork (Ne3/Ne6/Nf2) that wins the exchange by hitting queen and rook, choosing a quiet positional/developing move from a winning position; medium: same missed knight fork but the prize broadens beyond the exchange to a full piece (queen+bishop, or queen via a check-fork), with a few outliers that are self-hangs or non-knight tactics.

1080.label: Top: in a won endgame the player skips an immediate, free capture (usually an undefended rook) by pushing a pawn, shuffling the king, or giving a pointless check — the win is only delayed, not lost; medium broadens to free bishop/pawn captures, missed one-move mates, and faulty conversion/promotion technique, and bleeds into actually hanging one's own piece (Qa4/b4/Bf4).

1075.label: Top: in a winning middlegame the player fumbles a queen-centered decisive moment—half play a quiet king/queen move that squanders a forced mate, half actively hang or trade the queen (or grab material into mate); medium keeps the winning context but blurs toward king-safety collapses (king walks into mate) and broader tactical misses where the queen is involved but not always the lost piece.

1078.label: Top boards uniformly squander a winning passed pawn by advancing/promoting it prematurely instead of the precise capture-the-blockader, move-order, or promote-with-capture finesse, allowing a blockade or lost promotion race; medium blurs into broader passive or premature committal moves (passive rook placement, premature queen sortie, wrong pawn break) that squander a winning position and sometimes hang material rather than purely missing the win.

1085.label: Top: player invariably grabs material with the KING, skipping an available forcing check/mate (checks-before-captures) and either hanging the recapture or throwing away a forced win; medium broadens to captures with any piece (bishop, rook) plus pure move-order slips that likewise forgo the forcing winning line.

1089.label: Top: a side move (queen sortie, developing move, or premature knight thrust) ignores the central pawn tension and leaves the e5/d5 pawn to be grabbed by a simple capture (dxe5/exd5), losing a clean pawn instead of the forced ...exd4/exd5; medium blurs to the same theme via natural developing moves (Nf6, g6) and occasionally a missed tempo-gaining capture (cxd5) rather than outright material loss.

1093.label: Top boards are uniformly greedy queen captures of a pawn-defended piece (Qxc5/Qxd6/Qxg5) punished by instant pawn recapture for a minor piece or rook; medium broadens to hanging the queen any way — walking it onto a pawn-controlled square without capturing, or dropping it to a rook/knight, sometimes over a 2-3 move refutation.

1082.label: In drawn passed-pawn/promotion races the player makes a materially-safe pawn or king move that surrenders control of the race; top boards are dominated by tempo losses or king misplacement that abandon the defending piece's grip on the promotion square (often allowing a fork that wins the promotion-guard), while medium boards blur into wrong trades into lost/drawn pawn endgames, premature passer pushes that get blockaded, and hanging the blockading piece.

1095.label: Top boards are opening pawn moves that open a line — most often clearing a diagonal so a bishop captures the queen (Bxd8/Bxd1); medium broadens to any opening move hanging a piece or pawn via pins, forks, discovered attacks, or simple undefense.

1086.label: At peak the player skips a forced mate-in-one (overwhelmingly the h-file mate Qh2#/Qh1#) in favor of a quiet, non-forcing queen or king move; at medium it blurs into missing other decisive forcing resources in won/drawn endgames — a free rook (Qxf1+/Qxh1+), a saving perpetual, the correctly-directed mating check (Qh1+ vs Bd3+/Qd3+), or a faster mate — mixed with a few near-zero positional inaccuracies that share only the 'quiet move instead of the forcing line' surface pattern.

1084.label: Top boards uniformly miss exf6, the pawn-takes-queen capture that wins Black's en-prise queen on f6, by playing a quiet/passive move that lets the queen flee and grab e5; medium blurs into passive or non-forcing moves squandering a winning/equal position—skipping a free rook (Bxa8) or bishop (Rxd7) capture or an active king move rather than specifically winning the queen.

1096.label: Top boards are uniform: in a clearly winning position White plays a quiet/developing move and misses a forcing knight shot (Nxg6/Nf5/Nxf7/Ng6) that wins material; medium blurs this in two directions — missing other forcing tactics (queen checks, discovered attacks, rook invasions) and, increasingly, playing a passive coordination-breaking move that actually hangs own material rather than merely skipping a win.

1088.label: Top: a quiet/developing opening move (skipping an available forcing capture) ignores a standing tactic and hangs a full minor piece, most often to a knight fork or knight capture; medium blurs the lost material to the exchange or a pawn and occasionally flips direction to a missed free capture rather than a true hang.

1091.label: Top boards center on a natural-looking queen/piece sortie, check, or developing move that either hangs material outright (Nxe6, Qe2, e6) or skips a concrete winning tactic/tempo (Rd1, Rhe1, Qc7); medium blurs the same 'natural over concrete' habit into positional, move-order, and trade errors (greedy captures, queen retreats, wrong recaptures, endgame king walks) that squander a winning edge rather than dropping a piece, so neither a single motif nor outcome dominates.

1097.chip: Trades key defender for pawn (broadly hangs)
1097.label: Top boards uniformly surrender the sole passed-pawn blockader (bishop/knight/rook) for a single pawn in drawn endgames, converting a hold into a loss; medium blurs to other endgame material giveaways—leaving a queen hanging by missing the recapture, or a move-order/omission error that loses the pawn race.

1094.label: Top: a trivial immediate forced win is skipped for an aimless materially-safe move — 8/10 a back-rank mate-in-one (Qb8#/Rb8#), 2/10 a queen-winning Nh6+ — with no own material lost; medium blurs to longer forced mates and decisive forcing sequences squandered by the same passive play, though a few medium boards are merely inferior moves that let the opponent off rather than a clean missed win.

1092.label: Top boards are near-uniform: a premature d-pawn push (d5–d4 or d4–d5) intended to chase a knight that instead releases tension/overextends and surrenders the player's edge, refuted by a knight leaping to a central outpost (Ne4/Ne5); medium broadens to e- and g-pawn pushes (and a couple of mistimed captures) that likewise squander the advantage, with the refuting knight sometimes just retreating safely or winning material rather than always grabbing an outpost.

1090.label: Top boards are laser-focused: in the opening White/Black consistently fails to grab the free hanging b5/b4 pawn or play the winning Bxb5/Bb5/Ba4 pin, with the bishop as the recurring agent throwing away a winning edge; medium blurs this into broader queenside bishop-and-pawn material lapses, where the direction flips toward hanging one's own piece (rook to Bxc1, bishop to Nxc6) or missing other bishop tactics rather than purely skipping the b-pawn win.

1100.label: At the peak the player overlooks a forced checkmate (frequently mate-in-one, often by moving the very piece that enabled the mate or grabbing lesser material); at medium strength this broadens to skipping any decisive winning resource—material-winning tactics, pawn grabs, or the one critical thrust—in favor of a slow repositioning move.

1109.label: Top boards uniformly pass up a winning forcing knight check (Nxd6+/Nxe6+/Nxe3+) for a passive or greedy move; medium boards blur to any missed forcing continuation (bishop/pawn checks like Bd4+/exd6+, Ne6+, or a defensive trade), with punishment ranging from a squandered safe win to hung material to forced mate.

1105.label: Top boards almost all place/leave the QUEEN en prise for an immediate free capture (with a couple missing a free queen/rook capture instead); medium broadens to hanging other pieces (rook, bishop, fork-won exchange) and even non-material lapses—squandered mating attacks, patzer checks, and positional misjudgments.

1098.chip: Walks into king-exposing check (or lost defender)
1098.label: Top boards are mostly king moves or greedy captures that walk straight into a forcing check on the now-exposed king (Re6+, Re7+, Re8+#, Re2+), losing material or getting mated; medium blurs the trigger to rook/queen moves that abandon a key defender or open a line, so the refutation broadens to back-rank mates, exposed-king checks winning the exchange, and offside-piece/trap tactics.

1103.label: Top boards consistently miss a minor-piece (almost always a bishop) move that attacks a rook to win the exchange; medium broadens to knight/pawn forks of two pieces and bleeds into a few pure hanging-rook or king-safety blunders.

1107.label: Top boards are uniformly king moves that retreat or drift away from the center/promotion square in lost K+P endgames, forfeiting the tempo/king-activity race (no material hung, often near-0cp dead-lost positions); medium blurs to include passive pawn pushes and knight repositions that likewise waste the tempo and fail to centralize the king.

1099.label: Top boards are tightly about mistiming the critical knight exchange/capture — the player skips or mis-orders eliminating a dominant knight (e.g. Bxf5/Nxg5/Bxe5), either hanging material or missing the win; medium keeps the knight as the decisive piece but blurs into broader knight tactics (forks with check, discovered attacks, blockade breaks) that are likewise allowed or overlooked.

1108.label: Top boards uniformly recapture/capture immediately and hang the dark-squared bishop by skipping a forcing zwischenzug (almost always an intermediate check like Bxc3+/Bxd7+/Bxe7 first); medium boards generalize the same wrong-capture-order error to dropping other pieces (knight on e4, queen on a5) or merely forfeiting a pawn/exchange, where the missing finesse is sometimes a queen trade or quiet capture rather than a check.

1110.label: At the peak the constant is a quiet safe move in an already-won position that skips a free capture of a hanging piece — overwhelmingly a king grabbing an undefended bishop (Kxg5/Kxe4/Kxa3), with one knight-takes-knight variant; at medium the signal blurs away from captures into quiet king/minor-piece moves that merely drop the opposition or a tempo in pawn endgames (Kb6, Kc5) plus a fork blunder, so only ~6/10 are true missed winning captures.

1101.label: Top: a forced mate or decisive winning check was available but the player threw the win away with a passive king move or greedy capture (never playing a check); medium broadens to playing a check that's the wrong one or wrong move-order, and to missing saving perpetuals rather than only outright wins.

1106.label: Top boards consistently decline the simplifying rook capture/sacrifice (Rxf5+, Rxc6+, Rxf6+, Rxf3) of Black's last knight that liquidates into a trivially won K+P endgame, instead pushing a king/pawn; medium blurs to any liquidating capture of the last minor piece (knight taking knight/bishop, Nxd6/Nxd3/Nxf4/Nxf5, even plain king centralization), still always in a won endgame, with a few boards instead hanging the rook on the omitted exchange.

1102.label: Top boards constantly decline the winning forcing rook exchange/capture with check on the open file or back rank (Rxd1+/Rxe1+), either squandering a won position or walking into back-rank mate; medium boards keep the same missed forcing rook trade but blur the moving piece (knight/bishop/pawn/queen) and the consequence (wrong capture-order, hung material, or allowed mating attack).

1104.label: Top boards are uniformly quiet/slow rook moves (usually Rd8 on an open file, plus a couple wrong-piece captures) that skip an available forcing tactic which wins material/the game — a materially-safe 'missed win'; medium blurs in two directions — the move broadens beyond rooks (cxd5, Nbxd4) and, critically, shifts from merely missing a win to actively hanging material or king safety (Rb8 hangs, Re1/Rf1 dropping f2 or walking into mate, Rd8 allowing Qxe4), so the peak 'missed forcing tactic' theme becomes a mixed 'slow move that ignores a tactic and frequently loses material.'

1114.label: Top boards are committal pawn moves (captures/pushes like cxb3, c5, hxg3, axb6) that throw away a winning position, with punishment split between dropped material (released tension) and pure loosening (opening lines to own king, freeing enemy pieces); medium broadens to bishop/knight moves and shifts toward materially-safe moves that simply skip a stronger tactical or positional blow.

1117.label: Top boards are materially-safe KING moves in a won/holding endgame that throw away the result (wrong king square or skipping a capture like Bxc6/Kxe6); medium broadens the same omission to PAWN moves—premature pushes or exchanges (b6, c5, e5) and queenside king drift—that forfeit the win/draw rather than hanging own material.

1113.label: At the peak it's a tempting knight sortie/fork (with a couple of queen captures) that throws away a winning position by either hanging the piece or trading off the key piece into equality; at medium it blurs into any tempting active move—rook lift, pawn break, bishop capture—that squanders the edge, more positionally than by outright material loss.

1121.label: Top boards are sharply defined: a quiet/aimless move (pawn push, rook shuffle, queen relocation) ignores a clean forcing king-attack line — a forced mate, winning king-hunt tactic, or saving perpetual-check draw; medium blurs this into greedy captures and king-safety-weakening pushes that surrender the initiative or invite the opponent's decisive king attack rather than missing a strict forced mate.

1115.label: Top: ignores a pending/forced rook exchange (best move ~Rx...) and hangs a full rook outright — queen in one case, pawn in another; Medium: same skipped rook tension but the outcome blurs from a clean rook hang to merely dropping the win/advantage (missed simplifying capture or letting the rook invade).

1119.label: Top boards uniformly skip a clearly winning own-knight capture (Nxd4/Nxe4/Nxc4/Nxe5/Nxd5) from a winning position, choosing a safe developing or prophylactic move (a6/Nf6/Bg7/g3/Qe7) that throws away the win; medium boards mostly repeat this (notably missed Nxc4), but blur to include failing to rescue an already-attacked knight that then simply hangs.

1111.label: Top boards are self-destructive king walks and king-weakening pawn pushes that expose the player's own king and hasten the loss in difficult positions (with a couple simply hanging a rook/knight); medium blurs into broader self-inflicted concessions—hanging a bishop, abandoning a defensive guard or pawn-restrainer, weakening pawn pushes, and even tossing away a clear win.

1126.label: Top: a materially-safe but passive king (or retreating knight) move that wastes the critical tempo needed for a decisive capture/promotion in passed-pawn endgames, throwing away the win; medium narrows to passed-pawn king moves that skip a mandatory pawn capture (fxg6, axb5), though ~2/10 boards were actually 0cp best moves.

1122.chip: Hangs piece or walks into mate
1122.label: Top boards are self-inflicted king/pawn moves that either walk the king into a forced mate (open the shelter, abandon the back rank) or hang a full piece by chasing into a fork or deserting a defender; medium keeps the self-inflicted theme but blurs to pawn pushes and king walks that undermine a defender/pawn shield and drop a pawn, exchange, or piece — material loss rather than outright mate, with a few purely positional weakenings mixed in.

1112.label: Top: a rook move offering a trade or contesting an open file that loses material — the forced exchange exposes a deflection/fork/back-rank tactic (or skips an immediate free capture); medium keeps the trade-loses-material theme but blurs the piece (also queen/bishop/king moves) and the consequence (simplifying into a lost pawn/passed-pawn endgame, not just an immediate middlegame tactic).

1123.label: Top boards are nearly uniform: a quiet/developing move (often castling) passes up a forcing winning tactic against the enemy king, frequently the Greek Gift Bxh7+ sac (with a couple instead hanging own material like the Bg5/Nc6 drops); medium boards blur outward to any quiet, positional, or tempo-losing move that forgoes a concrete tactic—winning a pawn (Qxb2), exploiting an outpost, or a non-king shot—and now roughly half drop the player's own material via trapped pieces, allowed forks, or losing exchanges.

1125.label: Top boards are uniformly ...Bxd1-style bishop captures of the enemy queen played in the wrong move order, letting the opponent recapture the queen and net a full piece (or even mate); medium broadens to other capturing pieces and squares (knight Nxf6/Nxb3, pawn gxf5, bishop Bxf3/Bxe7) and to missed intermezzos (e.g. Rxh1+/Bxb4+ first), where grabbing the queen immediately squanders the larger material win.

1124.label: Top boards play a quiet move and skip a forcing QUEEN check that's either mate-in-one or wins material; medium keeps the 'missed forcing winning shot' theme but the check broadens to other pieces (knight Nc2+, pawn c3+, bishop Bxf5+) or occasionally a non-check winning resource.

1118.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player skips a knight fork—almost always hitting the queen (often netting queen/exchange/piece via a forced Nxe7+/Nxg7+ follow-up)—and instead makes a slow pawn/queen/bishop move; medium: same won-position-plus-passive-move signature, but the missed shot broadens from pure queen knight-forks to rook/bishop knight-forks, plain knight/bishop captures, and even quiet best consolidating moves, so the 'knight fork' specificity dissolves into 'missed winning move'.

1116.label: Top boards are uniformly the queen left en prise by a developing/move-order move that ignores a standing capture or forking-check threat; medium keeps the ignored-threat hang but blurs to rook/knight losses and an occasional missed free-piece capture.

1128.label: Top boards are a bishop developed to f4/f5 walking straight into the enemy e-pawn's capture (Bf4/Bf5 → exf4/exf5) for a clean lost piece; medium blurs to a bishop hung to a different pawn (Bc5 → dxc5) plus other opening developing blunders — a knight sac (...Nxd4), a Dutch-style ...f5 push, and tempo-losing developments (Bg2, Be7).

1120.label: At the peak the move is a tempo-wasting forcing rook check (Rh8+/Rh7+, even one non-blunder) in a won endgame that skips the decisive capture/simplification; at medium it blurs into outright missed free captures (queen/rook/minor) and greedy pawn-grabs that overlook a forced mate—nearly always a winning position where the decisive move was passed up, with only a minority actually hanging own material.

1135.label: Top: a premature/wrong-move-order capture or recapture self-inflicts loss of the player's own material (rook/queen/exchange), almost always punished by a knight fork; medium keeps the same wrong-order-trade error but the refutation blurs to also include king-safety/mating attacks or a plain recapture of the hung piece rather than strictly a knight fork.

1127.label: Top: a winning side (almost all endgames) plays a slow/passive move and overlooks a FORCING decisive continuation — immediate promotion push, forced mate, or a clean material-winning tactic (fork/discovered check); medium keeps the 'winning-but-skipped-the-decisive-move' core but blurs to broader endgame tempo/timing and positional slips (king-march or pawn-push mistiming, missed contesting move) that merely fritter the win, with a couple borderline/non-blunder cases mixed in.

1133.label: Top boards uniformly skip a FORCED back-rank checkmate (mate in 1–3) in favor of a greedy material-winning capture; medium blurs to missing back-rank tactics that merely win material/the queen rather than mate, plus passive non-forcing moves that squander (or even allow) a back-rank attack.

1132.chip: Premature pawn push wrecks structure (often pawn endgame)
1132.label: Top boards are uniformly committal pawn advances (frequently a push the opponent answers with the bypassing h5!/g5+) that ruin one's own PAWN-ENDGAME structure by letting the foe fix, bypass, or liquidate; at medium it blurs to structure-wrecking concessions in rook endgames, king-safety/middlegame positions, and even non-pawn moves that liquidate into the same lost or crippled structure.

1129.chip: Hangs rim bishop to pawn thrust (minor)
1129.label: Top boards are uniform: a developed bishop left on the rim/active diagonal is trapped and lost over 2-3 moves by an enemy pawn thrust (g4/h5/a5/b5/c4), usually after skipping the freeing ...h5/retreat; medium blurs to other minor pieces (knights) being attacked or won by pawn advances or tactics, plus a few softer harassment/tempo and off-theme endgame cases.

1136.label: Top boards are clean one-move piece hangs—any piece (knight, bishop, queen, even a pawn), frequently an unsupported aggressive check—dropped for free to an immediate capture; medium keeps the self-inflicted material loss but broadens to pieces lost more slowly (trapped queens, multi-move refutations) and a few tempo-/king-safety sorties into attack.

1134.label: At the peak, a winning side plays a move that exposes its own king or strips a key defender, allowing a decisive check or forced mate (boards 2,3,4,5,8,9); at medium this blurs into generally squandering the won position — still occasional forced mate (med 1,4) but now also hanging a piece or burning a tempo (med 2,3,5), so the invariant is 'blunder away a winning endgame' rather than a specific mating motif.

1137.label: Top boards are uniformly premature opening KING WALKS (Ke2/Ke7/Kd2/Kf2) that forfeit castling and expose the king to a tempo/pawn-winning refutation; medium blurs this into king-exposing moves across later phases and broader king-safety lapses (castling into an attack, king sorties allowing forks/skewers, even pawn/queen moves cracking the king), increasingly leading to concrete material loss rather than just lost tempo.

1131.label: In sharp, usually-winning positions the player throws away the result; at the peak it's overwhelmingly queen-centric—hanging its own queen or missing a queen-winning capture—while medium boards blur to any piece (rook/knight/bishop/exchange) and split roughly evenly between hanging material and missing a forced win or free capture, with no consistent direction.

1142.label: Top boards almost uniformly leave a corner rook hanging to the enemy queen (Qxa1/Qxa8/Qxh1/Qxh8, plus one diagonal queen-fork); medium blurs to hanging other material—knights, bishops, or rooks—often still to a queen capture but also via simple captures, forks, and trapped pieces.

1140.label: Top: in clearly winning K+P/promotion endgames the player makes a safe king or pawn move (or premature promotion) that abandons the decisive configuration — the mating net (Bg7+Nf6#, Rb1#), the winning opposition, or the queening-square blockade — throwing away a forced mate or win rather than hanging material; medium narrows to pure pawn-endgame king moves that squander the one key tempo/blockading square (Kg2/Kf7) needed to convert, with ~3/10 boards being non-blunders that dilute the signal.

1141.label: Top boards almost uniformly hang a piece—usually a bishop (Bc5/Bc4)—straight to a d-pawn capture by ignoring central tension (best is exd4/cxd4/exd5); medium keeps the opening-phase self-inflicted material loss but broadens the mechanism to pawns and pieces dropped via forks, discovered checks, pins, and bad retreats over 2-3 moves.

1130.label: Top boards skip a unique forced win — mate-in-one, mating continuation, or knight fork (the single move within 50cp); medium blurs to missing the only drawing/defensive resource in rook & pawn endgames, plus stray greedy/positional errors.

1143.label: Top boards are over-ambitious pawn advances that hang own material or collapse a good eval (the lost unit varies—queen on 1, exchange/rook on 6-7, pawn on 9), with two misfires (bishop move on 2, fully-correct push on 10); medium blurs the pawn-push constant by adding other over-extending moves (rook captures e2e5/h8h2, knight sorties) that likewise drop material or squander a winning eval.

1138.label: Top: a forced mate/decisive win is on the board and the killing blow is a knight check/sac/fork, but the player plays a safe or greedy queen/rook move instead; medium broadens to wins delivered by rook/pawn/bishop and to greedy captures that not only miss the win but flip the eval (hanging material).

1146.label: Top boards are pure queen-grabs of a single undefended bishop (queen decisive on every board, ~60% a missed free capture vs ~40% hanging one's own piece to the enemy queen); medium broadens the target from bishop to any undefended pawn/rook/piece and bleeds into adjacent queen-driven tactics (forks, king-safety).

1145.label: Top boards are premature pawn promotions whose new queen is captured for free; medium boards broaden to unfavorable trades/greedy captures (eliminating a passer or trading queen-for-rook) that liquidate into a lost position.

1153.label: Top boards squander a winning/drawing position by skipping the one decisive capture (Nxf6, Rxf7, Nxf5, Nxe8), while medium broadens to missing any single critical move — including quiet repositioning (Nc4) or non-capturing breaks — that still converts the advantage.

1149.label: Top boards squander an already-winning position by playing a safe-looking move/wrong capture instead of the strongest material-winning capture (frequently a queen or rook capture delivered WITH CHECK, e.g. Bxc5+/Qxa8+/Bxd4+); medium boards blur this to skipping the decisive shot more broadly — a deflecting capture that forces mate (Rxa2+) or an endgame-losing trade (Rxd2) rather than a clean piece-winning capture.

1150.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where the king goes the wrong direction (or grabs an irrelevant pawn) and forfeits the promotion race; medium broadens to endings with pieces still on (rook/bishop/queen) where a passive or misdirected king move squanders the same decisive tempo.

1139.label: Top boards are uniformly a ROOK abandoning its central/supporting post to chase or grab a (wing) pawn and squandering a winning/clearly-better position, usually letting an opponent passer decide; medium keeps the 'piece leaves its key square for a lesser target' core but blurs to other pieces (knight, bishop, even a pawn move) and to premature/misplaced moves that toss the edge, occasionally crossing into a missed forced win/mate or an outright hang.

1148.label: Top boards are constant: natural opening developing/pawn/castling moves that self-hang material (pawn, exchange, or piece) to a deflection/skewer/discovered-attack tactic one or two moves later; medium blurs the phase into the middlegame and broadens toward positional or king-safety moves that drop a pawn or squander a winning advantage rather than cleanly hanging a piece.

1147.label: Top boards are passive non-capturing king/pawn (and rook) moves that decline the single saving resource and lose outright—surrendering a drawn pawn endgame, hanging a queen/rook, or walking into back-rank/king-trap mate; medium broadens to quiet moves that merely squander a winning advantage (missed forcing line/mate, tempo loss) rather than always hanging material.

1144.label: Top boards peak on greedy captures (usually the enemy queen) that overlook a forced refutation — back-rank mate or a missed perpetual/faster mate; medium boards blur into hanging a piece or pawn via a quiet non-capturing move (castling, pawn push) that simply drops material to an overlooked tactic.

1152.label: Top boards are uniformly the passive ...Qe7 to defend an attacked f6-knight (tempo loss, blocked f8-bishop, e-file self-pin punished by O-O/Re1); medium blurs to other tempo-wasting queen sorties (Qe6, Qe2, Qa4) that lose time or walk into d5/Nd4 forks, with a few non-queen misplacements (Rf1/Qf2 hangs, Rc2 missed win) diluting the pattern.

1155.label: Top boards constantly hang a knight that jumped to f5/f6 to attack the enemy queen (refuted by a simple capture like exf5/Bxh5); medium blurs to knights hung on any square (e2/e4/d5/f4) and the occasional greedy capture, with rare outliers hanging a bishop (Bd6) or just losing tempo (h4).

1158.label: Top: a greedy/loose knight move (Nxe4, Nxe5, Nd4, Ne5) drops a full piece for at most a pawn to a simple immediate recapture in the opening; medium broadens to other unsound opening moves (Na5 bishop-hunts, Bg4/Bb4 misjudged pins, Bc5) that instead leak material over a 2-3 move tactical refutation (Bxf7+, Qa4+ fork, fxe5).

1160.label: Top boards are uniformly rook trades that transition into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn endgame; medium blurs the exchanged piece (adds a queen trade and king moves that merely permit the rook swap) and mixes in some unrelated hanging-piece/missed-win noise.

1154.label: Top: in already-lost endgames a pawn push or piece relocation abandons a strong/defensive square and concretely loses material or allows mate within a few moves (varied pieces — bishop, knight, pawn, queen); medium broadens to similar 'loose' abandoning moves where the cost is more positional/tempo (passive relocation, conceding an outpost or open line) without always a clean single-ply hang.

1151.label: At the peak, in a losing/critical middlegame the player skips the sole defensive resource (usually a rook move like Rc2/Re6/Rh4/Rd1) and instead hangs material or walks into a forced mating attack (king-safety dominant); at medium activation this broadens to skipping the only good move in equal-to-winning positions, so it also covers missing a winning fork/exchange or allowing the opponent's fork rather than purely defensive collapses.

1164.label: Top boards consistently play a materially-safe move that skips grabbing the undefended enemy queen (via mutual-attack diagonal/rank or knight fork); medium blurs to skipping other free winning captures (rook/piece) or a decisive breakthrough, but the missed free queen grab stays the central pattern.

1161.label: Top: in a winning position the player captures or trades the queen (often recapturing/swapping) for a material-safe outcome that throws away a forced mate or much stronger win; medium blurs to other materialistic grabs (pawn, bishop, or king moves) that likewise skip the win, and a few self-inflicted cases let the grabbed material hang to a fork/pin in the refutation.

1157.label: In a winning opening, a natural king-safety/developing move squanders a concrete tactic: top boards are almost all castling (O-O) that misses a knight strike (Nxd4/Nb5/Nd5), while medium broadens to other passive developing/relocating moves (knight retreats to c3/c6, rook to c1) that miss or walk past the win.

1162.label: Top boards uniformly play a move that ignores or enables a KNIGHT tactic (fork, capture, or mate) costing material (queen, exchange/rook, or piece); at medium the weapon and loss blur — still mostly knight forks/captures, but broadening to back-rank/queen mates and pawn or queen-attack refutations where a knight isn't always the punisher.

1159.label: Top: a pawn push/capture that dissolves a locked, drawn/held pawn fortress in a king-and-pawn endgame, handing the opponent a decisive passed pawn or king penetration; medium blurs to premature pawn breaks opening the position more generally (often middlegame, exposing diagonals/files or dropping a pawn) plus a few non-pawn moves that abandon a holding setup.

1156.chip: Hangs minor piece to pawn (often fork)
1156.label: Top boards consistently hang a minor piece (bishop/knight) in the opening to a pawn — usually a d5/d4/e5 pawn fork of two pieces, sometimes a plain pawn capture (exf6, cxd3); medium keeps the pawn-fork core but blurs into broader opening blunders like knight forks, missed pawn wins, and positional/king-safety errors.

1166.label: Top boards are uniformly a queen check refuted by QxQ, hanging the queen outright; medium keeps the same self-defeating check motif but blurs the checking/capturing piece beyond the queen (rook- and bishop-deliveries captured by rook/bishop/queen) and sometimes the punished move also squanders a forced mate rather than purely hanging.

1167.label: Top: a slow/irrelevant move (pawn push or piece relocation) ignores a forced mate against its own king and gets checkmated; medium broadens to distraction moves that ignore a decisive material threat or crushing attack—and occasionally a missed forced win/mate—rather than strictly mate-in-1/2.

1170.label: Constant across both: from a winning/advantageous position the player makes a self-defeating material decision; at the peak this centers on trading the queen for a minor piece or pawn but blurs to include under-/failed promotions and a knight hung on a defended pawn, while the medium position narrows back to the unfavorable queen trade that throws away the win.

1168.label: Top boards are all unsound g6 captures (bishop or pawn) that rip at the enemy king's pawn shield but hang a piece/material and squander a winning position; medium broadens to other king-shield and kingside captures (Bxh6, fxg4) plus a few unsound non-kingside trades, mostly losing own material though a couple instead miss a winning tactic.

1169.label: Top boards uniformly fail to parry an immediate mating threat (king-safety: Qg2#/Rd1#/Qc7#, or king/defender stepping into the mate); medium blurs this to ignoring any existing decisive threat — material-winning tactics (discovered attacks, forks, hanging pawns/pieces) and a few marginal tempo-losing moves — so the punishment splits between forced mate and heavy material loss.

1174.label: Top: a materially-safe queen move—almost always offering a queen exchange—that dissolves a forced checkmate into merely winning; medium keeps the same 'safe move throws away the mate' theme but blurs the agent and target, adding rook moves, pawn-grab captures, and a few cases that downgrade a decisive (non-mating) win rather than a forced mate.

1163.label: Top activations squander a winning/near-equal position via a tempting forcing move that backfires — peaking on greedy captures and checks (pawn/bishop) like dxe5+ and Bxd5; medium broadens to king repositioning (Kd4/Kd7) and wrong recaptures, with direction split between hanging own material in the refutation and merely missing the cleaner win (~2/10 not real blunders).

1173.label: Top boards are tightly unified: a queen move (or king/pawn move) that strips away the king's last defender or shelter, allowing decisive checks/mate (with 2-3 instead missing a forcing win like Qe5+, Ne6+, Qxe5); medium blurs this into king walks onto open lines (Kb1, Kf1), line-opening pawn pushes, and queen trades/retreats that surrender king safety, initiative, or material rather than a clean mating exposure.

1171.label: Top: in roughly level/drawn middlegames and rook/minor endings the player makes a natural passive developing or file-occupying move and overlooks a forcing capture or rook/minor-piece exchange that would win material or hold equality (with two greedy captures that walk into a refutation); medium blurs the direction — the same passive, tempo-wasting move now allows the opponent's forcing capture/fork, hanging material rather than just missing one's own win.

1172.label: Top boards uniformly play a slow, non-forcing developing move and miss a decisive queen-check king hunt (Qh8+/Qh1+) in an already-winning position; medium keeps the missed-forcing-win theme but broadens to forced mates spoiled by wrong move-order or wrong capture, plus occasional non-queen winning shots (Ne5/Be7/Rxc1) and even a couple of hung-own-piece cases.

1177.label: Top boards uniformly play a natural opening/developing move while missing a forcing QUEEN check (Qa4+/Qa5+/Qh4+/Qh5+) that wins material by exploiting an uncastled king or diagonal weakened by ...f6/f5; medium keeps the same king-exploiting check theme but blurs to wrong-route queen checks (Qd5 vs Qa5+) and non-queen forcing intermezzos (Bxf2+) that also punish the exposed king.

1165.label: Top: a voluntary BISHOP exchange (Bxc6/Bxd6/Bxc3/Bxe3) relieves central tension and throws away a clear advantage instead of a stronger non-capturing move; medium blurs the capturing/captured piece to knight/rook/queen/pawn and more often backfires from a mere even trade into outright hung, trapped, or endgame-losing material.

1180.label: Top boards are clear self-destructing blunders that either hang a piece outright (knight/rook/queen/exchange) or fatally expose the king to forced mate; medium blurs the same theme across a varying piece while mixing in missed wins (free pawns/forced mates skipped) and positional/tempo drops, so the constant peak signal is 'losing move that drops own material or king' but the exact fault and direction wobble at medium.

1176.chip: Hangs material ignoring central tension (any piece)
1176.label: Top boards are one-move opening blunders that drop material (often a queen or bishop) by developing/advancing a piece instead of simply recapturing in the central pawn tension; medium keeps the 'fail to resolve central tension → lose material' theme but blurs to multi-move refutations and varied pieces/pawns (knight, rook, pawn), even one case of winning less material than available.

1179.label: Top: in a lost/critical position an active non-defensive move (pawn push, centralization, king relocation) ignores the decisive threat and is immediately punished by hanging a piece (most often a rook) or walking into a forced (frequently back-rank) mate; medium keeps the same threat-ignoring active-move root but blurs in severity, often only conceding a tempo or a slower/partial material loss rather than an instant catastrophe.

1178.chip: Missed queen check winning rook (often Qxa1+)
1178.label: Top boards are uniformly the skipped one-move queen check Qxa1+ (once Qxc8+) capturing an undefended back-rank rook in a winning position; medium keeps the same missed queen check exploiting the back-rank king geometry but blurs the target square (Qxb1/Qxh1/Qxf2/Qxb2) and occasionally wins a pawn or a faster mate rather than a clean rook.

1175.label: Top: severe endgame moves (often a pawn push or king step) that throw away a winning/drawn result by mixed means — material hung via deflection, allowing a passed pawn to promote, or missing mate/queen-trading into a lost pawn ending; medium keeps the 'squanders the endgame' theme but blurs to much milder cases — tiny inaccuracies that still keep the win plus plain material hangs (skewer, greedy capture).

1182.label: Top boards pivot on a knight as the decisive piece, split between hanging one's own knight (often the d6 outpost lost via move-order slips like Rd3/Rg1, or outright as Nd3/Nc3) and missing Bxg5 to grab White's knight; medium blurs further toward failing to capture/trade an enemy knight (Bxe4, Bxe5, Bxd6) and looser knight-retreat/positional errors.

1189.label: Top: opening moves that ignore a bishop bearing down an OPEN diagonal and capture the undefended queen (Bxd8/Bxd1), losing Q for B; medium keeps the queen-for-bishop loss but blurs to queens on varied squares (e2/d1/d8) and to indirect exposures—clearing a blocker or moving a pinned defender—plus a couple of outliers (declining a free bishop, back-rank mate).

1186.label: Top boards are immediate, single-ply knight blunders—the knight left en prise or its defender removed in the opening, turning equal to lost; medium keeps the self-inflicted minor-piece loss but blurs to bishops too and to multi-move refutations (forks, trapped knights, zwischenzugs) that win the piece over 2-3 moves.

1185.label: Top boards uniformly play a quiet, materially-safe move and miss a forcing knight sac/capture (Nxf7/Nxf2/Nxc3/Nxe4) that exploits an exposed/uncastled king; medium boards keep the 'safe move squanders a winning/equal-plus edge' core but blur the tactic — knight checks (Nf6+) plus bishop/rook captures (Bxg2, Rxe3), pawn breaks (dxc3), queen grabs (Qxa7), and even pure positional/endgame slips (Be7, Kb6).

1190.label: Top: already worse, the player makes a non-forcing ROOK move that abandons a critical back-rank/file instead of the saving Rxe8/Rxf8 trade, getting crushed by a decisive knight fork or back-rank mate; medium keeps the 'skip the dangerous-rook exchange and get punished' theme but blurs the piece/move (queen centralization, pawn push, even a pointless rook check) and the tactic (passed-pawn promotion, deflection), still hanging material to a forced refutation.

1184.label: Top boards uniformly pass up a winning capture of a centralized enemy knight (overwhelmingly Nxd5, also Nxe5/Nxe4/Nxd4) in favor of a slow developing or castling move—a pure material-safe omission; medium positions keep the missed knight grab but blur to include other neglected captures/trades and even cases where a non-capture best move (Na5, Rb8, Bd7) or a wrongly-played capture is involved.

1188.label: Top: in won endgames a materially-safe pawn/quiet move skips the one precise winning continuation, usually the forcing check d3+; medium broadens to missing non-check precise winning/holding moves (pawn races, repositioning) that let the win slip toward a draw, with a few boards instead hanging material over 2-3 moves.

1181.label: Top boards are uniformly passive/quiet moves that overlook a free capture of the opponent's undefended queen (Rxd8, Nxd2, Nxe7, etc.); medium loses the queen focus and blurs into assorted passive moves that overlook tactics and drop material — trapped pieces, king-safety collapses, even mate-in-one — often hanging the player's own material rather than missing a capture.

1187.label: Top boards: player skips the only prophylactic/defensive move (or removes a key king-defender) and is hit by a forced mate or queen-winning attack; medium blurs to passive/inaccurate moves that allow a strong attack or squander a winning advantage without forced mate (also forks, back-rank, lost initiative).

1191.label: Top boards walk the king/a piece straight into a forced checkmate by ignoring the single forcing reply (king exposed); medium boards keep the king-into-mate core but broaden to also ignore a forcing check/fork that wins the queen or decisive material.

1194.label: Top boards are constant: a queen move that loses the queen via a hang (often a knight fork like Nf1+/Nxf7) or a clearly bad queen-for-rook trade; medium blurs into losing material more generally to a tactical oversight—including king-safety moves (Ke2, Kh7, Kd7, Kf8) and bishop/rook moves that hang a piece, the exchange, or walk into mate.

1198.label: Top: in a winning endgame the player ignores the single precise minor-piece resource (knight/bishop maneuver or sacrifice) and instead plays a natural king advance, promotion-into-capture, or useless check, throwing away the win; medium keeps the 'only-correct-resource-skipped' theme but blurs the piece (rook maneuvers, king-safety/fortress technique) and includes drawing as well as winning positions plus a couple of near-zero-cp non-blunders.

1202.label: Top boards uniformly play a slow/passive move that skips a winning QUEEN check (Qh5+/Qh4+/Qc6+) which mates or wins material; medium blurs the qualifier — still mostly forcing checks but broadening to bishop checks (Bb5+) and even non-check forcing wins (knight forks, pawn breaks like h4), with the invariant being the squandered forcing tactic (~half also drop the player's own piece a move later).

1192.label: Top: player voluntarily captures into a queen trade that liquidates a clearly winning kingside attack, a forced mate, or a free piece; medium broadens to premature or wrong-order/wrong-piece queen captures that skip a bigger win or even drop material in the recapture.

1193.label: Top: a knight greedily captures a pawn defended by another pawn in the opening (Nxd5/Nxb5/Nxd4), hanging the piece to a simple recapture for just a pawn; medium blurs to other piece-for-pawn losses—bishop sacrifices (Bxh3, Bxg6) and bishop-for-knight trades—and even drifts into king-safety walks (Ke6), so the 'minor-piece-for-a-pawn' core stays but the move type and phase widen.

1195.label: At the peak, a single-good-move critical position is blown from won/drawn to lost by a quiet king or knight move that hangs the player's own material, with a bishop almost always in the decisive line (the piece hung, the unsound sac, or the missed saving/winning move); medium broadens to non-bishop drops (e.g., a knight retreat conceding the advantage) and even includes a near-equal non-blunder, mixing in some missed-win cases.

1199.label: Top: in a won position overlooks a one-move capture of an undefended enemy rook (sometimes queen/knight), playing an idle pawn or king move; medium broadens to other hanging targets (bishop, queen) and blurs into leaving one's own rook hanging or a king-safety lapse.

1201.label: Top boards consistently skip a trivial pawn-take of a hanging bishop/rook in an already-winning endgame (dxc5, cxd6, fxe3); medium broadens to missing captures of hanging rooks/knights with assorted pieces (queen, bishop, pawn, rook).

1200.label: Top boards are uniformly passive/tempo-losing rook (or king) moves in rook-and-pawn endgames that abandon active placement and let the opponent's passed pawn run to promotion; medium blurs the piece (king, pawn, even knight/queen) and the consequence, broadening to general endgame tempo loss and a few non-pawn-race errors (forks, queen checks, mate).

1204.label: Top: a king move steps straight into forced mate-in-1/2 (king-safety blunder, nearly always immediate checkmate); medium blurs to king-exposure and other moves that concede decisive material via checks/forks rather than always immediate mate.

1183.label: At the peak, the defending side in a drawn (occasionally lost) endgame plays an inferior—usually king—move that misses the unique saving resource (saving capture, drawing trade, or king centralization), converting the draw to a loss or accelerating forced mate; at medium it blurs to passive pawn pushes, near-zero inaccuracies in already-lost positions, and even a winning side squandering the win, so direction and severity both loosen.

1196.chip: Passive move ignores urgent demand (often hangs)
1196.label: Top boards are natural quiet opening developments—frequently a bishop (…Bd7, Be2, …Be7)—that ignore a concrete demand (a dxc6 capture, a pin, central tension) and hang material; medium broadens to any passive move (castling, knight/king repositioning, a routine pawn move) that skips the position's urgent requirement, increasingly squandering a forced win rather than strictly hanging a piece.

1203.label: Top: a quiet developing/pawn move overlooks a bishop snatching an undefended pawn on the long diagonal to win the exchange (Bxg7/Bxg2/Bxb7/Bxb2); medium broadens to other missed long-diagonal grabs (queen Qxb7/Qxg7, Be4 winning a full rook) and blurs further into assorted missed tactics (forks like Bd3/Nb3) plus a few greedy/hanging captures.

1208.label: Top boards are sharp opening blunders that hang material within 1–3 moves, dominated by an overextended knight sortie (Nxf7/Ng4) or a pawn move leaving the e5/g5 knight en prise to a queen capture or fork; medium keeps the canonical Nxf7 knight-hang, while a few top outliers blur into positional king-weakening/tempo losses (g4, Qe3, Kd2, O-O).

1209.label: Top boards are consistently slow/passive queen moves (retreats or shuffles like Qe1/Qe3/Qh3/Qe2/Qf4) that decline the demanded forcing continuation, surrendering the initiative and either missing a winning shot or letting the opponent's attack crash through; medium blurs the piece to any non-forcing move (rook, pawn, knight, even king) that likewise skips the active/tactical continuation.

1197.chip: Greedy capture misses forced win (often queen)
1197.label: Top boards are consistently greedy captures (frequently a queen move) that spurn a forced mate or decisive queen-led attack while in a winning position; medium broadens to grabs/retreats that miss other winning ideas (pawn promotion, exchange-winning tactics) or, in already-lost spots, walk the king into a faster mate rather than squandering a win.

1206.chip: Misdirected king loses endgame race (often pure pawn)
1206.label: Top boards are pure pawn endgames where the king is sent the wrong way (or a pawn is pushed) and an arithmetically decisive pawn race is lost; medium broadens to rook/other endgames and tempo-wasting pawn pushes where king activation/centralization was the only saving plan, still flipping wins or holds into losses without hanging material.

1210.label: Top boards are uniform missed free captures of an undefended central enemy knight (f4/e4/d5/d4/e5) — a clear skipped win in the opening; medium keeps the 'missed winning capture' theme but blurs the target to a pawn (Nxe5), the exchange (Nxf4), or just eliminating a dominant knight, and a couple of cases drift into allowing an enemy fork instead.

1207.label: Top boards all throw away a decisive (mostly winning) position with the queen sitting in the critical line—but split evenly between hanging material outright (Rf4, g3, Qe6+, Qxe2, Bb4+) and skipping a forced winning capture (Rxa3+, Qxd8+ ×2, Bxf8, dxe5); medium boards keep only the 'blunders the win' theme while the piece and direction blur further, adding knight/rook/pawn hangs and even quiet positional/tempo squanders (Nf6+, Rg1, g4) where the queen need not be involved.

1212.label: Top boards hang a piece outright (rook/bishop/knight/queen lost to an immediate recapture, discovered attack, fork, or losing trade — even a couple back-rank mates); medium boards blur into slower self-inflicted losses where a passive, greedy, or tempo-wasting move concedes material or a key advantage over 1–3 moves (trapped pieces, pawn-race losses, surrendered outposts) rather than an immediate hang.

1217.label: Top: develops a bishop to Bg5/Bg4 to pin a knight, but the pin is illusory and a knight tactic (Nxe4 hitting g5, or Bxf7+/Bxf2+ followed by a Ng5+/Ne5+/Ne4+ fork) wins the bishop; medium keeps the 'pin/develop a bishop to an attacking square that fails' theme but broadens to other squares (Bb4, Bb5) and other refutations — a pawn break that breaks the pin (Nxd5), a queen fork (Qa4+/Qb5+), a simple recapture (Nxb4), or mere tempo loss (...f6/...Be6).

1215.label: Top boards all revolve around an en-prise queen the player mishandles—either failing to grab the free enemy queen or removing a defender that leaves its own queen hanging; medium boards blur to general material/capture errors (wrong recapturing piece, premature capture allowing a zwischenzug) where the queen is no longer the sole focal point.

1220.label: Top boards are materially-safe king moves in a won endgame that squander a forced mate/promotion instead of the one precise win; medium blurs to other pieces (pawn, minor, rook tempo moves) that throw away a winning advantage, with a couple drifting into outright hangs.

1219.label: Top boards uniformly play a slow developing/structural move while skipping a bishop capture of an undefended rook (winning the exchange or a full rook); medium keeps the hung-rook-capture theme but broadens the capturing piece to knight or queen as well.

1213.label: Top boards are uniform: in King's-Gambit central tension White (or Black) plays a quiet developing move (Nc3, c3, Nf3, h3, f3, Be3) instead of the winning central capture fxe5/dxe5/fxe4, squandering the edge—about half merely forfeit the win, half drop a pawn a move later; medium broadens to other tension-ignoring quiet/flank moves (h4, g3, Bc4, Bg5, even the piece-hanging Ba3) and to both colors, still letting unresolved central tension cost material/advantage.

1218.label: Top: in a clearly losing endgame, ignores the opponent's about-to-promote passed pawn(s) by playing an irrelevant pawn push, king walk, or passive piece move instead of the only defense (capture, blockade, or tempo-check); medium broadens to promotion-race situations more generally—mutual races where the player mishandles the timing (even from a winning side, flipping toward a missed win) and to wasting the one critical tempo against a dangerous enemy unit.

1211.label: Top: a quiet/greedy/king move played instead of an available forcing check (Qf6+, Qe5+, Be3+, d3+) that holds the edge—usually conceding material in the 2-3 move refutation; medium broadens to slow moves skipping the one precise active continuation (capture or attacking move) without an immediate hang, merely squandering a winning/advantageous position.

1221.label: At the peak the move throws away a winning/equal position by hanging a piece to a 1-3 move tactic, with a bishop usually the decisive piece (Bxg5+, Bxe5, Bxf6 dropping the queen, Bg5 undefended); at medium activation it blurs into non-material ways of squandering the advantage — king-safety lapses (Bf7+/Bxf7+ sacs, allowing Ndb5/Ba3), premature central breaks, and tempo-losing pawn grabs — so the constant is 'a blunder that converts a won/equal game into lost/equal' rather than any single hung piece.

1222.label: Top boards are razor-consistent: the player captures a centrally-posted knight (e5/d5/d4) and the opponent's PAWN recapture forks/double-attacks two pieces (bishop+knight, or piece+pawn) to win material with interest; medium positions keep the 'lose material on a central capture' core but blur the mechanism—sometimes a simple recapture of a defended piece (queen/rook hanging), a move-order error that ignores an already-attacked piece, or a zwischenzug/discovered attack rather than a clean pawn-recapture fork.

1214.label: Top boards all decline a forcing queen trade (Qxe2+/Qxd2+/Qxe7+/Qxa5) and instead develop or attack, with the refutation winning the now-undefended queen; medium boards blur the constant — the skipped best move broadens from a queen trade to any equalizing/tension-resolving capture (e.g. bishop trades Bxd3/Bxf1, central d4), and consequences range from a hung minor piece to merely a lost advantage.

1205.label: Top: in losing/drawn endgames a king, rook, or pawn move hangs material (most often the rook, e.g. Rxa2/Rxd6/Qxf7) or burns the tempo/defender in a passed-pawn race; medium broadens to dropping other pieces (bishop/knight) via tactics (discovered attacks, trapped pieces) and king-safety/back-rank walks, sometimes drifting out of pure endgames.

1231.label: Top: Black's greedy opening knight pawn-grab (mostly Nxe4) leaves the knight exposed and loses it to a Qa4+ check-fork recovery; medium keeps the greedy knight pawn-grab but blurs the refutation to other recaptures/forks (e.g. Nxe5 punished by Qxd5+Nxd5 c7-fork, or cxd5).

1226.label: Top boards are opening pawn/developing moves that open the king's light/dark diagonal for a decisive Qh5+/Qh4# (or leave the queen on c3 to be pinned by ...Bb4); medium broadens to general queen-line exposure—queen chased after Qa5, defenders removed enabling Qh4+/Qxf2+/Qxg6+, or the queen lost to a check/fork—with the queen the decisive piece (as attacker or pinned victim) on nearly every board.

1229.label: Top boards are uniformly missed winning knight checks (fork/discovered/clearance) that win a full rook from a materially-safe winning position; medium boards stay forcing-check-based but blur to include rook discovered-checks (Rf4+) and rook-saves, with the prize loosening to the exchange or a draw rather than always a full rook.

1227.label: Top boards uniformly squander a win by playing a natural capture/developing move instead of a forcing intermediate check (zwischenzug) that wins material or mates; medium boards blur to skipping any critical forcing/tempo move (non-check rook lifts, repositioning, or precise checks), and a minority instead self-inflict a hang by stepping into a fork.

1216.label: Top boards uniformly decline the engine's best move—a forced simplifying rook exchange (Rxe8+/Rxd1+/Rxd7, plus a couple of queen swaps)—that would clinch the win or hold equality; medium boards keep the rook/major-piece-exchange theme but blur in direction and form (forcing a queen trade, winning the exchange via Nxd8, grabbing a dangerous rook with Rxc8, or even avoiding a losing rook trade/back-rank mate).

1223.label: Top boards are early queen sorties (Qb3/Qb6/Qf3) that get hit by a knight fork (Nd4/Ne5/Nd5) or a Bxf7+/Nxe5 break and lose material — with ~25% instead being winning positions where the slow queen move skips that same Bxf7+/Nxe5 tactic (a missed win); medium keeps the 'exposed piece walks into a fork/double-attack' core but broadens the piece beyond the queen (bishop Be7/Bb2, knight Nd2) and adds occasional missed mates/wins, so direction is genuinely mixed.

1224.chip: Hangs piece to discovered check (often queen)
1224.label: Top: a knight off e4 (or other blocker) clears the e-file, hanging the queen to a discovered check from the e2-queen onto the e8-king in the opening; medium keeps the unblock-into-discovered-check theme but broadens the line (2nd-rank discoveries from a king stepping onto rank 2, bishop/pawn recaptures removing a file-blocker) and the loss (queen or exchange), with a couple of looser fork/king-safety tactics mixed in.

1234.label: Top boards are all pure king-and-pawn endgames where the losing side moves its king the wrong way (passive/retreating or toward the wrong wing), forfeiting the defensive march/counter-race; medium broadens to other lost or difficult endgames and non-king passive moves, with several near-best (0–15cp) cases blurring it from a clean blunder into 'misdirected king activity in lost endgames'.

1230.label: Top boards consistently squander a near-winning position by playing a quiet/natural piece move (rook lift, bishop reposition, slow queen/knight develop) instead of a crushing kingside attack — usually Qh5 or a b1-h7/c2-h7 battery aimed at h7; medium boards keep the same 'quiet move forfeits the win' core but broaden the missed continuation to central breaks (e5, Qd4), mating shots (Qh3/Bf6), and a minority that actually hang own material (queen/piece dropped over 1-2 moves).

1225.label: Top boards uniformly hang the queen in the opening—ignoring a direct attack from an invading bishop (or dropping the queen into a knight's range) and playing a routine developing/pawn move instead of the saving capture; medium boards keep the 'failed-to-capture in a winning opening' theme but flip direction and broaden, mostly MISSING free captures of a minor piece or pawn (Nxc4, dxc6, Bxg4, hxg4) and occasionally hanging a rook rather than the queen.

1239.label: Top boards uniformly skip an immediate, clean one-move grab of the opponent's completely undefended queen from a winning position; medium boards still miss winning the enemy queen but the capture requires extra precision — correct move-order (Rxd8 before Qxc4), the specific recapturing piece (Raxd8 to keep the blockade), or first using an attacking bishop (Bxg3) — and the squandered edge is sometimes large rather than outright decisive.

1232.chip: Hangs material on forcing move (often check)
1232.label: Top boards are constant: an over-ambitious forcing move—usually a check or knight/queen sortie—that directly hangs the player's own material (knight, queen, or exchange, sometimes over a 2–3 move refutation); medium blurs this by adding boards that instead miss a forced win/defense or make a positional trade that surrenders the advantage rather than outright hanging a piece.

1240.label: At the peak the player is already winning and plays a premature forcing check with the bishop (Bd4+, Bxf7+, Bg2+) instead of the clean capture/trade, hanging that bishop for free; medium positions keep the hung-bishop core but broaden the mechanism beyond checks to other mishandling (walking into a pin with Bg5, trapping it via Qe7), with boards 2/3/9 (and medium 1) being non-blunders that add noise.

1241.label: Player relocates a piece to a square where it's lost—either captured outright or refuted by a short tactic (fork/double-attack); top boards are dominated by knight moves hung directly or to a quick fork, while medium broadens to bishops, rooks and even pawn pushes and includes a few positional/tempo self-inflicted losses rather than clean hangs.

1236.label: Top boards are weakening kingside pawn pushes (h6/h5/e6) from a level opening that invite the Nxg6 sac, shattering structure and dropping material; medium broadens to other self-weakening opening moves (d6, Kb1) that hand the opponent an attack or material in a roughly equal position.

1235.label: Top: ignores an immediate queen mate-in-one (Qh7#/Qh2#/Qg2#) on an open diagonal against the castled king, grabbing material or playing an unrelated move instead of the forced defensive block; medium broadens to allowing forced mates-in-two (Qh6–Qg7#, Qg4+–Qg7#) and even back-rank rook mates, plus a few looser king-safety collapses.

1237.label: At the top it's a near-uniform premature rim knight sortie (...Na5, occasionally the mirror Na4) attacking the c4 bishop that abandons f7 and is refuted by the Bxf7+ king-hunt; at medium it blurs into assorted king-safety-neglecting tempo moves (flank pawn pushes like a6/g4/h6, bishop grabs, knight hops) that hang material to a variety of king-side tactical refutations (Qh5, Qg4, Qh4+, Bxf6) rather than Bxf7+ specifically.

1242.label: Top: in mostly-winning/critical positions the player overlooks the single decisive resource—a free capture (Nxh4/Qxg5), a saving O-O, king escape, or forcing check/move-order—and plays a passive move that throws away the win or walks into mate; medium broadens to lost positions where the lone correct defensive king move (Kg8/Ke8/Kf7) is the only thing staving off back-rank mate, with two self-inflicted hangs (Qe8, f3) making the direction mixed.

1246.label: Top boards are self-inflicted material losses where the played move drops own piece—rook, queen, bishop, or knight—either to an immediate free capture or within a 2–3 move refutation; medium boards blur the piece-type further and broaden toward slower eval-dropping moves (queen retreats, king-safety/pawn weakenings) that concede material or a winning attack over several moves rather than instantly.

1250.label: Top: a move strips a defender (or removes a blocking/guarding pawn) and the opponent's KNIGHT wins the now-undefended pawn/piece, frequently via a fork or capture-with-tempo; medium keeps the same 'leaves material undefended' mistake but the punishing piece broadens to any piece (queen Qxd4, rook Rxf7, bishop Bxa8) rather than specifically a knight.

1238.label: Top: in a balanced/drawn endgame a greedy capture or careless king/rook move drops a piece—most often a rook, also bishop/knight—to a tactical refutation that usually begins with a check or back-rank threat; medium keeps the self-inflicted hang but broadens upward to dropping the queen or walking into forced mate (with a couple merely squandering a winning trade).

1245.label: At the peak it's constant on quietly squandering a clearly winning eval by skipping the only strong continuation (materially-safe positional/tempo omissions like c3-for-f4, a5-for-g4, h3, Re8); at medium activation it blurs into outright material loss — hanging pieces and walking into tactics (Qxf4, dxc4, allowed forks and mate threats).

1247.label: Top boards are immediate material drops—a greedy capture or careless reposition that hangs a piece (rook/knight/bishop/queen) for a ~500cp swing; medium boards broaden to repositioning/pawn moves that neglect a defensive duty (king safety, pawn or passed-pawn defense), losing material or getting mated over the next 2–3 moves rather than on the spot.

1244.label: Top: in a clearly winning/better position the player skips a concrete forcing tactic (usually a check like Rd1+/Bxe5+/Qxf5+/Nf7+, sometimes a winning capture) and plays a slow non-forcing move, squandering the win; medium keeps the 'squandered advantage' theme but blurs into weakening/slow moves that not only miss the forcing line but actively hang material or allow a mating attack (king_safety pawn pushes, unsound rook sacs).

1252.label: Top boards consistently play a king-neglecting move that walks into a forced (often immediate mate-in-1/2) checkmating attack; medium boards keep the exposed-king theme but blur toward decisive material loss (forks, pins, back-rank, check-winning-a-rook) and even non-king positional slips, plus one missed-mate case.

1254.label: Top boards throw away a winning passed-pawn/promotion endgame via a pointless tempo-losing check (chiefly rook, also queen) that lets the enemy king activate or a pawn queen; medium broadens to other tempo-wasting or wrong-direction moves (passive king retreats, queen misplacement, non-check) that likewise squander a winning position.

1253.label: Top boards consistently throw away a forced MATE (ranging from mate-in-1 to mate-in-12) by choosing a natural developing/trading/tempo move that's still materially safe and leaves a winning edge; at medium the pattern blurs from 'mate' to 'winning combination/attack' and even move-order or positional slips, so several boards merely forfeit a decisive tactic or hang material rather than a literal checkmate.

1251.label: Top: in a winning endgame a tempting queen check or capture grabs material (or the wrong target) and throws away the cleanest path—a forced mate, free piece, or faster conversion—yet usually stays winning; medium blurs to a rook/pawn forcing move (e.g. f4+ instead of Rxh4) that lets the opponent defend and squanders the win down to equality.

1233.label: Top boards: a tempting forcing move (a capture or check) trades off the player's key attacking/defending piece and squanders a winning position; medium boards keep the 'active move throws away the edge' theme but broaden the mechanism to outright hangs, missed mating/saving tactics, and even slow passive moves.

1259.label: Top boards are quiet bishop pushes onto an undefended square (h6/a6/h3) lost for nothing; medium broadens to bishop captures/sacs (Bxg7, Bxf7+) that grab a single pawn but get recaptured, still dropping a full minor piece in the opening.

1248.label: Top boards almost always overlook a winning-or-saving queen/bishop intermezzo check (Qc5+, Ba6+, Qxf5+, Bb5+) played as a quiet move instead; medium boards keep the same 'missed forcing check' core but blur the checker to include knight and plain capturing checks (Nxf5+, Bxd5+, Qxd5+) arising from positional/fork themes.

1243.label: Top: a g-pawn push (g6/g3) to chase the queen off h5/h4 opens the e-file and long diagonal, letting the queen check (Qxe5+/Qxe4+) and fork-capture the now-exposed corner rook (h8/h1); medium keeps the identical g-pawn-chases-queen pattern but the booty broadens beyond the rook to other material the queen's central capture nets (pinned bishop, a knight via Qxd5+, or the exchange via a knight sac).

1228.label: At peak activation a decisive forcing move (usually a check or capture, e.g. exf6+, Rxb2+, Qf3+, Rxe8+) is on the board and the player instead picks a slow/natural/greedy alternative — about half squander a forced win/mate (1,3,4,6,8) and half walk into material loss or mate (2,5,7,9,10, where the best move was a calm defensive one); at medium activation the positions are less sharp and the same natural slow or greedy moves mostly just hang material or lose tempo (Bxh4, Bxc5, Qf4, Bxh6, Rd1), so direction is genuinely mixed between 'missed win' and 'hung material'.

1261.label: Top boards cleanly hang an undefended piece — a knight leaping to unsupported d5 or a bishop on g4/g6 stripped of its defender (queen recaptures); medium keeps the hung-piece core but blurs into material lost via tempo slips, positional trades, move-order errors, and allowed forks.

1258.label: Top: a developing move drops an undefended minor piece—almost always a bishop, occasionally a knight or queen—to an immediate pawn capture in the opening; medium blurs to hanging only a pawn (or losing material from a rim-placed/misplaced piece) rather than a full piece.

1255.label: Top boards uniformly squander a winning advantage by skipping a clear bishop capture (Bxg5/Bxc6/Bxd4) that nets a full piece; medium keeps the 'passive move instead of the available winning capture' theme but broadens the missed shot to knight captures (Nxe4/Nxd4/Nxg4), recaptures of other pieces, and even pawn breaks (b4), with a few cases where the lazy move also hangs own material.

1265.label: Top: a materially-safe move (almost always a rook) that ignores a one-move capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, throwing away a winning position; medium keeps the free-queen-grab theme (e.g. Rxa8) but blurs toward other missed simple winning captures/recaptures like a wrong-piece recapture on d5.

1263.label: Top boards squander a winning (or drawing) position via a slow king/rook move, greedy capture, or bad trade that hangs or loses the QUEEN as the pivot of the refutation (fork wins it, bad queen trade, or hung queen); medium boards keep the 'throw away the advantage by losing material' core but blur the lost piece to a rook/knight/exchange rather than strictly the queen.

1260.label: Top: a near-winning side plays a materially-safe, non-forcing opening move (castling, bishop retreat, quiet pawn move) that squanders a concrete knight sacrifice — almost always Nxf7, occasionally Nxc3/Nxf2; medium keeps the 'winning position, quiet move skips the forcing shot' core but blurs the tactic itself to other knight strikes (Ne6 sac) and even non-knight winning moves (central exd5, precise capture).

1266.label: Top boards decline a forced mating rook check—usually to snatch a pawn—throwing away mate-in-one/forced mate; medium boards decline a forcing rook check that merely preserves the winning attack/initiative, settling for a pawn-grab or quiet reposition that only shrinks the edge.

1262.label: Top boards hang a specific piece (queen, knight, or rook) outright—by ignoring a direct threat or a move-order error that leaves it en prise; medium blurs into any self-inflicted material loss, adding dropped exchanges, bad recaptures, and king-safety walks straight into mate.
