1249.label: A passive/tempo-losing move (retreat of a dominant piece, flank pawn push, or side-pawn grab) throws away a winning advantage; at the top the abandoned piece's role exposes the king to a decisive attack, while medium blurs to any slow/greedy move punished by general material or positional erosion (sometimes own rook/knight/pawn or king falling over 2-3 moves).

1264.label: Top: a knight abandons a critical kingside defensive square (classic Bxg7/Qxh7+ motif), often to grab a pawn, and the player's own king is mated by force; medium broadens to any piece or pawn move (king walks, ...g8/g8 blocks, pawn pushes, developing/retreating minors) that removes a defender or opens lines, triggering a self-inflicted collapse into mate or lost material.

1268.label: Top: rook grabs a dangerous passed pawn and is immediately recaptured (by king/knight/bishop/pawn, often with check), losing rook-for-pawn in an already-lost endgame; medium keeps the same rook-for-passed-pawn trade but the capture is sometimes near-best defense rather than a clear blunder.

1256.chip: Pawn capture opens own king (vs. drops material)
1256.label: Top: a tension-resolving pawn recapture/capture (classically axb4 or hxg5) rips open a file straight toward the player's own king in an opposite-castling/storm setting, handing a decisive attack rather than losing material outright; medium keeps the premature pawn capture/recapture that opens lines but blurs the punishment from pure king attack to simply dropping material (hanging knight/pawn, allowed fork, Qh4+ shots).

1269.label: Top boards consistently hang or trap a knight that's attacked by a pawn in the opening (ignoring exf6/dxc6 or fleeing to a trappable square); medium broadens the lost piece to also include a fianchettoed bishop and an over-extended early queen getting captured/trapped by similar pawn advances.

1257.label: At the peak, a slow non-forcing move (flank pawn push/knight maneuver) forgoes a winning forcing queen check and lets the opponent's king attack or decisive tactic crash through; at medium it broadens to passive/prophylactic moves that skip any forcing check (bishop checks, captures, intermezzo) and so squander a winning initiative or even hang material.

1267.label: Top boards consistently skip the neutralizing ...Bxe5 and drop material to a centralized knight's fork/infiltration (Nd7 hitting queen+bishop, Ng4/Ng6+); medium keeps the knight-tactic theme but blurs to other forms—skipped ...Bxf3, kingside knight attacks, king+rook forks (Nf6+/Nxe7+), and trapped or hanging own knights.

1273.label: Top boards uniformly miss the one precise winning pawn break (almost always b4) in pure king-and-pawn endgames, playing a materially-safe slow king move or wrong capture that lets Black blockade with ...c5; medium blurs to other timely breaks (a4/b5/h5/d6) and tempo-losing king moves, with a few outliers tipping into actually hanging a pawn/piece to a knight fork or back-rank shot.

1275.label: Top boards are winning passed-pawn endgames where the player skips the one decisive forcing line—a check-promotion or a rook trade/sac into a won pawn ending—and instead plays a passive king/pawn move that lets the opponent hold via perpetual check; medium broadens the pattern to other won positions (premature pawn pushes, missed mating knight move, missed queen trade) and even non-endgame cases, blurring the constant 'skipped forcing conversion' across phases and into a couple of material-dropping opening moves.

1270.label: Top: a rook is left undefended on an open file/diagonal and grabbed for free by the enemy queen (Qxa5/Qxh4 etc.); medium broadens to any hung piece (bishop, knight, exchange, even a pawn) and to other punishments — still mostly a free queen capture, but sometimes a knight fork, a Bd4+ zwischenzug, or (rarely) a missed-win tempo loss.

1272.label: In a winning/better position the player plays a slow, inferior move that throws away the edge instead of the decisive continuation; top boards are clearly-won positions skipping a forcing king-safety tactic (check/capture/fork like Nxb6+, Qg1, Nf6+, Nxe1/Nxe2+), while medium blurs to merely-better positions where the missed move is quiet precision (pawn breaks, recaptures, king activation) and several cases tip into actually hanging material.

1277.label: Top boards are all pawn CAPTURES that release a blockade/tension and, after the recapture, hand the opponent (connected) passed pawns or a fortress; medium broadens to any tension-releasing pawn move (advances like h4/d5 that provoke a structure-wrecking recapture) and even piece trades that open lines/destroy a key structure for the opponent's counterplay.

1274.label: Top: a passive king/piece move in a won endgame skips a concrete winning capture — almost always a free hanging rook, occasionally a knight fork; medium: blurs to passive/tempo-losing king moves that squander a winning or critical endgame without any clear free capture.

1271.label: Top: throws away a won game by prematurely trading (Nxf3+/Bxf6/Nxf6+) or a slow move instead of establishing/exploiting the pin on the kingside f3- or f6-knight; medium keeps the same 'squander the winning edge with a trade/slow move' theme but the pin motif blurs to other squares (c3, d3) or other missed winning tactics (and occasionally even hangs material).

1278.chip: Quiet move skips queen trade (or piece)
1278.label: Top boards are constant: a passive queen (sometimes king) reposition that abandons a game-saving queen trade/simplification (Qxg3/Qxf4/Qxe6) and is punished by lost material; medium blurs to broader quiet moves (king shuffles, premature captures, slow pawn/king moves) that skip a forcing resource—trading queens, saving a hanging piece, or an exchange-sac—and lose material or squander the edge.

1279.label: At the peak it's uniformly a pawn (73%) or bishop (27%) CHECK that the enemy king simply captures—handing back the checking unit and releasing the king from the d-file/mating-net pressure or attack (incl. unsound Greek-Gift Bxh7+); medium blurs the 'check' requirement to non-checking captures (Bxd6, Bxd3+) and even quiet moves (Kd3, Qb2) that likewise let the king escape or leave a piece hanging, squandering a winning/attacking position.

1285.label: Top: a premature queen trade with check that downgrades a winning position into a small edge, skipping a more decisive tactic—almost always a knight fork that wins the queen; medium keeps the 'throw away a win in a winning position by a simplifying/inaccurate move' core but blurs the played move (not always a queen-trade-check) and the missed tactic (knight forks, but also pins, move-order shots, and forced mates).

1280.label: TOP: in clearly won endgames with kingside pawn tension, the player releases it—capturing or playing a slow waiting move—instead of the winning lock/break/advance (f5/g5/g6/a5/hxg6), and the constant is 'tension released in a won position' (frequently a 0cp non-blunder, not always an actual win-throw); MEDIUM blurs this by adding middlegame tension and tension-releasing captures that actually hang material or merely shrink the advantage rather than purely missing a lock.

1286.label: Top boards uniformly hang the undefended c4/c5 Italian bishop after a tension-ignoring developing move (d4, O-O, Qf3, Re8, Ng4) that allows a free Bxc4/Bxc5; medium blurs this to other hung/retreating bishops (Bf5 to Bxf5, Bb3) and even missed/allowed tactics (skipping the winning Bxe3 knight-fork, allowing Nxb5–Nc7+ fork).

1281.label: Top boards are uniformly structure- or king-weakening pawn pushes (c4, g5, f5, h4, b4, b6, etc.) that squander a draw or win with no piece hung — purely positional; medium broadens to weakening/tempo-losing moves that are sometimes non-pawn (Bd8, Rd1, Kd6) and whose refutation turns concretely tactical (checks, knight forks, even mate, or a wrong capture hanging a piece).

1287.label: Top boards uniformly skip an immediate winning check — overwhelmingly a forced mate (Qf2+, Qg2+, Qf6+) — in favor of a quiet or greedy capturing move; medium broadens slightly, still mostly missing a winning check but occasionally one that wins decisive material rather than mate, or even a non-checking quiet win (Nf3, mate in 6).

1284.label: Top: a passed pawn is advanced—almost always with a check—letting the enemy king step directly in front to blockade it (or hide behind it as a pawn-shield), squandering a winning position; medium broadens to non-checking pawn pushes and even tempo-wasting rook/king moves that likewise let the passer be permanently blockaded or rounded up, sometimes outright losing the pawn.

1293.label: Top boards mostly hang a major piece—predominantly rooks (plus one queen)—by placing it en prise or vacating its defense, with two outliers (a wrong-capture trade into a lost endgame and a squandered forced mate); medium broadens the hung piece to minors (bishop, knight) and overloaded-defender losses while keeping the same self-inflicted material loss.

1292.label: Top boards are uniformly QUEEN checks that immediately drop the queen for a pawn or minor piece (e.g. Qxg2+/Qe4+ into a bishop, Qxg8+ into a rook recapture); medium broadens the checking piece to bishop sacrifices (Bb3+, Bxf2+) and occasionally to non-checking material giveaways or greedy captures that miss a win, but the constant is a forcing check that loses the player's own piece for inadequate compensation.

1288.label: At the peak the player makes a safe (often king) move in a drawn/won endgame that misses a clean winning capture — twice a free queen, once a bishop; at medium it blurs into safe non-capturing king moves that fail to convert (e.g., missing a forced mate), with broader tempo-loss, lost-blockader, and king-safety squanders rather than missed captures.

1294.label: Top boards are passive but materially-safe opening moves that miss a bishop pin/deflection (Bb5/Bb4/Be6/Bg4/Bh6) winning the enemy queen; medium boards keep the 'winning-position-overlooks-a-tactic' core but broaden the shot to pawn breaks (d5/e5/c6) and captures (Bxg7) that win general material or the exchange rather than specifically the queen.

1282.label: Top boards cleanly drop a piece—most often a knight, frequently after a greedy ...Bxb5-type capture or a defender-abandoning retreat refuted by simple recapture or a short forced sequence; medium keeps the material-losing core but broadens toward exchange losses and positional/tempo errors that squander a winning edge without always conceding a clean piece.

1276.label: Already losing in the endgame, the player fails to neutralize the opponent's passed pawn—at the peak by skipping the key capture of its supporter (Kxf6, Bxd2, Kxf5, Kxg3) so it promotes into a forced mate; medium boards are the same missed stop-the-pawn capture (Kxf5, Rxf2+), while top also blurs into blockade/king-route race errors (Ke7, Kc3, Rxh7+).

1289.label: Top boards are nearly uniform: a queen trade-offer/repositioning move (Qe2, Qd7, Qg2, Qd2, Qb3...) that leaves the king exposed to a forcing check winning the player's own material, when stepping the king to safety was best; medium broadens the piece (rook/bishop/king moves, self-obstructions that block the king's escape) and adds a couple of materially-safe slips that miss a win (allow perpetual or slower mate).

1290.label: Top boards are all speculative minor-piece captures/sacs in the opening (knight on f7/f2/e4/e5, once Bxf7+) that hang the piece for a single pawn and are refuted by a clean recapture; medium blurs to broader greedy/unsound captures and opening moves (Qxd6, Rxd5, ...c5, premature castling) that lose material or squander a near-winning advantage.

1299.label: Top boards are kingside g/h pawn pushes/captures that lose a tempo or wreck the player's own structure and squander a winning-or-equal position (rather than cleanly hanging material); medium broadens to other tempo-wasting moves (king retreats, castling, rook lifts) that hand the opponent a tempo-gaining check or pawn break, with a minority instead dropping a pawn/piece to a tactic (fork, undefended pawn).

1296.label: Top: in a winning position the player voluntarily trades/captures with the queen (Qxd5, Qxe2+, Qxc7+, Qxf7), simplifying into rough equality instead of a winning capture, fork, or mate; medium blurs to other simplifying exchanges (Bxe7, Nxe4) that release the attack and let the opponent consolidate.

1291.label: At the peak the player hangs a ROOK in a drawn rook endgame (e.g. a king move like Kc5 leaving Rd1 undefended → Rxd1); at medium activation it blurs to hanging a BISHOP (fxe3 dropping the d5 bishop) and bleeds into missed wins/saves (missed exd5, missed Rxe7+) and trivial tempo losses, so only 'endgame material error with a rook on the board' is reliable across all boards.

1303.label: Top boards are uniform: Black hangs the e5 pawn (plus two White Bd3 cases) by playing a natural developing/tempo move instead of the freeing ...e4 advance/central pawn break, and the central pawn falls; medium boards blur into broader 'skipped the one correct move' errors where assorted natural moves (Bxg6, b4, cxd5, f3) drop material or squander a winning advantage rather than specifically hanging e5.

1302.label: At the peak the player plays a materially-safe move while overlooking an immediate decisive shot — a one-move forced mate or an outright queen-winning capture/fork; medium positions keep the 'missed decisive win' core but blur it to multi-move mating combinations, queen-winning back-rank combos, and 'wrong-capture' decisive wins, with a few outliers that instead hang the player's own material.

1298.label: At the peak, over-optimistic knight sorties (to the rim or chasing the enemy queen) that lose tempo and drop material 2-3 moves into the refutation; at medium it blurs to bishop/rook/king/pawn overreaches refuted by defender-removal hangs, back-rank shots, or forks.

1307.label: Top boards are consistently the same error—leaving the fianchettoed bishop undefended on the open long diagonal so Bxg7/Bxb2 wins it cleanly (sometimes by moving a piece that shielded the diagonal, plus one positional tempo-loss and one rook hang); medium blurs to adjacent long-diagonal/fianchetto faults—an overloaded rook dropping a knight, a passive bishop tempo-loss, and a fianchetto move that skips a winning ...Bxg2 capture.

1305.label: At the peak this is uniformly the open-e-file Petrov failure: skipping the required ...Qe7 and instead moving the e4 shield-knight (or grabbing a pawn / developing Bd6, ...f6), which hangs the queen to a Nc6+ discovered check down the open e-file; at medium it blurs to simply hanging the undefended e4 knight to Qxe4 and to other knight-related material drops (a fork, an endgame knight misstep) rather than specifically the queen via discovery.

1283.label: Top: throws away a winning/favorable position by missing the one precise tactical or tempo-gaining resource (e.g. Re4, Rxf3+, Rg7+), but the peak is genuinely split with outright hanging a piece or walking into mate; medium broadens to squandering near-equal positions with positional, tempo, or piece-trapping inaccuracies — mechanism (missed-win vs hung-material vs bad-trade) is mixed throughout.

1297.label: Top: an aggressive move—usually a check (Qc5+, Rxc7+, Bxf7+, Qd4+)—is played while the player's own king is already under a forced mating attack, so the only defense is ignored and the player is mated or drops the queen; medium blurs to non-checking active/greedy moves (grabs, defender removals, retreats like Qxc4, Nxe5, Rh6, Rac8) that similarly ignore a decisive threat, allowing back-rank mates or losing material.

1300.label: Top: committal pawn pushes/captures that self-destruct the player's own pawn structure or strategic asset, squandering a winning (or equal) position; medium blurs to rook/knight/king moves that abandon a defensive post, hanging material or advantage to a refuting break or tempo move — so the damage spans positional collapse to outright material loss.

1295.label: Top boards uniformly leave the QUEEN en prise to an enemy KNIGHT capture for grossly inadequate compensation; medium keeps the knight-recapture motif but broadens the hung piece to rooks and bishops (with one case captured by a bishop instead).

1301.label: Top boards uniformly skip a winning bishop-capture tactic (Bxe6 or Bxd4+, frequently with check) in favor of a quiet retreat/develop/castle; medium boards keep the missed-bishop-capture core (Bxg6, Bxf5, Bxh6, Bxc3+, Bxe5) but blur into other captures like a rook exchange sac (Rxe6) or capturing with the wrong piece.

1308.chip: Traded active piece into lost endgame (often knight)
1308.label: Top boards consistently capture/trade off a dominant centralized knight via an even recapture, gifting the opponent dangerous passed pawns or a winning pawn majority and a lost endgame; medium keeps the trade-a-well-placed-piece theme but blurs to bishop trades and looser simplifying captures (wrong-piece grabs and even outright hung pieces) that misjudge the piece's value into a worse position.

1309.label: Top: promotes a pawn to queen on a square where it's immediately captured (usually by a rook on the promotion file), hanging the new queen and squandering a won position instead of playing the prep/intermezzo first; medium keeps the premature-promotion theme but broadens the refutation to other recapturing pieces (king/knight/bishop) and to promotions that ignore a forced mate or allow a saving perpetual rather than pure material loss.

1313.label: Top: cleanly throws away a winning position by hanging a piece (often moving its sole defender) or missing a forced mate (usually mate-in-1); medium: blurs into greedy pawn-grabs, tempo loss, and positional/endgame slips that quietly surrender the same large advantage.

1314.label: Top boards are uniformly a slow/passive move that overlooks a forcing winning pawn check — frequently the f5+ king-and-rook fork — that wins material outright; medium broadens beyond pawns to other winning forcing shots (discovered checks like d6+/fxe5+, knight forks like Nd4+, even mate-in-one), with the constant being a passive move skipping a forcing material-winning check rather than the specific f5+ motif.

1306.label: At the peak a slow/passive move fails to win a trapped enemy knight (g7, g2, b3, b3, b7), throwing away a winning edge; at medium it blurs into any tempo-losing/passive move that squanders the advantage—now frequently by hanging the player's own piece or a pure positional give-back, with the knight no longer always the target.

1304.label: Top boards are clean 7th-rank skewer/back-rank rook checks that win material (usually a rook, sometimes queen/bishop) in already-won positions; medium broadens to deflection and other forcing checks—prize and even checking piece blur (incl. a queen check), with a couple of defensive/losing outliers.

1317.label: Top: a passive 'safe' developing/pawn move overlooks a free, undefended enemy bishop (b5/g4/b4/g5) in the opening, throwing away a winning piece; medium blurs to missing other hanging pieces (notably knights, e.g. Bxd5) and broader missed winning captures/tactics, with a few cases shading into self-hangs and positional errors.

1312.label: Top boards are king moves that throw away a drawn-or-losing endgame—hanging a piece (Q/N/R), walking into a mating net, or ceding critical tempo to a passed pawn; medium keeps the same game-losing effect but broadens the moving unit to knight, rook, queen, and pawn (and occasionally a thrown-away win), so what's constant is 'an inferior endgame move that collapses the position' while the mechanism and piece blur.

1320.label: Constant across all: a reflexive forcing check played instead of the stronger (often quiet) winning move; at the peak it throws away a concrete forced mate (frequently also hanging the checking piece — queen/rook/bishop/knight), while medium boards blur to the same tempting check merely squandering a decisive/winning advantage rather than a forced mate.

1310.label: Top: a quiet/passive or natural-looking move (developing move, retreat, non-forcing check) squanders a winning position by overlooking a concrete material-winning tactic — free hanging piece, fork, or free pawn; medium blurs to plausible moves that throw away a winning or equal position via tempo loss, positional concession, or allowing the opponent's own tactic, so the 'win' missed is often positional/forcing rather than clean material, and several lines actually lose material in the refutation.

1322.label: Top boards uniformly skip an immediate pawn promotion with check (c1=Q+, e8=Q+, f8=Q+) that forces near-instant mate, instead playing a slow king/piece move; medium blurs this to passing up any fastest forced win in a won endgame — including a winning queen check (Qxg6+) rather than only promotions.

1319.label: Top: ignores an existing attack or mutual tension (often on the long diagonal) and leaves a piece—usually a bishop, sometimes the queen/rook—hanging for an immediate free capture; medium broadens to less-direct material loss, including walking into a fork, abandoning a piece's defender, or playing a quiet/tempo-wasting move that drops material over the next 2-3 moves.

1318.label: Top boards are winning middlegames where a slow, non-forcing or wrong-order move leaves the player's own rook (occasionally queen/bishop) en prise for a free capture; medium blurs into the endgame, where a tempo-wasting move (e.g. ...b6 instead of ...Rxd5) throws away a won rook/pawn ending the same way.

1323.label: Top: a greedy capture or wrong recapture wastes the single tempo needed to stop the opponent's passed pawn, so it queens by force and a win/draw becomes a loss; medium blurs to broader endgame tempo-loss or piece misplacement (not always a capture, and sometimes only squandering the win into a draw) that fails the passed-pawn race or critical defensive task.

1315.label: Top boards: a clearly winning opening is thrown away with a knight central to the decisive line, predominantly via self-inflicted greedy or careless moves that hang the player's own material (sometimes over 2-3 moves); medium boards keep the won-position + knight theme but blur toward missed winning knight captures/tactics, and the punished/lost piece itself varies.

1321.label: Top boards are razor-consistent: a passive/quiet move overlooks a decisive central knight capture (Nxd5/Nxd4/Nxe5/Nxe6/Ne4) that wins material via fork or discovered attack; medium boards keep the 'safe move skips the forcing shot' core but blur the tactic — still often a central knight strike (Nxd5/Nxf4/Ncxd5), yet drifting into other quiet moves that squander a winning edge or even allow the opponent's tactic, so the knight/'missed-win' signature weakens.

1311.label: Top boards are constant: the only/best move is to capture or trade off a centralized knight on e4/e5/d5, and skipping it (passive/wrong-order move) usually lets that knight deliver a fork or check (hangs material); medium broadens the knight's square to c6/d4/f3/f4 and tilts toward simply missing a free knight capture (clean missed win).

1316.label: At the peak it's king moves in clearly-won endgames that merely lose tempo or lengthen the mate (near-0cp inaccuracies); at medium it blurs to other pieces (rook/pawn/bishop) and to more severe cases of actually throwing away the win (h6 vs g5+) or hanging material via a tactical refutation (Kg2→skewer), so the feature spans optimal-but-slow technique through genuine blunders.

1325.label: Top boards consistently play a natural, non-forcing move from a winning position that skips a concrete winning tactical shot (capture, queen centralization, or pawn break) while staying materially safe; medium boards blur toward walking the king into mate or hanging material outright.

1327.label: Top: from a winning middlegame, plays a passive/non-forcing move (queen, pawn, king, or wrong-piece retreat) and overlooks a forcing tactic whose key shot is a rook capture or exchange sacrifice winning material; medium keeps the 'missed forcing win' theme but broadens the winning shot to any capture (bishop/knight) or even a forced mate, with one or two cases where the skipped tactic actually leaves own material hanging.

1328.label: Top boards are uniform: the player grabs the queen with the natural immediate capture but skips the required intermediate check/zwischenzug (Rxg8+, fxe6+, Be3+, Nd3+), leaving its own piece (rook/bishop/knight) hanging to a 1-move refutation; at medium the pattern blurs to any natural move that skips a move-order finesse or coordinating move, mixing self-hangs (incl. back-rank/discovered-check mates) with pure missed wins.

1326.label: Top boards are almost all the missed pawn capture exf6 winning a knight while the player makes a safe recapture/quiet move; medium blurs to other material-winning captures (dxc6, Bxc3, Bxf3, exchange sacs) and occasionally drifts toward recaptures that hang material or non-opening cases.

1324.label: Top boards are all queen moves (usually greedy material grabs) that ignore an immediate mating threat against their own king and allow forced checkmate; medium keeps the 'ignored the opponent's forcing refutation while playing for activity/material' theme but blurs to other pieces (rook/bishop) and to refutations that merely win material, initiative, or tempo rather than delivering strict mate.

1331.label: Top boards uniformly skip a forcing Qh5+/Qh4+ that wins the h8/h1 rook against a king bared by the missing f-pawn, playing a quiet developing move instead; medium boards still miss the same early queen check but the king-exposure now stems from a self-inflicted ...f6/f4 push and the payoff blurs from the rook down to a pawn, structural damage, or a move-order finesse.

1338.label: Top: a quiet, non-forcing king/rook move in a won endgame that skips the decisive capture/check or faster mate; medium blurs to bishop/knight moves and more 0cp false-positives, with a couple actually hanging material rather than just being slow.

1329.label: Top boards uniformly ignore an existing mate-in-one threat against the player's own king (usually while greedily grabbing material); medium broadens to longer forced mates (M2–M16) and king-walk blunders, occasionally degrading to plain material loss or a squandered own forced mate.

1330.chip: Squandered win with quiet move (king attack)
1330.label: Top boards squander a clear win by playing a slow/quiet pawn, king, or queen move instead of the forcing continuation against an exposed king (mate-in-one, decisive check, or queen tactic winning material); medium boards keep the 'passive move lets the advantage slip' core but blur the king-attack specificity, broadening to general positional/defensive lapses (retreats to dead squares, declining to castle, slower mate routes, failing to activate a rook) where the missed line is positional rather than a direct king hunt.

1333.label: At the peak it's almost uniformly a clean knight fork (Nd3+/Ng6+/Nd5+ etc.) that checks the king and wins a rook outright, overlooked in favor of a passive or greedy material-safe move; at medium the rook-winning target stays constant but the tactic broadens to pawn and bishop forks plus discovered-attack and deflection checks, still skipped for a natural pawn-grab or quiet developing move.

1335.label: Top: materially-safe but passive, tempo-losing rook/king/pawn shuffles that abandon a forcing active continuation (Rh2, Rxc8, Rd2+, Rg6+), collapsing a clearly winning position into equality; medium keeps the passive/imprecise-move theme but blurs the consequence — now the quiet move also hangs material, misses a forced mate, or turns a drawn position into a lost one.

1336.label: Top boards skip an immediate forced checkmate on the exposed enemy king (often a literal mate-in-1 like Qg6#/Qxd8#/Qb3#) by playing a safe capture, fork, or knight retreat instead; medium broadens to longer forced mating attacks (mate-in-10 via discovered check, slower king-hunts) plus the occasional hung piece, but the constant is choosing a materially-safe move over a winning king attack.

1340.label: Top: a materially-safe king/piece move skips the single best move — usually grabbing a hanging enemy queen (Rxb8, Rxd1, Rxh4) in an equal/drawn endgame; medium broadens to any free hanging piece (e.g. Rxg5 winning a loose bishop), with a few peak boards instead missing the lone drawing resource rather than a capture.

1332.label: Top boards share a clean peak—in a near-lost endgame the player ignores the single best move, usually a free major-piece grab (Bxc3/Rxb8/Rxh4) or the sole-saving Kc4, and instantly collapses to mate; medium keeps the 'only one critical move existed' core but blurs in direction, mixing a missed queen-capture (Rg8 instead of Rxh4) with a quiet move that hangs material to an in-between check (f5).

1348.label: Top boards are uniformly the defending KING marching the wrong direction (away from the passer's promotion path), letting the opponent's passed pawn queen uncontested; medium broadens to other neglect of the passer—wrong-piece blockades (bishop instead of king), tempo-wasting rook/pawn moves, or grabbing material—that likewise let it promote.

1342.label: Top boards: a bishop is the decisive piece and the player typically hangs, traps, or fails to use its own bishop (losing material or skipping a bishop tactic); medium blurs to hanging other pieces (knight, exchange, pawn) and more missed wins, with the bishop only sometimes central.

1341.label: Top: a premature queen sortie to an exposed central square that's chased with tempo (and sometimes drops a piece left behind); medium blurs it to a queen left exposed/trapped — at times via a non-queen move — or harassed for outright material loss (or an advantage squandered).

1344.label: Top boards uniformly ignore a knight fork (almost always Nf7, answerable by Kxf7) and play a quiet developing/castling move that hangs the queen; medium boards broaden to ignoring other tactics—pins, discovered attacks, non-f7 forks, king-safety/tempo errors and even a couple of missed free captures—hanging a rook or minor as often as the queen.

1337.label: Top boards drop White's bishop on c4 when the e4-knight wanders off (best was Bd3), losing it to ...dxc4; medium broadens to either color hanging a minor piece—bishop on c5 or knight on e4/e5—to a free pawn capture out of a level opening.

1343.chip: Hangs pawn in lost endgame (king move)
1343.label: Top: in an already-lost endgame the player makes a passive king move that abandons a pawn (sometimes a rook), deepening the loss; medium: broadens to other passive/greedy moves (rook, bishop, pawn pushes) and more often walks into a forced mating net rather than just shedding material.

1346.label: Top boards are uniformly near-0cp slow king marches/pawn pushes (plus a couple of spite checks) that delay the engine's most direct capture while the position stays 100% winning—pure tempo loss; medium boards keep the same skip-the-direct-capture pattern but blur in severity and piece (king, pawn, plus bishop/rook moves) where the wasted tempo balloons from 0–14cp into genuine 175–435cp blunders that throw the won endgame to a draw or loss.

1347.label: Top: a faulty capture or unsound sacrifice—often a minor piece (Greek-Gift bishop sacs, knight grabs, greedy pawn-wins)—that loses material to a clean recapture or zwischenzug, usually in the opening; medium keeps the 'loses own material' core but blurs the mechanism, adding quiet developing/pawn moves that walk a piece into capture or undermine its support, with the loss widening to the exchange or a pawn and the refutation including forks as well as recaptures/zwischenzugs.

1334.label: Top: in a winning endgame the player ignores a free hanging enemy rook and instead plays a king/pawn move that hangs their own rook; medium blurs to skipping a free bishop/queen capture or merely missing the winning capture without actually losing material.

1349.label: Top: a materially-safe move in a won position skips a clearly winning capture (queen, rook, exchange, or pawn); medium broadens to missing the best continuation generally — often a quiet positional move or pawn push rather than a capture (with one case actually hanging material).

1354.label: Top: a slow king move (occasionally a pawn move) wastes the critical tempo in a won/drawn rook endgame, squandering the precise rook tactic or promotion while material stays safe; medium blurs to pawn pushes and rook moves and mixes in cases that actually hang material rather than just missing the win.

1353.label: Player makes a materially-safe but passive/slow move (king walk, quiet pawn push, or rook reposition) and overlooks a concrete winning continuation; at the top the missed win is usually a forcing decisive shot (mate-in-2, free capture, skewer, infiltrating tactic), while medium boards blur toward missing precise endgame technique/tempo (king marches, piece activation, correct move order).

1358.label: Top boards consistently hang the queen — left en prise, pinned, or forked — to a one- or two-move opening refutation, while medium positions broaden to knights, bishops, and pawns dropped to the same kind of immediate opening tactic.

1351.label: At the peak the player passes up a clear material-winning move—usually a decisive tactic/fork in an unclear position; at medium strength it blurs into squandering already-won positions via passive or self-obstructing play (often passed-pawn conversion) and sometimes hanging material outright.

1345.label: At the peak the player reliably passes up the engine's clean, often game-deciding capture—frequently substituting a pointless check (Bf4+, Bd6+, Bc3+, Bg7+) or a wrong/routine capture; medium boards blur this into smaller missed captures (a pawn, Kxh6) or even non-capture best moves, with direction genuinely split between ~6 squandered wins and ~4 cases where ignoring the capture hangs the player's own queen/rook.

1339.label: At the peak it's a uniform pattern: in a winning opening the player makes a greedy knight pawn-grab (Nxe5/Nxf4/Nxd5/Nxe4) that gets cleanly recaptured, hanging the knight for a pawn (a couple top boards instead hang the knight by leaving it undefended); at medium activation the hung-knight core blurs into general squandering of a winning opening advantage — tempo-losing checks/pawn moves (Bb5+, f3), wrong-knight/positional captures, a trapped bishop, and even allowing a knight fork.

1350.label: At the peak it's a quiet, non-forcing move (queen shuffle, passive retreat/regroup, slow flank or developing push) that ignores a concrete demand—central tension, a direct threat, or a defender's duty—ceding the initiative and frequently losing material over the next 2-3 moves; at medium the pattern blurs into related lapses (greedy pawn grabs, king-weakening pawn advances, rooks to undefended squares, and missed central breaks) that likewise concede initiative or material, with the piece/tactic involved varying widely.

1357.label: At the peak the player hangs their own queen, bishop, or knight to a single-piece fork/deflection/overload tactic; at medium the pattern blurs to also include skipping a winning capture, king-safety mating collapses, and structural/positional concessions—but every board turns on mishandling the one critical piece whose capture or neutralization was decisive.

1362.chip: Hangs piece on greedy capture (often queen)
1362.label: At the peak, a material-grabbing capture ignores an existing threat and drops the queen to a simple recapture; at medium the same threat-blind capture instead loses a bishop or knight, often via a zwischenzug/move-order refutation.

1355.label: Top: from a winning/drawn position the player passes up the clean winning capture (best move is a capture in ~9/10) and instead plays a flashy check or quiet king/rook reposition that usually hangs material to a knight fork or back-rank mate; medium keeps the declined-capture core but blurs — the skipped best move is sometimes a quiet faster-mate/pawn break rather than a capture, and the move merely squanders the win (slower mate, reduced edge) instead of outright hanging.

1365.label: Top: an aggressive/greedy opening move (frequently abandoning the guarded c5 bishop) leaves a piece hanging to a simple or short-tactic capture — almost always a bishop, occasionally the queen; medium blurs to hung knights and pawns and even non-material king-safety/positional blunders.

1356.label: Top: a brash queen move (often a pointless check) abandons the king's defense/back rank or a key guard, squandering a fine position and inviting a mating attack or material-winning tactic; medium blurs the piece (knight/bishop/rook/pawn) and broadens the abandoned duty from king safety to defending a hung pawn/piece, but still ends in lost material.

1361.label: Top is uniformly a slow, tempo-wasting move—usually a non-urgent pawn push—that fails to contest open files or force a rook trade, letting the opponent double rooks on the 7th/2nd rank for a winning initiative; medium keeps the 'passive move cedes the initiative' core but blurs to other slow moves (queen/knight/king) and broader punishments—back-rank mates, discovered attacks, and outright piece hangs.

1359.chip: Squandered win with flashy check (often discovered)
1359.label: Top boards throw away a winning/mating position by choosing a tempting forcing check (very often a discovered check) over the quiet, simple decisive continuation; medium boards keep the same 'flashy forcing move beats the clean win' pattern but blur from strict checks to any enticing forcing capture/trade that dissipates the advantage — direction is mixed (some merely miss the cleaner win and stay materially safe, others actively hang a rook/exchange over the refutation).

1367.label: Top: a materially-safe move (usually a greedy capture like Nxa8/Qxh8) overlooks a forcing check that wins the queen outright or delivers mate, the single best move being a check in every board; medium keeps the missed-forcing-tactic theme but blurs it — checks now include knight-fork/intermezzo checks winning lesser material (rook/exchange/piece), and a couple of boards are quiet winning moves or even a non-blunder rather than clean queen-winning checks.

1366.label: In winning/better positions a natural developing, repositioning, or pawn-advancing move throws away the edge; top boards directly hang material (pawn h7/b2, Bg5, exchange) or skip a clean winning capture (Nxe4/Qxd2/Bxb7), while medium boards broaden to plausible moves that permit an equalizing or winning tactical resource (fork, discovered/perpetual check, mating attack).

1373.label: Top boards are all pawn pushes that try to gain a tempo by chasing the enemy queen but instead hang a pawn or fatally expose the own king (Qg3+, Bb4+, Bb5+ etc.); medium keeps the same queen-chasing pawn-push motif but broadens the cost from a dropped pawn/exchange to outright king collapse and forced mate (Qxa7 mate, Rf8+ mate).

1369.label: At the top the player is in a won position and skips the decisive blow — a forced mate or a free capture — playing a non-finishing move that keeps it merely winning; at medium this blurs into missing the most-efficient win generally (free material, tempo, or mate downgraded to a large edge), with a couple of noisy boards (a non-blunder, a self-hung bishop) and even some drawn positions spoiled into losses.

1364.label: Top: a key kingside defender is pulled away (or the king itself shuffles/weakens its pawn shelter), punished by a forced kingside mating attack; medium broadens to any move that abandons a defensive duty, punished by a decisive attack or tactic (fork, discovered check, hanging piece) that wins material rather than always mating.

1363.label: Top: liquidates the active rook with a check-recapture (Rxd7+/Rxe2+ etc.), converting a winning or defensible position into a lost-or-drawn king-and-pawn endgame; medium broadens the liquidating check-capture to queen trades and to moves that also forfeit forced mates or lose material.

1368.label: Top boards are uniformly a (often centralized) knight snatching a wing pawn (g6/g4/g3) that is immediately recaptured—losing a full knight for a pawn and frequently ripping open a file toward an uncastled/exposed king; medium blurs to other pieces grabbing pawns (Bxg6, Qxg2 walking into a trap, Nxd4) and looser material-losing greed, with some non-greedy noise (endgame/tempo errors, even a best move).

1352.label: Top: from a winning position a slow pawn move (usually a flank push harassing an enemy knight) ignores the concrete demand—often failing to grab/recapture a hanging knight—and squanders the edge by hanging material or missing a winning capture; medium broadens to the kicked knight ignoring the threat and jumping forward to fork or invade (Nc7+, Nf2, Ne3) for a tactical/king-safety collapse.

1371.label: Top boards uniformly squander a clearly winning position (a free queen/rook capture or forced mate) by playing a pointless check that lets the king escape ('patzer sees a check'); medium boards keep the squandered-win-in-a-winning-position theme but blur from checks to other tempo-wasting suboptimal moves (greedy pawn-grabs, wrong move-order, king missteps).

1375.chip: Hangs material to pawn push (often double-attack)
1375.label: Top: an aggressive pawn push meant to attack TWO enemy pieces at once (double-attack/fork attempt) backfires and drops the player's own material (pawn, exchange, rook, or even mate); medium broadens to single-target pawn kicks, passed-pawn advances, and even a capture that likewise hang material via a tactical refutation.

1376.label: At the top a reflexive recapture squanders a forced mate or a decisive winning check/zwischenzug; at medium it broadens to skipping an intermediate check or non-mating tactic that wins material (exchange/piece/queen) rather than delivering mate.

1372.label: Top boards consistently pass up one's OWN forced, almost-always-queen-delivered checkmate (or queen perpetual) by grabbing material or playing a quiet/non-checking move; medium keeps the 'skip the forcing win' core but blurs the delivering piece (pawn mates, knight forks) and the direction (often walking into/allowing the OPPONENT's forced mate instead of missing one's own).

1377.label: Top: king moves in pure pawn endgames that mishandle tempo/opposition in a promotion race—typically letting the opponent advance with a tempo-gaining check (e.g. d5+) or botching promotion order—though several peak boards are engine-approved 0–2cp non-blunders; medium blurs to pawn pushes (a3, b5, b6, h6) and rook/bishop-endgame races where a single mistimed king or pawn move similarly concedes the race.

1381.label: Top: in an endgame the player captures with the rook (usually a pawn, often with check) to trade off its sole blockading/defensive rook, turning a holdable/drawn position into a loss; medium broadens to other endgame-conversion slips — misplaced rook, tempo-wasting king moves or checks, and allowing an unfavorable trade.

1383.label: Top: pure king-and-pawn / promotion endgames where one imprecise king move throws away the theoretical result (squandering a draw in some, a win in others); medium broadens to rook endgames and tempo/opposition positions and occasionally to non-king pawn/queen moves, with several boards being 0cp non-blunders and direction mixed.

1384.label: Top boards uniformly drop a rook for the exchange by leaving it en prise to an enemy knight or bishop (whether by moving the rook onto the attacked square or by abandoning its defender); medium keeps the rook-for-exchange theme but the attacking unit blurs to also include pawns and tempo/fork shots, with a few outliers hanging the queen or walking into mate.

1382.label: Top boards uniformly hang or trap the dark-squared bishop (g5/h4) by skipping the resolving Bxe7 trade (caught by ...g5 or a direct ...Bxg5/Bxh4); medium blurs to other failures to resolve piece tension or capture in the right order — sometimes hanging a different bishop/piece via a skipped zwischenzug, and sometimes merely missing a winning intermezzo/fork rather than directly losing material.

1374.chip: Missed deflection check winning queen (or material)
1374.label: Top boards uniformly skip a deflection-sacrifice check (luring the king off a defended square) that wins the enemy QUEEN, opting instead for a quiet move, pawn grab, or plain queen trade; medium positions keep the 'missed forcing check' core but blur the target and motif — deflections, zwischenzugs, move-order finesses, and even knight forks that win a rook or knight or force mate rather than strictly the queen.

1380.label: Top boards are consistently passive or decentralizing king moves (or tempo-wasting pawn pushes in lieu of king activation) that surrender endgame activity/tempo and deepen an already losing or drawn position without hanging material; medium blurs in two ways — the move broadens to other passive piece placements (Nf6, Na2, Bc7) and the consequence broadens from slow deterioration to king moves that outright hang a piece or walk into forced mate.

1378.label: At the peak a tempting forcing check (most often a queen check, e.g. Qxf8+, Qh5+, Qxh5+) is played instead of a free capture or cleaner win, either hanging the player's own piece or merely squandering a clean win; at medium the same premature-check error blurs across rook, knight, bishop and even pawn checks, with the punishment ranging from a hung knight/rook/bishop to just a lost tempo.

1370.label: Top: a pointless check (e.g. Rb2+/Rb3+/Ne5+) in a won rook endgame that squanders the win by skipping the decisive king-centralizing tempo (Ke4); medium keeps the tempo-wasting/wrong-priority theme but blurs into non-check moves—piece relocations or pawn pushes that abandon a defensive file/duty or skip the critical break—letting own material (pawn, rook, or queen) fall over the next few moves.

1379.label: Top boards are king moves in sharp, single-resource endgames that miss the one precise win (forced mate, fork, queen-capture) or the only drawing break—occasionally also hanging material; medium broadens to non-king imprecisions (pawn push b4, queen retreat Qb7) that stay materially safe but skip the most forcing winning line.

1392.chip: Hangs piece in unsound sac (often Nxf7)
1392.label: Top boards are tightly constant: knight pseudo-sacrifices grabbing a pawn on f7/f2 (Fried-Liver-style) that simply hang to a clean recapture, losing a piece for a pawn; medium blurs to any piece hung via an unsound capture or move — rook sacs (Rxf7), the Greek-gift Bxh2, and knights stepping onto attacked squares (Ne5/Ng5/Ng3/Nc2).

1389.label: Top: a quiet developing/slow move (Be7, Bb2, c3, Nc3) is played instead of the urgent pawn break or active continuation, cleanly forfeiting tempo and the initiative; medium broadens to passive moves that also abandon a specific defensive duty (defender of f7, a promotion square, the 7th rank) or skip a tactical strike, so the punishment ranges from positional collapse to outright loss of material or mate.

1385.label: Top boards are a winning side declining the decisive passed-pawn push/promotion (sometimes a forced mate) in favor of a slower edge; medium boards broaden the 'decisive move' to any winning continuation that advances or supports the passer (or saves a tempo before it slips), and bleed into a few non-promotion misses and material losses.

1391.chip: Hangs queen on a check (or piece)
1391.label: Top boards are uniformly queen checks that drop the queen onto a square defended by an enemy knight (f6/e5/e7/c6/f3), hanging it for free; medium keeps the forcing-check-that-hangs-material theme but blurs into other captured pieces (rook recapture, knight check, an f7 bishop sac) and slower material loss via tempo.

1393.label: Top boards are uniformly pure king-and-pawn endgames that throw away the promotion race via a tempo-wasting king move or wrong capture/push order (win→draw/loss); medium keeps the lost-promotion-race theme but broadens to queen-endgame races and a couple of plain hanging-piece blunders.

1386.label: Top boards are king moves—frequently captures (Kxh6, Kxe4, Kxe6, Kxh7)—that lose or fail to win a K+P passed-pawn race, with several being 0–13cp non-blunders in already-lost positions; medium broadens to non-capture king moves and pawn pushes that lose tempo, misplace the king toward the wrong wing, or skip a winning pawn break.

1390.label: Top: in a clearly winning pawn endgame the player makes a slow, materially-safe move (usually a passive king move) and misses the single precise winning continuation—nearly always a pawn breakthrough/advance—throwing away the full point to a draw; medium broadens to any missed precise endgame move (king activation, blockade, bishop holding a square), where the slip sometimes only trims a winning edge or fails a critical saving defense in an already-losing position rather than squandering a clean win, and even includes a couple of near-best moves.

1395.label: Top: the queen abandons a forced mate by grabbing material (typically capturing a rook), trading the kill for material; medium: broadens to any piece (rook/knight/pawn) skipping the decisive check or forcing line — either snatching material or playing a passive non-forcing move — sometimes even walking into the opponent's mate.

1399.label: Top boards consistently squander a won opening by trading the key bishop (Bxe6/Bxc6) instead of playing the decisive d5/dxe7 break; medium blurs to quiet developing moves (Nc3) and other trades (Bxc5) that skip the same d-pawn advance, with ~3 boards instead simply hanging the player's own minor piece.

1388.label: At the peak the squandered resource is a clean forced checkmate (often discarded by grabbing material with a capture or playing a 'safe' king move); at medium it blurs to forced wins generally, where a still-winning but non-mating/greedy move replaces the decisive line.

1394.label: Top boards play a quiet developing/queen move and overlook a forcing material-winning knight capture (overwhelmingly Nxe5); medium keeps the missed-capture core but blurs the shot to other winning captures/tactics (Bxe5, Nxf6+, Qxa2) and a few cases where the quiet move actively hangs own material rather than just skipping a win.

1387.label: Top: plays an irrelevant check or material grab instead of capturing the enemy passed pawn one step from promotion, letting it queen decisively; medium broadens to also abandoning the blockading piece or king's defensive post (plus one missed tactical combo) that lets the passer promote.

1398.label: Top: a materially-safe quiet/retreating move overlooks the position's one clean forcing winning blow (en passant→Nd3+ fork, f5 outpost→Ne7+ fork, e-file pin Rxe5, Bxe5+/Bh7+ sacs); medium: blurs to missing the single decisive best move—still often a tactic (Na3, Ne5, Qa5+, Rb5+) but broadening into positional, defensive, or merely faster-mate continuations rather than always a clean material-winning shot.

1396.label: Top: premature passed-pawn/endgame pawn pushes that squander a forced mate or winning king/knight move; medium narrows to pawn-endgame pawn pushes that convert a clear win into a draw — materially safe but result thrown away.

1397.label: At the peak the move is almost always a king-safety error in an already-lost middlegame — the king walks into the open (Kf3, Kd1) or a piece that shielded the king/back rank is removed (Nc3, Rd8, Rxf5), accelerating forced mate; at medium this blurs into outright material hangs, where greedy or careless captures and rook/queen relocations drop a piece to a tactic (fork, pin, deflection, Greek-gift, back-rank) rather than purely exposing the king.

1400.label: Top: a quiet developing move (Be7, ...d6, ...Nf6, etc.) ignores the f7/c7 weakness and hangs the exchange/queen to a knight fork (Nxf7 or Nc7+); medium keeps the 'developed-into-a-fork' theme but blurs the target square (f2, c3) and occasionally drifts to non-fork opening material drops (Qxb8, Nxg7+) or a tempo/mate oversight.

1404.label: Top boards uniformly drop the queen for free via an early queen sortie or ignored attack on it; medium keeps the opening piece-hanging theme but broadens to hung minor pieces (knights/bishops) and pin/fork/discovered-attack losses, even an allowed mate-in-one.

1403.label: Top boards all center on a knight tactic with mixed direction—either hanging a piece (knight/bishop/rook) or skipping a winning Nd6+ fork; medium blurs both the piece and the direction, folding knight hangs/forks together with general material drops (missed Bxb7/dxc6, hung pawns) where the knight is only sometimes the decisive piece.

1402.chip: Hangs material to tempo refutation (often knight)
1402.label: Top boards are passive opening knight relocations/retreats (Ned7, Nb6, Neg4, Nc6) that hang a pawn/piece to a tempo-gaining pawn push (typically e5/d5) — or, against the uncastled king, skip a winning Nc2+/Nd3+ fork; medium keeps the same 'loose opening move punished with tempo' idea but blurs the piece to queens (Qf5/Qh5/Qb6), bishops (Be7/Bd3), and pawns (f4/b3), so direction splits between hung-own and missed-win.

1407.label: Top boards consistently lose Black/White's own bishop in the opening—typically by failing to resolve a pin/tension (the g4-vs-h3 motif) so it falls en prise or to a trapping push—while medium boards blur to other mishandled minor pieces, adding knights that walk into refutations and bishops dropped to tactics, with some cases shading into pure positional/tempo loss.

1405.label: At the peak a quiet knight retreat/reroute (Na2, Ne1, Nd1, Ne6) — plus a passive h5 advance — passes up a concrete forcing resource (capture, check, fork like Nc6, or the b5 pawn break), squandering a winning or holdable game; at medium the skipped active move is the same idea but the passive choice broadens to king walks, bishop reroutes, rook retreats and even castling, while a few boards (Nf4, Rd8, dxe5) instead outright hang material or grab a bad capture.

1409.label: Top boards uniformly fail to capture the knight with the h-pawn (hxg6/hxg3), walking into a queen discovered check that wins the h-file rook or mates; medium blurs to other unaddressed material-winning tactics—knight/bishop forks—where the threatening piece is left unmet.

1408.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed Qxg5/Qxg4 grabbing an undefended knight for free in the opening; medium broadens to other strong queen moves—active g5 sorties/double-attacks (Qg5) and free knight captures on other squares (Qxd6)—plus a few non-queen tactical misses.

1410.label: Top boards are uniformly greedy captures—usually winning the exchange or snatching a rook—that get refuted by a tactic costing back more material (or skip a stronger blow); medium blurs into positional grabs and missed wins, including non-capturing pawn pushes and back-rank mate misses, that squander the advantage.

1418.label: In a winning endgame the player skips a forcing check—at the top a queen fork that cleanly wins a rook (grabbing a pawn or playing a passive king move instead); at medium it blurs to forcing checks winning other material (knight/bishop/exchange) or even forced mate, sometimes just choosing the wrong checking square.

1406.label: Top boards are uniform: a KNIGHT recaptures/grabs a pawn and lands on an undefended central square (e4/e5/d4/d5), getting taken for free — a clean piece-for-pawn blunder in the opening; medium broadens the greedy opening pawn-grab to other capturing units (pawns, bishop) and to indirect refutations (discovered attack, fork, overloaded defender, move-order/positional concession) rather than just a direct recapture.

1413.label: Top boards are flashy knight checks (with a stray bishop/queen check) thrown from an already-winning position — the king simply escapes or the checking piece is captured for free; medium blurs to other premature checks, fork attempts, and even a non-check pawn lunge that likewise tosses away the win (sometimes hanging the mover, sometimes missing a free capture).

1414.label: Top boards are uniformly greedy captures (bishop/knight/queen/rook) that backfire by hanging the player's own piece or walking into mate, while medium blurs to include non-capture material grabs and captures that squander a forced win/draw rather than purely losing material.

1417.label: Top boards hang a piece or fail to remove an active enemy knight that then captures the loose material, with a knight central to nearly every refutation; medium blurs this to knight/pawn forks, pawn-level losses, and a few tempo/missed-advance errors.

1415.label: Top boards are queen moves left en prise to a direct capture or short tactic (Bxd5, Nxg4, Bxg3, or a forcing fork) from winning positions; medium keeps the queen-loss theme but blurs into other pieces being lost or trapped plus tempo/positional errors, with two missed-win exceptions.

1416.label: In a decided position the player plays a quiet/non-forcing move that ignores the one critical forcing resource; top boards are split between grabbing a free undefended rook (Rxh8/Qxd1/Rxh1/Qxc8/Qxe8) and avoiding a one-move forced mate (Kh3/Kh2/exf4/Bh6), while medium blurs to missing other captures (bishop/queen), patzer tempo-checks, and back-rank mates that needed a preparatory check.

1412.chip: Hasty pawn push wastes win (vs king move)
1412.label: Top boards are pawn-endgame hasty pawn advances that squander a decisive winning advantage (often a forced win/mate) when the precise converting move was a king move or accurate capture; medium broadens to other premature pawn breaks plus a few non-pawn moves that similarly throw away the winning conversion.

1423.label: Top boards consistently play a quiet/materially-safe move missing a forcing queen- or bishop-check that wins material or mates (frequently a Bd4+ bishop fork netting a rook, or a queen check like Qd5+/Qc5+); medium broadens to actually playing a check, just the wrong/imprecise one instead of the precise winning forcing check.

1411.label: Top boards uniformly skip grabbing a free, undefended enemy piece that wins decisive material (Rxb4, Kxe2, Bxa1, exd4, Qxa7), often hanging their own piece in the process; medium boards broaden the same 'missed winning resource' theme to non-free tactics—capturing a key defender (Qxd6), a queen-winning check (Qh5+), or resolving tension—where ignoring it lets the player's own king/structure collapse.

1422.label: Top boards are self-inflicted king-exposing moves (opening lines, blocking escape squares, or walking into checks) that permit a forced checkmate; medium blurs this to king-weakening moves that instead concede decisive material via checks and forks rather than always forced mate.

1419.label: Top: from a clearly winning position a quiet non-forcing king/pawn move throws away the win — half directly hanging a piece (queen/rook/bishop/pawn), half skipping a forcing conversion (intermezzo check or move-order); medium keeps the 'slow move squanders the win' skeleton but broadens into positional and endgame-technique squanders, with a couple of non-mistakes.

1426.label: Top: a forcing Qa4+/Qa5+ diagonal check exploiting the loose b4-knight and uncastled king is skipped, throwing away a winning advantage (with a flip-side tail where allowing that same b4-knight's Bc2/Bd3+/Nc2 fork hangs the exchange); medium broadens to the identical check hitting loose knights on c4/b5 or merely chasing the b4-knight with a3 instead of winning it outright.

1421.label: Top boards are uniformly a knight grabbing a central pawn (e5/d4/d5) that gets refuted by a tempo-gaining intermezzo—usually an in-between check (Bxd7+, Bxe2, Bxd2+)—winning back the stranded knight or more; medium blurs to other greedy/premature captures and moves (pawn grabs, queen sorties, rook shifts) punished by a similar zwischenzug, fork, or king-safety tempo blow.

1401.label: Top: an opening priority-of-threats/desperado tactic—usually after an enemy bishop infiltrates to f3/g4—that wins the OPPONENT'S queen is overlooked, either by a passive move or by recapturing with the wrong piece (often hanging one's own bishop/rook); Medium: blurs into later-middlegame priority-of-threats tactics where the direction flips—more often dropping one's OWN queen to a fork/desperado/discovery or losing the exchange—plus some king-safety/mating oversights.

1424.label: Top boards uniformly miss a clean winning capture whose recapture is impossible because it opens a file/diagonal onto a pinned or x-rayed piece (Rxb5, Bxd5, Nxe5, Qxg6, Qxg3), playing a slow queen/knight/king move instead; medium boards keep the 'threw away a won position with a quiet/wrong move' core but blur the motif to any decisive tactic — forcing checks/mates, discovered-check queen wins, or rook sacs — rather than strictly the pinned-recapture capture.

1432.label: Top boards are uniformly a rook (occasionally a queen) moved—often a greedy pawn grab—onto an enemy bishop's open diagonal and captured for free; medium keeps the same bishop-diagonal capture motif but broadens the hung unit to knights and queens as well as rooks.

1427.label: Top: a quiet 'ask-the-bishop' opening move (almost always h3, also Bb3) skips a tactic that wins Black's loose pinning bishop on g4 (or g5) — via Bxf7+/Ng5+ fork, hxg4, or Qa4+; medium broadens to passing up other material-winning opening shots against various loose pieces/pawns (exf4, cxb4, dxe5, Bxf2+/Nxe4+) and even some lines where the played move outright hangs material to Bxf7+.

1425.label: Top boards: in a winning/clearly-better position the player picks a slow, passive or tempo move instead of the available forcing shot, squandering a clean win (mate, queen, exchange, pawn); medium broadens so the quiet move not only misses a win but also concedes the initiative and lets the opponent's tactic win material, making it a near-even mix of 'missed win' and 'hung material' across varied pieces.

1431.label: Top: a greedy capture or premature pawn push grabs immediate material instead of a more precise resource (in-between check, stronger capture, structural preservation, or forced mate), usually losing material or a win in the refutation; medium blurs to passive/tempo-losing king/rook moves and hanging-piece placements that skip a stronger active continuation, plus one or two boards that aren't real mistakes.

1428.label: Top: invariably neglects the forcing/defensive queen exchange (Qxh4/Qxd5/Qxe5/Qxc6, etc.) that removes White's attacking queen, instead playing a quiet developing or king move that allows mate or decisive material loss; medium keeps the same skipped-queen-trade core but broadens to other saving simplifications (e.g., a rook liquidation like Rxd4 into a won pawn endgame).

1420.label: Top: a piece (peak = rook, broadening to queen/king/bishop) vacates the single critical square where it was holding back mate/material or sustaining a winning attack, either missing a decisive shot or accelerating a forced loss; medium: the same critical-square desertion but mostly rooks (plus a knight/pawn) abandoning an active file or defensive post, costing a key pawn or tempo in technical (rook) endgames — direction genuinely mixed between missed wins and self-inflicted collapses.

1430.label: Top boards uniformly decline a free, undefended central pawn the queen could grab (almost always Qxd4/Qxd5) for a check, developing move, or castling in the opening; medium broadens to other free captures (Qxe4/Qxe5/Qxf5), spills into the middlegame, and the declined or wrong-piece move sometimes also hangs material itself.

1429.label: Top: prematurely shoves a passed pawn one square toward promotion (skipping king/piece activation) so the enemy king steps in front and blockades the promotion square—two cases instead lose it to a knight fork—collapsing a won/drawn endgame; medium keeps the same premature-push intent but the refutation blurs to deflection, capture, pawn-race loss, or mate, and even includes cases where the push was actually correct.

1440.label: Top boards are clean failures to blockade/capture an already-far-advanced passed pawn (7th-rank passer), letting it queen for free or with forced mate after grabbing material or pushing an irrelevant pawn; medium broadens to losing the promotion race by one tempo — king or piece left a square too far (king races, misplaced bishop/knight) to stop the runner.

1439.label: Top boards leave a piece en prise to an immediate free capture—usually the just-moved bishop/rook grabbed outright, or the queen lost to a one-move knight fork; medium boards broaden the same 'material dropped' pattern to short multi-move refutations: knight forks with check, discovered attacks, removing-the-defender sequences, and a couple of king-safety collapses.

1434.label: Top boards are uniformly ill-timed central pawn breaks (mostly ...d5) that undermine the player's own structure and hang a pawn; medium broadens to other premature/tempo-losing moves that drop material or allow tactics (forks, a hanging rook), with a recurring minority instead squandering a winning center.

1441.label: At the peak the player invariably answers a winning opening position with a quiet developing move and overlooks a forcing winning queen check (Qe5+/Qe4+/Qe3+/Qe7+, usually snatching the undefended corner rook); at medium activation this blurs into missing other forcing wins (e.g. a Nf6+ sacrifice) and, in a minority, quiet moves that instead allow the opponent's forcing check/tactic—so direction drifts from clean 'missed win' toward 'hangs material'.

1437.label: Top: the engine's best move is a direct queen-capture trade (Qx...) that the player declines with a passive king move, flank pawn, or queen sortie—leaving its own queen hanging or condemned to passivity and converting a drawn/tenable game into a lost one; medium broadens to include declined queen-trade OFFERS (e.g., 19.Qd2) where refusing the exchange loses material to tactics rather than hanging the queen outright.

1435.label: Top: a voluntary queen-or-rook exchange that simplifies a winning/drawn position into a lost (usually king-and-pawn) endgame; medium blurs to rook trades into merely inferior rook endgames, plus a few outright major-piece hangs and positional draw-throws.

1442.label: Top boards are uniformly an early uncastled f/g-pawn push that strips the king's e1-h4/e8-h5 diagonal and is refuted by Qh4+/Qh5+ winning material; medium blurs to other pawn/piece moves that open a different diagonal toward the king (Bb4+, Qa4+, discovered check on c1) or weaken a line for a decisive tactic, so the constant 'Qh4+/Qh5+ on the king diagonal' generalizes to 'any line-opening that hands the opponent a winning check/attack'.

1445.label: Top: a winning side throws away a forced mate or queen-winning combination by abandoning the key square—almost always trading/relocating the QUEEN that powered the attack; medium broadens to any piece (bishop, rook, knight, even pawn) playing a routine or greedy move that misses the sole decisive forcing tactic (mate, deflection, fork) in a critical position.

1446.label: Top boards uniformly skip a free capture of an undefended enemy KNIGHT (23...Rxe2, 25...Bxe4, 26...Rxf3, 24.Bxd7, cxd6), taken cleanly by a rook/bishop/pawn while an autopilot move throws away the winning piece; medium keeps the hanging-knight theme but broadens the capturer to queen/pawn (Qxa6+, Qxf6, Qxf3, dxc6) and the target can look defended (Bxe5), with a minority blurring into other skipped winning shots (missed Rf2#, slow mate, king-safety lapse).

1438.label: Top: a slow, tempo-losing move (knight/pawn/queen shuffle) while the enemy queen sits loose on b2/b7, skipping the decisive b-file rook swing (Rab1/Rb1) that challenges it; medium keeps the 'don't chase the exposed queen' core but broadens the queen's square (c6/e7/h2/d5) and the challenging resource (rook to any file or a tactic), with the consequence blurring between lost initiative, hung material, and a missed clean material win.

1443.chip: Hangs material via rook activation (often Rd8)
1443.label: At the peak it's a natural-looking rook lift onto an open file (often Ra8–d8 'activate on the d-file') that squanders a winning/equal position, most commonly by leaving material hanging in the refutation (Rxb5+, Bxd8, h7, c5); at medium the moved piece broadens to queen/bishop/knight/king and the punishing mechanism blurs further into missed winning captures (Qxc7, Nxg5), bad queen trades into lost endings, and slow positional drift, so neither the piece nor a single direction is constant.

1448.label: Top boards are clean one-move opening blunders that hang a piece outright (most often a rook to a centralized queen sweeping an open long diagonal/file, plus knights/bishops and one central pawn); medium keeps the 'lose material in the opening' theme but broadens the mechanism to material dropped over 2-3 moves (forks, trapped pieces, king-exposing checks, ignored threats) and even bleeds into a few purely positional/tempo-losing opening moves with no immediate capture.

1450.label: Top boards are direct one-move piece hangs—most often a rook dropped to immediate capture; medium boards broaden to own material lost over a short 2-3 move refutation (abandoned defenders, premature/greedy captures, move-order errors, or self-trapped pieces).

1433.label: Top boards are uniform: in an endgame the player captures a piece (a knight in 8/10, occasionally a bishop) to simplify, but the recapture dumps them into a lost or drawn pawn endgame — surrendering the very piece that restrained White's passed pawn, which then promotes; medium blurs the move type — still endgame-conversion blunders (a rook/knight capture into a lost pawn race), but also non-capturing errors like king retreats that abandon the blockade or hang a rook and pawn pushes that let the opponent's passed pawn queen or harvest a pawn.

1451.label: Top: a routine knight developing move in the opening hangs material (often the queen, also rook/piece/pawn) to a forcing blow—typically a long-diagonal bishop check (Bc6+/Bxf3+) or knight fork, with one outlier being a missed mate-in-one; medium broadens to other quiet/non-forcing piece moves (bishop, rook) that lose material to a wider range of tactics (removing-the-defender, queen-trapping, promotion, or a missed counter-capture).

1449.label: Top: a quiet opening move (esp. Bd3/Bd2/f3) skips the engine's forced Nxc6 and leaves the d4 knight hanging to ...Nxd4 for a clean piece; medium keeps the 'failed to resolve central tension / skip Nxc6' theme but blurs the lost material — a hung pawn (e5), an unsound Nxf7 sac, or even walking into a mate (Nd6#).

1454.label: Top: in a won position passes up a forcing rook check (almost always a skewer) that wins material, playing a materially-safe but inferior move; medium keeps the 'missed forcing winning check' core but blurs the qualifier — adding knight checks/forks and checks that win via mate/mating-net rather than pure material — with a couple of off-theme outliers (a hung-piece blunder, a 0cp non-mistake).

1444.label: At the peak it's consistently a self-exposing move—king tucked to a 'safe-looking' square or a rook leaving the back rank—that walks into a forced mating attack and throws away a winning position; at medium it blurs into broader defensive lapses (abandoning king cover to grab material, removing/overloading a defender, even a plain hanging piece or tempo loss) that surrender the king's safety or a won game.

1459.label: At the peak, all boards are razor-sharp K+P king moves that surrender the opposition/key square and flip a dead draw into a loss; at medium it blurs into king moves in already-lost endgames (often with rooks/knights/queens present) that lose only 0–25cp and are negligible non-errors merely occurring in opposition-themed endings.

1452.label: At the peak, a bishop move vacates the key blockade square/diagonal (or wastes a tempo) in a lost endgame, letting the opponent's passed pawn run and queen; medium broadens the moved piece to pawn/knight moves (f4, Nxf4) that likewise ignore the promotion threat, while a couple of outlier top boards instead drop a piece to a tactic.

1456.label: In a winning opening, plays a quiet developing/castling/king-safety move and skips a material-winning tactical shot; top boards are dominated by the queen grab on b7 (Qxb7) with a few other piece-winning captures (Nxg6, Nxe5, Bxa6), while medium broadens the target/shot to exchange-winning bishop grabs (Bxg7, Bxb2), en passant, and occasionally non-capturing best moves.

1458.label: At the peak the player makes a natural/safe developing or castling move and overlooks the winning Nxf7/Nxf2 knight sacrifice on the king's weak f-pawn (Fried Liver / mirror); at medium it broadens to other missed knight strikes — forks (Nf2), captures on h2/e6/f6, knight checks — with a handful of cases where the wrong knight capture or move-order actually hangs material.

1464.label: Top boards: in an endgame the player gives up the minor piece blockading/defending against a passed pawn (almost always a bishop captured by the enemy king), throwing away a win/draw; medium broadens to a hung knight blockader and bishops captured by a rook, with a few outliers (optimal pawn pushes, tempo losses) that aren't true blunders.

1453.chip: Hangs material on tempting check (top: rook-for-pawn)
1453.label: At the top a rook captures a pawn WITH CHECK but is simply recaptured, dumping a whole rook for a pawn and a winning/holding position; medium blurs to other tempting checking captures (exchange or queen sacs) and to checks that needlessly liquidate the position — sometimes throwing away a win or forced mate rather than strictly hanging material.

1457.label: Top boards are constant: a greedy pawn-grab in a won endgame, almost always with the king (e.g. Kxh4, Kxh6, Kxg4, Kxa4), that trades away the winning structure and is refuted by an immediate recapture; medium blurs this into rook pawn-grabs (Rxa7), premature passer pushes (b4, g6, f3), and even minor move-order/tempo slips that barely cost eval, plus an opening bishop-hang outlier.

1461.label: Top boards leave a piece—most often a rook—en prise for an immediate one-move capture (typically by removing its defender or walking into a pin/fork), while medium boards blur to slower material losses (pawns, knights, the exchange) conceded over a 2-3 move refutation via weakening/tempo-losing or defender-abandoning moves rather than a clean instant hang.

1462.label: Top boards: a king (occasionally rook) walks onto a square creating a fatal alignment, losing material to a check—usually a skewer/pin/fork on king+major piece, or a forced trade into a lost pawn ending; medium blurs to include rook moves and other endgame slips (mishandled passed pawns, tempo-losing or deflecting checks) that concede material or the advantage.

1465.label: Top boards are uniformly tempting knight checks—almost all intended as king/queen forks—where the very forking knight is simply recaptured (Nxe2, Rxf2, Nxf3), flipping winning to losing; medium broadens to non-fork checks (discovered/sac checks, even a bishop check) and partly shifts direction toward squandering a forced mate rather than purely hanging the piece.

1466.label: Top boards are passive king-safety defenses (often ...Nh7/Rf8) that skip the saving/winning central pawn break (...d5/d4); medium broadens to any quiet or retreating move that forgoes a stronger dynamic resource — a tactic, centralization, exchange-win, or pawn break.

1463.label: Top boards remove the king's last defensive piece and are mated; medium broadens to defenders of other pieces (back-rank rook, f2-square, undefended bishop) punished by mate or by grabbing the now-loose material.

1447.label: Top: Black uniformly declines the favorable central pawn capture (dxc3/exd4/dxe4/dxc4/cxd3) that resolves central tension, instead playing a slow developing move, castling, or pawn push — squandering a win (sometimes hanging material outright); medium blurs the constant to any missed tension-resolving move (tactical sac, recapture, pawn break/push), now also from White's side and occasionally a greedy capture that backfires.

1460.label: Top boards put the queen at the center of the decisive line (it's the moving or the lost unit) where abandoning a defensive duty or ignoring a standing threat hangs a piece or allows mate; medium keeps the same neglect-the-threat theme but the dropped unit blurs across knight, bishop, and pawn, with a couple of boards merely missing a free capture rather than hanging their own material.

1455.label: Top boards consistently substitute a quiet/slow move (frequently a king move) for a forcing QUEEN check/tactic, ceding a free tempo that throws away a won or drawn position—often leaving the queen itself hanging; medium positions blur this to other passive tempo-losing moves (rook/bishop retreats, pawn pushes) and non-queen forcing continuations, with direction split between hanging own material and merely missing the forcing win/draw.

1469.label: Top boards are uniform: a move that opens a file or removes a key defender lets an enemy ROOK crash onto the open line/back rank for mate or won material; medium blurs the punishing piece, where the same defender-removal/line-opening instead exposes the king to queen or bishop attacks (Qh4+, Bxh7+ Greek gift, Ba6+, Qd4+) rather than a clean rook invasion.

1472.label: Top boards consistently drop a knight to a one-move capture in the opening, almost always fixable by the resolving trade Nxc6; medium broadens to include bishops and to knights lost via other mechanisms (illusory pins, retreating to an undefended square), but the constant remains hanging a full minor piece to a simple capture.

1470.label: Top: voluntarily trades the only active rook/bishop for a knight and gets recaptured, collapsing a drawn/losing position into a clearly lost pawn or rook endgame; medium blurs to include bishop targets (Kxe7), king recaptures, and a few near-equal/engine-approved trades that aren't true blunders.

1471.chip: Hangs piece on defended capture (often knight)
1471.label: At the peak it's a single-ply capture—usually a knight, frequently with check (Fried Liver/Scholar's/fork dreams)—onto a square whose overlooked defender simply recaptures, losing a piece for a pawn; at medium the same defended-square capture (queen/bishop too) blurs into multi-move refutations where the loss is sealed over 2-3 moves via trades, follow-up forks, or a flashy check that abandons a cleaner win.

1467.label: Top: a capture or king move that strips away a defender of the player's OWN king (usually via a pawn/piece capture), opening lines for a forced mate; medium blurs the target — removing defenders of key pawns/squares or exposing the king, costing material or the game rather than always mate (plus a couple of near-false-positives).

1436.label: Top: the player's most powerful rook is directly traded or grabbed off for a pawn/knight (the rook itself moves), discarding a winning or equal position; medium keeps the lost-rook theme but broadens to indirect surrenders—a pawn push or knight move that abandons the rook, or a simplifying exchange into a lost endgame.

1477.label: Top: a quiet opening move leaves the player's own knight en prise (almost always Nf3 to e4 or Nf6 to e5), refuted by a trivial pawn capture (one king capture); medium keeps the hung knight but broadens to knights lost after grabbing a pawn (Nxd4) or a retreat, plus occasional mere pawn/tempo losses rather than a clean piece.
