1468.label: Top: a queen move (showy check or greedy pawn grab) throws away a forced mate while material stays safe; medium broadens to any piece (rook/bishop/knight/king/pawn) squandering a winning advantage, with a few cases bleeding into slow material loss.

1473.label: Top boards are a clean queen mate-in-one against a king entombed by its own pawns (player plays a safe/quiet move instead); medium broadens to longer forced mates and other overlooked decisive queen-led forcing wins, with a few cases that are just the best material or drawing/endgame resource rather than mate.

1476.label: Top boards are clean: in a clearly winning position the player plays a quiet/positional or merely-aggressive move that skips an available forcing win (hanging-piece capture, check sequence, or mate), an omission rather than a self-hang; medium blurs the pattern — it still includes missed forcing wins (incl. wrong-forcing-move choices like a non-mating check), but broadens to self-hangs (exd7, Bg5), allowing enemy tactics/forks (Qe6, Bb6+), and a draw→loss endgame, so roughly half are squandered-win omissions and half are advantage-losing blunders.

1475.label: Top: an over-aggressive opening move attacking the enemy queen with 'tempo' (Bg4/Bg5/Nd4) cleanly hangs a full minor piece to a queen capture or zwischenzug refutation; medium keeps the same queen-chasing impulse but broadens the punishment to counterattack/king-safety exploitation, pawn-chase (c5), or mere tempo/positional loss rather than always a clean piece.

1481.label: Top boards are uniformly the premature Bxf7+ bishop sacrifice with check (once Bxf2+) that drops a full piece for one pawn with no attacking follow-up; medium keeps the unsound-opening-sacrifice theme but blurs the mechanism—still mostly Bxf7+, but adding a bishop hung to a fork-check (Bb5 into Qa5+), a knight move that opens a decisive check (Nb5 into Bb4+), and a pawn push (h5) that abandons an already-developed bishop—so the constant 'check' and 'f7' cues loosen into 'any unsound minor-piece offer/hang in the opening'.

1484.label: At the peak, every flagged move is a forcing check in a 100%-winning endgame that wastes a tempo—often spoiling a faster mate or breaking an existing mating net (e.g. Nf4+, Ng6+ liberating the trapped king); at medium strength the pattern blurs from 'check' toward generic tempo-loss in won endgames, adding quiet non-checks like rim-knight retreats (Nh7) and pawn pushes (f5)—and crucially many flagged checks (and pushes) are actually 0cp non-mistakes, with a few outliers being real material/draw blunders (Qf2 misses a free queen, Kh5 throws a draw).

1478.label: Top: in a won/mating position, plays a tempting forcing check (usually a queen check, sometimes a rook) that hangs the checker or throws away the forced mate instead of the decisive capture; medium broadens to other won-position misplays, including non-checking abandoning moves and a near-equal case.

1489.chip: Hangs material or walks into attack
1489.label: At the peak the player collapses a fine/winning position through varied self-defeating moves—most often hanging or trapping own material, but also missing a free winning capture (Kxf6), making a losing forcing trade, or walking into a tactical/mating refutation; at medium it narrows to mostly hanging a piece/pawn to a simple capture or exposing the king to a mating attack.

1482.chip: Fails to stop passed pawn (rook→queen EG)
1482.label: Top boards are uniformly rook endgames where a materially-safe but careless move (often a greedy pawn grab or passive shuffle) fails to blockade or get behind the opponent's passed pawn, letting it promote; medium blurs to queen/pawn endgames with the same passer-neglect plus some unrelated careless moves (hanging a piece, king-safety lapses, lost tempi).

1479.label: Top: declines a clean, immediate free capture/recapture of a hanging piece (constant: a quiet developing/king move played instead of an obvious ~500cp recapture, often a minor piece on f3/c3 or a free enemy queen) — own material is lost; medium blurs to broader tactical/positional oversights where the best move was a capture or stronger tactic but a king-safety, endgame, or wrong-piece move was chosen, with smaller eval swings.

1491.label: Top boards are split—greedy recaptures that hang material (queen/piece via a refutation) and reflexive captures/trades that miss a forced mate—plus tempo-losing 'free' checks (Nd1+); medium narrows to the natural materially-tempting move (greedy capture dxc6, or Nd1+ check) thrown in a winning position, with no single piece or SEE signature unifying them.

1486.label: Top boards self-inflict a minor-piece loss in the opening—almost always a bishop via unsound f7/f2 sacs or undefended placements (a few knights too); medium boards keep the 'lose material early' theme but broaden to dropping central pawns through careless opening moves rather than hanging a whole piece.

1490.label: Top boards are losing king-and-pawn endgames where a king misstep or pawn push loses the pawn race and lets the opponent's passed pawn promote (with one outlier hanging a knight and one being the engine move); medium broadens to rook endgames and other king/rook missteps that similarly let connected passers run, sometimes also squandering a draw or win.

1488.label: Top boards are razor-consistent — every one passes up a free capture of the opponent's undefended ROOK (Nxa1/Bxh8/Nxd8/Bxa1/Nxg1, etc.) in a materially-safe equal position, instead playing an aimless king or pawn move and throwing away the won exchange (a clean 'missed win'); medium boards blur away from the specific hanging-rook capture into other single-only-move critical blunders — greedy captures that actually hang the player's own piece (Nxe5, Nxd2 walking into mate) and lost-position inaccuracies — so the unifying thread softens to 'chose the tempting/aimless move at a critical only-move point' rather than strictly missing a free rook.

1483.label: Top boards are king-exposing/self-weakening quiet moves that walk into a check or fork and lose material in a short refutation; medium blurs to any quiet middlegame move (varied piece/mechanism — fork, deserted defender, tempo/move-order slip) that drops a piece or large advantage to a forcing tactic.

1485.label: Top boards constantly retreat or play a quiet move and overlook a clean forcing shot — a check or capture (often grabbing an undefended pawn like g4, or a sac/fork winning a piece) that wins material; medium boards blur this, sometimes still missing an active winning resource but more often just choosing a passive move that misses the precise defense or even invites the opponent's counterattack.

1474.label: Top boards are uniformly a rook capturing a (usually passed) pawn in a losing endgame that is immediately recaptured (rook surrendered for a pawn); medium blurs to other losing-position rook give-aways (a hanging rook check that grabs nothing) and even a non-rook material blunder (a queen drop dropping pawns).

1493.label: Top boards are nearly all rook moves that self-drop material or walk into mate (back-rank/h-file, capture, pin), while medium blurs the piece to queen, bishop, pawn or king that blunders into an immediate tactic (fork, skewer, pin, hanging capture).

1494.label: Top boards revolve around a decisive queen — usually hanging one's own queen (or another piece) via a natural-looking move, occasionally missing a free capture of the enemy queen; medium broadens into general material blunders and king-safety-weakening moves that hang pieces or invite a crushing attack.

1487.label: Top boards are clearly-winning positions blown by skipping the single free capture of a hanging enemy rook (occasionally queen); medium broadens to merely better/equal positions where the player instead actively hangs own pieces or fails to win material of any type (bishop, pawn, exchange), shading from 'missed win' toward 'hangs own piece'.

1495.label: Top boards uniformly play a routine developing/retreating move (Be2, Nf3, h3, Nb6...) that passes up a winning opening knight fork — Nb5/Ndb5/Ndb4 hitting c7/d6 — with no material hung; medium boards blur this into missing the single best move more broadly: other tactical strikes (Nxd5, Bxf7, Nxe4), central pawn breaks (d5/f4/c4), and move-order precision, with a few even drifting toward letting own material/structure suffer.

1502.label: Top boards are uniform: the queen makes a greedy capture and is immediately recaptured (single-ply, ~6-point loss); medium broadens to queens lost over a 2-3 move refutation (Rxf2+...,Qxf1+ mates) or that abandon a back-rank/mate defender, plus non-capturing queen moves walking onto an attacked square (Qb5, Qe8).

1496.label: Top: a clearly winning middlegame is thrown away by one natural/greedy move that EITHER hangs material to a tactical refutation (knight fork, discovered check, queen invasion, exchange sac) OR overlooks a forced mate while grabbing safe material; medium keeps the 'squanders a won position' core but broadens to smaller-magnitude slips, king-safety/positional drift and endgame technique (and even near-0cp non-blunders), splitting roughly 50/50 between hanging own material and missing the win.

1498.label: Top boards are consistently passive/mistimed king moves in endgames that squander a tempo or abandon a defensive resource (turning drawn/winning into lost); medium blurs to other pieces (rook, bishop, queen, pawn) and into the middlegame, still playing a slow move instead of the urgent active break/capture/defense, with a couple of non-blunder outliers and only ~2 boards directly hanging material.

1492.label: Top boards: a passive or king-weakening move ignores the position's forcing demands and permits a forced (usually mating) attack on the player's own king; medium boards keep the passive-move-instead-of-forcing-counterplay theme but blur into merely dropping material (hung rook, lost pawn/fork) or squandering a winning/equal advantage.

1499.label: Top boards are remarkably uniform: a greedy capture—almost always ...Nxe5 (or a ...Bg4 pin/...Qxh6 grab aiming at e5)—overextends and hangs a piece to an Re1 pin, a Qd1–g4 discovered attack, or an f4/tempo hit; at medium activation the e5-capture motif blurs into broader overextension, where king moves (Kd7, Kh7, Ke1, Kf2) and loose developing/grabbing moves expose material to checks, pins, and forks, so the constant is 'own material dropped to a tactic after an overeager move,' with the greedy-e5 specificity holding only at the peak.

1500.label: Top: in winning/holdable passed-pawn races the player plays a tempo-wasting king move (or needless capture/side-pawn push) instead of immediately pushing the decisive passer, squandering the win or draw; medium broadens to any slow endgame move that neglects efficient passer progress — pushing the wrong passed pawn, idle checks/rook shuffles, or even hanging a piece — so the constant 'king-move tempo loss in a pawn race' blurs into general failure to advance the right passer.

1505.label: Top: a purposeless rook check (in rook endgames) that drives the enemy king to a stronger square, squandering a win or draw by handing over tempo; medium keeps the same wasted-check motif but broadens the checking piece to knight and queen, including checks that additionally hang material or force a losing exchange/trade-down.

1501.chip: Passive king move forfeits tempo (sometimes other piece)
1501.label: TOP: consistently passive/retreating KING moves in pure endgames that concede tempo and activity instead of centralizing or restricting the enemy king (materially safe, 0–11cp up to letting slip a forced mate); MEDIUM: broadens to passive or over-eager rook/knight/bishop/queen/pawn moves that likewise surrender the initiative, sometimes losing material in the refutation or walking into mate.

1507.label: A slow, non-forcing/preparatory move is played instead of the demanded concrete forcing line; at the peak this almost always squanders the player's OWN winning tactic (double attack, forced queen trade, free piece) while own material stays safe, whereas medium boards blur the same 'quiet instead of forcing' habit into walking INTO the opponent's tactic — a pawn fork (d5/e5), deflection (Rh7+), or trap (b4) that hangs material.

1511.label: Top boards are unsound forcing checks/sacrifices in an already-winning king attack that hang material and let the attack fizzle (Kf2+, Qxg7+, Rh2+, Rxg2+); medium blurs toward quiet positional moves and skipped/converted forced wins (Bd4, Qh4, Kf7) that squander the advantage rather than literally sacking.

1512.label: Top boards are all quiet/passive KING moves in a won endgame that skip an immediate forcing win — most often promotion-with-check (c8=Q+, a1=Q+, g8=Q+) or a forced mate/perpetual; medium broadens the same 'passive move skips the forcing line' to ROOK moves and to missed forcing checks/forks (Bg4+, Rc4+, Ne3+, intermediate g4+), with the move materially safe in every case — though several top boards (2, 6, 7, 8) are non-blunders, lowering reliability.

1504.label: Top: uniformly plays a materially-safe move while overlooking a winning forcing rook check (or rook mate) that exploits the exposed enemy king; medium keeps the missed-rook-check core but blurs to other forcing resources (non-rook/pawn checks, a drawing check) and to positions where the player also hangs material instead of just missing the win.

1503.label: Top boards are consistently failures to handle an enemy g5/g4 knight raiding f7 — missing the h3/h6 antidote (plus a couple of Nc7+ forks and one greedy Nxe5/failed Bxf7), almost always throwing away a winning position; medium broadens to general mishandling of enemy knights — missed knight-kicking pushes (a4/b4/g4/h3), walking into captures/forks, and hung pieces — with genuinely mixed direction (mostly squandering a win, sometimes missing a forced one).

1509.label: Top boards are uniformly purposeless knight checks (Nx+) that abandon a dominant outpost or defensive/blockading duty and squander a winning or holding position; medium blurs the 'check' requirement to include quiet knight relocations (and once even a bishop check) that likewise forsake the strong square, with outcomes ranging from outright hung material to pure tempo/positional loss.

1514.label: Top boards hold a winning/drawn position and squander it by greedily grabbing material with a capture (rook/bishop/pawn, e.g. Rxe6+, Rxd2+, Rxf6, Bxd1, Bxd4+) instead of the forcing win/mate/perpetual; medium broadens to quiet non-capturing moves (Ra8, Ne6) that likewise abandon the decisive forcing line, and the direction blurs between hanging own material and merely missing the win.

1508.label: Top boards drop a full piece—usually a major piece (rook/queen)—to a forcing capture/recapture that walks straight into a refuting tactic (back-rank, removed-defender, miscalculated grab); medium boards keep the same own-material-loss but blur to pawns and minor pieces lost more slowly via quieter positional slips (king walks, pawn pushes, vacating a defender).

1506.label: Top boards uniformly hang a knight in the opening by ignoring an immediate pawn capture (exf6/dxc6/exf3) or lunging to an undefended square; medium boards keep the same root cause—neglecting central pawn tension (fix is almost always dxe4/cxd5)—but blur from losing a knight to broader positional/tempo damage.

1515.chip: Missed attack on exposed king (usually check)
1515.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed forcing CHECK (Qh4+/Qh5+ or Bg3+/Bg6#, sometimes mate) by queen or bishop that punishes a self-wrecked, exposed enemy king after a quiet developing move; medium keeps the exposed-king/kingside theme and the Qh4+ motif but blurs the method, adding non-check blows like a knight maneuver (Nh4) or a check-plus-fork (Qh4+ then Nxf4+).

1497.label: Top: player declines the engine's best move, which is always a knight capturing the enemy's strong centralized knight (NxN), squandering the advantage; medium broadens the target to bishops/other pieces and to looser knight-capture tactics where the best move may be a quiet/queen move and the declined capture often means lost material rather than just a missed win.

1519.label: Top: uniformly early-opening queen CHECKS (Qa4+/Qa5+/Qb4+) that lose tempo to a developing interposition which blocks-and-attacks the queen, frequently dropping material via fork/hanging piece; medium keeps the premature queen-sortie-attacked-with-tempo theme but blurs it to non-check queen moves (Qc3, Qc5, Qd3) and mixes in outcomes from hanging the queen outright to missing a forced mate.

1516.label: At the peak the player passes up a clean forced mate that hinges on the queen — usually a queen capture-with-check or queen-delivered mate — playing a safe, slower move instead; at medium this blurs to skipping the fastest queen-decisive conversion more broadly (including an under-promotion that should have been a queen), with a sizable minority instead hanging their own queen, but the queen is the decisive piece on nearly every board.

1521.label: Top boards are uniform: in a won position the player plays a quiet (usually king) move that ignores a free capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen, squandering the win; medium blurs the 'capture-the-queen' constant into squandered wins generally—missing a promotion (g8=Q) or grabbing a rook instead of taking the hanging queen.

1520.label: Top boards are uniformly passive/misplaced KING moves in pawn endgames that lose a critical tempo and fail to activate toward the decisive zone (king is the constant at the peak); medium broadens to the same activity/tempo failure made with other pieces—passive bishop/rook repositioning, pointless knight checks, and weakening pawn pushes—where the 'king' specificity blurs but the passive, tempo-wasting endgame intent persists.

1524.label: In drawn positions the player loses their own material; top boards almost always hang the queen outright (directly or after a forced 2-3 move refutation), while medium broadens to other lost material/tempo-wasting queen moves and a couple of missed winning queen captures.

1510.label: Top: the player hangs the queen and it is snapped off by an enemy bishop (board 8 instead drops the exchange/rook), often squandering a forced mate; medium broadens both dimensions — the hung piece becomes a rook (or knight/bishop) and the captor may be a knight or rook (plus a couple of wrong-capture-order/wrong-piece cases) — but the constant is leaving one's own material en prise for free.

1517.label: Top boards all hang an undefended knight that an enemy bishop snaps up for a near-free piece; medium keeps the hung knight (occasionally a bishop) but broadens the capturer to rooks, queens, pawns, or knights.

1513.label: Top boards squander a won (or equal) position by skipping a clear free capture—twice by merely threatening an enemy piece instead of taking it—while medium boards blur into hanging the player's own material or premature positional breaks that throw away the same edge.

1522.label: Top: passive king move in a won endgame that fails to capture/neutralize a decisive passed pawn, squandering the win without losing material; medium blurs to other quiet pawn/piece moves and to merely-drawn-or-worse positions that likewise skip the single forcing solution.

1518.label: Top boards are impulsive 'patzer' checks that throw away a forced mate, most often by outright hanging the checking bishop or rook (e.g. Bf6+/Rxf6, Be3+/Kxg7, R1d2+/Bxd2); medium blurs the constant 'forced-mate-squandered-by-check' core into greedy capture-checks and trades (Qxf7+, Bxe8+, Bxd7+) that liquidate or release pressure and into materially-safe checks that merely miss the faster win, so the squander shifts from losing material to skipping a forced win and the piece that falls varies (bishop/rook, occasionally queen).

1525.label: Top boards are optimal/near-optimal simplifying captures (usually a rook recapture) liquidating a clearly-won endgame with ~0cp loss; medium blurs to the occasional win-throwing rook-for-pawn trade (winning→drawn) plus quieter non-capturing simplifications.

1527.label: At the peak it's always a tempting forcing rook move (check/capture/pawn-grab) that either hangs the rook outright or abandons a key defended pawn/support duty; at medium the piece blurs to any unit (king/pawn/bishop as well as rook) and the mechanism widens from hanging material to quietly squandering a winning edge by abandoning a passed-pawn or defensive duty.

1530.label: Top: queen greedily grabs a flank pawn (b7/b2/g2/g7), leaving it stranded/trapped or skipping a stronger capture or mate; medium keeps the greedy queen grab but blurs the target square (d4/h7/h1) and occasionally other greedy material-grabs that backfire into a trapped or hung piece.

1534.label: Top: a bishop greedily captures a fianchetto/edge pawn (b2/g7/b7/g2) and is instantly recaptured, dropping a minor piece for a pawn in the opening; medium broadens to the queen and other pieces snatching defended pawns, punished by recapture, a queen trap, or a recovering fork.

1533.label: Top boards are queen/rook captures that voluntarily simplify a won or drawn position into a lost pawn endgame; medium broadens to minor-piece trades and rook-for-bishop exchanges (with a couple of outright piece hangs blurring the peak).

1526.label: Top boards consistently mishandle flank pawn tension—a passive knight/pawn move letting axb5/hxg6/hxg4 open lines (often winning material or wrecking structure); medium blurs the same line-opening idea into central breaks (exd6+, dxe5) and other ignored-tension/move-order refutations.

1523.label: Top boards burn the one critical tempo on a slow king walk, pawn push, patzer check, or greedy grab and skip the forcing rook capture/sacrifice that wins or saves the game; medium broadens to passive queen/knight repositioning moves that not only miss the decisive pawn-break or capture but actively hang material to the opponent's fork or recapture.

1537.label: Top boards uniformly leave the queen en prise on g4/g5 to an enemy bishop along an open long diagonal (Bxg4/Bxg5); medium broadens to the queen lost to minor-piece captures on other squares, including a knight grabbing it with check (Nxg6+).

1531.label: Top: an opening pawn push (d5/f5/f4/c4) leaves a central e4/e5/d5 pawn undefended for an immediate one-move free capture (cxd5/dxe5/Nxe5); medium broadens to central pawn advances or captures—often into the early middlegame—that drop the pawn or material through undermining its defender, pins, or short follow-up tactics rather than a clean single-move grab.

1529.label: Top: in a drawn/holdable endgame the player makes a passive king/knight move and ignores the SOLE saving move, which is a capture (queen, pawn, rook, or bishop); medium keeps the 'one and only good endgame move missed via a passive king/knight shuffle' core but blurs the capture specificity, the saving move often being a quiet blockade or king/knight repositioning instead.

1536.label: At the peak it's an over-aggressive opening knight jump/sortie that directly hangs or traps the knight itself for nothing; at medium it broadens to queen and bishop sorties and to indirect material loss (queen trapped, defender removed, exchange dropped), still over 1-3 moves of refutation.

1535.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a direct capture of the opponent's completely undefended queen (Qxh1, Bxc7, Bxe4, Bxd6, etc.), playing a quiet/positional move that lets the queen escape; medium blurs this to winning the queen via other capturing pieces or short tactics (Nxc2, Nxe2, Bxe2) and to other missed material wins (rook with Bxh8, bishop with axb4, back-rank mate Qxb1+, exchange Rxd5), plus a few near-0cp non-blunders, making it a 'missed winning capture' feature anchored on the enemy queen.

1532.label: Top boards consistently decline the correct central pawn capture (dxc4/dxe4/exf5) and drop material—usually a central pawn, sometimes a full or forked piece; medium boards blur into tempo-losing positional/developing moves that ignore the d/e/c-file tension, mixing outright hangs with skipped winning captures.

1528.label: Top: in a favorable middlegame the bishop is the decisive piece — the player either misses a winning bishop attack (Bh6/Bxh7+/Bxh3) or makes a greedy/loosening move that a bishop refutes; medium: same squandering of a winning/favorable position but the decisive piece blurs to rook/knight/queen and direction stays genuinely split between missed wins and hung material.

1544.label: At peak the player plays a safe non-winning move that skips an immediate forced checkmate (Rh4#, Ra7+/Rgb7#, Qh5+/Qh7#); at medium it blurs to skipping decisive material-winning lines (e.g. c4 winning the d7 knight), with one outlier instead hanging its own pawn (Qe7 dropping h5).

1545.label: Top boards are almost uniformly a pointless queen check (Qb3+, Qc5+, Qh6+, Qg5+) that the opponent trivially blocks or sidesteps, displacing the queen off a key square and throwing away a winning/equal position instead of the consolidating or tactical shot; medium keeps the same tempo-wasting 'patzer check' theme but broadens the checking piece beyond the queen to bishops and other pieces (Bh3+, Bc5+, Bxd4+, Qa4+), and the squandered edge occasionally tips into outright material loss.

1540.label: From a winning position the player throws away the advantage two ways that the feature can't cleanly separate: at the peak it's a near-even split between outright hangs of a major piece (rook/queen/bishop, sometimes via a fork) and passive/inferior moves that skip the only winning shot; at medium it blurs almost entirely toward materially-safe but inferior moves that miss the single precise winning tactic or forced mate, with grabbing/trapped-piece cases the rare exception.

1541.label: Top boards throw away a concrete forced mate by playing a slow, quiet, materially-safe move (often a queen reposition or aimless pawn push) instead of the forcing checking sequence; medium blurs this to missing any forced win — extending or abandoning mates, overlooking material-winning tactics (skewer, free rook), and greedy/offside pawn-grabs that merely stall the decisive conversion.

1546.label: Top: a slow flank pawn move or passive piece retreat in a winning position skips a decisive, materially-safe central pawn break (fxe6/dxe5/exd5/dxc3); medium broadens to other dawdling moves and wrong-direction captures that overlook the stronger central strike, occasionally even letting own material slip.

1539.label: Top boards center on a single bishop as the decisive free piece — either the player hangs it on an exposed square (Bh3/Ba6/Bb7/Bh6) or overlooks a free bishop capture (Bxg8/Bxh8/Bxg1); medium positions keep the bishop-centric free-piece tension but blur direction and piece, adding exchange-winning Bxf1 grabs, move-order bishop losses, and knight-fork tactics (Ne4+, Nxc2) attached to the same hanging-bishop motif.

1550.label: Top boards consistently hang a ROOK—frequently via a needless check (Rg6+, Ra2+, Rxf6+)—that the enemy KING recaptures (Kx...), downgrading a forced mate to a still-won endgame; medium blurs by broadening the recapturer to pawns (fxe6, axb5, fxe3) and the dropped piece to other majors (queen), still in winning positions, with several boards actually sound sacs or mere tempo losses.

1549.label: Top boards play a forcing-looking check from a winning/drawing position that hangs the checking piece (most often a bishop or knight) to a recapture that simultaneously frees the king; medium boards blur this to checks that merely waste tempo or drop the advantage without literally hanging material (and even include a sound check), with the constant being the impulsive check rather than any one piece.

1548.label: Top boards consistently play a careless move that removes the sole defender (or ignores an existing threat), allowing immediate checkmate or a clean piece win (Nxg5, Bxd7, Bxh5, Rhg8); medium blurs this into any self-inflicted material loss—walking the king into mate/checks, allowing forks or back-rank mates, or simply hanging a piece/pawn—so the hung target varies and a few are missed wins rather than direct hangs.

1547.label: Top boards uniformly skip castling and leave the king stuck in the center, where it's punished by checks on open files/diagonals (Qb4+, Re8+, Rhe8+) with O-O/O-O-O the clear best; medium blurs the move type to greedy pawn grabs, bishop trades, and slow tempo-losing repositions that similarly neglect king safety, where the engine's top move is no longer always castling.

1538.label: TOP: Black fails to resolve the Bg4–Nf3 pin with Bxf3 — retreating to h5 (hit by g4) or grabbing d4 (refuted by a Qxd4/Bb5+ intermezzo) and hanging the bishop/material; MEDIUM broadens to White's mirror Bg5/Bxf6 retreats and to cases where the skipped Bxf3 was a missed winning capture rather than an outright self-hang.

1552.label: Top boards all leave an en-prise queen uncaptured (usually answering it with a passive king move) in a winning/equal endgame; medium blurs to ignoring a free rook/exchange capture (and occasionally the careless move also hangs own piece).

1551.label: Top: player instantly recaptures the 'intruding' piece and hangs a full minor piece because the correct order required a forcing in-between move first (a check or more-forcing capture, e.g. Bxf6/Bxc3+/Nd6+/b3+); medium keeps the same premature-capture mechanism but broadens the cost from a dropped minor piece to throwing away the whole win — letting a fork land or skipping a mate/promotion/checks-before-captures sequence.

1555.label: Top: a quiet/passive move overlooks a forcing check that wins material or forces mate (the check is the lone winning move); medium: same missed-check theme but broadens to include playing an inferior/wrong-piece check instead of the strongest forcing one, with the win ranging from mate to material gain.

1543.label: Top boards are uniformly a king declining to recapture a sacrificed bishop on f7 (Kxf7) and retreating instead (Kf8/Kh8); medium blurs to king-captures of other hanging pieces (Kxg7/Kxh8) and, more loosely, to broader critical-king misjudgments—retreats, walking into forks/discovered attacks, and greedy captures that skip the key recapture.

1542.label: Top boards are uniform: a rook relocates onto an open file/square that enables a knight fork, check, or discovered attack winning the rook or exchange (knight decisive ~8/10, with 2 being missed forced wins rather than hangs); medium blurs the moving piece to bishop/queen/king/pawn and the refutation to varied tactics (queen infiltration, hanging piece, missed draw/win), so neither 'rook' nor 'knight' stays constant.

1553.label: Top boards all hang the queen in a winning position—either moving it onto a capturable square (frequently with a check) or ignoring it being en prise; medium boards keep the 'drops own material while ahead' core but broaden the victim to knights, the exchange, and pawns lost via skewers, forks, removed defenders, and a few tempo/positional collapses.

1557.label: Top: a flashy knight check that simply hangs the knight (or its only support) to an immediate capture, a clean full-piece loss from drawn/winning/unclear positions; medium keeps the same hung-checking-knight motif but blurs to multi-move refutations (Kg1 then Qxf2) and to cases where the check chiefly squanders a forced mate/win (Qf2#, Rg8#) rather than just dropping material — with one borderline non-blunder.

1560.label: Top boards are all decisive RxX rook trades (frequently a needless tempo-check) declined while completely winning, skipping a trivially won king-and-pawn endgame; medium blurs this by adding trades that only secure a draw, non-check rook retreats, and even a king grabbing the wrong piece instead of the rook.

1554.label: Top boards are invariably a bishop flung at the opponent's fianchettoed bishop (h6/h3/a6/a3) and lost for free; medium blurs to queen sorties (Qh5/Qa6) and greedy pawn-grabs into the same fianchetto flank that all hang.

1559.label: Top: a clean forced checkmate was available (mate-in-1 up to mate-in-12) but the player chose a materially-safe move that only kept a winning position; medium holds the same mate-missing core but blurs to also include piece-winning tactics (Qxa8+, Nxe7) and slower/alternate forced wins.

1558.label: Top boards: a natural developing/castling move directly hangs a piece in the opening — varying across queen, rook, bishop, knight, or pawn — to a one-move capture, fork, or trap; medium blurs the direction, adding slow/natural moves that instead miss a forcing tactical win or squander a winning advantage, with only some still losing material outright.

1563.label: Top: passive/irrelevant moves (queen retreats, pawn pushes, king steps) ignore a forced-mate threat while skipping the necessary forced queen trade, so the king is mated; medium broadens to ignoring decisive material threats—undefended pieces, knight forks, pawn promotions—and even skipping material-winning queen trades, so the loss is material rather than mate.

1562.label: Top boards are tightly clustered on self-weakening king-safety blunders—removing the king's last defender or marching the king into danger—that allow checkmate or a decisive attack; medium positions blur this into broader self-inflicted moves in losing/lost positions that hang material outright (e.g., Rb1 dropping a rook) or concede positional/tempo damage (a4, g5) rather than always exposing the king.

1564.label: Top boards uniformly ignore an advanced/passed enemy pawn that had to be captured or blockaded, getting punished by promotion or a supported pawn-capture-with-check (exf2+/bxc2+/exd7+/gxf7+) that wins material; medium keeps the advanced-pawn core (e7 push, c6/a6 promotion, gxh7+ storm) but blurs into other neglected urgent threats—loose bishops, pins, and even a missed perpetual—that likewise cost decisive material.

1556.label: Top: a knight greedily grabs a pawn in the opening (Nxe5) and squanders a winning advantage by hanging the piece or stripping a defender off the king; medium blurs to any squandering move—pawn captures, quiet tempo-wasters, and defensive lapses across phases—that collapse equal or already-losing positions, frequently straight into king-side mate.

1561.label: Top boards are constant: a knight move (in the opening, from a drawn/holding position) that abandons a key defender—h7/h2 for a Greek Gift, or g5/e6/e4—or walks straight into a capture, losing material or conceding a decisive kingside attack; medium blurs to other pieces (bishop, rook, queen, pawn) making passive retreats that release pressure or hang material, and shifts partly from direct material loss toward positional/tempo collapse (with one missed Greek Gift).

1571.label: Top: snaps off the queen immediately and hangs its own attacking knight by skipping a saving zwischenzug-check (typically Nxe7+/Nf3+/Nd3+); medium broadens to skipping any intermediate move — rook trade-off first, bishop relocation, or pawn/bishop checks — that would have saved a non-knight piece or won extra material.

1570.chip: Missed winning queen check (often Qa4+ fork)
1570.label: Top boards uniformly skip a queen check that forks the king and a loose minor piece—almost always Qa4+—choosing a passive natural move (a3, O-O, Bd2, a6) while staying materially safe; medium keeps the missed winning queen check but broadens beyond the clean Qa4+ fork to other forcing checks (Qa5+, Qb5+, Qd5+, even Qxd4+/Qxe4+ capturing with check) that win material via a short sequence rather than a one-move fork.

1568.label: Top boards are pawn moves—overwhelmingly hxg6 (also exd5/bxc6/c6/c5)—that blow open a file or diagonal and hang the player's own material, most often the rook to Qxh8 or a piece to a capture-with-check/fork; medium broadens beyond pawns to king, knight, and bishop moves that likewise open a line or abandon a defender, hanging material to a check, fork, or king-hunt.

1567.label: Top boards center tightly on the f7/f2 focal point—either hanging a piece with an unsound Nxf7/Bxf2 sac or skipping the textbook Bc4/Ng5 strike; medium boards blur the same theme into broader opening king-attack misjudgments (Greek-gift Bxh7+, missed Ne5/Nxg5 strikes, and various tactical blunders that hang material off the f7 square).

1575.label: Top boards are uniformly hangs of the player's OWN BISHOP—left undefended, trapped by its own pawn, or losing it after a defender is removed (Ne4, g6, Bg4, O-O, Qd2); medium blurs to hanging other pieces (knight Ne5/Bg5, rook Qe8, pawn) plus some king-safety/positional blunders that aren't clean piece-drops.

1565.label: Top: rook/queen desperation checks in already-lost positions that the king calmly sidesteps, sacrificing the checker or pulling a defender off post to force immediate mate; medium keeps the same purposeless-check idea but blurs to minor-piece checks (bishop/knight) and milder consequences where the check merely loses material, wastes a tempo, or squanders a faster win rather than allowing instant mate.

1569.label: Top: a reflexive pawn-chase of the enemy queen overlooks capturing it outright (free hanging queen, ~+6); medium: the same queen-chasing pawn/piece move blurs into either hanging own material to a tactic (Nxg6, Bxg6+, Bxf3, Bxb4, Qxa6) or missing a different win (queen trap Nc4, bigger capture Bxg5).

1574.label: Top boards are consistently slow/passive KING moves (retreat or king-safety) chosen over the engine's active/forcing alternative; at medium activation the piece blurs (queen/bishop moves also fire) and so does the consequence — sometimes hanging a pawn or bishop, sometimes missing a forced win/mate, sometimes skipping the only defensive resource, so neither a clean 'Hangs' nor 'Missed' direction nor a single piece holds.

1566.label: Top boards are near-uniform: from a dead-equal middlegame the player fires an aggressive check—overwhelmingly Qh5+—that simply hangs the queen to a capture along the open 5th rank (a few instead lose via a queen-for-rook trade, a tempo-wasting check, or a back-rank slip); medium boards blur well beyond clean queen-hangs into any self-defeating move that throws away an equal-or-defensible position—hanging a piece to a pin, walking the king into a mating net, allowing a decisive queen trade/passer, or ignoring a back-rank/mate threat—so the constant 'self-defeating check that drops the queen' diffuses into general game-losing blunders.

1577.label: Top: a natural, materially-safe move (castling/developing/king-walk) passes up a forcing material-winning shot, almost always the long-diagonal Be4/Bg2 hitting an undefended a8/h1 rook (board 4 is the lone self-inflicted grab); medium keeps the 'safe move skips the one critical reply' core but blurs the target—often just a tempo/precision loss or a smaller material/positional drop rather than a clean long-diagonal rook win.

1572.label: Top: a greedy material grab (capture/pawn-push) ignores an immediate, usually mate-in-1 threat and self-mates the player's own king; medium keeps the forced-mate theme but broadens the losing move to king-walks and quiet pushes, and blurs further into plain material-losing blunders (hung piece, queen lost to a fork, positional collapse) that aren't mate.

1576.label: Top boards uniformly skip a winning CHECK (capture-check or forced mate) for a natural quiet move; medium broadens to non-check forcing captures/tactics and the chosen move frequently hangs material outright rather than just throwing away the win.

1578.label: Top boards consistently throw away a clearly winning position with a quiet/king-march or pawn move that gets punished by a knight tactic (fork/check, e.g. Nc4, Nd8+, Nd7+, Nd5+); medium boards keep the same 'imprecise move squanders a won position' core but blur the instrument to include rook checks (Rf6+), bishop/pawn captures, blockades, and missed captures/mates rather than always a knight.

1582.label: Top boards miss a forced mate/win whose decisive move is a rook delivering check (Re1#, Rb3+, Rh4+); medium keeps the missed-forced-mate-via-check pattern but the checking piece broadens to queen, pawn, or knight (Qf4+, b3#, Ne5+).

1580.label: Top: a king step or removal of a blocking piece that hangs the QUEEN to a forcing rook check (usually a discovered check); medium keeps the same self-exposing-to-a-rook-check motif but blurs the prize, losing a rook/exchange or walking into rook-delivered mate instead of always the queen.

1579.label: A non-urgent 'own-agenda' move (king walk, repositioning, flank pawn push, pawn-grab) that ignores the position's decisive demand and loses material; top boards lean to endgame own-agenda moves that let an enemy passed pawn promote or leave a hanging piece, while medium broadens to middlegame king-safety pawn pushes and pawn-grabs that walk into a refuting tactic (fork, discovered attack, mating net).

1587.chip: Hangs piece to short tactic (often knight)
1587.label: Top boards consistently hang a minor piece or queen to a 1-3 move tactic (mostly knights left attacked/undefended); medium blurs into pawn losses (self-blocking, overloaded defender) and some tempo/positional slips, with a few missed-win and endgame outliers.

1573.chip: Traded active bishop for knight (any piece)
1573.label: Top boards almost uniformly exchange a strong, active bishop for a knight via an even recapture (Bxf6/Bxd5/Bxc6/Bxd6), surrendering the bishop pair and attacking chances when a tempo pawn push (e4/e5/c4) or a tactic kept the edge; medium keeps the same 'liquidate an active piece for a knight' idea but broadens the capturing piece and motive — bishop/knight swaps on f3/c3, an exchange sac (Rxf3), pawn grabs, and capture-before-preparation move-order errors — all throwing away a clear or winning advantage.

1581.label: Top boards are defensive king-safety blunders in already-losing middlegames that expose the king or remove its lone defender, converting a resistable position into forced mate (often shedding a piece in the refutation); medium blurs into a grab-bag of eval-dropping blunders—missed tactical wins, hung pieces, allowed forks, and advantage-trading moves—rather than pure king-exposure.

1583.label: At the peak the mistake is underpromoting a pawn (to a knight) and throwing away a completely won endgame; at medium it blurs into a different conversion blunder—a king move (Kc6) walking into a knight fork—so the constant is 'squandering a won endgame in one move' while the mechanism shifts from underpromotion to a tactical/fork error.

1584.label: Top boards consistently liquidate/hang the queen — the only perpetual-check or defensive resource — converting a holdable but losing endgame into forced mate; medium broadens to also include surrendering the defensive rook (rook-for-knight trade) alongside the queen hangs.

1588.label: Top boards consistently squander a winning position by playing a quiet/routine developing or tempo move instead of an immediately winning knight capture (bxc6/dxc6/exf3) that then lets the knight escape; medium blurs the capture into other missed winning shots—central pawn breaks/strikes (e5, f5, dxe4, f3)—and increasingly into hanging one's own piece by walking into a tactic or unsound sac.

1589.label: Top boards throw away a decisively won endgame either by hanging major material (rook/queen via skewer, or pawn over 2-3 moves) or by missing a trivial forced win (immediate promotion, free-queen capture, mate); medium keeps the won-endgame squander but blurs the mechanism toward quiet pawn pushes and king walks that drop material more gradually, plus the occasional missed winning capture.

1594.label: Top boards are uniformly lost endgames where a rook/king move leaves the rook trapped or captured over the 2-3 move refutation (often the actual best move, fired on exposed-rook losing positions); medium blurs into middlegame positions and other moving pieces (bishop, knight, king) where the rook is still the typical piece hung — plus occasional non-rook material loss or a missed pawn-endgame win.

1591.label: Top: Black mishandles the f6-knight attacked by White's e5 pawn — retreating it to a losing square or ignoring the threat — and hangs it for ~200-300cp; medium blurs to any unaddressed opening threat (by either color), failing to meet a tactical/attacking idea and thereby dropping material or allowing a decisive king attack (Qh5/Qh4+/Nf5+/forks).

1592.label: Top boards uniformly hang the player's own QUEEN to a tactical capture delivered with check (Bxd2+, Rxf6+, Bxd4+, Nd3+); medium keeps the same 'lose own material to a check' motif but broadens the victim to rooks, knights, or the exchange (and occasionally allowing mate).

1599.label: Top boards uniformly skip a free, simple capture of an undefended hanging rook in a winning position, letting it flee; medium boards keep the same 'overlooked a free capture' pattern but broaden the missed piece to any major/minor piece (rook, queen, or bishop).

1595.label: Top boards constantly skip a winning queen capture delivered with check (Qxc4+, Qxb3+, Qxd4+) to settle for an inferior still-winning move; medium blurs to winning captures without check (Qxg4) and includes false positives where the played move was actually best/optimal-conversion.

1602.label: Top: a materially-safe move (usually a knight/bishop/queen retreat) declines a free ROOK win (Qxh5, Rxa5, Bxf5, Nxe5) in a won opening; medium keeps the 'skip the winning capture' theme but blurs the prize to a minor piece (Qxg5) alongside the rook grabs.

1596.label: Top: in drawn/won positions a quiet positional/endgame move (passive rook/knight/bishop placement, off-tempo pawn push) lets the opponent's usually-connected queenside passed pawns roll unopposed, or ~40% misses a forcing shot (Qxf5+, Nxc5+, Nxc3+ fork, Bxg2/Rxd1 finesse); medium keeps the 'throws away the holding/winning move' core but blurs the mechanism toward king-safety and back-rank/deflection lapses (Qh5+, Re6+, Rh8+, mating nets) alongside the same passed-pawn concessions.

1597.label: Top boards are uniformly opening knight-hangs—either developing/moving a knight onto a square a pawn or piece attacks (Nf3 into ...gxf3, ...Nxe5 into Qe2, ...Nxd4 into Be3) or ignoring a standing attack on a developed knight (h3/Bxf4 vs ...dxc3, ...e6 vs exf6); medium blurs the victim to other minor pieces (e.g. dropped bishop on h5, a bishop move that loses the f6-knight) and to broader material loss, including queen-greedy/check moves and a couple of materially-safe missed wins.

1604.label: Top boards are uniformly classic Greek Gift sacrifices (Bxh7+/Bxh2+) that simply hang the bishop because the supporting attackers are absent and the king safely captures; medium broadens the target square to include the analogous Bxf7+ sac, but the constant theme is an unsupported bishop sacrifice against the king that drops a full piece.

1586.label: Top boards are constant: greedy knight captures (Nxe5/Nxd4/Nxf5/Qxe5) grabbing a pawn that hang the moving piece—or invite a mate/fork—to an immediate refutation; medium blurs to unsound but non-capturing central knight sorties (often Nd5/Ne5/Ne4) that overextend onto an undefended square and lose material, with a couple of non-knight overreaches (Kf2 draw, ...b5) mixed in.

1585.label: Top boards are immediate, premature pawn promotions in a won endgame that skip a needed prep move (a4, Kd7, king-off-the-g-file)—often hanging the new queen to a skewer/fork or letting the opponent counter-promote into a draw; medium broadens to other hasty winning-position moves (a king advance abandoning a pawn, a developing move walking into a fork) that likewise throw away the win.

1603.label: Top boards are self-inflicting moves (pawn breaks, defender removal, or a king step) punished by a capture-with-check that wins material or forces mate; medium broadens to king moves that walk into non-capturing checks, fork-checks, and the occasional pure material grab where the check is incidental.

1601.chip: Hangs material to bishop diagonal (often queen)
1601.label: Top boards consistently lose the QUEEN to a bishop diagonal pin/skewer—king and queen left aligned and punished by the recurring bishop (typically ...Bc5 vs Qd4/Qe3, also Bg5/Bd4/Be5); medium blurs this into a broader 'bishop wins material on a diagonal' theme, adding rooks lost to bishop forks/captures/tempo-checks (Bb3 fork, Bxb1, Bxf4+ then Bxh2) and other king-on-diagonal skewers, with a couple of non-bishop outliers (knight-mate, queen pawn-grab).

1600.label: At the peak: a quiet developing bishop move (Bd3/Bd2) that hangs the d4 knight to an immediate ...Nxd4 in the opening (no recapture due to the Bb4 pin / blocked queen); medium blurs to other quiet or structural moves (pawn captures, a bishop trade) that instead drop a rook to Qxa8/Qxa1 or surrender a central pawn.

1606.label: Top: in lost endgames a king move (rarely knight) fails to catch, block, or stay in the square of the opponent's passed pawn, allowing/speeding promotion; medium blurs to rook moves, trades, and captures that similarly mishandle a passer—sometimes squandering a win or drawing rather than just accelerating a loss.

1605.label: At the peak the player declines an available simplifying queen exchange (Qxh6/Qxe5/Qxd3/Qxe1...) and instead plays an aimless or tempo-losing queen move — frequently a check — that lets the opponent's attack or passed pawn become decisive; at medium the constant 'skipped Qx trade' theme remains but the replacement move blurs to any passive piece move (e.g. Kh2, pawn pushes) rather than only a queen move/check.

1593.label: Top boards uniformly skip a forcing winning QUEEN check (frequently a capture-with-check), the player instead playing a slower non-check or wrong-piece check; medium blurs to also missing the correct queen-check square, a rook check, or even a quiet winning queen move.

1598.label: Top: trades the queen (usually a capture/check) to dissolve a decisive attack into equality, declining quieter queen-keeping moves; medium broadens to other pieces — knight and rook exchanges, plus outright hanging captures and greedy grabs — that likewise squander a winning position by simplifying or giving back material.

1610.label: Top: moves that walk the king straight into an immediate (often back-rank or direct Qg2#/Rg4#) checkmate; medium broadens to allowing slower mating attacks by removing key defenders and occasionally overlooking one's own forced mate.

1607.label: Top boards are clean opening material drops—an early knight/pawn/bishop move (Na5, Ne5, f5, g5, a6, Bxf2+) that abandons defense of the e5 pawn or the f7/king square and is instantly punished by Bxf7+ or Nxe5; medium boards blur to broader opening errors—weakening/tempo-losing moves (Qe6, f3, Qa4, Ng5) and pieces left to a fork—that lose material or advantage over a few moves rather than a single clean capture.

1608.label: Top: a developing or pawn move in the opening leaves a minor piece — almost always an undefended bishop (or removes its sole defender) — to be captured for free; medium broadens to knights/pawns and short 2-3 move refutations (deflection, fork, wrong capture-order, move-order errors) that win the loose material rather than a clean one-ply grab.

1609.label: Top is constant: a passive bishop/knight developing move drops a full piece to a forcing tactic, almost always an f7/b7 hit (Qxg4 free piece, Bxf7+, Qb3/Qd5/Qh5 double attacks on f7+b7); medium blurs into careless pawn pushes/retreats (e5, f5, c6, b6, exd5) that lose just a pawn or collapse positionally rather than cleanly hanging a piece.

1615.label: Top boards skip the single winning continuation—a free capture or forced mate—by playing a materially-safe king move or wrong-square check; medium blurs into broader winning-technique lapses (wrong-file check, rook in front of its pawn, premature rook trade) that throw away the won endgame.

1621.label: Top: forced back-rank mate-in-one, almost always a rook landing on Rc1# (or Ra1#) with escape squares sealed, declined for a routine pawn/king/rook move; medium broadens to mate-in-two and other rook delivery squares (Rg1#, Re3#, Rb8+, Rc8+, Ra1+) but is still the same overlooked rook back-rank checkmate.

1614.label: Top: a winning position is squandered by a slow queen/bishop/rook move that misses a forcing pawn break/advance (best move is a pawn push in every peak board); medium keeps the 'passive move throws away the edge' pattern but the overlooked winning resource blurs beyond pawn pushes to include piece moves and tactics (knight forks, captures, trapped-rook traps).

1611.label: Top boards peak on a winning side playing the natural simplifying queen capture/check (Qxd7+, Qxd1) instead of the stronger forcing line, missing a bigger win or mate; medium broadens to other pieces' obvious forcing moves (knight capture Nxe4, rook check Re1+), where the outcome blurs from merely skipping a win to conceding decisive counterplay or even getting mated.

1622.label: Top boards uniformly play a king-weakening or off-target move that ignores a building kingside attack, most often allowing the textbook Greek Gift Bxh7+ mating sacrifice; medium boards broaden to other self-inflicted king exposures (castling/walking into a check or knight fork, shattering the king's pawn cover, even a smothered mate) plus a couple of central/queenside material drops.

1619.label: Top boards split evenly between Bxc3+ and Bxc6+ — a bishop capturing a knight with check that prematurely trades off the strong pinning/pressuring bishop, surrenders the bishop pair (or a key outpost), and usually skips a stronger move (often a queen capture like Qxd4/Qxd5 or a bishop retreat); medium narrows to Bxc6+ but blurs in the cost, ranging from a mere positional/structural edge to losing a full piece via the wrong capture order.

1618.label: Top boards are uniformly king-safety errors—an already-lost side makes a king or pawn-shield move that exposes its king / opens lines and converts the loss into a forced mate; medium keeps the 'already-losing, self-hastening move' core but blurs into adjacent categories (hanging a piece, mistimed pawn pushes, passed-pawn/trapped-piece mishandling) that accelerate the loss rather than strictly exposing the king.

1616.label: Top: an always-queen pointless check that the king simply sidesteps, wasting a critical tempo and squandering a lost-but-fighting or won position; medium keeps the queen-check core but blurs to include rook checks and move-order/wrong-piece checks, where the waste means skipping a forced mate, a material-winning capture, or a saving defensive move.

1613.label: Top boards are passive/irrelevant moves (often a flank pawn push) that ignore the position's single most urgent demand — almost always letting an opponent's passed pawn promote in a losing-but-savable spot; medium boards broaden that ignored demand to king safety, allowed forks, or walking into a forced mate, with a couple instead missing a forced mate or key defensive capture.

1612.chip: Hangs piece, king move not Qxg5
1612.label: Top: king retreats (f7→g6/e8/e7, h2→g1) instead of the sole winning Qxg5/Qxg4 capture of a hanging knight, abandoning its own g4/g5/h5 bishop which is then taken for free; medium keeps the king-move-skips-Qxg5 motif but blurs into other piece moves (queen, knight) that skip capturing some other hanging enemy piece (rook, bishop) or convert a win, similarly dropping material.

1620.label: At the peak the move is materially safe but skips the quiet pawn move (almost always b3, also b4/b6/f6/g6/c6) needed to challenge, cage, or block the opponent's active BISHOP, letting it reposition to a dominant square or escape a trap; at medium it blurs to restraining other minor pieces (e.g. an offside knight via Rc8/c6) and to looser prophylaxis omissions — and several medium boards drift into outright hung pawns/pieces or tempo/king-safety blunders rather than pure restraint, so the bishop-via-b3 core is only partially constant.

1628.label: Top: in a materially safe position the player overlooks a simple, free capture of an undefended enemy rook (winning a rook or the exchange, often forfeiting a forced mate), choosing a quiet king/pawn/rook move instead; medium blurs the target from 'rook' to 'any decisive winning resource' — missed forced mates, promotions, exchange-winning tactics, or winning tempo moves — passed over for a quiet or reflexive checking move.

1625.label: At peak strength the player hangs the queen on the e-file (e5/e6, punished by Rxe5+/Rxe6+) by ignoring the mutual tension instead of resolving it with Qxe1+; medium boards keep this same queen-on-e-file/Qxe1+ motif, while some top boards blur the hung material to a rook, bishop or knight.

1623.label: Top boards uniformly hang material to a forcing tactical refutation (frequently a capture-with-check, but the lost unit varies: king-net, bishop, pawn, exchange, rook); medium boards blur this into tempo/positional concessions and pure missed wins (grabbing a free pawn, a mate-in-2), so the constant is 'a move that overlooks the most forcing line' while the direction (self-hang vs. skipped win) is what diffuses.

1626.label: Top: in a losing position a passive/king-exposing move allows a FORCED MATE by king attack (back-rank or king-hunt), declining the only defense—usually a queen-for-rook sac; medium blurs the 'mate' core into losing decisive material (hanging pieces, endgame collapse) to the same kind of attack.

1631.label: Top boards are unsound knight pseudo-fork sacs on f7/f2/c7 (à la Fried Liver) that Black/White simply recaptures, netting a piece for a pawn; medium blurs to any opening move that hangs a minor piece—overlooked recaptures, ignored attacks on a hanging knight/bishop, or tactics that drop a knight.

1627.label: Top: queen checks driven to the edge/corner (Qa8+, Qh8+, Qh1+) that hand the king a flight square and throw away a forced mate or won game; medium broadens to rook (Rh1+) and other forcing checks, with more cases being a reflexive check chosen over an available mate-in-one or the quiet winning move.

1629.chip: Hangs material moving a guard/blocker (often knight)
1629.label: Top boards are uniformly a knight quitting a critical blocking/defending square (file or diagonal) so the queen, exchange, knight, or even mate falls to an intermezzo or newly-opened line; medium blurs the deserting piece to any unit (king, bishop, pawn as well as knight) and occasionally shades into missed wins / wrong-capture choices rather than pure hangs.

1632.label: Top: in a won position the player leaves the queen en prise on a tempting square—usually a forcing check captured by a pawn/bishop (2 hang a rook instead); medium keeps the hung-queen core but broadens into plain rook hangs, losing piece trades, and one materially-safe missed-tactic.

1634.label: At the peak the player overlooks the one saving defense and walks the king straight into forced mate (back-rank/king-safety); at medium the same blindness to the opponent's immediate decisive reply blurs from mate into dropping major material—hanging a queen/rook or allowing a winning fork/promotion.

1635.label: Top: in a clearly winning opening the player pushes a pawn instead of grabbing a free, undefended hanging minor piece (mostly knights, one bishop on g4), letting it escape and throwing away the win; medium narrows to the same undefended-knight capture (Qc7 instead of taking on c6), while a couple of top boards instead drop the player's own material or a tempo, blurring direction.

1617.label: Top boards are uniform: a slow non-forcing move (pawn push, king tuck, queen redirect) declines the position's demanded forcing queen trade/capture or simplification, hanging material or walking into a mating attack; medium keeps the queen central but blurs both the resource (missed pawn breaks, bishop/king moves, e.g. hxg3/Bxe7/Kc3) and the direction (mixing hung material with greedy/wrong trades and missed wins).

1630.label: Top: in clearly winning/mating positions the player makes a quiet queen or king move that declines an immediate free capture of an undefended enemy queen or rook (Qxh1, Bxf7, Kxd4, Rxa7, Bxc2, Nxf8), letting the opponent trade or save the piece and converting a forced mate into merely winning; medium blurs into broader winning/critical-position material lapses — taking the wrong (lesser) piece, hanging one's own queen, dropping a pawn, or even allowing back-rank mate — and several boards (4,7,10,8-med) are non-blunders or minor inaccuracies.

1633.label: Top boards: from a winning position the player skips the decisive queen trade/capture (Qxd7+/Qxe7+/Nxd8) and hangs their own queen; medium broadens the dropped piece to a bishop or knight (e.g. unsound fork) while the queen stays the central punishing piece.

1641.label: Top boards reflexively capture a rook (occasionally bishop/queen) instead of an immediate or near-immediate forced mate (often mate-in-one with the king already netted); medium broadens to grabbing the queen/rook while skipping a longer but still forced checkmate, the move staying materially safe so it's a missed win rather than a hang.

1643.label: Top boards are textbook one-move queen-invasion checkmates on h7/h2 (knight covering the king's escape, own rook blocking f-file), where the player instead chases the queen with a pawn; medium broadens to other invasion squares (Qxa2#) and mate-in-2 nets, plus a few endgame/line-opening moves that merely lose material rather than allow forced mate.

1645.label: Top boards are quiet developing/castling/flank moves that ignore the central pawn tension and get hit by a forking pawn break (d4/e4/e5) that double-attacks two pieces and wins material; medium boards keep the same 'ignore the tension, allow the break' error but broaden the punishment to breaks that mainly gain tempo, space, or a structural edge rather than cleanly forking/winning a piece.

1637.label: Top boards are king-exposing moves (greedy captures near the king or king walks) that strip pawn shelter / open a file/diagonal and allow a FORCED MATE; medium broadens to king and piece moves that weaken safety but only lose material or tempo (e.g. capture-with-check, retreats), often falling short of mate.

1638.label: Top positions hang a specific piece outright—usually a greedy or careless capture (Rxb6, Rxd3, Rf2) or a move that drops a rook/knight/queen, even walking into back-rank mate; medium positions blur into broader self-inflicted blunders that lose material or squander a winning/drawn edge—removing a key defender, premature captures, or positional/tempo errors.

1642.label: Top boards constantly skip a full-piece-winning queen capture (often Qxd2/Qxc6/Qxd3, frequently because the recapture loses to a fork); medium blurs to missed captures by any piece (Rxc6, Bxe4, Nxe5, Qxa5) plus a few positional/defensive misses that squander the win, with the played move usually materially safe rather than hanging.

1640.label: At the peak, a capturing trade in an already-losing endgame (mostly rook, also bishop/queen) liquidates into a pawn-promotion race the opponent queens first — typically by grabbing a supporting piece or trading queens rather than the real passer; medium narrows to a rook capturing the wrong target, but ~3/10 are the forced/best move, so it reads partly as a lost-promotion-race position detector.

1644.label: Top boards peak on a winning queen check missed in an open-king / absent-f-pawn position—most sharply White's crushing Qh5+ on the open e8–h5 diagonal; medium blurs to the color-mirrored Black Qh4+ on the open e1–h4 diagonal, where a quiet pawn/piece move squanders the forcing check (and sometimes even drops g7/material in the refutation).

1624.label: Top: a free enemy bishop sits on g4/g5 and the player skips the 100%-winning Qxg4/Qxg5 (in ~half also abandoning the d1 queen to ...Bxd1); medium keeps the same missed free-bishop grab but blurs the square (e.g. Qxa4+) and occasionally needs a non-queen recapture (Bxe7).

1636.label: Top: a careless move (often abandoning a central pawn/square like d4/d5) throws away a clearly winning position and is punished by a queen check or capture, frequently on e6 / the a2-g8 diagonal; medium: the squandered position is smaller or already worse and the refutation broadens beyond the queen to knight/pawn forks, discovered checks, or mate, so the material lost (pawn, piece, exchange, or just the edge) varies.

1649.label: Top boards throw away a draw/win when a king-move or check fails to stop an enemy passed pawn, and the promotion is forced through by coming WITH check or by INTERPOSING against the player's own check; medium broadens to slower tempo-losing king/queen moves that simply let the pawn advance and queen without the check trick.

1651.chip: Hangs material to overlooked tactic (or mate)
1651.label: Top: from winning/equal positions a natural or greedy move (often a pawn/piece grab like Qxc6, Qxe4, Nxc3) walks into a concrete refutation that loses material over the next move or two (occasionally just skipping a winning shot); medium broadens the overlooked tactic from material-winning refutations to king-safety/mating nets (Qe3+, Rh-file mates, a7+ Nc7#) and favorable forced simplifications.

1650.label: Top boards are speculative Greek-Gift-style bishop checks (Bxf7/f2/h2, also Bc6+) that hand over a full bishop for a pawn with no attacking follow-up; medium keeps the 'forcing check that loses material' theme but broadens the giveaway piece to knight/rook/pawn checks (and a few that squander a win/mate rather than hang outright).

1647.label: Top boards are clean rook trades/captures that liquidate a holdable or winning position into a lost king-and-pawn endgame (connected passers/active king decide); medium blurs to broader simplifications and positional concessions (pawn pushes, passive rook moves, hung defenders) that likewise convert a good position into a lost one.

1654.label: Top boards squander a clearly won/forced-mate position through a queen-centric one-move blunder, split ~50/50 between missing a free enemy queen/rook capture (e.g. Rxd7, Nxg5, Rxb3) and hanging one's own queen or king (e.g. Re7→Qxf8, Kb1→Qe1#); medium positions keep the 'threw away a winning position' theme but blur the decisive piece to rooks, bishops and knights and lean slightly more toward missed captures, with direction genuinely mixed.

1653.label: Top: opening developing moves (esp. Bc4/...e5) leave the e1-h4 / h5-e8 diagonal bare and hang material to a queen check (Qh4+/Qh5+/Qxe5+/disc. check); medium keeps one Bc4→Qh4+ board but broadens to other king-safety lapses (Ne5 invasion) plus an endgame positional outlier, and direction blurs from hangs toward one missed Qh5+ win.

1655.label: Top: an active/tempo move (often attacking the enemy queen) abandons a key defender or skips the forced resource, punished sharply—usually by queen infiltration or mate; medium broadens to any tempo-seeking or 'active' move that instead hangs/traps a piece or concedes a positional resource, with more varied (non-queen) punishment.

1646.label: Top boards uniformly miss a material-winning, forcing rook capture delivered WITH check (Rxe4+/Rxg7+/Rxc5+/Rxf5+) in favor of a passive consolidating move; medium broadens to any skipped forcing tempo-winning move — rook/queen checks (Re1+, Rh7+, Re7+, Qe2+) or minor-piece captures (Nxc3, Nxe5) — losing the strict rook+capture+check specificity.

1652.chip: Hangs material on tempting check (medium: quiet)
1652.label: Top boards are flashy FORCING moves—mostly checks, some greedy captures—that hang a piece or squander a winning edge instead of the solid (often itself forcing) winning line; at medium the pattern blurs to quieter, non-forcing tempo-losing moves that simply miss the winning tactic, and the direction splits between true hangs (~6/10) and wasted/missed wins (~4/10).

1639.label: Top boards are near-uniform: a rook (occasionally queen) greedily captures an enemy passed pawn, usually with check, and hangs the major piece to the king's recapture, squandering a won or drawn endgame; medium blurs to assorted passed-pawn endgame blunders that still drop material/the result—recapturing with the wrong piece, hanging a piece while blockading, or making a quiet/king move that lets the passer promote (mate).

1648.label: Top boards are the canonical rook/a-file 'put the question' pawn push at a bishop (h3/h6/a3/a6) that wastes a tempo and squanders a clear advantage or a concrete missed win; medium broadens to other tempo-wasting flank pawn pushes (e.g. b5) — and an occasional analogous slow developing move — where the refutation more often outright loses material rather than merely skipping a win.

1664.label: Top boards are uniformly structure-wrecking pawn advances that liquidate a holding/favorable pawn chain (turning draw→loss or win→draw); medium blurs to include king moves that abandon defense of the key pawn structure and other premature endgame advances.

1665.label: Player ignores a completely undefended enemy queen they could win for free; top boards are pure queen-takes-queen captures, while medium positions broaden the capturing piece to knight, rook, bishop, or pawn (and occasionally the skipped capture coincides with hanging the player's own queen).

1661.label: Top boards are uniformly rook moves that fail to deal with an enemy passed pawn—placing the rook on a square that doesn't control the promotion square or wasting the tempo-gaining check needed to hold; medium blurs this to include king moves, pawn-race tempo losses, and other endgame defensive errors (with a minority hanging the rook or missing a mate), but the constant is mishandling a passer in a rook endgame and letting it promote/win.

1663.label: Top boards are clean rook-for-rook exchanges (Rxf8/Rxe8/Rxd1) that surrender a key defender, the open file, or a winning move-order, turning a tenable/winning game worse; medium keeps the unnecessary-rook-capture core but blurs the consequence — sometimes the capture outright hangs the rook, grabs the wrong piece, or trades away a forced mate/forcing tactic.

1656.label: Top: in a won middlegame the player grabs material (capturing queen/knight/pawn) or plays a natural queen move instead of the single precise forcing shot — a sacrifice, intermezzo, or check like Rxe5/Qg8+/Ne7+/exf7+ — and is hit by a forcing refutation that wins material or mates; medium broadens the wrong move to quiet king/pawn retreats (Kh8, Kd3, h6) that mostly walk into forced mate, so direction blurs between missed wins and self-inflicted losses.

1666.label: Top boards are quiet/passive moves (mostly queen/bishop repositioning) that stay materially safe but skip a forcing, usually material-winning continuation; medium blurs the direction by adding passive moves that not only miss the stronger line but actively allow an opponent's tactic—often a fork—to win back or capture the player's own material.

1667.label: At the peak the constant is a self-inflicted king-safety collapse — a king walk or removal of the lone defender that ignores an immediate threat and concedes a forced mate (Qxd2#, Qxe6+/Qe7#, check-fest mating nets); at medium it blurs into simply hanging a major piece (rook/bishop) or conceding a back-rank/discovered-attack refutation, but always a self-inflicted move in a losing/tense middlegame that flips the game into an immediate decisive loss.

1660.label: In every board the player skips the needed central-knight capture (Nxd5/Nxd4/Nxe4): top boards thereby drop a full piece (the dropped piece varies—knight, bishop, or queen—from the unresolved central knight), while medium broadens to losing just a pawn or to lasting positional damage (shattered structure, squandered advantage) from the same ignored central tension.

1657.label: Top: from a clearly winning middlegame a natural/greedy move (often a capture) overlooks a decisive forcing win — a knight fork or forced mate — settling for a smaller material gain; medium broadens to actively hanging a piece or queen outright, frequently to an enemy fork, sometimes from merely worse rather than winning positions.

1662.chip: Hangs major piece or allows mate
1662.label: Top boards are won positions thrown away by a self-inflicted blunder that hangs a major piece (queen/rook) or steps into a one-move mate; medium blurs to slower multi-move refutations and a pure positional missed win.

1659.label: Top boards relocate a defending knight or (later) rook off a key square so material hangs to a capture/threat on the vacated square (mate in #8); medium blurs into trapped-piece and positional squander, with ~3/10 boards instead being missed forcing wins (Re3, c6, Rc8).

1671.label: Top: in won/lost endgames the player makes a passive non-forcing move (slow pawn push, wrong rook move) instead of the one critical resource — a tempo check or capture — letting the opponent's passed pawn queen (occasionally just hanging a free piece); medium blurs to the same passive-instead-of-critical idea via wrong king moves that allow promotion/mate.

1672.label: Top: a natural-looking move (recapture, development, king-step) in a winning or equal position ignores the position's single critical resource — usually a sharp tactic (Nxh5, Qxd4) or the sole defensive move (Bxh6, Ne2, Kf7) — producing a 250–620cp collapse; medium preserves the 'only one move within 50cp' signal but blurs into quieter positional and endgame/move-order misses with smaller swings, and direction mixes squandered wins with outright hangs.

1658.label: Top boards almost always capture/recapture a CENTRALIZED KNIGHT in the wrong move order (or with the wrong piece, e.g. Nxf6 vs Bxf6), which hangs the player's own material or trades off a winning/attacking advantage; medium blurs the captured target to other premature grabs and recaptures (rook, pawn, queen) and broadens the punishment to deflection, fork, or pawn promotion rather than a simple back-rank/own-piece hang.

1674.label: Top: in a won position the player makes a routine central pawn capture (exd4/fxe4/dxe5) and misses the decisive Qh4+/Qh5+ check that forks king and h1/h8-rook along the open e1-h4/e8-h5 diagonal left by the missing f-pawn; medium keeps the same missing-f-pawn kingside theme but blurs—the win can be a longer Qh5+ sacrificial attack rather than a clean fork, the squandering move may be a passive retreat (Bb3) instead of a capture, and occasionally the greedy grab simply drops a piece to a different tactic (Nxc6).

1676.label: Top: a knight greedily grabs a central pawn (d4/d5/e5) and is instantly recaptured, hanging a full minor piece for a pawn; medium broadens to other capturers/squares (bishop and pawn grabs like Bxd5, Bxb4, Nxe4, Bxe6) plus a few non-capture moves that likewise drop a piece for a pawn.

1675.label: Top: in a winning middlegame the player skips a decisive queen move delivered with check (capture/sacrifice/zwischenzug that wins material or mates) for a non-forcing move; medium blurs to rook checks/exchange-sacs that win into pawn endgames, with the forcing-check piece no longer strictly the queen.

1673.label: At peak: from already-lost positions the player declines the critical defensive capture of an infiltrated rook (instead pushing a pawn, walking the king, or grabbing with the queen) and walks into a short forced mate; at medium this blurs to hanging a different piece (knight/queen) or merely missing/slowing a clear material win rather than getting mated.

1679.label: Top: a developing/non-central move—usually a bishop sortie like Bc5—ignores the f4-e5 pawn tension and gets refuted by a clean fxe5/fxe4 grabbing the abandoned central pawn; medium keeps the same 'abandon the center tension' theme but broadens the punishment beyond the simple pawn grab to a pawn fork (Bf4), a trapped knight (Nd5), a tempo-losing retreat (Bd3→exf5), or a premature recapture (Nxe4).

1669.label: Top: from a winning position a greedy capture or king-exposing move lets the opponent's forced mating attack through (or squanders an own forced mate), nearly all king-safety collapses; medium blurs the strict-mate constant into broader squandering of the advantage — hanging material (exchange/pawn/queen), allowing perpetual/counterplay, or a positional slip rather than guaranteed mate.

1682.label: At the peak the player skips a single clean free piece capture (rook on f1, bishop on f7/g6, rook on a3/e1) that trivially converts a won endgame; medium positions blur into missed forced mates (wrong checking square, omitted Qg7+) and the occasional self-hang (Qb1??), plus a couple of near-0cp non-mistakes.

1668.chip: Missed forced mate, grabbed queen (any capture)
1668.label: Top boards are queen captures that ignore a forced mate-in-1/2 or stronger win while staying clearly winning; medium broadens the grabbed piece to rooks/pawns and the consequence often flips to actually hanging the mate (e.g., walking into a back-rank Re8# or Qg2#) rather than merely skipping a faster one.

1683.label: Top boards play a quiet/passive move — a rook retreat, king step, or routine recapture — that forfeits a concrete forcing tactic, most often a knight fork/check (Nf6+, Nxf3, Nxe4); medium boards blur the same 'passive move skips a forcing shot' theme to other tactics (a queen trap via g4, a rook counter-attack) and impurely into directly hanging material or walking into back-rank mate.

1678.label: Top: a passive bishop-to-d2/d7 move that breaks a pin but skips a forcing queen tactic (Qg4/Bb5+/Qb4+/Qxg7) in a winning position; medium blurs to any quiet/non-forcing move (rook, recapture, other bishop) that skips the stronger line and increasingly just allows a fork or concedes structure rather than purely missing a clean win.

1681.label: Top boards uniformly trade the queen (Qxd8/Qxa1/Qxg1) to defuse a winning attack on an exposed king, converting a near-mating advantage into equality; medium blurs to any major-piece capture/trade (rook for queen, hung queen via a distracting move, a promoted queen instantly recaptured) that simplifies away a winning or mating position, sometimes missing a forced mate.

1685.label: Top: a natural-looking developing move (esp. ...Nf6/...Qf6) abandons the e5 center pawn and is refuted by fxe5/dxe5, losing material with tempo (plus a couple of fork/trap variants); medium keeps the same 'developing move punished by a pawn break' motif but broadens the break to c4/c5/dxe4 that traps a developed piece or wins a pawn, with some cases only costing tempo/space rather than clean material.

1688.label: Top: in an endgame the player declines an immediately capturable hanging enemy rook (occasionally a queen, board 3), usually by fleeing with the king instead of taking the free major piece—turning a draw/loss into forced mate; medium narrows to the rook case where the win is skipped by a piece retreat (Ra1 rather than Kxb5) rather than a king flight.

1687.label: Top boards are king-safety blunders—often a greedy material-grabbing capture—that walk the own king into an immediate forced mate-in-1; medium blurs to allowing mate-in-2/3 (and a couple of overlooked own mate-in-1s or a lured-piece loss), but the forced-checkmate theme stays constant.

1689.label: Top: with central tension unresolved, a passive developing/pawn move skips the forced capture (exd4/cxd5/exd5) and hangs a bishop (on c5/c4) — sometimes a dropped central pawn or a ...d4 fork of Nc3+Be3; medium: blurs to broader passive opening moves that drop a piece or the exchange to tactics (Bxf7+ then Nxe5+, Nb5–Nc7+, the e5 fork), with a couple of cases being just a bad positional trade.
