1690.label: Top: in clearly winning middlegames, plays a quiet/passive or developing move (slow pawn push, premature trade, retreat) instead of the decisive forcing tactic — a fork, check, or 7th-rank/file infiltration — leaving material safe but squandering the win; Medium blurs the same quiet-in-a-sharp-position habit into less-than-winning spots and into cases where the lazy move actively hangs material or allows the opponent's fork/check, so the direction drifts from pure 'missed win' toward 'hangs'.

1684.chip: Hangs minor piece in opening (often bishop)
1684.label: At the peak the feature fires on hanging a minor piece in the opening either way—premature bishop sacs/misplacements (Bxf7+, Ba6) and knights grabbing a defended pawn (Nxd5/Nxe5/Nxe4), plus one early-queen blunder (Qg5); at medium it narrows almost entirely to unsound bishop play, mainly the toothless Bxf7+ sacrifice and Bc4 walking into ...dxc4.

1691.label: Top: a quiet/developing/retreating move skips the one forcing capture or defense (often Nxe5/Nxd5/Bxe6) and loses cleanly to a sharp tactic — discovered check, knight fork, double attack, or mate; medium: the same neglect of the needed capture/defense persists but blurs into slower pawn losses and positional retreats (e.g. Nh2, Ba7, Nxc3) that drop material over a move or two.

1692.label: Top boards play a move (usually a rook) that walks into a check-driven refutation (Qd8+/Rd1#/Qxb7#/h1=Q+) winning material or mating; medium broadens to non-check tactical refutations (queen forks, infiltrations, back-rank checks, tempo losses), and several boards squander/miss a win rather than strictly hang material.

1680.chip: Passive K/Q move skips rook capture
1680.label: Top: in a level/drawn position the player makes a passive king or queen move instead of the single critical capture of a hanging enemy rook (or the rook-mate-stopping defensive capture), hanging the equalizer or walking into rook mate; medium blurs to any passive K/Q move that declines the sole saving capture/defense and drops material or allows mate — the rook specificity loosens (king-walks, queen-mates, move-order misses).

1693.label: At the peak, the move hangs material—most often the queen—by walking into an opponent's decisive forcing check on an open file/diagonal; at medium activation the lost piece blurs (rook/knight/bishop) and the direction flips toward materially-safe moves that miss a winning forcing check or mate-in-one.

1698.label: Top boards uniformly drop the queen onto a square covered by an enemy bishop on a long diagonal (Bxg2/Bxd7/Bxc6 etc.), winning queen-for-bishop from a winning position; medium boards keep the queen-hang core but broaden the capturer to rooks (Rxf3+, Rxa2-type) and to pawn/line-opening moves that expose the queen, while diluting with a few tempo-loss/missed-conversion cases.

1696.label: Top: consistently leaves a full minor piece (usually a knight) en prise via an intermediate capture or removed-defender tactic; medium keeps the self-inflicted material loss but broadens the hung unit to bishops, the exchange, or even allowing back-rank mate.

1697.label: At the top the player hangs the rook—almost always via a meaningless spite check—in an already-lost middlegame; at medium it broadens to hanging the queen (and occasionally a bishop), often through greedy or miscalculated captures rather than pure checks.

1694.chip: Squandered win via bad capture (any piece)
1694.label: Top boards are forcing captures/checks (bishop, queen, or knight) from a winning position that hang the piece or liquidate into equality; medium broadens to quieter trades/captures that hand back the advantage, including a rook-for-knight grab that loses a pawn endgame.

1686.label: Top: in winning positions the player picks a premature check or wrong capture/move-order, missing the cleaner forced win and often hanging material (Nxd5+ vs Nxe4+, Qxd6+, exd6, Re6 over Nxe7+); medium broadens to aggressive queen/rook sorties seeking attack/counterplay (Qg4, Qg3, Rc3, Nc2) that overlook the stronger move and frequently drop material — direction is genuinely mixed between hung-own and missed-win.

1699.label: Top: in pure K+P endgames a king move (or wrong-order pawn trade) abandons or ignores the decisive passed pawn, letting it be captured and turning a clear win into a draw; medium broadens to positions with pieces on board and to pawn pushes that shove the passer onto a hanging square — same theme of squandering the winning passer, though one medium case is a near-zero inaccuracy and another a king walking into mate.

1695.label: Top boards: in a lost/critical endgame the player makes a passive or irrelevant piece move (often a knight, e.g. Ng3/Nxa3, also a passive rook or premature pawn push) that ignores the opponent's promoting passed pawn (occasionally a forced mate), losing material or squandering the only saving/winning path; medium narrows to a bishop stepping straight into the king's capture while the passer queens.

1705.label: Top positions consistently miss a trivial free capture of the opponent's hanging bishop (dxc5/Bxc4/Nxf1/Kxe4) in a winning position; medium broadens to the opposite direction — losing one's own bishop via an unsound sac (Bxf2+) or a greedy capture (Qxf5) — so the bishop is the constant invariant while the missed-win vs. hangs-own direction is inconsistent.

1704.label: Top: a premature central pawn break (e4/e5/d5) opens the center with the king uncastled/pieces undeveloped and drops a clean pawn to a simple tactic; medium broadens to flank and endgame pawn pushes (h5, c5, f6, d6) that likewise hang a pawn or, in ~30%, collapse the structure/king safety rather than lose material outright.

1700.chip: Blows winning edge surrendering bishop (any piece)
1700.label: Top boards are remarkably constant—in a winning/better position Black or White parts with a bishop too cheaply (premature capture/trade, outright sac, or release of a pin/tension) and collapses the eval toward equality or worse; at medium the 'bishop' specificity blurs into squandering the advantage with any piece or pawn—a wasted bishop pin, a queen retreat that gets trapped, a tempo-losing pawn push, or a hung minor—so the unifying thread is 'gives material/tension back and blows the edge,' less reliably via the bishop.

1703.label: Top: a self-inflicted move (removing a key defender or ignoring an attack) drops own material and is refuted by a knight tactic — a fork, an Nf3+ sacrifice, or a knight capture of the queen; Medium: the same 'drops own material by undefending' theme but the refutation broadens beyond knights to bishop captures, pins, and even a missed-win case (Ra1).

1702.chip: Traded major piece into lost endgame (often K+P)
1702.label: Top boards voluntarily swap the last queen or rook into a clearly lost king-and-pawn endgame where White/Black's passed pawn or pawn majority decides; medium keeps the same last-major-piece trade but blurs the target ending (sometimes a lost piece endgame rather than pure K+P, or merely throwing away a win into a draw).

1706.chip: Hangs pawn via pawn move (often piece)
1706.label: Top: a pawn push or recapture (often vacating a central defender like c3→d4) drops a clean pawn to the opponent's tempo-gaining capture; medium keeps the careless pawn move but the loss broadens to a full piece, the exchange, or positional/king-safety collapse (plus an occasional non-pawn capture).

1701.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a careless king move (occasionally a pawn push) abandons a pawn or the critical tempo, letting the enemy king grab the pawn and create a decisive passer; medium keeps the slow-move-drops-a-pawn theme but broadens to rook and other endgames (and other move types), with a few outliers being tactical/mating conversions rather than pure pawn losses.

1711.label: Top: a one-move blunder drops a specific piece for nothing (rook/bishop, but also queen/knight) by grabbing material or retreating/advancing onto an undefended square; medium keeps the same hang-a-piece pattern across queen/rook/knight while blurring to also include a few boards that miss a forced mate or walk into one.

1709.label: Top boards consistently skip a forced mate / decisive kingside sacrifice (Bxh7+, Rxh7, Qf6→Qg7#) in favor of a quiet, materialistic, or trading move; medium broadens to any missed winning attack — purposeless checks (Re1+, Rb8+), wrong recaptures, or slower-mate/defensive lapses — where the chosen move is sometimes still materially safe but occasionally hangs own material into the refutation.

1670.label: Top boards are uniformly king-exposing g-pawn pushes (...g6/g3) punished by dark-square mating attacks (Bh6+Qg3→Qxg6+/Qg7#) or an exchange loss (...Bxf1); medium broadens to other weakening kingside pawn advances (f5/h5/g5) plus a tail of unrelated passive/tactical lapses.

1712.label: Top: player greedily grabs the QUEEN with a check (Rxe2+, Bxc3+, Qxe7+, etc.), settling for the recapture/trade and missing a forced mate or a winning intermezzo/move-order; medium: the same greedy check-capture pattern but the captured target blurs to rooks, knights, or even a pawn while still skipping the bigger material win or forced mate.

1713.label: Top boards overlook a single forcing blow — usually a queen mate-in-one or knight fork — with direction split between missing the player's own winning capture/mate (Qxf1#, Nxc2, Bxf3) and allowing the opponent's (Qxc2#, Nxg5+, Rxf2); medium keeps the same 'failed to calculate a decisive tactic' theme but blurs the tactic type to breakthroughs, king-walk mating nets, and losing trades.

1710.label: Top boards are consistently flank/wing-pawn pushes (b/c/g/h) thrown forward for counterplay that backfire into hung material, allowed mate, or a squandered won position; medium blurs the file constraint, adding premature central-pawn advances (d/e/f) and pure tempo-wasting pushes that likewise lose material or throw away the advantage instead of defending, developing, or cashing the win.

1716.label: Top boards are uniformly a knight grabbing a defended central pawn (Nxe5/Nxe4) or hitting a central outpost (Nfd4) and being instantly recaptured for a pawn; medium blurs to other minor pieces (Bxd4), undefended outpost jumps (Nd5), and even leaving an already-placed knight hanging via a developing move (Nbd2).

1722.label: Top: a safe/slow move misses a winning knight fork (almost always with check) that wins material outright; medium broadens to forcing knight checks/sacrifices that deliver forced mate or win material via a combination rather than a pure single-move fork.

1720.label: Top: in a losing K+P endgame the king marches the wrong direction—usually to grab a pawn (Kxa2/Kxd3/Kxh5)—abandoning the blockade or critical square and losing the pawn race; medium broadens to any tempo-wasting wrong-direction move, including non-grabbing king detours and slow pawn pushes (h5, a3) that lose the promotion race.

1715.label: Top boards are uniformly a passive king/pawn (or aimless knight) move that skips the active, tempo-gaining knight check (Nd5+/Nc6+/Ne4+/Nf4+) saving the draw or winning material; at medium the saving resource blurs to a rook check, a quiet king move, or simply rescuing a hanging knight, so the constant 'knight-check' peak loosens into 'any missed active tempo move.'

1724.label: Top boards are winning rook endgames where a tempo-wasting rook check drives the enemy king to a better square instead of the quiet improving move, bleeding mate/win margin; medium broadens to queen checks and wrong-piece/wrong-square checks that toss away a forced mate (and occasionally outright hang material).

1714.label: Top boards are uniformly forced back-rank mates after the player removes/neglects its sole back-rank defender (usually a greedy queen/rook capture); medium blurs to other king-safety collapses—f2-square mates and a discovered-check king walk—but still hands the opponent a forced mate.

1719.label: A slow or wrong-move-order move that abandons a defender or ignores a defensive necessity; at the top this hangs concrete material (often a pawn, sometimes a piece/queen) within 1-3 tempo-gaining moves, while medium boards broaden the same 'removed defender' idea to king-safety/pawn-shield collapses that allow decisive king attacks or back-rank mates.

1723.label: Top boards are knight sorties hung for free in the opening—overwhelmingly Ng5 grabbed by ...Qxg5 (also Nh4/Nh5/Nxe5)—while medium keeps the premature-sortie theme but broadens beyond the knight, adding a bishop jump (Bb2 dropped to Qxb2) and a rook lunge (Ra6 taken by Bxa6), plus Ng4/Nh4 leaps that lose material the same way.

1721.label: Top boards are constant: a greedy capture—almost always grabbing the queen—walks straight into a forced back-rank/king-safety mate; at medium the grab broadens to lesser pieces (knight/bishop/rook) and the punishment blurs from forced mate to simply hanging the player's own material or collapsing into a lost/drawn position.

1707.label: Top: in a lost endgame the player makes a quiet king move that ignores an adjacent saving rook/queen/bishop capture and walks straight into forced mate; medium broadens to missing or mis-choosing the strongest capture (greedy or wrong recapture), losing an exchange or piece rather than getting mated.

1718.label: Top boards are uniformly a rook (occasionally king) shoved to an exposed/passive square that self-destructs material within 1-3 moves (direct capture, deflection, back-rank mate); medium broadens the relocated piece to knights, bishops and kings and the punishment from an outright hang to forks, traps, mating nets, or surrendered advantage.

1708.label: Top boards are sharp blunders where a natural king/piece move (knight, queen or rook; several king-safety mating nets) hangs material or walks into a forced mate via the opponent's single decisive forcing reply; medium broadens to quieter tempo-losing or repositioning moves and missed winning/drawing resources, where the refutation is slower or positional rather than a clean one-move tactic — so direction is genuinely split between hanging own material and missing a win/defense.

1729.chip: Allowed losing trade into endgame (often queen)
1729.label: Top boards are queen moves that permit a forced queen exchange liquidating into a lost king-and-pawn endgame (peak constant); medium blurs to rook/bishop trades into lost endgames, plus a few that instead hang the queen to a deflection or walk into mate.

1726.chip: Hangs piece on open e-file (file/tactic blurs)
1726.label: Top boards uniformly develop/centralize a piece (mostly knights, also bishops) while the king sits on the open e-file, losing it to a recapture-with-check (Rxe3+/Qxe4+/Rxe5+); medium boards keep the 'hangs a piece by neglecting king/defender' core but blur to other files and tactics — direct captures (Qxd6), pins (Qxe5), discovered checks (exd5+), removed defenders, and king-walks in endgames.

1717.label: Top: from winning/tense positions a passive piece move—often the queen retreating or repositioning off a key coordinating square—skips a decisive forcing tactic, sometimes even hanging material to a multi-move refutation; medium blurs to equal-or-already-losing positions where natural king/pawn/rook moves mostly lose tempo or walk into shorter tactics rather than missing a clean forced win.

1728.label: Top boards constantly overlook an immediate forced checkmate (Qf8#, Qxb7#) in a won position; medium boards keep the 'winning position, played inferior squandering move' core but blur the win from mate-in-1 to any forcing material-winning continuation (Qxg6/Qxe6+/Qb7+) or a tactic the chosen move walks into.

1734.label: Top: ignores an already-present attack/fork and plays an unrelated developing or repositioning move that hangs the queen, almost always to a knight; medium keeps the 'ignore existing threat → hang material' core but broadens the lost piece to rooks/the exchange (and the attacker to bishops).

1725.label: Top boards are king-and-pawn promotion errors where the king sits wrong relative to the passer—queening prematurely so the fresh queen is captured (king too far) or stepping the king the wrong way and abandoning the pawn it should escort; medium blurs this into rook endgames and tempo/move-order slips where the king (or rook) drifts off the passed pawn it was supposed to support, sometimes turning a win into a draw rather than literally hanging the queen.

1727.label: Top boards leave a knight en prise in the opening for an immediate one-move free capture (typically Nxd4 met by ...Qxd4, or a c3-knight abandoned to dxc3); medium broadens to minor pieces lost over 2-3 moves via trapping sorties (Na4, Nb4) and tempo-losing developing checks, plus a stray endgame slip.

1730.label: Top boards are routine queen recaptures that skip a winning intermediate move (zwischenzug) and leave a minor piece (knight or bishop) hanging; medium broadens the hung material to the queen itself (or a tempo-loss missing the saving trade).

1732.chip: Missed pawn break vs centralized knight
1732.label: Top: in a winning position the player skips the decisive central pawn break (c4/f4/d6/g5) that dislodges an enemy knight entrenched on e5/d5, a materially-safe omission squandering the edge; medium keeps the centralized-knight theme but blurs to flank pawn breaks (g4/f5), picking the right capture/which knight to take, or general mishandling of the knight tension, occasionally even allowing the knight's own tactic.

1738.label: Top boards: in a won endgame the player advances a pawn or steps the king instead of grabbing the undefended piece blockading their passed pawn — constant motif but the capture target varies (rook, bishop, or knight, usually a king-capture); medium narrows to the knight blockader specifically (Kxa2, Kxf6).

1733.label: Top boards consistently hang a freshly-promoted queen by promoting a pawn (almost always to Q) onto a square the opponent already defends, instantly losing the new queen and squandering the passed pawn; medium boards blur this into broader passed-pawn mismanagement — premature/mistimed pushes, wrong move-order in pawn races, and greedy advances that cost the passer's value (and sometimes hang material like a rook) rather than literally hanging a queen on the promotion square.

1740.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed winning queen check (Qa4+/Qh5+/Qa5+) that exploits an uncastled king on an open diagonal to win material after a routine pawn/developing move; medium keeps the exposed-king-exploiting theme but blurs to other missed forcing shots (queen forks like Qe4+, bishop sacrifices like Bxf7+, knight forks, pawn-break tactics, or picking the inferior check) and occasionally edges into actually hanging a piece.

1741.label: Top boards uniformly miss the crushing Qh4+/Qh5+ queen check exploiting the open e1-h4/e8-h5 diagonal left by the absent f-pawn (a materially-safe move squandering a winning position); medium broadens to other missed wins in winning positions — non-check queen shots (Qd4, Qxd4) and even a back-rank mate (Re1#).

1737.label: Top: opening tactical blunders where a knight is the central refuting/hung/moving piece, mostly hanging material or walking into mate (with a few missed-win/tempo omissions); medium blurs to other tactical motifs (forks, Greek gift, discovered checks) and even endgame positions where the knight's role weakens or vanishes.

1731.label: Top boards uniformly decline the winning central pawn capture (dxe5/dxc6) while d-pawn tension is live — either passing up free material or, in ~half, leaving their own piece to fall after the refutation; medium blurs to broader mishandling of the central tension: recapturing the key square with the wrong piece (Bxe5/Nxe4 instead of fxe5/dxe4) or pushing past it (e5), plus a few looser missed-tactic/trapped-piece cases that drift off the pure pawn-capture theme.

1735.label: Top boards uniformly squander a winning/edge position by playing a passive, tempo-losing move instead of the dominant central knight outpost jump Nd5/Ne5; medium broadens to other strong knight moves—Nd4, Ng4, Ne6/Nxe6 and Nxg4 forks/captures—still passing up a forcing knight resource (with occasional non-knight winning shots).

1745.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed g-pawn capture of an enemy bishop parked on h6 (the available gxh6 that wins or equalizes is skipped for a quiet developing move); medium blurs the capture square and piece — gxh5/gxh3/gxh4, Bxe6/fxe6, even grabbing a knight (Nxa2, Bxh4) — and adds a couple of 'hung-own' outliers where the player's own piece instead falls to a kingside h-file bishop tactic.

1743.label: Top: a quiet developing bishop (Bd6/Be7/Bc5/Bd3) abandons the g7/g2 pawn on the open long diagonal, so the enemy fianchettoed bishop grabs the pawn and then the trapped corner h8/h1 rook for the exchange-plus-pawn; medium broadens to pawn, queen, and knight moves that open or vacate the long diagonal, where a bishop OR queen captures the corner rook, snaps off undefended diagonal pawns (b7/c7), or forks two minors.

1736.chip: Hangs major piece into pawn endgame
1736.label: Top boards: a queen (or rook) captures the opponent's dangerous passed pawn with check and is recaptured into a still-won king-and-pawn endgame, only squandering a faster win/mate; medium broadens to rook or queen trades that also grab pieces (not just passed pawns) and dump an actually winning or drawn position into a drawn or lost pawn endgame.

1744.label: Top boards constantly capture/trade off the player's own rook—its sole counterplay/back-rank defender—converting a tenable position into a lost endgame (or, in the back-rank/promotion cases, walking into mate); medium keeps the 'voluntary losing capture' core but blurs the piece, adding queen-for-rook trades, hanging-piece grabs, king captures, and promotion self-mates.

1751.label: Top: in clearly winning pawn endgames the player plays a slow centralizing king move instead of advancing the decisive passed pawn, losing the single tempo that turns the win into a draw; Medium: the same king-move-not-pawn-push theme persists but blurs in severity (often only delaying a forced mate rather than losing the win), with several flagged king moves actually being optimal/0cp false positives and one case that hangs material outright.

1739.label: Top: a queen move—frequently an aimless check—vacates its critical defensive/tactical square and throws away a winning position; medium: any piece (king, rook, bishop, pawn) similarly neglects a key square or duty, squandering the advantage with inconsistent punishment (hangs material, forced losing trade, walks into a fork, or even mate).

1746.chip: Flashy check over winning move (often knight)
1746.label: Top boards are showy knight checks (often double-check) played instead of the winning discovered check, so the king just sidesteps with no follow-up; medium broadens to queen/rook (and bishop) checks chosen over the correct quiet capture, mate, or only saving move—sometimes squandering a win, sometimes hanging material in a drawn position.

1742.label: Top boards squander a won endgame by a premature pawn push (or piece relocation) that ignores a winning capture/check and hangs own material within 1–3 moves; medium boards blur to pure pawn/king-endgame timing moves that merely lose tempo or allow mate, and sometimes aren't even blunders.

1754.label: Top: king moves stepping directly into a forced mating net (one-to-three-move checkmate, king's own pawns sealing escape squares); medium blurs to broader king-safety lapses — exposing or self-trapping the king, sometimes only losing material or enabling mate via self-block — mixed with several off-theme material/tempo blunders and one non-blunder.

1747.label: Top: a clearly winning endgame thrown away by a premature/wrong pawn push that skips the single precise winning continuation; medium broadens to other inferior endgame conversions (rook misplacement, wrong recapture, hanging tactics) and even merely-drawn/equal positions blown by hasty advances.

1749.label: Top boards constantly mishandle a forced rook exchange on a contested open file (c/d/e) — declining the trade or allowing it on the opponent's terms — liquidating into a lost pawn/rook endgame or dropping material; medium blurs the same file-exchange into a back-rank mate, with a few missed winning rook captures.

1752.label: Top boards throw away a winning/won position by skipping the decisive move—usually the winning queen trade (Qxe3) or capturing a hanging rook/queen—often instead exposing/advancing the king or hanging their own piece; at medium activation the pattern blurs to pure king-safety collapses where the king walks into a forced mate (Rf2#/Rg3#).

1753.label: Top boards vacate a key square (e3/f7) or pull a defender so the opponent lands a winning check/fork that usually nets the queen or a major piece; medium broadens to any overlooked forcing tactic — queen tempo-hits, exchange sacs, back-rank mate — so the feature splits between hanging material and missing the precise winning blow.

1756.chip: Greedy capture trades key defender (any piece)
1756.label: Top boards are rook/bishop captures that trade off the player's sole back-rank/king defender (or key attacker), squandering a won position; medium broadens to knights and even non-capture misplacements that still surrender a critical piece for material or tempo.

1762.label: Top boards consistently hang one of Black/White's own pieces (bishop, queen, or rook) for free—typically by moving the piece's sole defender or ignoring a mutual queen attack instead of capturing first; medium boards blur the pattern away from outright material loss toward broadly squandering a winning position (missed forcing wins, aimless tempo-loss moves, positional/king-safety errors).

1750.chip: Hangs piece to forcing tactic (often check)
1750.label: Top: a move ignoring a forcing diagonal check (Qa4+/Qa5+ or Bb5 pin) that exploits an uncastled king and a loose bishop to win material over 1–3 moves; medium: broadens to other forcing refutations—forks, back-rank mate, discovered check, and greedy/trapped pieces of any type—still losing own material.

1761.label: Top: a pawn push meant to chase/attack an enemy rook that backfires—mostly hanging own material (or allowing mate/perpetual, sometimes missing a stronger forcing win); medium keeps the failed rook-chasing tempo idea but broadens the move type to any tempo move (king/bishop/rook retreat or push, occasionally chasing a queen) and mixes hangs with positional/tempo loss.

1763.label: Top: a slow/passive move ignores the central pawn tension, letting the enemy break (almost always ...f4, also c5/d4/c4) crash through where the engine wanted a central capture (exf5/exf4/cxd5/dxc5) for a decisive positional edge; medium keeps the 'skipped the critical tension-resolving capture' core but blurs to kingside/flank tension (hxg3, hxg5), non-pawn captures (Nxh4, Nxe5, Nxe4), and occasionally a direct king-safety collapse rather than a pure central break.

1759.label: Top boards consistently push a pawn or king instead of the one critical rook capture/sacrifice that neutralizes an enemy passed pawn a step from queening, letting it promote; medium boards broaden to any decisive endgame move missed—winning skewers, free captures, mate-in-one, or a king move that hangs the rook—not strictly passed-pawn races.

1760.label: Top: in zero-margin endgames the single saving move is skipped — frequently a free enemy-queen capture, though several peak boards instead drift the king/knight and hang own queen/knight or allow a decisive promotion (mixed missed-save vs hung-own); medium narrows to the clean case of a missed free enemy-queen capture (Nxb6).

1757.label: TOP: a greedy pawn capture—usually a move-order error—hangs the player's own piece/queen or tears open their king in a winning position, with the refutation winning more material; MEDIUM broadens to a greedy king recapture that leaves the king exposed and skips the one balancing move (e.g., a fork).

1764.label: Top boards consistently pull a key defender off the player's own king (knight from f6, bishop from e4, queen from e2/e3, the lone defensive rook), triggering a forced mate or decisive attack; medium boards blur to misplacing a well-placed piece or burning a critical tempo (move-order errors, slow advances) that merely squanders the advantage or hangs material rather than directly exposing the king.

1769.label: Top boards are constant: a bishop (occasionally queen) walks onto an undefended deep square—almost always Bxc7 or ...Bc2—where the enemy queen grabs it free in one move; medium blurs to other hanging modes (greedy ...Bxg7/Bg4 minors recaptured, leaving an already-attacked bishop en prise, queen/pawn hangs), still self-inflicting opening material loss.

1766.label: Top: from a clearly winning endgame, the player throws it away—usually grabbing a tempting capture/check/promotion in the wrong move-order (or simply hanging a piece), dropping a rook or queen; medium blurs to less-winning, non-endgame positions where the edge is squandered via a losing queen trade, a wrong-way king march, or allowing a fork.

1771.label: Top boards are uniformly missed forced checkmates (frequently mate-in-1/2, typically by reflexively grabbing material instead of delivering mate); medium blurs to any missed decisive win—winning tactics, promotions, or merely faster mates—reached not just via greedy captures but also pawn pushes, retreats, and move-order slips.

1768.label: Top boards are uniformly the Bxf7+/Bxf2+ bishop sacrifice against an uncastled king (a quiet/developing move played instead throws away a winning advantage); medium broadens to other king-hunting bishop sacrifices—Greek Gift Bxh7+/Bxh2+ and Bxg7+ against castled kings—plus a few other missed forcing wins/mates.

1770.label: Top: a won endgame (often a forced mate) is thrown away by hanging one's own piece—usually a rook, sometimes the queen or a promoting pawn—frequently via a careless check or king step the opponent simply captures, collapsing the full point into a draw; medium keeps the winning-endgame check/king-move motif but blurs to technique/tempo slips (aimless checks, king runs that let the king escape) that fail to convert without actually hanging material, plus a couple of true queen hangs.

1774.label: At the peak it's a winning ROOK landing on the 8th/1st rank (Re8+/Rd8#/Rf1+/Rd1#) declined for a slow, materially-safe move; medium boards keep the missed back-rank blow but blur the piece to the QUEEN (Qc8#/Qd8+/Qe8+) and occasionally a rook infiltrating the 7th/6th rank (Rd7+/Rf6+).

1755.label: Top: declines the engine's best knight capture (typically Nxe5/Nxe4) in the opening for a quiet developing/retreating move, hanging a pawn/piece/exchange to a 2-3 move refutation; medium blurs to other captures (Bxb5, Rxc3) and a few pure missed wins.

1773.label: Top boards are tight: a specific piece (queen/rook/knight/king) vacates a critical guard square and is punished by a check/tactic that wins material or forces mate; medium blurs to any move that neglects a defensive duty (tempo loss, allowed fork/7th-rank invasion) and hangs material, with both piece and outcome (material vs. mate) varying.

1765.label: Top boards squander a won endgame via faulty simplification — typically trading/sacrificing a rook (recaptured by a pawn) or a losing king move that drops into a drawn/lost K+P ending; medium broadens beyond pure endgames to other pieces and middlegame king-safety/tactical/positional moves that throw away a winning (or holdable) position.

1775.label: Top boards are tight: a greedy capture (usually a rook grabbing a pawn/piece, sometimes a queen/bishop) vacates the back-rank defender and is refuted by a back-rank check then a pin that wins back the player's own piece; medium blurs to any defensive lapse (failing to castle, tempo-wasting, dropping a blockade) punished by checks/tactics, with outcomes sometimes being mate, promotion, or a fork rather than a clean piece-hang.

1777.label: Top boards consistently skip a clearly winning bishop capture — typically Bxh6 (a decisive sac/attack on a misplaced knight) or Bxa3/Bxa6/Bxh3 (free material) — in favor of a quiet developing or prophylactic move; medium blurs this to choosing the wrong bishop capture (Bxf5 over Bxh6) or missing the correct winning bishop move/placement (Bxf1, Be6).

1778.label: Top boards are uniformly a queen snapping an undefended enemy knight on h4/h5 (Qxh4/Qxh5) in the opening from a winning position; medium broadens to other capturing pieces (bishop) and target squares (g5, h7, d5, c4), occasionally an undefended bishop instead of a knight, and a couple require a short tactic rather than a one-move grab.

1772.label: Top boards are nearly all king moves (occasionally a rook stepping off a defensive post) that relocate the player's own king to a more exposed square, inviting a forced check/mate sequence; medium blurs the moving piece to anything (knight, bishop, queen, pawn push, rook) that ignores or enables the opponent's forcing attack on the king, shading into plain hung pieces and even missed-mate move-order errors.

1779.label: Top boards are opening moves (greedy pawn-grabs or careless developments) that hang a minor piece — bishop or knight — most often to an a-file queen check (Qa5+/Qa4+) forking king and loose piece; medium keeps the self-inflicted material loss but broadens beyond the opening into the middlegame and beyond the a-file to other diagonal checks (Qb6+, Qc5+) and follow-up knight-fork refutations (e.g. Bxf7+ then Ne5+).

1782.label: Top: queen left en prise to a directly-attacking bishop (ignoring it with a pawn/development move → Bxd8 wins queen for bishop); medium keeps this dominant bishop-attack pattern but also blurs to include moving the queen onto a defended square (e.g. Qxa5 → Rxa5).

1783.label: Top boards are uniformly a trivial one-move grab of the opponent's completely undefended queen (player instead makes a passive, materially-safe move from a winning position); medium blurs the capture into slightly less obvious forms — a queen win via recapture/fork or a forced trade, occasionally where the safe-looking move actively loses, with one outlier that's a fork-induced rook hang rather than a missed queen capture.

1748.label: Top boards are bishop retreats or wrong recaptures that waste a tempo and skip the active, usually material-winning continuation; medium broadens the piece to pawn pushes, knight relocations and queen sorties, with the consequence ranging from pure tempo/initiative loss to allowing a fork or outright hanging a rook.

1776.label: Top boards are tempting checks or forcing pawn pushes in the endgame (most often a knight check, hanging that very knight) that the opponent refutes with one simple capture, throwing away winning/equal positions; medium boards keep the forcing-move-punished core but blur into non-checking moves, missed defensive resources, and tempo-wasting checks where the refutation is sometimes positional or mating rather than a clean material grab.

1767.chip: Premature pawn capture activates enemy king (often check)
1767.label: Top: a pawn capture WITH CHECK in a won/equal endgame that the opponent simply recaptures with the king (Kx...), activating it and forfeiting the win, instead of the precise intermediate check, king centralization, or knight fork; medium keeps the 'activate-the-enemy-king' theme but blurs the trigger to non-checking captures, premature pawn pushes, and king retreats (recapture sometimes by pawn/queen, and a couple of near-equal non-blunders).

1785.label: Top: a passive king move ignores a free capture of an undefended enemy piece, nearly always a hanging rook (one queen, one own-bishop hang), in drawn/losing endgames; medium blurs the 'free capture' core into passive king/knight moves that simply miss the one saving/winning resource (king centralization, pawn break, or perpetual-check tempo) rather than a literal hanging piece.

1780.label: Top boards all play a quiet developing move that overlooks a pawn capture (usually ...dxc3, also exf3/dxc6) winning a hanging enemy knight in the opening, letting the opponent recapture and equalize; medium boards blur to general opening central-tension mishandling—missing material wins, releasing tension prematurely, or unsoundly pushing/hanging pawns.

1784.label: Top: in a won endgame an idle pawn push/check/king move skips a trivial capture of an undefended enemy piece (constant: free capture squandering a forced mate; the piece is most often a rook but also knight/bishop/queen), while medium blurs into squandering the cleanest decisive win generally (missed mate-in-1, missed fork, non-endgame, plus several minor inaccuracies or non-blunders).

1790.chip: Hangs piece to pawn thrust (mostly bishop)
1790.label: Top: opening moves that let a pawn advance (a5/b5/c4/c5/g5) trap or fatally attack the player's own bishop on b6/c4/b3/f4/h4, losing it over 2-3 moves; medium keeps the 'piece trapped by pawn thrust' motif but broadens the victim to other minors (knight on h5/d4 hit by g4/c3) with a few stray tempo/positional losses outside the bishop-trap pattern.

1787.label: Top: a queen move squanders a winning/safe position—hanging the queen, walking into mate, or skipping a crushing tactic with the queen central to the refutation; medium broadens to king/rook/pawn moves that throw away wins (or draws) via mixed failure modes (hung piece, allowed mate, missed win, positional collapse).

1797.chip: Hangs piece to enemy king (often rook)
1797.label: Top boards uniformly leave a rook en prise to the adjacent enemy king in a rook endgame (king grabs it for free); medium keeps the hang-to-king pattern but broadens the piece beyond rooks (queen, knight) and occasionally a recapture/losing trade rather than a clean king capture.

1793.label: Top boards all hinge on the queen: a greedy lesser capture either misses exf6 winning Black's en-prise queen or hangs the player's own queen/rook to a capture (often with check); medium blurs this into greedy captures that drop a rook, bishop, or knight (Qxb2, Rc8, Nxb7, Bxh2) to analogous tactics, with direction genuinely split between missed wins and self-hangs.

1786.label: Top boards consistently hang the player's own bishop after a greedy pawn capture that throws away a winning position; medium positions keep the same greedy pawn-grab trigger but broaden the cost to also hanging the queen or knight, or exposing the king to a decisive attack/mate.

1791.label: Top boards are clean king-safety blunders that open or ignore a forced mate against the player's own (often uncastled) king; medium positions broaden to king-hunts that merely win material—dropped queen/rook, knight forks, or pawn-grabs/passive moves that expose the king without immediate checkmate.

1796.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed ...b5/f5 (or b4) pawn-break fork striking the queen+bishop on the a4/c4 (or g4/e4) alignment after a quiet developing/grabbing move; medium blurs into other winning pawn-break double attacks (d5/e4/e5/g3 hitting queen+minor) plus a few off-theme king-safety lapses that actually hang the own king.

1789.label: At the peak the player hangs a developed bishop (typically on f4, e.g. to ...exf4) to a central pawn capture, the defining failure to resolve central pawn tension; medium boards keep the same tension-mishandling theme but broaden the cost—dropping a pawn or knight, missing a winning center capture (dxe5/Nxe5/Bxa6), or conceding pawn structure—so the unifying error is tension-handling, not one specific hung piece.

1794.label: At the peak a single decisive knight is mishandled—either hung (boards 3,5,6,7,8) or its winning fork/tactic skipped (1,2,4,9,10); at medium the 'missed-forcing-shot / dropped-piece' theme persists but the pivotal piece blurs from knight to bishop/rook (e.g. Bd3+, Rxd5+, Re2+), and direction stays genuinely split between hanging and missing.

1788.label: At the peak a single move collapses a winning/equal opening—roughly half greedy or wrong captures that drop material and half quiet developing/retreating moves that ignore a live tactic—and at medium activation it blurs further toward king-safety lapses (f2/f7 attacks) and skipped defensive resources, so it reads as a generic 'throws away the opening advantage' feature spanning hung material, missed wins, and tempo loss.

1798.label: Top boards uniformly miss a forcing queen check winning a hanging piece (Qxa6+/Qxc6+) after a slow safe move; medium keeps the winning-position-missed-forcing-blow theme but broadens to other forcing wins (Qxd8+, Nd6+, Qxg7, king-attack resources) and occasionally allowing the opponent's tactic (fork/free capture).

1800.label: TOP: in won king-and-pawn endgames the player plays a king move instead of pushing/escorting the passed pawn, occasionally throwing away a forced mate or the clean win (f7-vs-g7, Kf3-vs-Kxh4, Kb5-vs-g7); MEDIUM broadens to any slow supporting move (queen, knight, rook, and rook/back-rank endgames) chosen over the direct forcing win — but ~6/10 boards are 0–9cp non-blunders, so the underlying 'play the king, not the pawn' signal is real yet only sometimes an actual error.

1804.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgame misjudgments—trading/simplifying into a lost K+P ending or botching opposition/break timing (converting a win or draw); medium blurs to broader pawn-play timing errors (passed-pawn placement, premature pawn breaks) plus wrong-colored-bishop and already-lost cases.

1801.label: Top: a knight (or bishop) deserts a defensive duty—dropping its own major piece or stepping into a forced mate; medium keeps the self-inflicted material loss but broadens the moving piece to pawns/rooks and the punishment to forks and king-attacks rather than only direct hangs/mate.

1781.label: Top: a queen move abandons a key defensive duty (blockade, perpetual check, or its own/king safety) and is punished by a deflection or tactic that loses material—usually the queen itself; medium blurs in two ways—non-queen pieces (knight/rook/bishop/king) and a majority of materially-safe moves that instead MISS a winning queen check/capture (Qc4+, Qxg7+, Qxc6+, Qc8+, Re6+), with one noise board (forced-mate-anyway Qf1).

1806.label: Top: king moves in losing pawn endgames that walk into a tempo-gaining pawn check (g4+/h5+/e5+) driving the king back — mostly 0–2cp non-blunders; medium broadens to king/piece placements that allow a rook or queen check (Rd8+/Qd7+/Qc3+/Nf4+) winning material outright, plus one catastrophic outlier.

1795.label: In a winning opening the top boards squander the advantage with a natural, materially-safe knight capture/recapture (often Nxe4, sometimes a quiet Qe2/Nc3/O-O) that skips the lone forcing win (Bxf7+, Nf6#, d5+ or pawn-break); medium blurs to a quiet knight retreat (Nf3) missing the same decisive shot—though a couple of boards (Nxe4 refuted by ...d5, Ng5+) instead hang a piece outright.

1792.label: Top boards consistently decline an immediately available capture of a free, undefended MAJOR piece (queen or rook — frequently a mutual-hanging tempo race where declining also drops one's own queen); medium broadens to any undefended piece (bishop/knight) and dilutes with a few borderline/non-capture cases (endgame and positional slips).

1809.label: Top boards are almost all queen moves that abandon a defender or step into a tactic, hanging the player's own material (knight, rook, or pawn in the refutation); medium boards broaden the moving piece to bishop/knight/king and the lost material varies, with a handful instead just degrading or squandering a winning position rather than dropping a clean piece.

1799.label: Top: a routine opening developing move overlooks a free FULL piece — frequently the queen (grabbing a hanging enemy queen via Bxd8/Nxd4, or saving one's own queen left en prise with Qxg4/Qxg5); medium blurs to lesser captures and merely winning the exchange (Bxe8/Bxa8), and to picking an active/tempo move instead of the clean capture.

1812.label: Top boards are a clean move-order error — grabbing a rook/minor/pawn instead of trading or capturing queens first, which hangs the player's own undefended queen along an open diagonal; medium boards keep the same 'capture before resolving the queen' fault but broaden the punishment to king-safety collapse, back-rank mate, or simply throwing away a winning eval rather than a literal queen loss.

1802.label: At the peak: in an already-losing middlegame the player declines the only saving move (capturing White's hanging queen) and instead marches the king—or pushes a weakening pawn—straight into a forced mate; the medium board is the same king move into a short forced mate after skipping a queen-capture, while a few peak boards blur into simply losing material/a knight or passed-pawn into a lost endgame rather than mate.

1807.label: Top boards squander a clearly winning/better position via an unfavorable trade or greedy capture (queen/rook/bishop—often a 'spite' capture or simplification that revives the opponent); medium blurs into outright hanging a piece on an undefended square and positional/king-safety concessions that throw away the same advantage.

1815.label: Top: in a winning position the player chose a quiet/safe move and missed a forcing knight check that forks the king and rook to win the exchange (Ne2+, Nf3+, Ne7+, Nc6+); medium keeps the same missed knight fork/check motif but broadens the booty — sometimes winning a bishop/minor piece (Nc7+) or rook plus pawns rather than strictly the king+rook exchange.

1814.label: Top: in a won endgame the player makes a non-decisive move (lesser capture or premature pawn push) that skips the decisive win of an enemy ROOK by capture or skewer; medium keeps the 'winning position, skip-the-win' core but blurs both target (rook→queen/knight, even pin/fork lines) and direction, with some premature pushes/grabs instead hanging the player's own piece (knight, bishop, or trapped queen).

1810.label: Top boards lose the queen via a direct queen move that hangs it outright or trades it for less/into a lost endgame; medium broadens to non-queen moves (castling, king/pawn/bishop moves) that leave the queen en prise or strip its defensive duty, plus more even-material trades into lost positions.

1813.label: At the peak, nearly every board hangs the QUEEN to a knight-fork CHECK (Nf5+/Nxe3+/Nf6+), squandering a winning/mating position to a single forcing reply; at medium the constant is still 'won/drawn position thrown away by an overlooked forcing check,' but it blurs to other forcing motifs — skewers winning a rook (Kxf3→Rf1+), promotion-checks, and king-into-mate walks (Kh2→Nf2#, Bg3→Qxg2#) — plus a few 'missed forced win/blockade' cases and one non-fit (board 8 is best).

1811.label: At the peak, a self-inflicted tempo-grab move (usually shoving a pawn/piece at the enemy queen) hangs material and is decisively answered by an intermediate enemy queen check or mate, dropping a knight/rook/queen or a winning edge; at medium the 'tempo-grab that backfires' theme holds but the punisher blurs—rook checks (Rxe2+), bishop/knight blows (Bf4, Nf3), missed forks (Na4), and structural/mating refutations replace the pure queen check.

1808.label: At the peak the queen is the constant — nearly every board hinges on a queen decision, and ~6/10 skip a free winning queen capture/tactic (Qxg5, Qxd5, Bg5 queen-trap, Qh4+, Qxd6, Rxf1) while ~4/10 push the queen into losing/trapping own material; at medium the queen anchor blurs to any piece (bishop/knight/pawn moves) and the direction shifts almost entirely to hanging or trapping one's own material via short refutations.

1817.label: Top boards consistently ignore a Bg4 pinning/pressuring the f3-knight (no h3), letting ...Bxf3 or ...Bxh2+ remove the kingside defender and hang a minor piece a few moves later; medium broadens to other defensive lapses—moving the f3-knight itself or a weakening pawn push that abandons a key guarded square and drops material (plus a couple stray grabs).

1818.label: Top: a passive/retreating queen move abandons a critical defensive duty (back-rank guard, key diagonal, perpetual) and immediately hangs material or allows forced mate; medium broadens the piece to any (pawn, king, rook, knight) and blurs the direction toward ignored threats and positional tempo-losing moves that surrender a key resource without always losing material outright.

1820.label: Top boards are uniformly a rook check (Rh8+/Rxh7+/Ra8+) left undefended and grabbed by the king, squandering a won position—occasionally an unfavorable queen-trade check; medium blurs toward queen checks and forcing moves that lose material more indirectly (interposable check missing mate, premature capture, or trade skipping a cleaner win).

1816.chip: Traded last piece into lost endgame (usually bishop)
1816.label: Top boards uniformly trade the last minor piece (a bishop) into a lost king-and-pawn endgame where the opponent's passed/majority pawns run unopposed; medium broadens to knight and rook-for-bishop trades into other lost simplified endgames, with some genuine noise (a correct trade, a greedy capture, and a pawn push that aren't lost-endgame trades).

1819.label: Top boards are tightly king-exposure blunders—removing the queen/pawn/knight that shields the king (or moving the king itself) to allow a forced mate or immediate queen loss; medium blurs into plainer self-inflicted hangs of any piece (queen, knight, bishop, pawn-grab) plus a few slow/tempo-losing moves that still drop material or hasten the player's own mate.

1826.label: Top boards play a quiet/natural developing move (usually castling) and miss a materially-safe winning central pawn break (d4/d5/e5) or the Ne4 trap of the f6-queen; medium keeps the 'quiet move skips a winning tactic' core but blurs the winning blow to other shots — capturing a pinned piece, a knight outpost (Ne5), a flank break (b5), or a mating attack.

1805.label: Top boards are winning rook endgames where the player flees/retreats the king from a check instead of capturing the free (often checking) rook and hangs it; medium broadens to other passive or greedy non-rook moves—pawn-grab move-orders, king-exposing pawn captures, idle queen checks—that either drop material more slowly or simply skip the winning capture, so direction is mixed.

1822.label: Top boards are clean knight hangs in a winning middlegame—the knight is moved to or left en prise (or its defender abandoned) and dropped to a simple capture; medium broadens to also hang bishops/rooks, trade a minor piece for a pawn via greedy grabs, and even (rarely) skip a forced mate.

1821.label: Top: in endgame promotion races the player burns the one critical tempo—usually grabbing an irrelevant pawn with the rook/king or making a passive/distant move instead of checking, pushing, or blockading—and lets the opponent's passed pawn queen; medium blurs the consequence and phase, where the same irrelevant tempo-wasting move instead allows a decisive threat broadly (mate, skewer, advancing passer, or a squandered/ missed win), including middlegame positions.

1803.label: Top boards are uniformly passive king/quiet moves that ignore a forced queen capture-or-trade and so hang the queen (or walk into mate); medium keeps the same 'ignore the queen tactic and drop material' core but blurs the piece — still mostly queens, yet now also losing a rook (bad rook-trade into lost endgame), a bishop, or the exchange to a fork.

1827.chip: Hangs material, missing winning capture (often queen)
1827.label: Top: from a winning position the player ignores a free enemy queen (or other decisive capture) and instead plays a move that hangs their own queen/material; medium blurs to generic material-losing or positional blunders in non-winning positions with no free-queen theme.

1832.label: Top: a king or pawn move in a king-and-pawn endgame that releases central tension or breaks a blockade, letting the enemy king infiltrate into a winning square (no material hung, purely positional collapse); medium broadens to any piece (rook, bishop, knight) abandoning the key guarding square, still allowing enemy king infiltration or an unstoppable passed pawn.

1825.label: Top boards are sharp line-opening pawn pushes or defender removals/pulls (f6, f5, g4, c4, Bg5, Qxb4, Nb7, Nbc6) that hand White a decisive king-side sacrifice or attack (Greek Gift Bxh7/Bxh2, Bxg6, Qh5+) winning material; medium blurs into slower tempo-wasting or positional moves that merely neglect king safety while the attack builds (b6, Bd7, Qg5, Nh6, hxg4), plus a few that simply hang a piece or walk into a fork.

1833.label: Top: in lost passed-pawn endgames the king is shuffled to a passive edge/corner instead of centralizing, capturing the key supporting piece, or blockading — though several top boards are 0cp 'lost anyway' non-blunders; medium narrows to the decisive cases (king_safety/positional) where the edge-bound king accelerates promotion or forced mate.

1824.label: At the peak the player almost always passes up a clean FORCED MATE or decisive king-side/back-rank/discovered-check attack, instead grabbing a pawn, playing a quiet positional move, or executing the right idea in the wrong order; at medium the constant 'skipped the strongest forcing line in a winning/drawing position' holds but blurs from pure mate into non-mating decisive tactics (winning material, only-saving moves, endgame king marches) and a few cases that simply hang material.

1828.label: Top: in a winning/sharp position the player botches the decisive combination centered on the enemy queen—either a quiet/wrong move that skips the winning queen capture or a wrong-order capture that leaves a piece (queen included) hanging; medium blurs the pivotal piece to rooks/exchange and minor-piece tactics, and the direction is split between missed queen-wins and self-inflicted hangs.

1831.label: Top: a greedy queen capture (almost always ...Qxe4 grabbing a pawn) gets pinned or skewered on the open e-file against the uncastled king; medium blurs this into queens—and occasionally other pieces (pawn/knight captures, king moves)—overextending into forks, harassment, or newly opened files/diagonals that drop material.

1834.label: Top: a natural developer or castling move leaves a piece cleanly en prise with an enemy knight central to nearly every refutation (Bc4 dropped to Ne5, Bxc6+ on c6, or the recurring Nxc3/bxc3/Bxc3+ fork) — piece type varies but the en-prise-in-the-opening + knight motif is rock-solid; medium keeps the opening material-loss theme on some boards (Nf3 allows d4 winning the a1-rook, Bg5 drops the c3-knight, Nd7 hangs d5) but blurs into slower multi-move losses, trapped pieces (Bxa7), one missed win (skips Bxf7+), and several middlegame king-safety collapses (b3 Ba3#, g6, Kg7, g5) where the clean single-knight refutation fades.

1838.label: At the top it's almost uniformly ...Nxf2, an unsound knight-for-one-pawn sacrifice on an illusory queen+rook fork refuted by the calm Kxf2; at medium it blurs to Fried-Liver-style Nxf7 sacrifices refuted by Kxf7 — same error of giving up a full knight for a pawn that the king simply recaptures.

1830.label: Top boards are uniformly king moves that walk an already-exposed king into a forced mate in lost positions (Kb3/Kc4/Ka3 etc. shortening mate); medium blurs the edges—still king-exposure themed but broadening to passive moves hanging a piece, allowing a back-rank mate, and even squandering won positions, so direction mixes hung-own with the occasional missed-win.

1835.chip: Skips central capture, hangs piece (often knight)
1835.label: Top: player declines the natural central pawn capture/tension and hangs a knight to an advanced enemy pawn (Nc3/Nf6 into a pawn, exf3, dxc6); medium keeps the 'neglected central capture' theme but blurs the consequence into merely dropping a pawn or positional/tempo loss (and one allowed knight fork).

1823.label: Top boards: squanders a winning/better middlegame by failing to find the single precise rook move (Rd7/Re1/Rc7/Rd1/Re8 to an open file, the 7th rank, or as a defensive resource), usually then hanging a rook or bishop to a tactic the rook move would have prevented; medium boards keep the 'one precise move was skipped' core but broaden the saving move to any piece (knight/bishop/pawn/queen), so the punishment splits ~6/10 clean material loss vs slow positional/tempo drift.

1842.chip: Losing blunder: mate or hung material (queen)
1842.label: Top boards are clean self-inflicted decisive losses—king walked into forced mate or queen hung outright—with the queen the decisive piece in nearly every refutation; at medium it blurs to include smaller material hangs, tempo/positional slips, and a missed winning tactic, so it reads as a broad 'decisive blunder' feature rather than one motif.

1829.label: Top: in clearly-winning endgames a capture, king-march, or wrong move-order fails to stop the opponent's passed pawn, letting it advance or promote and squandering the win; medium broadens to equal/drawn endgames where the same neglect of the passer flips the result to a loss.

1840.label: At the peak, boards are already-losing middlegames where a passive king/pawn move (Kh3, f3, g3, Nd7...) overlooks an elementary pawn capture that wins the opponent's hanging queen (dxc5, exf6, fxg4); at medium the pattern blurs to any passive king/pawn move in a lost position that squanders the best resource — sometimes a defensive king move or a tempo-wasting pawn push with no actual capture available — and occasionally even hangs Black's own piece, so it mixes pure missed-captures with general passivity.

1837.label: Top boards are uniformly a queen check that simply hangs the queen to a rook capture (or rook interpose-and-capture), throwing away a winning game; medium broadens the checking piece (rook hung to knight, wrong-piece check) and the direction (some are toothless checks that miss a forced win/mate rather than outright hangs).

1845.label: At the peak, in clearly winning middlegames the player overlooks a forcing queen check that delivers forced mate (Qd4+, Qa1+, Qh5+) and instead plays a slow pawn push or materialistic grab; at medium the constant is still a missed forcing winning move but it blurs to checks that win material rather than mate and to non-queen forcing shots (rook checks like Ra3+, knight checks like Nh6+, or quiet winning rook redeployments).

1847.label: Top boards are knight checks (Nf3+, Nxc2+, Nxd6+) that hang the piece outright or burn a key tempo/trade off the best piece for a pawn; medium blurs the checking piece to bishop and pawn (Be3+, Bd4+, exf7+, g5+) and broadens the cost to squandering a winning position via a strong-piece trade or even skipping a forced mate.

1839.label: Top boards are overwhelmingly a missed Bxf7+-style sacrifice/blow against the uncastled king's weak f7 square (played a quiet develop/castle instead); medium blurs to other winning opening tactics — an attack on f2, a knight fork (Nb4xc2), or a central capture (exd5) — sharing the 'safe quiet move skipping a forced win in the opening' core.

1836.label: Top: a bishop greedily captures a rook (Bxa8/Bxa1) to win the exchange but removes the long-diagonal king defender or walks into a forced tactic, exposing the king; medium broadens to other greedy material grabs (knight capture, premature b1=Q, snatching the bigger rook) that skip a needed intermezzo/move-order and hand back material.

1849.label: At the peak the player moves a piece (knight/bishop ~50/50) off a defensive duty and leaves its own minor piece or pawn hanging—frequently snapped off with tempo or check (Qxb7, Qxf4+, Rxa4, Qxc8+, Qxa2); at medium activation the constant 'undefended piece left by a piece move' blurs into pure tempo losses, king-safety/castling lapses, trapped pieces, and missed faster mates rather than clean material hangs.

1841.label: Top boards uniformly ignore a free, undefended enemy queen (occasionally a hanging bishop on f6) instead of capturing it; medium boards keep the hanging-queen miss but broaden to passive king-safety/defensive moves that skip the free capture and walk into forced mate.

1852.label: Top boards are king moves in passed-pawn endgames that step to the wrong square (often the back rank), failing to catch/blockade the passer so it advances or promotes with a tempo-gaining check and forces mate; medium blurs to smaller tempo-losing king moves and occasionally a different piece (rook/queen) misplaced relative to the passer.

1850.chip: Hangs rook in losing trade (sometimes queen)
1850.label: Top boards are remarkably uniform: an active rook trade or pseudo-sac (frequently a check like Rxf7+/Rd1+) that dissolves a dominant doubled-rook/two-rook setup and hands back a winning position; medium boards keep the self-inflicted rook exchange that squanders the win but blur the piece (occasional queen hang) and the mechanism (some trades walk into a knight fork rather than hanging the rook outright).

1843.label: Top: in 100%-winning openings the player declines the free central knight grab (constant best move Nxe5/Nxe4), throwing the win away either by hanging material in a flashy line (Bxf2+, Qd8) or by a quiet omission/allowed tactic (a6, a3, Bd3, Bd6→Nxf7, Nxc3→Bxf7+); medium blurs the winning shot to any material-winning capture (Rxb4, Nxd5, bxa5, Nxh5) and shades into positional dawdling, so direction is genuinely split between hangs and misses.

1844.label: Top boards are uniform: a greedy capture grabbing material while the player's OWN king is under a decisive attack, usually walking into immediate checkmate; medium blurs away from captures into broader king-safety blunders—king walks into mating nets and quiet/tempo-losing moves that ignore the refutation, plus a few off-theme hangs.

1857.label: Top boards are clearly winning endgames where the player plays a safe non-decisive move that skips a forced win — usually a free capture (gxh4, Rxd5, Rxd4) or the only winning king/pawn move — while medium positions blur the pattern into general tempo-losing quiet moves and a few cases that actually hang own material to a knight fork (Rf3→Nd4+), plus one non-blunder.

1853.label: Top boards hang a piece or exchange by capturing/recapturing in the wrong order or skipping a required intermezzo (zwischenzug/check); medium blurs into king-safety lapses and plain undefended-piece hangs, with one outlier being a missed free capture (reverse direction).

1848.chip: Hangs queen to king-capturing check (major piece)
1848.label: Top boards are laser-uniform: an (almost always queen) check the enemy king simply captures for free, hanging the piece outright — only an occasional rook-hang varies it; medium blurs the same theme to other major-piece losses and forcing-move errors (a rook walking into a skewer, an inferior check that misses mate, a king-weakening pawn push), still broadly punished by the opponent grabbing the dropped material.

1863.label: Top: trades a dominating rook for a knight, collapsing a won rook-vs-knight position into a theoretically drawn/lost pawn endgame; medium broadens to surrendering the more active piece (bishop) for a knight as a structural concession — but ~4/10 are noise (capture is best, or the real error is a missed mate / wrong capture order).

1846.label: At the peak it's a king-stripping pawn capture (esp. fxe5/cxd4) that lets a queen check on the opened diagonal (Qh5+/Qh4+) win a rook; at medium it blurs to other opening captures/developing moves that lose material via undefended pieces, opened diagonals (Bxb2), or knight forks (Nd5/Nd6+) — with one board a missed Qh5+ win rather than an actual hang.

1858.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where an inferior king route or skipped pawn break (e5/f5/h5/cxb5) flips a draw or win into a loss with no material hung; medium keeps the same losing positional king/pawn move but broadens to bishop, rook, and even queen endings (and occasionally lets material slip over 2-3 moves).

1861.label: Top: a quiet/misplaced move pulls a piece (knight, bishop, queen, pawn) off its critical defensive or restraining square (or skips the only resolving move), squandering a winning/better edge into equality; medium: the same desertion but punished concretely — the freed enemy delivers forks, sacrifices, or wins material (Nd5, Ng5, Nxh6+, hung bishop/queen).

1862.label: Top boards are bishop sorties to h3/h6 (plus some queen lunges) that abandon a defensive duty—an undefended pawn, a piece's defender, or back-rank safety—and hang material to a refutation exploiting that duty; medium blurs the attacker to queen, rook, and knight moves that likewise vacate a key defended square/piece and get punished.

1864.label: Top boards are tempo-losing king retreats (and a few pawn pushes) that squander a won or drawn king-and-pawn/rook ending without hanging material, the king-move + missed-conversion theme being constant; medium blurs this by adding bishop/queen tempo moves, other endgame types, and one knight-fork material loss, while several flagged positions (Rh1, Rf1, Qa1, Bc2, Qf8+) are actually engine-best non-blunders, diluting the signal.

1856.label: Top: in the opening the player hangs the queen to a knight fork or outright knight capture (esp. Qe3 allowing Nxc2+, or failing to recapture allowing Nxd1); medium broadens beyond the opening and beyond the queen to other knight forks (rook/exchange via Ne7+) and king-safety blunders that walk into mate.

1855.label: Top boards are passive king moves (64%) made in already-lost positions that walk straight into a forced mate or strip the king's last shelter; medium broadens to other misguided/passive moves (pawn pushes, knight/bishop/rook shuffles) in lost positions that instead hang material or squander the one critical defensive/counterplay tempo—mechanism (mate-walk vs. hang vs. tempo-loss) is genuinely mixed.

1860.label: Top boards are greedy opening pawn-grabs/captures (dxc3, exd6, Nxe5, d3) from a roughly equal position that leave the player's own knight en prise for a near-free win; medium keeps the same greedy capture (dxc3, dxc6) but the refutation is a king-safety/positional collapse rather than a clean knight hang.

1859.label: Top: a quiet or king move (0% captures) overlooks a tactic—often a capture-with-check or knight fork—and lets a minor piece or the exchange fall, with ~2/10 instead king-safety blunders that miss a win or allow mate; medium keeps the hung-piece core but blurs to include misjudged/greedy captures that get trapped and to major-piece (rook/queen) losses.

1854.label: Top boards are greedy materialistic captures—queen-grabs, recaptures, or removing one's own defender—that hang material or wreck king safety and throw away a winning position; medium broadens to any imprecise non-capturing move (rook shuffles, king/pawn pushes, knight reroutes) that likewise squanders a winning or favorable advantage.

1867.label: Top boards consistently play a safe/pointless move (pawn or piece shuffle) while a hanging enemy queen is capturable in one move (Bxf8, Nxc2, Rxg8, exd8=Q); medium blurs from the literal queen-grab to any skipped decisive shot in a won position (accelerating a mate, a piece-winning tactic), with the king/queen still safe so it's a missed win rather than a material loss.

1865.label: Top boards throw away a won/equal position with a forcing queen check or capture that hangs material (Qxf7+ Scholar's-mate sacs, Qxb1+ queen-for-rook, Na8+), with a few quiet king/pawn moves walking into mate or missing fxe3; medium blurs toward greedy material-grab captures that drop a piece or squander a tempo (queen-for-rook trade, pawn-grab hxg4 missing Nd5).

1866.label: Top boards consistently pass up a crushing queen kingside infiltration (Qh6/Qxh6, Qh3, or Qf6) from an already-winning position; medium boards broaden to other missed kingside attacks (queen to h4/h5/e4 or bishop f6) and occasionally unrelated winning moves (queenside rook invasions, endgame precision), so the 'queen-to-the-king' core blurs into a general 'missed winning continuation.'

1871.label: Top: squanders a winning position with a slow king/rook/knight or wrong-pawn move instead of immediately pushing (or clearing the path for) the decisive passer; medium broadens to missing the required setup—zwischenzug check, correct promotion order, or removing the blockader/defender—needed to force the same promotion.

1876.label: Top boards play a quiet/non-forcing move and miss a decisive winning queen check (Qxg7+, Qh7+, Qd7+, Qb7+) that mates or wins the queen/rook; medium boards keep the missed-forcing-check theme but broaden the delivering piece to rook or bishop checks (Bf4+, Ra3+, Rxf7+, Qe3+) winning material or saving a draw.

1874.label: Top boards are in a winning position and overlook a decisive forcing check—almost always a queen strike to e6/d5 (Qxe6+/Qxd5+)—playing a slow safe move (rook shuffle, knight/king retreat) instead; medium blurs to other immediately decisive tactics (mate, pawn promotion check, knight fork) and even includes forcing checks that themselves hang material, mixing the 'missed win' direction with a few 'hung own' cases.

1872.label: Top boards always have a promotion or forcing check/queen-trade available (often c8=Q+ or g8=Q+) that the player declines for a quiet king or pawn move; medium broadens to skipping any single best forcing/precise move (sometimes a check-first sequence or a non-checking centralizing move), with severity ranging from harmless tempo loss to throwing away the win/draw or hanging material in the refutation.

1875.label: Top: plays a tempo-wasting queen check that hands the enemy king a flight/shelter square, converting a forced mate into a merely winning position instead of the fastest capture/mate; medium broadens to other tempo-losing moves (king and rook moves, not always checks) that squander the quickest win, with a few near-equivalent non-blunders mixed in.

1873.label: At the peak the feature is razor-sharp: the player almost always leaves or moves a KNIGHT onto an undefended square — frequently while greedily grabbing a defended pawn (Nxe5, Nxe4, Ng5) — and it's recaptured for nothing; at medium activation the piece-type and mechanism blur, so the hung material becomes a bishop, queen, or even a dropped pawn, lost not just by direct recapture but via forced exchange sequences, a knight fork, or a trapped piece, with one outlier (Kf2) merely surrendering a winning edge rather than material.

1869.label: Top boards are constant: from a winning position the player (usually with the queen) reflexively grabs the obvious invading rook instead of the decisive move that wins the hanging enemy queen (a move-order/wrong-target error); medium boards blur this from a queen-win to a missed or self-inflicted forced mate (back-rank Rg1#/Re1#, Qg8#) — and direction splits between hanging own material and merely missing the kill.

1870.chip: Hangs piece on greedy capture (often queen)
1870.label: Top: the queen greedily grabs a (usually defended) bishop and is met by an immediate simple recapture, losing queen-for-minor; medium broadens the capturing piece to rooks/pawns and the punishment beyond plain recapture to walking into a mate or merely an even trade that squanders a winning edge.

1879.chip: King fails to stop passer (pawn endgame)
1879.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a wrong-way king (chasing, passive blockade, or stepping to the edge) fails to stop/catch the opponent's passed pawn—often walking into forced mate; medium broadens to endgames with extra pieces (rook/knight/bishop) and includes a couple of cases that throw away a win or last-ditch resistance rather than a dead-lost position.

1881.label: Top: in a winning position the player makes a lesser capture (usually a pawn) and overlooks a stronger capture of hanging enemy material — an undefended rook/queen or winning the exchange; medium blurs into suboptimal piece moves (knight retreats/recaptures) that surrender the edge positionally rather than missing a clean material win, with 2-3 boards instead hanging the player's own piece.

1880.label: Top: a self-inflicting move — a king walk into the open, removing a defender, blocking an escape square, or opening a line/diagonal — fatally exposes its own king and permits a forced checkmate; medium keeps the same king-exposure theme but blurs toward exposures that merely lose material or tempo (e.g., walking into a fork or shortening an already-lost mate) rather than always delivering immediate mate.

1877.label: TOP: in a lost-but-playable middlegame the player rejects the ONLY saving queen trade/capture and instead makes a king step (occasionally a queen retreat) that walks straight into forced mate; MEDIUM keeps the 'walks into mate / king-safety collapse' core but blurs the saving move beyond queen trades (piece development, promotion, rook relocation) and even includes already-winning positions where the chosen move merely concedes a faster mate or a delaying exchange.

1886.label: Top boards hang a bishop or rook to a short forcing tactic—abandoning a defender, a move-order slip, or stepping into capture; medium broadens to lost exchanges/queens (and forks over 2-3 moves) but mixes in several positional drifts and missed-wins.

1883.chip: Hangs win to knight tactic (often fork)
1883.label: Top: a capture/trade from a winning position self-inflicts a decisive loss punished by a knight landing with a fork, check, or mate (boards 7–8 instead lose to a bishop x-ray / queen recapture); medium keeps the same winning-to-losing self-inflicted blunder but blurs the punishment beyond knight forks to queen/bishop grabs of a hung piece and king-hunt mates.

1888.label: Top boards are clean free grabs of an undefended/hanging queen in the opening (Bxd8/Bxd1/Nxd8/Nxd1) skipped for a quiet move; medium boards still win the queen but the capture is embedded in a fork or short tactic (taking the wrong forked piece, or needing an intermezzo), blurring the pure hanging-queen pattern.

1882.label: Top: a won endgame where the player walks past an immediately capturable undefended enemy piece (usually a rook, twice a queen, once a bishop), playing a materially-safe king/pawn move instead of the free grab; medium keeps the won-endgame king/pawn-move habit but blurs from a literal free capture to missing the one precise winning conversion (a promoting pawn push, holding the promotion square, or correct king route).

1878.label: Top boards are king/queen moves that directly hang or stop defending material decisively (piece varies: queen, rook, bishop); medium blurs into pawn pushes that strip away a piece's defender plus a couple positional/missed-win omissions.

1889.label: Top boards are uniformly a safe/passive move that overlooks a bishop clearance/deflection sacrifice WITH CHECK (Bxf2+/Bxh2+/Bf7+) opening a line to capture the undefended enemy queen; medium keeps the forcing-check-wins-the-queen core but blurs to knight sacs and mate-in-X shots, plus a few inverted cases where the played move instead hands the opponent the queen/rook via an enemy check (e.g. Qb5→Bd6+, dxc5→Qxa1).

1851.label: At the peak a passive bishop retreat declines a forcing opening continuation (a tension-resolving capture, Bb5+ check, or Qh4+ combination), flipping equality into a lost game; at medium it blurs to any quiet move—knight reroute, queen sortie, pawn push, even castling—skipping the critical resource, with punishment ranging from positional collapse to outright hung or trapped pieces.

1884.chip: Trades rook into lost ending (or hangs it)
1884.label: Top boards uniformly trade the last rook off the board into a misjudged, hopelessly lost pawn endgame where the opponent's passed pawn(s) queen faster; medium blurs the action from a clean exchange to also simply hanging the defensive rook outright—still surrendering the only piece restraining the passer and letting it promote.

1887.label: Top: all greedy pawn-grabs or unsound sacrifices that hang a minor piece (knight ~60%, bishop ~40%) in the opening, instantly refuted by a recapture or Qh5-style double threat; medium keeps the same materialistic capture theme but broadens to moves that squander a winning attack (Nxa4, Bxf7+) and even a king-weakening pawn push (f6) punished by Qh5+, so the loss is sometimes the advantage/attack rather than raw material.

1890.chip: Hangs piece to ignored threat (often knight)
1890.label: Top boards are uniformly opening move-order/threat-ignoring errors that hang a knight (e.g. trading the Bg5 instead of Nxe4, or allowing bxc3/exf6/gxf3) with a knight central to every refutation; medium broadens the hung material to other pieces (trapped queen, bishop, positional knight loss) and adjacent themes (king-safety, tempo) while the punishing tactic still features a knight.

1868.label: Top: a quiet developing/pawn/castling move in a won opening lets an enemy long-diagonal bishop grab the uncaptured corner rook (Bxh8/Bxa8/Bxa1); medium broadens to other material losses after skipping a capture — a knight fork winning the a1 rook, a trapped h8 rook, or an unsound bishop sac — plus some boards merely miss a free bishop rather than hang the rook.

1896.label: Top boards collapse a won or forced-mate endgame into a dead-drawn 0.00 by hanging a major piece (rook or queen) to immediate king capture; medium blurs the mechanism to knight hangs, losing trades, and missing the only winning/drawing move.

1895.label: Top boards are passive rook/queen retreats (or simplifying trades) in drawn endgames that surrender activity and throw the result; medium blurs to king and bishop moves and captures across mixed phases and result-states, all sharing the theme of a passive/retreating/simplifying move that cedes initiative and worsens the outcome.

1894.chip: Hangs piece via rook move (often Rxh7)
1894.label: Top boards are greedy rook pawn-grabs (usually Rxh7) that hang material when the rook or its recapturing piece gets trapped/undermined a move later; medium blurs to broader loose or passive rook moves (and some other pieces) that drop material to a tactic or skip a material-winning move.

1893.label: Top boards are passive queen retreats (Qf6/Qg6/Qg3-type) that decline the standing resolving queen capture/trade—usually Qxd5/Qxf5—either squandering a clear material win or directly hanging own material; medium broadens to other pieces (Nxe5/Kh7/Kg1/Rd2-type moves) that likewise ignore the available queen trade, leaning more toward self-hanging material or a king-safety/back-rank collapse, making the direction genuinely mixed between 'Missed' and 'Hangs'.

1899.label: Top boards consistently overlook an immediate forced checkmate (mate-in-1 or short forced mate) and instead play a purposeless or greedy move that lets the opponent escape into perpetual check; medium boards broaden to missed multi-move wins, winning captures/tactics, and even failure to seize a saving perpetual, collapsing a decisive edge into a draw or equality.

1891.label: Top: a queen check (usually grabbing a pawn) immediately recaptured for almost nothing—frequently by a bishop on a long diagonal; medium broadens to other checking/forcing major-piece moves (rooks, queen trades) that lose material or skip a mate to recapture.

1902.chip: Traded rook into lost pawn endgame (major piece)
