1902.label: Top boards constantly capture-trade a ROOK to simplify into a misjudged worse/losing pawn endgame (with one truly optimal Rxh6+ and one ~11cp non-mistake mixed in); medium blurs the traded piece to queen/bishop-for-rook and adds a move-order/tempo slip plus a greedy piece-grab that ignores a promoting passer.

1897.label: Top boards consistently play a safe, non-capturing developing or pawn move that passes up a decisive forced win in the opening — a forced mate (Qh5+/Qh4+) or winning the queen/a piece (Nxd2, Nxg6); medium boards keep the 'quiet materially-safe move that squanders a winning edge' core but blur the win type, ranging from missing material to mere positional drift, and some even let the opponent's tactic in (knight fork, trapped bishop) rather than a clean missed knockout.

1904.chip: Traded queens into worse endgame (often lost)
1904.label: Top: queen recaptures that trade queens into a clearly lost (usually pawn) endgame, surrendering perpetual-check/active-queen drawing or winning resources; medium: same queen-trade error but into merely inferior endgames with smaller eval swings and broader endgame types (rook/bishop/blockade).

1885.chip: Hangs piece in opening (often to pawn)
1885.label: Top boards hang a developed minor piece to a simple one-move pawn capture (exf3/exd4/Bxg2) or, just as strongly, make a positional pawn push conceding the center; medium broadens to quiet opening pawn/piece moves that drop material via slower tactics (forks, trapped pieces, passed pawns) or that merely concede space/tempo, sometimes into the middlegame and endgame.

1898.label: Top boards greedily capture (or play a quiet move) and overlook a forced checkmate—usually a back-rank mate-in-1/2; medium boards blur to missing decisive material wins (queen forks, zwischenzugs, trapped pieces) or letting a winning game slip toward a draw, sometimes even allowing the opponent to mate in return.

1903.label: At the peak, the player grabs tempting material in a winning opening position — usually a capture, with the piece varying (bishop, knight or queen taking rook/queen/pawn) — and is refuted by an overlooked intermezzo or check (gxf7+, Qa5+, Ne7+, exf6) that wins the material back; at medium the pattern blurs to non-capturing tempo-losing moves (e.g. Qh5) and unsound sacrifices that likewise skip the one accurate priority move, so the 'greedy capture missing the zwischenzug' core holds only loosely.

1911.label: Top boards are uniformly king-to-corner/edge/back-rank tucks in endgames that abandon activity and walk into checks, pawn promotion, or mating nets; medium blurs the pattern to any passive, non-defensive move (still often a king edge-move, but also a passive bishop/rook retreat or a weakening pawn push) that likewise fails king safety and concedes checks or a mating net.

1907.chip: Premature push hangs material (often central pawn)
1907.label: Top: a premature pawn push (c5/e5/f5/c4/b5) ignores the central tension and drops an undefended central pawn (boards 7/9/10 instead just concede space/structure); medium keeps the 'premature opening advance neglecting the center' theme but broadens the loss from a hung central pawn to general material—including flank pushes (b5/b4/e4/d4/f5) and even loose piece moves (Nd4/Nb7)—refuted by a central counterstrike.

1900.label: Top boards all spurn the decisive kingside Rxf6+/Rxf5+ rook-for-knight check in won king-and-pawn endgames (playing a materially-safe king move that keeps but doesn't cleanly convert the win); medium generalizes the same sacrifice to the queenside (Rxc6+).

1910.label: Top boards: a natural developing or pawn move ignores a one-move tactic/threat and concedes mate or an outright piece (often via a central pawn-break or deflection like e5/c4/a6, including a back-rank mate); medium boards broaden to the same blunder type but with more varied and slower refutations — forks, trapped/hung pieces, and lines that win 'only' a pawn or a piece over 2-3 moves.

1909.label: Top boards are all pure single-pawn-grab bishop sacs on h3/h6 instantly refuted by the g-pawn recapture with zero follow-up; medium broadens to include Greek-Gift-style sacs that do get a Qxh6 follow-up yet still fail, two-pawn grabs, and an occasional g6 target, but the constant is hanging the bishop to gxh-/fx- recapture for no real attack.

1906.chip: Hangs material to overlooked tactic (often bishop)
1906.label: Top: natural quiet/repositioning bishop moves that ignore the position's tactics—mostly removing a key defender so the opponent lands a decisive shot/hangs material, with a strong minority instead skipping a forced mate or winning attack; medium keeps the 'quiet move overlooks tactics' core but blurs the piece (rook, queen, king, pawn moves) and the motif (back-rank, deflection, plain tempo loss), making the hang-vs-missed-win direction genuinely mixed.

1905.label: Top boards consistently give up the queen via a forcing check/capture (often a wrong move-order, e.g. Qxc3+ instead of Rxc3, Qxe4+ instead of an in-between check), dissolving a forced mate or crushing attack into a mere edge; medium broadens to a more straightforward queen capture-sacrifice (Qxh6 for a pawn) that simply hangs the queen — so direction blurs between outright hangs (lose material) and safe-but-wasteful queen trades that only forfeit the win.

1901.label: Top: in a clearly won endgame the player makes a quiet, material-safe (usually rook, sometimes knight) move that skips an immediate forcing win — a winning capture, a knight fork, a mate-in-1, or an immediate pawn promotion; medium broadens to skipping multi-move forced-mate sequences (and even faster mates via checks), while several flagged boards are actually optimal and a few are outright hangs/walks-into-mate rather than missed wins.

1918.label: Top: uniform premature queen sorties (Qh5/Qh4/Qd5) or development that leaves the queen en prise to a knight/pawn in the opening; medium blurs into unrelated game-losing blunders—throwing away a won endgame or walking the king into mate.

1912.label: In a lost endgame the player makes a passive/retreating king move (occasionally a pawn move); at the peak this move declines a free capture of hung major material (rook or queen, sometimes knight/pawn), turning a fightable loss into forced mate, while at medium activation it blurs into merely suboptimal passive king placement (retreat to corner/edge or wrong direction) with no material actually available to take.

1917.label: Top boards uniformly play a quiet developing/repositioning move and skip an available forcing shot — almost always a knight jump to b5/d5 setting up Nc7+ (or Nd6+) forking king and rook — while the materially-safe move squanders a winning edge; at medium the constant blurs into other missed tactical/positional wins, and a sizable minority actually hang material outright (e.g. Qe7??/Bg6+ dropping rook or piece) rather than merely missing a win.

1920.label: In already-losing positions, plays a premature pawn push or king misstep that accelerates defeat—usually letting the opponent's passed pawn run instead of centralizing the king; top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames with passed pawns, while medium broadens to rook endgames and occasionally an outright hung pawn.

1921.label: Top is uniformly a knight leaping to an aggressive central/forward square (e5/d4/d5/b4/b5) that a pawn kick (c3/f4/a3/d3) traps or wins; medium broadens the piece (queen on e5/b2, rook on h6, plus knights) and the refutation method (forks, checks, double-attacks—not just pawn kicks) while keeping the 'overextended sortie punished for material/tempo' core.

1908.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player skips the available decisive capture (back-rank mate via Rxc1/Rxc8, a royal fork, or simply grabbing a hung piece) and is punished catastrophically—often mated or dropping the won material; medium: the same failure to convert blurs to non-capture decisive moves (a forced mate via check, the right endgame king move) with smaller swings, and direction is split between hanging own material/king and merely missing a materially-safe win.

1919.label: Top boards capture a pawn (usually with check) and get recaptured, trading away the sole winning rook/queen/bishop and collapsing a won game into a dead draw (insufficient material); medium boards are the same rook-for-pawn trade but only shrink a still-winning edge rather than reaching a draw.

1922.label: At the peak it's clean one-move ~one-piece material swings—usually hanging the player's own piece (frequently a knight) or, less often, missing a free enemy piece/capture; at medium it blurs into material lost through multi-move refutations driven by king-safety, pin, and fork weaknesses rather than an immediate single-move hang.

1913.label: Top boards are highly consistent: a natural opening developing move or greedy pawn-grab that loses own material to an immediate recapture or short tactic (usually a minor piece — knight/bishop, occasionally a pawn or the c3-knight); medium boards blur both the unit (queen hung on g2) and the direction, mixing in safe moves that skip a forcing material-winning tactic (missed Ne4/Qb4+/Bb5+) and pure tempo/positional lapses.

1914.label: Top: a natural opening/developing move skips the eliminating capture (Bxc3/Bxc6) and walks into a Nd4/Nd5 knight fork that wins the player's bishop (often forking queen+bishop or king+bishop); medium keeps the same skipped-priority-capture/move-order theme but blurs both the forked target (queen, exchange, knight, fork-with-check) and the punishment type (plain hung bishop, discovered attack, central d5 break, tempo loss) rather than a clean Nd4/Nd5-takes-bishop.

1915.label: Top boards uniformly hang a knight by placing/leaving it in a pawn's capture path in the opening; medium broadens to loosening pawn pushes (g4/f3/f4) that hang pawns or expose the king, plus other early material/king-safety lapses.

1928.label: At the peak, a natural developing/space-gaining move hangs the player's own material to a tactic—almost always knight-related (own knight left unguarded or dropped to an enemy knight fork); at medium activation it blurs into quieter pawn losses and missed-win tempo moves, with a knight still central to nearly every refutation.

1925.chip: Hangs piece in won endgame (often knight)
1925.label: Top boards: in a winning endgame the player drops a piece (most often a knight, but also a rook) by parking it on a capturable square or playing a pointless check, ignoring a clean free capture; medium boards narrow to the pure case of a knight moved onto an enemy-knight-controlled square and taken for free.

1926.label: Top boards: a natural opening development (usually a bishop, sometimes a knight) lands on a square hit by a pawn break (e5/d4/c5/b4) that forks two minor pieces and wins one; medium broadens to pawn breaks that also fork or trap the queen, plus a few non-fork hangs (trapped bishop, positional trade).

1931.label: Top boards constantly overlook a free en-prise enemy piece (queen ~6/10, else rook) and play an unrelated move that itself often hangs material; medium boards keep the missed-capture core but blur toward rook/knight targets and moves whose main fault is hanging own piece or allowing a refuting tactic rather than pure omission.

1924.label: Top boards are almost exclusively rook checks (Rc8+/Rg7+/Rc1+/Re5+) that the king calmly sidesteps, squandering tempo and the stronger quiet/capturing move; medium broadens to bishop and discovered/queen checks (Be3+, Ba2, Qb1+) and even a few near-optimal checks, blurring the 'check is bad' signal.

1923.label: Top boards are uniformly premature passed-pawn pushes to one square from promotion (e2/d2/b7/c7/f7) that gift the opponent a clean rook/bishop blockade in front of the passer and dissolve a won position; medium keeps the premature-push core (d7/b2/c2) but blurs into other tempo-wasting moves in promotion races — king steps, captures, and piece moves that remove the passer's support or let the opponent get counterplay/blockade.

1932.label: Top boards: the king is walked into the open or its pawn-shield/castling is stripped, allowing a forced checkmate; medium boards keep the same self-exposing king move but broaden the punishment to material loss via discovered checks/forks (with a couple slipping into merely faster mates or a missed simplifying win).

1927.label: Top boards uniformly skip the one winning central pawn thrust (d4/e5/e4/d5) that simultaneously forks bishop AND knight, choosing a safe develop/castle move instead; at medium the constant blurs to any winning central pawn break — often hitting just one minor piece, resolving central tension via a capture (fxe5), or in a few cases the passive move actually walks into the opponent's own fork/discovered shot rather than missing one.

1929.label: Top boards all initiate a capture/exchange (varied piece — knight, queen, rook, bishop) that backfires, either dropping material to the recapture/refutation or simplifying into a lost endgame/worse position; medium broadens to non-capturing loose moves (...f6, ...Qf5) whose refutation similarly wins material.

1933.label: Top: hangs own material by moving a piece — frequently the queen — off its defensive duty, leaving a rook/knight undefended for capture (Qb1, Qh4, Qxe5, Rhxh7); medium keeps the 'moved-defender hang' (Rb8, Qh6) but blurs to pieces overextending/hanging themselves directly (Nd4, Bf4, Bh5) and to skipping a winning tactic, so it fires broadly on 'throws away a winning/equal position.'

1936.label: Top boards are uniformly pointless rook checks (Rg1+, Rh8+, Rg2+, Re6+, Rh7+) that either hang the rook outright to a capture or squander tempo/material and convert a defensible losing position into a lost/mated one; medium broadens to other piece checks (e.g. Nf2+) and near-check piece offers like Rf5, where the move sometimes only forfeits a faster win rather than dropping material.

1916.label: Top boards are uniform: from a winning position the player skips a decisive forcing CHECK—usually mate or a winning check (Qh7+, Qxh7#, Ne2+, Rg7+, Qg7#)—and plays a passive/greedy move that throws the win away; medium blurs the direction and position quality, adding hanging a piece or pawn to an enemy check/fork (Qa5+, Qxd4+), missing non-mating tactics (Bxh3, Qxa6+), and even pure positional or endgame drift from equal/worse positions.

1930.label: Top boards are consistently a winning side throwing away a deeply-infiltrated dominant piece—most often a knight (also queen or bishop)—by relocating, trading, or grabbing a pawn with it so it's recaptured/neutralized in the refutation; medium broadens to other piece types and to move-order or missed-tactic errors that surrender or trade off the dominant restraining piece rather than consolidating.

1938.label: Top: from clearly winning positions, plays a routine develop/recapture (Nc3, Rxb1, Qxf3) instead of shoving an advanced c6/f6 passer with cxb7 or f7+ to queen, letting Black just take the pawn (Nxc6); medium: same theme blurs to other passed-pawn advances (e7, bxc2) and supporting moves that enable promotion, plus a couple of looser tempo/structure misses, sometimes from already-lost positions.

1941.label: Top boards consistently fail to play a winning knight fork of king and rook (Ne6+/Nf5+/Nd6+/Nd3+ etc.) that wins the exchange, opting for passive/greedy/wrong-check moves; medium keeps the same king+rook knight-fork core but blurs to include a king+queen knight fork, bishop tempo-checks, a zwischenzug, and even a missed mate-in-one — i.e. any missed winning forcing shot, still predominantly the knight fork.

1943.label: At peak activation the eval-flipping blunder is queen-centric — the player hangs their own queen (moving it onto an open line or into a fork/capture) or misses winning/promoting against the enemy queen; at medium activation the queen is only sometimes the protagonist and the pattern blurs into broader single-move decisive losses: allowing mate or back-rank/king-safety collapses, dropping pawns, or missing a forced win.

1940.label: Top: a queen move loses material—usually abandoning a defensive duty so the recapture/infiltration comes with check on a freshly-opened file or diagonal; medium blurs to any losing move (king walks into mate, queen dropped onto an attacked square or trapped, even a pawn push missing the win).

1947.label: Top boards: a greedy/natural capture (or piece placed on an attacked square) overlooks the opponent's discovered attack or double-check refutation and loses material; medium blurs to other refutations (forks, deflection, passed-pawn pushes) plus a few positional/defensive omissions and missed wins.

1939.label: Top boards consistently capture/trade the active rook (met by Kx) to liquidate into a clearly lost king-and-pawn endgame, surrendering the rook's counterplay; medium blurs this to lost minor-piece endgames, outright hanging the rook to Kxh1/Nxg2 via passive king or pawn moves, and even a king-safety walk into mate—all sharing the loss of the active rook.

1937.label: At the peak the move is a flashy/premature knight check that throws away a forced mate or a clean winning combination (with a few that strand/hang the knight, e.g. Nxa7+/Nc7+); at medium the pattern blurs to move-order/tempo knight checks that merely squander a large winning edge (centipawn drop) rather than a mate, occasionally drifting to a wrong-piece check or an outright hung knight.

1944.label: Top: an active move—usually a knight relocation or a capture—directly hangs a piece/pawn for nothing (Ng3+, Raxd1, Ng5, Nxd2, Nf4) turning a playable game into a loss; medium blurs into wrong-capture move-orders and positional concessions (creating enemy passed pawns, opening lines to one's own king, abandoning an attack) that surrender the advantage without a clean material hang.

1934.label: Top: in a won endgame the player squanders a forced mate by hanging their own queen (occasionally a rook) instead of the decisive capture, flipping a win into an equal/lost position; medium: still throws away the forced mate but more mildly — greedy pawn-grabs or king/queen relocations that merely delay or downgrade the mate while staying winning rather than dropping the queen.

1942.label: Top: aggressive forcing moves (captures, checks, fork/double-attack attempts for tempo or material) backfire—the opponent ignores the threat and counterattacks, hanging the player's own piece or exposing the castled king (with two boards actually missed wins and one not a blunder); medium broadens to quieter king-safety and positional moves (outpost retreats, castling, prophylaxis) that similarly expose the king or drop material, plus a couple that merely waste tempo or skip a faster win.

1935.label: Top: one decisive move throws a dead-drawn endgame—roughly half hang the bishop/knight outright (often a clumsy blockade square), the rest miss the only holding move and let an enemy pawn promote; medium blurs into king wrong-direction and tempo-loss errors, even flagging a near-0cp non-blunder.

1951.label: Top boards are uniformly missed Qh4+/Qh5+ checks exploiting the open diagonal left by the enemy's missing f-pawn (player instead develops/recaptures); medium positions broaden to other winning queen checks and forks (Qe4+, Qxe5+, kingside Qh5+) that punish an exposed enemy king beyond the strict f-pawn-hole motif.

1948.label: Top boards are uniformly king/rook moves that create a vulnerable alignment (shared rank/file, back-rank, stalemate geometry) walking into a decisive enemy ROOK check—skewer, back-rank mate, deflection, or check-forced trade—that wins the rook, mates, or drops into a lost pawn endgame; medium blurs the agent of refutation to other forcing tactics (knight fork Nd3+, bishop check Bg4+, queen pin/check Qb8/Qd8+, mating nets), and to plain king-passivity rook-endgame errors, where the self-created alignment still lets the opponent's forcing move decide the game.

1956.label: Top boards skip an outright free capture of an undefended queen or bishop (played a routine developing move instead); medium boards keep the missed free capture but skew to undefended bishops and looser cases — grabbing a pawn instead of the piece, or a quiet move over a stronger forcing capture.

1950.label: Top boards are uniformly flank pawn pushes (h3/h6/g4/g5/a3) that 'put the question' to an enemy piece and squander the advantage—either loosening the king's shelter (inviting Bxh6/fxg6/Ng3-type attacks) or skipping a sharper tactic/developing move; medium blurs the precise pattern, keeping some wing pushes (g6, a4, h6, g4) but adding generic tempo-wasting or move-order errors (rook, king, queen moves, premature captures) that likewise ignore the stronger resource.

1945.label: Top boards are tempo-wasting rook checks in pure rook endgames that drive the enemy king to a stronger central/queenside square instead of using the move for active king or rook play; medium blurs to queen checks and checks played in place of a concrete tactic or capture.

1959.label: Top boards are clean self-inflicted hangs of the queen or bishop left en prise to a single immediate capture; medium broadens to king-safety-weakening and positional/trade moves that still drop the player's own material, but over a 2-3 move refutation rather than in one ply.

1958.label: Top boards consistently give up the only defensive minor piece in a holdable/lost endgame—the bishop, either hung by a king move (1,5,8,10) or traded for a single pawn (3,6,7,9; a knight on 2)—turning a defensible ending into a lost one; medium blurs this to the defensive knight and to looser endgame mishandling of that piece (self-trapping it on 7, passive blockade on 6, failing to reroute/blockade passers on 4,9, hanging it on 8,10), plus a few near-equal king/tempo moves that dilute the signal.

1952.label: Top: a greedy material grab — almost always capturing a bishop (or knight) to 'win a piece' — overlooks a decisive refutation that either hangs the player's own piece, drops into a lost endgame, or allows back-rank/king-hunt mate or pawn promotion; medium blurs the direction by adding non-capture greedy/careless moves (king walks, pawn pushes that hang material) and missed-win cases where the grab only draws instead of mating or promoting.

1949.chip: Hangs or misses win in endgame
1949.label: At the peak it's a clearly winning endgame where a non-decisive move replaces the decisive one—roughly half skip a free material-winning capture (often Rook-takes-Queen via Rxd4/Rxd3/Rxf5/fxe5) and half hang their own piece by vacating a key defender/blocker; at medium it blurs into drawish king-and-pawn endgames where a king or pawn move (Kd5/Kxf3/h6) throws away the result, so the direction (hangs vs missed) and piece stay genuinely mixed and two top boards are already lost where the move is best.

1946.label: Top boards are uniformly the premature Bh6/Bh3 bishop-sortie that trades off the enemy fianchetto while abandoning the bishop's restraining/defensive duty (releasing a pin, dropping support of a piece/pawn, or wasting tempo with the king uncastled); medium blurs the specific move/piece, generalizing to ANY piece (rook, knight, queen, even a pawn) that vacates a critical defensive square or relocates pointlessly, in each case conceding material—often over 2–3 moves—or a decisive positional/king-safety edge.

1960.label: Top: a slow pawn move ignores a forcing combination—almost always the Rxe8 + c-pawn-to-c7 deflection that wins a full rook (passed-pawn promotion theme); medium keeps the 'inattentive move concedes material via a multi-move tactic' core but blurs to non-pawn moves and varied motifs (back-rank, forks, exchange sacs, deflections) and even outright forced mate rather than just material.

1961.label: Top boards are queen moves that abandon a concrete defensive duty (guarding f3/b2/f7, a hanging piece) and thereby hang major material or allow forced mate, with the missed resource almost always a queen trade; medium broadens to non-queen abandoning moves (e.g. Rxe5 leaving the queen en prise) and to merely dropping a single (passed) pawn rather than mate/major material.

1955.label: At the peak the player squanders a winning/equal (even mating) position with a tempting forcing queen move — a check or trade — that relieves pressure or hangs material; medium positions broaden to other tempting moves (pawn pushes, rook shifts, greedy queen grabs) that likewise abandon the precise winning continuation, with the direction genuinely mixed between hanging own material and merely missing the win.

1968.label: Top boards are all king moves in king-and-pawn (or king-bishop) endgames that surrender the opposition/correct king square and throw away a draw or win; medium blurs into general endgame tempo-loss and mispositioning with other pieces (pawn pushes, rook/queen moves), several only marginally suboptimal or 0cp.

1971.label: Top boards are greedy captures/forced trades that throw away a winning-or-equal position—about half hang the player's own material (bishop, exchange, even queen), half merely simplify into dead equality; medium broadens to positional captures and even non-capture pawn moves that surrender the edge or drop material to a tempo/fork.

1963.label: Top boards hang a piece outright via greedy captures or self-exposing moves (rook #2, queen #3, bishop #4, knight #10); medium narrows to king walks (Kc6, Kc2) that walk into a check/skewer and drop material or a holdable endgame, plus tempo/pawn slips that hang nothing — genuinely mixed.

1970.label: Top: a self-inflicted middlegame move that abandons a defensive post/duty and hangs the player's own material (varied piece — rook/queen/bishop/knight, sometimes the abandoned defender enabling mate); medium blurs toward broader neglect of the urgent king-safety priority (skipping castling/king-flight) that ends in mate or material loss.

1966.label: In endgames, a passive own-agenda king/pawn (sometimes bishop/rook) move ignores the opponent's single decisive threat, converting a holdable or drawn position into a loss; top boards cluster on pawn/king advances punished by passed-pawn breakthroughs or mating nets, while medium boards broaden to the same neglect punished by knight forks, skewers, pointless checks, or hanging-piece losses.

1965.label: Top boards uniformly hang a minor piece (usually the dark-squared bishop via b4-a5/c5, also Na5/Ne4/Nc6) by placing it where a pawn break (b4-c5, d5, a4, g4, e5) traps or wins it; medium blurs to other piece-losing tactics (knight forks, pins, mating attacks) and increasingly to materially-safe moves that skip the one saving capture/defense (Qxe5, Qxe3, Rxd4, Nxb3, Nxf3+), mixing 'hangs' with 'missed-win'.

1969.label: Top boards uniformly overlook a free capture of the opponent's completely hanging queen (playing an idle non-capture instead); medium broadens to missed free captures of rooks and minor pieces, plus a few other winning tactics (forks, trapping).

1967.label: Top boards squander a forced mate/win by immediately queening a pawn (e8=Q, e1=Q, a1=Q) — or once by grabbing material with a rook — instead of the precise winning move, while medium narrows purely to premature pawn promotion that lets the new queen be captured and collapses the win into a draw.

1972.chip: Hangs material chasing a knight (often fork)
1972.label: Top: a pawn push chases an enemy knight (on b5/b4, also g4/g5/e5) and walks into a royal knight-fork (Nc7+/Nc2+) that wins the exchange; medium keeps the 'chase-a-knight' theme but the punishing tactic blurs — forward knight leaps forking rooks (Nf7/Ng6), the knight simply grabbing material, or unrelated shots like Qxd4/Qh5+ mate.

1953.label: Top: the queen snatches the poisoned b2/b7 pawn and gets chased/trapped, losing the queen for a rook; medium keeps the same greedy queen b-pawn grab but the refutation broadens beyond trapping to forks, tempo-loss and positional collapse (plus a couple of unrelated loose king moves like Kg1/h3 allowing Bxf2+).

1977.chip: Hangs material with a check (often promotion)
1977.label: Top boards are a forcing check that throws away own material — most often a premature promotion (or rook-for-pawn trade) that walks straight into a capture; medium broadens to other forcing checks/trades (e.g. a queen exchange) that leave a piece hanging in the refutation.

1976.label: Top boards uniformly play a safe developing move (Nc3/d3/Bc4/Qe2/Bc5) that skips the immediate, forced queen check Qh5+/Qh4+ winning the h-rook by exploiting the missing f-pawn and bare king; medium boards keep the same missing-f-pawn king-attack theme but blur to other forcing wins (e.g. a Bc4 development trap, or checks exploiting combined e/f-pawn holes).

1973.label: Top boards are uniformly missed forced mates driven by the Qh6/Qf6→Qg7# maneuver (player picks a safe/passive move instead); medium keeps the 'winning position, skip the strongest move' theme but blurs from pure Qg7# to other mating nets (Qh8#, Qg2#) and even non-mate wins/saves (Greek Gift Bxh7+, positional Bh6, a drawing perpetual).

1962.label: Top: from a clearly winning position (+500..+700 or forced mate) the player makes a materially-safe, passive/quiet move and misses a decisive tactic or forced win (winning move varies — back-rank Rb8, overload Rac1, free Qxc2, exchange-winning Bf5, mate). Medium keeps the 'safe move that isn't best' core but blurs the winning requirement: edges that merely slip from advantage toward equal, and several where the inaccuracy actually allows the opponent a counter-tactic (fork) or comes from a non-winning position.

1978.label: Against an opponent with TWO queens and a forced mate looming, the player ignores the sole defensive resource—capturing one of the two queens (e.g. Qxc8/Qxa1/Rxe8)—and instead plays a passive or greedy move; top boards are clean forced mates (#-3 to #-14) where capturing a queen is literally the only survivable move, while medium boards blur to letting a queen escape into a crushing two-queen attack or heavy material loss rather than an immediate forced checkmate.

1980.label: Top: in the opening Black loses the dark-squared b4 bishop—retreating ...Ba5 into the b4 trap or leaving it to a Qa4+ fork—instead of the resolving ...Bxc3+; medium blurs to other tension bishops that should be exchanged (...Bxf3, ...Bxd2+) or are simply left hanging (Bg4 to hxg4), plus some king-safety/wrong-capture noise.

1981.label: Top: king steps straight into mate-in-one, ignoring the one defensive resource; medium broadens to any piece (queen/knight/pawn/rook) that allows a forced mate several moves deep—or merely a collapsing/material loss—rather than the sole saving move.

1979.label: Top boards are clean one-move puzzles where a quiet, materially-safe move (pawn push, rook/king shuffle) overlooks a single decisive capture—hanging bishop on d6, the queen on d7, the d3 passer; medium blurs the mechanism to any squandered winning/equal edge, adding passive retreats and quiet moves that also allow enemy forks (Nf6, Na5+) or trade into a lost ending, but the unifying error is failing to play the one critical (usually capturing) move.

1985.label: Top boards consistently miss a winning queen/rook trade-or-sacrifice (Qxf7+/Qxf6+/Qxe2+/Rxc7+/Rxf6+) that liquidates a won position into a trivially winning pawn/king endgame, instead playing a check or piece-keeping move; medium blurs into other missed winning tactics (exchange sacs, knight forks, discovered attacks) and a minority of boards that instead hang the player's own queen.

1982.label: Top: castling (O-O/O-O-O) that hangs the player's own material — queen, knight, or bishop, sometimes lost over a 2-3 move refutation; medium blurs to castling (and a few other king/rook moves) that stay materially safe but squander a winning tactic (tempo loss) or castle straight into an attack.

1983.label: Top: a passive/slow move squanders a won game by missing a forcing winning queen capture or infiltration (Qxh7/Qxa7/Qxa2/Qc8+); medium blurs to missed wins by other pieces (Bxb2, Rxb2, Qe1) and to slow moves that instead hang own material (Qe5 drops bishop, Rc5 drops rook) or even allow mate.

1964.label: Top: a greedy/careless capture (almost always the queen) leaves the queen undefended and is refuted by a bishop-sacrifice deflection/clearance check (Bxh7+, Bxh2+, Bb5+, Bg6+) that wins it with tempo; medium broadens to other hung pieces (bishop/knight/rook) and other punishing tactics (knight forks, diagonal queen forks, discovered attacks, plain hangs), even some missed wins.

1974.label: Top boards throw away a forced mate by choosing a natural capture or check (often a queen trade or capture-with-check) from a won position, keeping only a lesser win; medium broadens to skipping decisive material wins (rook/piece) and at times the same natural-move habit lets the opponent's own mate or fork land.

1988.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed, forcing Greek Gift bishop sacrifice on h7/h2 (Bxh7+/Bxh2+) in a winning position — a quiet developing/retreating move lets the opponent play ...h6/...Nf5/...g6 and permanently shut the attack; medium boards keep the same 'missed winning kingside shot' theme but blur the exact motif (retreating the h4/f3 attacking knight, choosing Bxe2 over Bxh2+, Ng5 instead of Bxh7+) and even leak into a couple of non-Greek-Gift missed wins (Bb2 trapped-piece, missing O-O-O while hanging a knight).

1986.label: Top boards are premature queen checks (Qa5+/Qa4+) that White/Black blocks with tempo (b4, Bd2), squandering the advantage and sometimes hanging a piece; medium broadens to bishop and even rook checks (Bb5+, Ba4+, Re1+) and blurs between actually hanging material and merely tossing away a winning edge or a stronger move.

1987.label: Top boards are pure rook/king endgame failures where the player abandons the blockade square (or skips capturing the runner) and the passer queens; medium broadens to hanging or misplacing the blockading piece itself (bishop/knight, wrong-pawn recapture) and a few tangential promotion-enabling slips.

1984.label: Top: a material-grabbing capture—almost always snatching a bishop—that ignores a stronger threat, either walking into immediate mate (king-safety) or a winning tactic (fork/zwischenzug/discovered attack); medium broadens to knight/queen grabs and even non-captures, but the same fatal threat-ignoring greed persists.

1991.chip: Conceded key square to king (often K+P)
1991.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a king move (occasionally a passive minor-piece move) surrenders a central square and lets the enemy king infiltrate to win pawns or the game—material never hangs outright; medium broadens to rook endgames, structure-freezing pawn moves, and passive piece retreats that cede a key square, even bleeding into king-safety/mating-net lapses outside the endgame.

1957.label: Top: a natural developing/castling/king move ignores the position's decisive knight tactic—either a knight fork (Ne2+, Nb4-c2+, Nxe3) or a hanging/undefended knight (Rxc6, Rxe5)—losing material; medium: the same neglect blurs from clean material loss into positional squanders, missed wins, and minor (pawn/bishop) drops, with a knight still the recurring decisive piece.

1994.label: Top boards are slow/routine/loosening moves (castling, Kh1, a6, a4, e4) that skip a decisive knight capture—nearly always Nxe6—to win material or shatter the enemy king; medium broadens the tactic to other knight captures (Nxc6/Nxd4/Nxe5/Nxg6) and increasingly blurs into self-inflicted material loss, hanging a pawn or piece outright rather than just declining a win.

1996.label: Top boards uniformly leave a piece undefended that an enemy rook captures for free (often with check); medium positions broaden to material lost to other attackers (queen, knight, king, even a pawn) and to adjacent motifs—trapped pieces, overloaded defenders, en passant—but the constant is a move that hangs own material with no recapture.

1989.label: Top boards uniformly walk the king into a one-move checkmate by ignoring a pre-existing queen-bishop diagonal battery (Qxg2#/Qxg7#/Qxc7#) when only an interposition saved it; medium boards still include one such battery mate (Qb2#) but more often blur into simply hanging a piece or losing material by overlooking the opponent's pre-existing tactical threat (overloaded defender, missed shot).

1997.label: Top boards are materially-safe slow KING moves in won endgames that skip a forcing promotion/mate/pawn-push; medium broadens to other quiet or mis-ordered moves (rook, pawn, queen) that likewise miss the decisive forcing continuation.

1975.label: At the peak, a quiet pawn or developing move in a clearly winning position drops a major piece—almost always the queen or rook (e.g. ignoring Rxh7, leaving the queen en prise on g6); at medium the pattern blurs to minor-piece hangs (bishop on b6) and still-winning positions where the error is merely missing a bigger capture (the enemy queen via Nxb5) rather than an outright hang.

1998.label: Top boards are tightly clustered: a passive, materially-safe move overlooks a forcing exchange/rook-winning CHECK (deflection/zwischenzug — Bxg7+, Qxf1+, Bxg2+, Bxf2+, Ne7+), constant at the peak; at medium the motif blurs away from checks toward other overlooked tactics (a queen-winning discovered attack, a pawn-winning queen-trade-then-gxf7+ sequence), and direction drifts from 'missed win' toward 'hangs material'.

1993.label: Top boards ignore an immediate queen capture (usually with check, e.g. Qxh1+/Qxc3+/Qxg8) and hang material whose type varies—rook, knight, or pawn—with two outliers being missed-win queen trades/positional drifts; medium narrows to the specific case of hanging the g1-knight to Qxg1+ with check.

1992.label: Top boards uniformly skip the central knight strike Nxd5 — which wins a free pawn by hitting the queen on b6 — in favor of a safe trade/developing move; medium boards keep the 'won opening, one precise winner ignored' frame but blur the tactic to any missed winning continuation (central breaks cxd5/d6, Bxf7+ sacs, Rc1+ checks, even premature queen sorties).

1995.label: Top boards uniformly hang a piece or the exchange by ignoring the opponent's immediate tactical reply — a knight fork (Ng5, Nc5+, Ne2+) or a zwischenzug/removal-of-defender capture; medium keeps the 'overlooked forcing tactic' core but blurs the direction, mixing in move-order/recapture errors, positional tempo losses (Rg1, Nf5), a back-rank mate, and a couple of purely missed material-winning shots (Rxc6, Rxc8).

2001.label: Top: a tempo-wasting queen check that drives the enemy king to safety and forfeits a forced mate or decisive material win; medium: the same purposeless/move-order queen check, but giving up smaller material or positional wins (and occasionally even hanging a piece to the escaping king).

2005.label: Top boards are almost uniformly the light-squared bishop dropped on g4 to a knight on e5 (Nxg4 wins a clean piece); medium boards blur into hanging other minor pieces and bishops to assorted tactics (forks, pins, skewers, trapped pieces) plus a few missed-win/positional drops, all in the opening.

2002.label: Top boards uniformly trade off an active bishop (Bxe2/Bxf3/Bxe7/Bxd7) to force a favorable queen exchange/simplification that squanders a winning position by releasing all the tension; medium broadens to other premature captures and move-order errors (knight/rook/pawn captures like Nxc5, dxe6, Rxf2, capturing before the preparatory Qg3/Rad1/O-O-O) that likewise release pressure or abandon the cleaner win.

2006.label: Top boards consistently skip a single forcing capture that wins the opponent's queen for far less material (Bxe3, Nxg4, Nxc5, Rxf6, Qxb4), settling for a tame trade; medium boards blur the queen-grab into other missed decisive shots—exchange/rook sacrifices and the strongest attacking continuation—plus an occasional self-hang (Na4).

2009.label: At the peak, the move leaves the player's own QUEEN hanging—either by removing its only defender/recapture or by ignoring a direct capture threat (with a couple of king-safety/mate outliers); at medium strength it blurs to hanging a minor piece (bishop) or dropping a pawn to a short tactical refutation.

2008.label: Top boards are over-aggressive captures or checks (Nf3+, Bxf2+, Bxf3, Rxb7+) that get refuted and drop varied material—knight, bishop, or most often the exchange—with a couple purely positional or leading to mate; medium narrows to a capture-with-check losing the exchange (a7b7) plus a positional capture (h4f6).

1990.label: Top boards consistently center on the thematic ...d4/e5 central break (peak: missing ...d4 that forks the c3-knight and e3-bishop in a near-winning position); medium keeps the central pawn-break judgment theme but blurs the direction — adding other break-forks (d5/e5 vs c6/e6, f6/d6), unsound advances that hang own material, premature ...e5 collapses, and a few unrelated tactical lapses.

2007.label: At the peak, an 'active' rook/pawn move vacates a critical king-defending square (often a rook leaving its defensive post), letting the opponent infiltrate for forced mate; medium blurs the punishment to material loss—abandoning a defender or king-shelter to allow a won piece, skewer/fork, trapped piece, or greedy pawn-grab that hangs the king/material in the refutation.

2000.label: Top: faulty captures/move-order slips that strip away a key defender and hang a major piece—often the queen; medium: broadens to any self-inflicted weakening move (pawn break or king step) that merely drops a pawn or exposes the king.

2004.label: Top boards constantly hang a full minor piece by declining to capture/recapture a deeply intruding enemy bishop (on c3/c6, usually by pawn) in favor of a developing move; medium blurs into broader missed captures/recaptures and development or king-safety lapses (e.g. Ke7) that also drop material.

2015.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where a materially-safe king move goes the wrong direction or burns a tempo, squandering a win/draw (but ~40% are 0–7cp non-blunders that merely share the pawn-endgame/king-tempo setting); medium broadens to rook/queen/bishop endings with the same tempo-losing or wrong-way king/piece move.

2012.label: Top boards almost uniformly drop the just-moved bishop on an attacked/undefended square (frequently g4/g5), captured for free or in a short forcing sequence; medium broadens to hanging any moved piece—rooks (c4, e6), knights (d4, e2), and even queen/capture moves that lose the piece or exchange.

2010.label: Top: in clearly winning positions the player skips a concrete forcing finish (mating sac, promotion-with-check, or winning capture/check sequence)—often grabbing a greedy capture that hangs own material in the refutation; medium: still-better positions blur into slow, non-forcing or wrong-tempo moves that merely squander the advantage (sometimes giving up a perpetual or walking into attack) without always losing material.

2003.label: Top: a greedy capture or advance opens a file/diagonal beside the uncastled or exposed king, dropping the queen for a rook to a recapture-with-check; medium broadens to hanging any material — pawns, minor pieces, fork-droppers, even mate-allowing moves — frequently without check and not always king-related.

1999.label: Top boards are queen-vs-pawn endgames where the king steps right beside its own passed pawn, wasting a tempo or inviting a tempo-gaining queen check instead of optimal placement; medium blurs into rook, bishop, and pawn endgames where misplaced kings or mistimed pawn pushes similarly botch the passed-pawn promotion/conversion.

2017.label: Top boards are pawn/king/rook moves that waste a critical tempo and throw away a winning endgame (with one outright hung bishop); medium blurs into drawn positions, wrong-piece/king placement, and several near-zero non-blunders.

2013.label: Top boards are uniformly greedy captures that strip away the sole back-rank defender (Rxc4/Rxb4/Nxg6/Qxe5...) allowing an immediate or short forced back-rank mate; medium blurs to other king-exposing moves — non-capture defender displacement, self-obstruction or king walks (Qh5, Rf2, Kf8), an occasional non-back-rank mate net (Qd8#), and a few plain material hangs (Ne5+, Nd4) rather than strictly back-rank.

2019.label: Top boards almost uniformly hang own material to a knight fork (constant theme: centralized enemy knight forking king+rook/exchange after the player's king or rook move); medium keeps the knight-fork core but blurs the material and motif—rook-vs-rook forks, discovered checks, plain hanging pieces, and even a few positional/missed-win drops.

2011.label: Top: a tempo move attacks the enemy queen (often via self-interference blocking the piece's own defender) but leaves an undefended minor piece/rook the queen simply grabs instead of retreating; medium broadens to hanging pawns or pieces snapped by a rook, and slower moves that ignore an already-hanging unit (with a few drifting into king-safety/mate cases).

2020.label: Top boards are uniformly premature Qh4+/Qh5+ sorties refuted by a pawn block (g3/g6) that gains tempo on the queen — squandering the advantage and often hanging the queen outright to Nxh5/Nxh4; medium boards keep the same 'premature check punished by a simple tempo-gaining block' pattern but blur the square and piece (Qg5+, Qa4+, Qh6+, Qh5, even a Greek-gift Bh7+), more often costing a pawn/advantage than the queen itself.

2014.label: Top boards are pure king-and-pawn endgames where the player skips the decisive winning/holding king maneuver—infiltration, centralization, or blockade—usually by shoving a pawn or stepping the king the wrong way while material stays safe; medium broadens to rook, passed-pawn, and king-safety endings (and even greedy king captures) with the same failure to make the correct king move instead of a careless pawn push or piece move.

2016.label: Top: a quiet/inaccurate move squanders a winning or comfortable opening and directly hangs a minor piece (knight or bishop) to a simple capture; medium blurs to material dropped over a short forcing refutation—hung pawns, tempo-based piece loss, plus an endgame slip—unified only by wasting the opening advantage.

2021.label: Top: a king move or greedy capture self-opens lines/squares so the opponent answers with a decisive check that forces mate or wins material with tempo; medium keeps the king-safety/check flavor but blurs into broader tactical refutations — allowing forks, leaving pieces en prise/trapped, even a missed win — that no longer center on an exposing check.

2024.label: Top: in won rook endgames a materially-safe rook check or routine capture squanders an immediate queen promotion (h8=Q-type conversion); medium stays on the same promotion-throwaway (rook check that abandons the passed pawn), while the broader top set also blurs into missing a forced mate or a free piece-capture.

2018.label: Top: from an already-losing position the player captures/trades away their most important defensive or counterplay piece (queen, rook, or bishop) for little, accelerating the loss; medium blurs into a grab-bag of other ways to worsen a lost (or winning) position—passive retreats, premature pawn breaks, removed defenders, missed wins/mates, and several near-0cp dead-lost captures that aren't real trades at all.

2026.label: From a winning position the player throws away the advantage with a self-destructive move; top boards are dominated by king moves that walk into a check or forced mate (king exposed), while medium boards blur into hanging/trapping pieces and ignored material threats.

2027.label: Top boards recapture/centralize with a knight in the opening (usually Nxe5, also Nd4/Nxd5) leaving the wrong piece hung so a pawn capture/fork wins material a move later; medium keeps the opening-knight-blunder theme but blurs to other knight moves (Ne4, Nxg5, one missed win) and even non-knight blunders (O-O, b3, Bh4) that hang a piece or allow a fork.

2034.label: Top: a reflexive Qxd8+/Qxd1+ queen-trade-with-check that abandons a winning queen attack or fork the queen should have delivered; medium broadens to any queen exchange (non-check trades, recaptures, even wrong move-order) that surrenders a win which may instead come from a knight fork, keeping the queen active, or grabbing a hanging piece first.

2022.label: Top: the queen is placed (or captures) on a square—frequently instead of a winning knight fork—that lets the opponent trade queens and simplify away a winning advantage; medium keeps the 'misplaced major piece invites a simplifying trade' core but blurs to other pieces (rook/bishop) and mixes in outright hanging material to a simplifying capture, with the specific knight-fork motif fading into general simplification.

2029.chip: Hangs dominant knight via faulty check (sometimes rook)
2029.label: Top boards uniformly surrender a dominant, centralized knight with a forcing 'fork'/check (Nx+) that the opponent's queen simply recaptures for insufficient value; medium positions blur to other faulty capture-checks (e.g. Rxf1+, Nd3+) where the queen again refutes the over-eager piece, but the recurring core is trading off the best minor piece via an unverified check.

2023.chip: Allowed passer to promote (often via check)
2023.label: Top boards are near-uniform purposeless tempo-losing CHECKS in a passed-pawn endgame that fail to blockade/attack/capture the opponent's promoting pawn (only-move was Rb2/Rb6 etc.); medium keeps that throughline but blurs the move type—adding pawn pushes (f4), piece attacks (Ra3), and rook trades (Rb5) that likewise ignore the passer—so a winning or held position collapses as the pawn queens.

2037.label: Top boards are self-defeating rook checks/sacrifices (Rxg2+, Re1+, Rf8+) that force an exchange sequence into a lost endgame or mate; medium broadens to other checking pieces (knight forks Nf3+/Nf6+, bishop Bb6+, queen Qxh7+) where the checking piece is simply captured for inadequate compensation.

2030.chip: Missed free queen capture (often king move)
2030.label: Top boards are king moves that ignore a hanging enemy queen and walk straight into forced mate or immediate loss of the player's own queen; medium boards keep the free-queen-on-the-board but blur the action to pointless checks, queen relocations, or wrong captures that merely squander the winning edge rather than always getting mated.

2035.label: Top: in a won position the player skips the decisive pawn-advance-WITH-CHECK (e3+, f3+, d5+, b6+, g6+, d7+, d2+) that deflects the enemy king off a defender or blockade to win a piece/exchange or promote, choosing slow centralizing/king moves instead; medium keeps the 'skipped a critical pawn resource for passive play' core but blurs the check requirement — the missed move is often just a non-checking pawn break or push (e5+/a5/h5+/g6+), and some boards are defensive/lost or even non-pawn (saving a bishop, Bf1), so the deflection-check signature is only partial.

2036.label: Top: from a winning opening position, skips the forcing long-diagonal bishop capture (Bxg7/Bxg2/Bxb7) that grabs an undefended pawn and nets the exchange, playing a quiet developing move instead; medium blurs to any missed capture of an undefended pawn that wins material — same long-diagonal/fianchetto targets (g2/b7/b2) but now also queen grabs (Qxg2, Qxd4) and off-diagonal shots (Bxc6+, Bxf2+).

2031.chip: Allowed enemy pawn to promote (any piece)
2031.label: Top: a defender's move — mostly a king walk, but also rook/queen — fails to control the promotion square, letting the enemy passed pawn queen (sometimes with check) in a won/drawn endgame; medium broadens to knight/bishop guards abandoning the square and even forced/best moves in already-lost positions.

2033.label: Top: a slow bishop/pawn developing move (or unsound sac) declines the undefended central e-pawn that Nxe4/Nxe5 cleanly grabs as the engine's clear #1, sometimes self-hanging a piece in the refutation; medium broadens to other passive moves in sharp open positions where the missed shot is usually still a central knight capture but the consequence shifts from a missed pawn toward a hung piece.

2025.label: Top boards consistently decline a free/winning capture (almost always a hanging knight) in a won position, playing a non-capturing king/pawn move that lets the piece escape; medium boards blur this into squandering winning/equal positions more broadly—mostly positional and endgame errors (king activity, blockade squares, pawn races) with only a couple of missed knight captures.

2032.chip: Hangs material eliminating advanced pawn (often queen)
2032.label: Top: capturing a dangerous advanced/passed pawn that instantly hangs own material — most often the queen to an opened diagonal (Bxd1/Bxg3/Bxb1), also bishop/exchange/pawn, with a few that just grab the pawn and skip a stronger winning capture (Qxf3, Qxa6); Medium: same advanced-pawn-elimination root but blurred — material lost widens to king-safety line-opening losses (cxb4, Kxg7, fxg4), the method broadens from capture to blockade/push (Rf1, d5), the direction broadens to missed winning forks/captures (Nxc3 vs Bxg7, gxf3 vs Nxf5), and a couple are purely positional/marginal pawn surrenders (fxe3, Rxd2).

2038.label: Top boards uniformly ignore an immediate mate-in-1 delivered by the enemy queen—almost always while chasing that queen for a tempo; medium keeps the same king-safety negligence but broadens to multi-move forced mates (mate-in-2 through mate-in-9, sometimes via rook/back-rank patterns) plus a few cases that instead just drop heavy material or skip a winning mate.

2039.label: Top boards are uniform: a greedy pawn/bishop capture opens the d-file or a diagonal (or creates a pin) and immediately hangs the player's own queen via Qxd5/Qxd4/Qxd8/Bxd8; at medium the grab still backfires but blurs to losing a rook or the exchange (Rxa1, ...Bxg1) rather than the queen, with a couple of greedy queen-grabs that instead walk into Bxf7+ Nd5# and one that merely skips a bigger capture.

2040.label: Top boards force a queen trade (via capture or check) that surrenders an available perpetual-check draw and walks into a lost K+P/rook endgame; medium boards blur into other forcing material errors in drawn endgames—hanging the queen, capturing the wrong rook, or dropping the exchange via a pointless check.

2045.label: At the peak it's consistently a materially-safe quiet move that skips the free capture of a hanging rook/knight/bishop (or a winning promotion) in an already-won endgame; medium blurs this to missing the single winning continuation more broadly — correct pawn push, promotion timing, or a knight fork in a pawn race — and includes a few 0cp non-blunders.

2042.label: Top: from a losing position, plays an irrelevant move that ignores an enemy passed pawn's promotion threat and abandons/hangs the rook blockading or guarding the queening square, dropping it for free; medium blurs the blockader to king/knight and broadens to passive 'irrelevant move' errors that neglect the passed pawn or critical task — sometimes only an eval/positional loss rather than a clean material hang.

2041.label: Top boards are king-exposing moves (frequently king walks) that permit a forced mating attack; medium blurs to self-inflicted blunders—king moves and others—that instead drop material to tactical refutations (checks, deflections, back-rank/exchange, passing pawns) rather than mate.

2044.label: Top boards uniformly play a slow/irrelevant move (pawn push, king walk, piece relocation) that ignores an enemy passed pawn's imminent promotion, letting it queen and win decisive material; medium keeps many promotion cases but blurs into ignoring other concrete decisive threats—skewers (Ra8+), back-rank mates (Qd8/Qd7+), and king infiltration onto the passers—via the same kind of slow move.

2047.label: At peak the player plays a passive, natural-looking move (Rb8, Qd8, Bc7, Nf4) and ignores a forcing QUEEN CAPTURE-WITH-CHECK that wins, equalizes, or saves (Qxd4+, Qxg2#, Qxf2+, Qxe1+, Qxf7+); at medium this blurs to missing any critical forcing/best resource — perpetual queen checks (Qe1+), non-check queen captures (Qxf4, Qxd7), rook-check defenses, or precise positional moves — and several medium boards instead simply walk into tactics or allow mate.

2046.label: At peak the player throws away a clearly winning (occasionally must-draw) endgame in a one-correct-move position by missing a forced mate or decisive tactic—sometimes flatly hanging a piece; at medium it blurs to smaller-edge or already-defensive endgames where the single needed move is a quieter king/rook placement and the eval swing is modest.

2043.label: Top: advances a passed pawn one square (or auto-queens) toward promotion in mostly-lost endgames where king activation/defense was correct, so the pawn is recaptured or the push wastes a tempo (impact ranges from negligible to mate-allowing); medium keeps the same premature-push theme but in equal/winning positions it squanders the draw or win, occasionally broadening to misplacing another piece.

2028.label: At the peak Black declines the critical ...Nxd4 central knight capture in a won-or-equal opening, playing a natural developing move that either forfeits a win or—more often—permits a material-winning refutation (Nd6+/Ndb4-Nxc2+ fork, discovered attack, pin, even mate); medium positions broaden the critical move to Nxe4/Nxd5 and occasionally a non-capture central priority (d4, O-O), with refutations skewing toward actively losing material.
